train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism with acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her mid-20s presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset shortness of breath occurring after recent elective gallbladder surgery. One year earlier she had been diagnosed with a lower extremity deep vein thrombosis without an identified precipitating cause and had received anticoagulation therapy for six months, since discontinued. She denied hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, obesity, or use of combined hormonal contraception, and there was no family history of hematologic or autoimmune disease. On initial assessment, blood pressure was 95/60 mmHg, heart rate 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 95% on supplemental oxygen at 3 L/min. Physical examination revealed swelling of the right lower extremity. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with incomplete right bundle branch block and an S1Q3T3 pattern. Laboratory studies showed troponin T 0.3 ng/mL (reference <0.1 ng/mL), pro-B-type natriuretic peptide 938 pg/mL (reference <125 pg/mL), and D-dimer 5.4 mg/L (reference <0.5 mg/L). Chest radiograph did not reveal other acute pulmonary abnormalities. Given the clinical picture, she was started on empiric anticoagulation with subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin while further cardiopulmonary imaging was arranged.

A man in his 50s with a two-decade history of recurrent asthma exacerbations presented to the emergency department with acute-onset respiratory distress and worsening dyspnea. Initial arterial blood gas analysis showed severe respiratory acidosis, with pH 7.142 and PaCO2 96.3 mmHg. He was treated with inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist bronchodilators, but his hypercapnia progressively worsened and his respiratory status continued to decline, prompting endotracheal intubation and initiation of invasive mechanical ventilation. On the ventilator he was noted to have markedly elevated airway resistance, such that pressure-controlled ventilation could not achieve adequate tidal volumes; pressure-support ventilation utilizing his spontaneous breathing effort proved more effective and was continued, with support levels adjusted to his inspiratory effort and tidal volume. Management included frequent inhaled bronchodilator therapy, intravenous corticosteroids, and ketamine used for sedation and its bronchodilator properties, along with analgesia. Over the following days his respiratory mechanics and gas exchange gradually improved, tracked by serial ventilator waveform and capnography parameters. He was subsequently weaned from mechanical ventilation, extubated, and discharged after approximately two weeks of hospitalization.

A pre-adolescent/early-adolescent male (approximately 12 years old) with no known comorbidities presented to the emergency department with left scrotal pain and swelling of 10 hours' duration. The pain began after voiding, was sudden in onset, described as prickling, continuous, and progressive, worsened with movement, and was associated with lower abdominal pain and swelling of the scrotum that arose suddenly and progressed gradually. There was no history of trauma, fever, vomiting, dysuria, weight loss, or known congenital genitourinary anomaly. Past medical, family, and allergy history were unremarkable; bowel and bladder habits were normal. On examination the patient appeared anxious. Vital signs were stable. Genital exam showed left testicular tenderness and swelling, a positive Deming's sign, negative Phren's sign, and an absent cremasteric reflex on the affected side. A clinical risk-scoring assessment for the acute scrotum placed him in an intermediate-to-high risk category. Initial laboratory studies were unremarkable, and serology for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C was nonreactive. Scrotal ultrasonography showed coarse echotexture with reduced/absent vascularity of the left testicle, a bulky left epididymis, and bilateral hydrocele (left greater than right).

An elderly female patient was brought in for sudden loss of consciousness and limb weakness. About four days earlier she had an episode of transient loss of consciousness while eating, followed by chest tightness partially relieved with sublingual nitroglycerin. On admission at that time, ECG showed ST-segment elevation in inferior, anterior, and posterior leads with reciprocal changes and a conduction block; coronary angiography demonstrated severe multivessel coronary artery disease with thrombus in the right coronary artery, and she underwent emergency percutaneous coronary intervention. About twenty hours before the current presentation, she developed subacute, symmetric, ascending limb weakness beginning in the bilateral upper limbs with numbness, progressing to the lower limbs with new urinary retention. Cranial CT was unremarkable. Past history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, and a prior stroke, with no preceding gastrointestinal or respiratory illness. On exam she was tachycardic (105 bpm, irregular rhythm) with blood pressure 169/97 mmHg and temperature 37.1°C. She had flaccid quadriplegia, hypotonia in all limbs, distal sensory loss, absent deep tendon reflexes, and bulbar findings including dysarthria, diminished gag reflex, and absent cough reflex. Cerebellar function and other cranial nerves were normal. Labs showed normal blood counts, CRP, electrolytes, and hepatic/renal function; elevated BNP (526.44 pg/mL) and procalcitonin (1.69 ng/mL); negative serologies for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, EBV, CMV, and HIV. Serum anti-ganglioside antibody testing was positive for several subtypes. Family declined lumbar puncture and electrodiagnostic studies could not be performed. She subsequently developed progressive respiratory muscle weakness requiring endotracheal intubation.

A 7-year-old boy presented to the pediatric emergency department with continuous, progressive left scrotal pain for 2 days, accompanied by scrotal swelling and redness. About 4 days prior to presentation, he had developed left lower abdominal pain, initially thought to represent gastroenteritis; the pain reportedly migrated to the left scrotum roughly 2 days before presentation, and the family attributed the scrotal redness to skin scratching, treating it symptomatically at home before seeking care due to worsening symptoms. There was no associated nausea or vomiting, no preceding trauma or surgical history, and no clear precipitating, exacerbating, or relieving factors. On examination, the left scrotum was red, swollen, tender, and the testis was high-riding; Prehn's sign was negative and the cremasteric reflex was absent on the affected side. The right scrotum was unremarkable. Vital signs were not notably abnormal. Laboratory testing showed no leukocytosis and a normal C-reactive protein level. Color Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum showed an enlarged, inhomogeneous, hypoechoic left testis with no detectable intratesticular blood flow; flow to the right testis was preserved and its architecture was homogeneous. Given the clinical and imaging findings, urgent surgical exploration was undertaken within an hour of presentation.

An older adult male presented to the emergency department by ambulance with bilateral knee pain accompanied by fever and chills for two days. He was unable to bear weight and denied any preceding trauma. Past medical history included type II diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. He had undergone a urologic procedure involving prostatic urethral lift, cystoscopy, and Foley catheter placement approximately two weeks prior. On arrival, he was febrile (101.6°F/38.7°C) and tachycardic (heart rate 105 bpm). Both knees were warm to palpation without overlying erythema or cellulitis. Bilateral knee effusions were present with positive bulge and patellar tap tests, and range of motion was limited by pain. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 17,700/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate greater than 140 mm/h, and C-reactive protein of 26.70 mg/dL. Blood glucose was 94 mg/dL, and renal function and electrolytes were within normal limits. Bedside arthrocentesis of both knees yielded turbid synovial fluid, which was sent for laboratory analysis including cell count, Gram stain, and culture. Empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics were initiated and orthopedic surgery was consulted for further evaluation and management of the bilateral knee effusions.

A young adult man (age band 20-29, male) presented to the emergency department with intermittent left-sided scrotal pain of moderate intensity, ongoing for 3 days. He reported that he had a previously known left varicocele and initially attributed the pain to this condition, which led him to delay seeking medical evaluation. Past urologic history was notable for a retractile testicle noted previously. Family history was notable for a male sibling who had undergone emergency scrotal surgery in the past for an acute scrotal condition. Vital signs were not specified in the available history. On physical examination, the left testis was swollen, firm, tender to palpation, and positioned higher in the scrotum than expected. The right testis and scrotal contents were otherwise unremarkable on exam. Color Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum was performed and demonstrated markedly decreased blood flow to the left testis compared to the contralateral side, with no other imaging abnormalities described. Given the clinical and sonographic findings, urgent surgical scrotal exploration was undertaken for further evaluation and management.

A man in his 60s with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, coronary artery disease (two coronary stents placed within the past year, on dual antiplatelet therapy), and obesity (BMI 31) was transferred to a stroke center after presenting to an outside emergency department with sudden left-sided hemiplegia. He had experienced severe tearing chest pain while driving that morning, which resolved by the time he reached the receiving hospital; he denied chest pain on arrival. He was conscious, cooperative, and non-aphasic. On examination he had left hemiplegia, left hemianopsia, and left facial weakness without facial drooping or slurred speech. Initial vital signs at the outside facility were BP 126/64 mmHg, HR 60/min, SpO2 98% on room air, glucose 170 mg/dL. On arrival at the stroke center, vitals were BP 108/51 mmHg, HR 53/min, SpO2 100% on room air, glucose 132 mg/dL, afebrile. ECG was normal. Labs showed elevated cardiac enzymes and creatinine 1.49 mg/dL. Initial outside brain CT showed a right parietal hypodensity without hemorrhage. Further neurologic workup including brain CT, brain CTA, and chest CTA was pursued to characterize the extent of intracranial and vascular findings.

A man in his late 40s presented to the emergency department with one month of right-sided "shoulder" pain that had progressively worsened. Six days prior, he had seen his primary care physician and was started on high-dose oral prednisone and as-needed ibuprofen, taken as directed, without improvement. He had been advised to obtain outpatient CT imaging but was unable to schedule it and returned to the ED due to worsening pain. He also reported a growing swelling near the right clavicle and intermittent fevers and night sweats over the past month, which he attributed to lack of home air conditioning. He denied weight loss, intravenous drug use, sexually transmitted infections, or known immunocompromise; he reported prior multi-year incarceration abroad with a negative tuberculosis test four months earlier. He is monogamous with his wife without barrier protection. Vitals: BP 157/100 mmHg, HR 75 bpm, temperature 98.6°F, RR 18, SpO2 100% on room air. Exam showed a warm, indurated mass at the right sternoclavicular region with severe pain on range of motion, especially adduction. Labs showed white count 9.41 x10^3/mcL without left shift, negative HIV screen, negative urine drug screen, ESR 55 mm/hr, and CRP 52.8 mg/L. Chest X-ray showed no acute abnormality. Contrast CT of the chest showed induration and stranding of subcutaneous fat with cortical destruction at the clavicular portion of the joint and increased intra-articular soft tissue density.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute appendicitis with perforation, localized peritonitis, and gangrene, with abscess
train_cases.note: A man in his late 60s presented to the emergency department with a 7-day history of abdominal pain and nausea/vomiting, with fever and altered mental status over the preceding 24 hours. Past medical history included chronic kidney disease, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and prior coronary artery bypass surgery. On presentation he was mildly febrile (37.6°C), tachycardic (110 bpm), with normal blood pressure; Glasgow Coma Scale was 11. Abdominal exam revealed tenderness in all four quadrants, most pronounced in the right lower quadrant, with distension but no overt peritonism. He reported obstipation for 3 days; bowel sounds were decreased, and rectal exam showed an empty rectal vault. Labs showed leukocytosis (12.9 x10^3/uL), markedly elevated CRP (27.1 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (11.5 ng/mL), acute kidney injury (creatinine 5.3 mg/dL), hyperglycemia (388 mg/dL), and elevated lactate (2.3 mmol/L). Abdominal ultrasound showed minimal free fluid. CT of the abdomen/pelvis demonstrated a large (13 x 7 cm) fluid collection predominantly in the right lower quadrant with diffuse free air within it, extending into the bilateral pararenal and perirenal spaces. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were started and emergency exploratory surgery was arranged for suspected intra-abdominal perforation with retroperitoneal abscess and septicemia.

A woman in her late 40s with a history of right hip arthroplasty performed 8 years earlier presented with about 1.5 weeks of left knee pain and swelling. She denied any preceding trauma, tick bites, sexually transmitted infection exposure, or personal history of autoimmune or inflammatory disease. She was initially evaluated by her primary care provider, who suspected patellar tendonitis and recommended conservative management. Due to worsening pain, she was seen at an urgent care the following day; C-reactive protein was markedly elevated at 256 mg/dL, while complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, and uric acid were normal. She was given a presumptive diagnosis and started on prednisone and hydrocodone, but her symptoms continued to worsen. She subsequently presented to an orthopaedic clinic, where she was found to have leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 11.8 K/µL and persistently elevated CRP of 239 mg/dL. She was admitted for further evaluation. Arthrocentesis of the affected knee was performed, revealing 60,800 nucleated cells/µL with 89% polymorphonuclear predominance and no crystals identified on microscopy. No vital sign abnormalities were documented in the available record. Further diagnostic workup, including joint fluid culture, was pursued to determine the underlying etiology.

train_cases.diagnosis: Benign neoplasm of unspecified adrenal gland
train_cases.note: A woman in her early twenties with an unremarkable medical, family, and psychosocial history presented to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision involving head trauma. She had a brief loss of consciousness lasting about 10 minutes, with an initial Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14 that improved to 15 within an hour, meeting criteria for mild traumatic brain injury. In the emergency department, vital signs were unremarkable, physical examination was normal, and non-contrast head CT was unremarkable. About ten days later, she was evaluated in an outpatient brain injury clinic reporting headaches, anxiety, and dizziness. At that visit, blood pressure was elevated at 160/100 mmHg (baseline had been normotensive), while the remainder of the physical exam remained unremarkable with no focal neurological deficits. Initial laboratory workup including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, insulin-like growth factor 1, and cortisol were all within normal limits. Urine drug screen was negative. However, plasma and urine-fractionated metanephrines were both markedly elevated (urine-fractionated metanephrines 1700 mcg/24 hours, reference <400; plasma-fractionated metanephrines 2.2 nmol/L, reference <0.50). Abdominal imaging was subsequently obtained to further evaluate this biochemical finding.

A 71-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a three-day history of general weakness, malaise, and fever. Symptoms began three days after his first dose of an immune checkpoint inhibitor given for a recurring, locally advanced basal cell carcinoma of the left cheek. He had a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor with liver metastases, on palliative treatment with everolimus and somatostatin receptor-targeted radionuclide therapy. A pre-treatment echocardiogram had shown findings compatible with an infiltrative cardiomyopathy and coronary artery disease. He was a retired farmer still living on a cattle farm. On presentation, temperature was 38.6°C, blood pressure 79/44 mmHg, heart rate 89/min, respiratory rate 27/min, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. He was somnolent without focal neurologic deficits. Heart sounds were regular with a systolic murmur at the third left intercostal space; lung auscultation was unremarkable. An ulcerating lesion (3x5 cm) was present on the left cheek without surrounding inflammation. Skin and joint exam were otherwise unremarkable. Labs showed CRP 96 mg/L, normal leukocyte count (5.5x10^9/L), and thrombocytopenia (107x10^9/L). Chest X-ray showed mild pulmonary venous congestion. Head CT showed no soft tissue abscess near the facial lesion. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and hemodynamic support with norepinephrine were started for suspected sepsis of unknown origin in an immunocompromised host. Blood cultures (both aerobic and anaerobic bottles) became positive with matching organism growth, remaining positive 72 hours into antibiotic therapy. A wound swab of the facial lesion grew different organisms. Repeat transthoracic echocardiography showed new mild mitral stenosis and tricuspid regurgitation, and transesophageal echocardiography revealed two mobile masses on the posterior mitral leaflet (9x8 mm and 15 mm).

train_cases.diagnosis: Other ectopic pregnancy without intrauterine pregnancy
train_cases.note: A woman in her early 30s, gravida four para two, presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period had occurred about two weeks prior, and her menstrual cycles were normally regular. Her surgical history was notable for a bilateral salpingectomy performed two years earlier at the time of a cesarean delivery, done for permanent contraception. On examination she appeared pale; formal vital signs were not detailed in the available record. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant, without rebound or guarding described. A urine pregnancy test was positive, and quantitative beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) was 1,735 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated an empty uterine cavity with no intrauterine gestational sac and a complex mass in the left adnexal region. No free fluid or other findings were described. Given the history of tubal surgery, positive pregnancy test, and absence of an intrauterine pregnancy on imaging, further evaluation and close monitoring were planned.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other ectopic pregnancy without intrauterine pregnancy
train_cases.note: A woman in her late twenties (gravida 5, para 1, living 1, prior spontaneous losses 3), with a history of prior lower segment cesarean section, presented with painless vaginal bleeding for 10 days, occurring after 10 weeks of amenorrhea and a positive urine pregnancy test 6 weeks prior. She reported no contraceptive use and had previously undergone uneventful self-administered medical abortions on three occasions. After noting vaginal spotting and presuming the pregnancy was non-viable, she self-administered oral and vaginal misoprostol 4 days before presentation. On arrival, she appeared severely pale with tachycardia (110-120/min) and blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. Hemoglobin was 6.4 g/dL; other labs were within normal limits. Speculum exam showed active vaginal bleeding; bimanual exam revealed a uterus consistent with 10 weeks size, ballooning of the cervix, and tissue palpable at the external os. Ultrasound showed an enlarged uterus (10 x 5.79 x 5.73 cm) with endometrial thickness of 7.4 mm in the upper uterine segment, a gestational sac located within the cervical canal containing a live embryo with crown-rump length 30.4 mm (consistent with about 9 weeks) and fetal heart rate 176 bpm.

A 48-year-old man presented after being transferred for evaluation of persistent chest and back pain lasting approximately 6 hours. His past medical history included hypertension, tobacco use, and alcohol use. On contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiography, imaging demonstrated involvement of both the thoracic and abdominal aorta with an abnormal aortic wall contour and a dissection flap. Shortly after presentation, the patient acutely developed paralysis of the left lower limb, and imaging/clinical assessment showed decreased blood flow to the left iliac arteries, consistent with a malperfusion syndrome affecting the lower extremity. Vital signs and additional exam details were notable for the acute onset of neurologic deficit (left lower limb weakness/paralysis) with diminished distal pulses on the affected side. No abdominal pain or renal dysfunction was reported at this time. Given the acute limb malperfusion, urgent intervention was pursued to restore blood supply to the lower extremities. Emergent angiographic evaluation was planned to define the extent of aortic involvement and guide revascularization strategy, including assessment of the origin of the dissection relative to the great vessels and iliac arteries.

A young adult male presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of sore throat and difficulty swallowing. He also reported fever, body aches, and a hoarse voice. Neck movement was painful, particularly on flexion. He denied shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, or chest pain. He had been unable to sleep for two nights and reported hallucinations with light sensitivity. He had no significant past medical history and no known drug allergies. Vital signs: heart rate 118 bpm, blood pressure 152/92 mmHg, temperature 39.1°C, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. He rated his pain as 10/10. Examination revealed bilateral tonsillar swelling. Laboratory studies showed CRP 185 mg/L, white cell count 29.7 x10^9/L, and neutrophil count 27.1 x10^9/L; venous blood gas was within normal limits. A lateral neck radiograph showed swelling of the supraglottic soft tissue with narrowing of the airway at that level. He was initially treated empirically with intravenous antibiotics per local sore-throat guidelines and referred for specialist assessment, where bedside flexible nasopharyngoscopy showed oedema of the uvula and bilateral aryepiglottic folds, with an adequate glottic airway and normally mobile vocal cords.

An elderly male presented to the emergency department with an acute episode of rectal bleeding followed by a syncopal episode. The volume of blood loss could not be quantified by the patient, but the syncope raised concern for a significant bleed. He had been seen approximately 5 weeks earlier for an acute abdominal illness that had been managed conservatively, with plans for elective surgery at a later date. On examination, he was of lean body habitus, in no acute distress, afebrile, and acyanotic. Mucous membranes were pink and moist with no scleral icterus. Abdomen was soft, nontender, nondistended, with no palpable masses and no right upper quadrant tenderness. Vital signs were stable: blood pressure 134/82 mmHg, pulse 86 bpm, respiratory rate 22/min, temperature 36.3°C. Initial labs including renal function, liver function, electrolytes, clotting panel, D-dimer and troponin were unremarkable. Complete blood count showed an initial hemoglobin of 11.9 g/dL, which decreased to 10.2 g/dL within 24 hours. No further episodes of rectal bleeding were observed after admission. Imaging of the abdomen obtained on the day of admission revealed a small cystic structure adjacent to the gallbladder region, with a thick-walled gallbladder and surrounding inflammatory changes causing loss of the normal fat plane between the gallbladder and the adjacent colon.

A 75-year-old male presented with a 3-day history of nausea, decreased oral intake, progressive generalized weakness, and fevers. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, GERD, COPD, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He had undergone a cystoscopy for urinary retention about one week prior, reportedly with normal findings. He reported long-standing heavy daily alcohol use (approximately one pint of vodka daily for over 20 years) and denied intravenous drug use or known immunocompromising conditions. On admission, vitals showed blood pressure 106/56 mmHg, heart rate 125 bpm, respiratory rate 25/min, and temperature 100.5°F. Exam revealed a nontender, distended abdomen with hypoactive bowel sounds, scleral icterus, jaundice, tachycardia, and a holosystolic murmur. Labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 13,660/mm3), hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, platelets 90,000/mm3, potassium 2.9 mEq/L, creatinine 1.70 mg/dL, magnesium 1.4 mg/dL, AST 54 U/L, ALT 41 U/L, ALP 131 U/L, total bilirubin 4.13 mg/dL, lactic acid 3.3 mmol/L, and urinalysis with pyuria and nitrites. He was resuscitated with IV fluids and started on empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis showed right lower lobe consolidation, mild esophageal wall thickening, a cirrhotic-appearing liver, and mild bladder wall thickening. He developed acute hypoxia requiring noninvasive ventilation and ICU-level monitoring. Blood cultures were drawn, and a transthoracic echocardiogram showed a mobile mass on the mitral valve leaflet.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A young adult male presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain. He reported 8-10 episodes of non-bilious vomiting without blood, and colicky, non-radiating abdominal pain rated 7/10. He denied cough, sore throat, rhinorrhea, diarrhea, melena, or dysuria. Past history included type 1 diabetes mellitus with prior episodes of ketoacidosis, managed with subcutaneous insulin but with frequent (4-5 times weekly) missed doses and no home glucose monitoring; he had stopped insulin 3 days before this visit. He also had a several-year history of hyperthyroidism, previously treated with an antithyroid medication that was discontinued months earlier without follow-up thyroid testing. On examination he was alert (GCS 15), temperature 36.4°C, pulse 145/min, respirations 35/min, blood pressure 135/69 mmHg, SpO2 99% on room air. Skin was warm and dry; the neck showed diffuse thyroid enlargement without nodules or bruit. Lungs were clear; heart rhythm was regular and rapid with hyperdynamic sounds. The abdomen was tense with diffuse tenderness and rebound. No leg edema was noted. Labs showed glucose 20.4 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 6.76 mmol/L, pH 7.21, anion gap 19 mmol/L, elevated white cell count and neutrophil percentage, suppressed TSH with markedly elevated free T3 and free T4. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Abdominal CT showed severe fatty liver with no surgical findings.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism with acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her late 60s presented to the emergency department after an episode of loss of consciousness that occurred one hour earlier. She reported retrosternal tightness and discomfort that began while walking, followed by syncope and a fall resulting in a forehead hematoma and an abrasion on the right side of her face. She regained consciousness spontaneously within a few minutes. Past medical history was notable for hypertension. On arrival, vital signs showed blood pressure 100/74 mmHg, heart rate 116 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on 3 L/min supplemental oxygen. Examination revealed a 3 cm x 3 cm subcutaneous forehead hematoma with minor overlying skin bleeding and an abrasion on the right side of the face. Cardiac examination showed tachycardia without murmurs; neurological examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed a markedly elevated troponin I level and a substantially elevated D-dimer level, with otherwise normal complete blood count, renal and hepatic function tests, coagulation studies, and electrolytes. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with ST-segment elevation of 0.1-0.2 mV in leads aVR and V1 and ST-segment depression of 0.1-0.3 mV in the anterolateral leads. Non-contrast computed tomography of the head and chest showed no acute abnormalities.

A 27-year-old man with no significant past medical or surgical history presented after a motorcycle accident with ejection from the bike. He was hemodynamically stable, alert, and oriented, GCS 15. Exam showed a glabellar laceration, facial and right hip/wrist bruising, diffuse minor lacerations, and an externally rotated, deformed right leg with intact distal pulses. Diffuse ecchymosis was noted over the lower abdomen, pelvis, back, and extremities, but none over the testicles or perineum. The pelvis was clinically unstable. Imaging revealed an open-book pelvic fracture, right acetabular and obturator ring fractures, sacroiliac diastasis, a left wrist dislocation, and a large presacral pelvic hematoma with active bleeding; FAST was negative and a retrograde urethrogram excluded urethral injury. He underwent preperitoneal pelvic packing, ICU monitoring, drain placement, and later orthopedic pelvic fixation, with an uneventful early recovery. Five days after the packing procedure, he developed acute-onset right lower quadrant abdominal pain and unilateral right testicular pain. On exam, the right testicle was difficult to palpate and appeared displaced higher within the inguinal canal compared with the left. Scrotal Doppler ultrasonography showed the right testicle measuring 4.4 x 2.7 x 2.3 cm with grossly unremarkable echotexture but no detectable arterial flow; the left testis measured 3.8 x 2.2 x 2.6 cm with normal echotexture and color flow. He had no prior history of testicular trauma, undescended testes, hernia, or genitourinary complications.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A teenage girl (early adolescence, no prior known illness) presented after a high-energy motor vehicle collision with multiple injuries. Prehospital assessment showed hypoxemia (oxygen saturation 90% despite high-flow mask oxygen) and a severely depressed level of consciousness; she underwent field endotracheal intubation for airway protection prior to helicopter transport. On arrival, vital signs showed marked tachycardia (heart rate approximately 195 beats/min), blood pressure 137/82 mmHg, oxygen saturation 99% on 100% inspired oxygen, and mildly elevated temperature (37.1°C), with persistent depressed consciousness. Physical exam revealed an open mandibular wound not extending into the neck. Imaging demonstrated a pelvic fracture with active bleeding, an open mandibular fracture without intracranial injury, an odontoid fracture, and a right medial malleolar fracture. Emergency angiographic embolization was performed to control pelvic hemorrhage, and antibiotics were started for the open fracture. After staged surgical fixation of the pelvic, odontoid, and mandibular injuries on the second hospital day, the patient developed high fever (up to 40.6°C) and persistent tachycardia (heart rate up to 175 beats/min) unresponsive to antipyretics, active cooling, and antibiotic adjustment. Sedation was discontinued, but her level of consciousness remained reduced. Brain MRI was unremarkable, and repeated infectious work-up was negative. The fever, tachycardia, and altered consciousness persisted over multiple days despite supportive measures, prompting evaluation for noninfectious causes of the unexplained hypermetabolic state.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her mid-70s with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, alcohol-related liver cirrhosis status post liver transplant, and severe osteoporosis presented to the emergency department with shortness of breath and wheezing. Approximately one month earlier she had been hospitalized for chest pain, back pain, and dyspnea two days after undergoing kyphoplasty of the lower lumbar spine for a compression fracture; during that admission she was treated for pneumonia with antibiotics and was noted incidentally to have a thin linear metallic density within the inferior vena cava, for which she was placed on a short empiric course of an oral anticoagulant that she completed prior to this presentation. She reports taking all home medications as prescribed, including erythropoiesis-stimulating agent injections, aspirin, levothyroxine, midodrine, and an opioid for pain. On current presentation, blood pressure was 169/77 mmHg, temperature 36.5°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 4.4 x10^3/uL, platelets 122 x10^3/uL, and renal function similar to baseline. Rapid testing was positive for influenza A. Chest imaging was obtained to further evaluate her respiratory symptoms and known vascular finding.

A man in his late 50s presented with 2 days of painless obstructive jaundice. Radiologic imaging obtained prior to admission had raised concern for a pancreatic head mass. Past medical history included dyslipidemia and a glucose metabolism disorder (prediabetes) diagnosed 8 months earlier, managed with dietary modification. On physical examination, the patient had a mild productive morning cough; no other significant findings were noted. Laboratory studies showed CEA 3.02 ng/ml, CA19-9 1.87 U/ml, CA15-3 20.99 U/ml, CA125 20.04 U/ml, AST 46 U/l, ALT 92 U/l, GGT 557 U/l, total bilirubin 15.8 mg/dl (direct 13.29, indirect 2.51), serum amylase 155 U/l, and ESR 46. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed diffuse enlargement of the pancreas, most pronounced in the head, with an ill-defined hypodense border, hyperdense gallbladder content, peripancreatic inflammatory change, and dilatation of the intrahepatic and main bile ducts. MRI confirmed acute inflammatory change in the pancreatic head. MRCP demonstrated a focal lesion at the lower head of the pancreas with low T1 signal, hypovascularity, and restricted diffusion, considered suspicious for malignancy, along with pancreatic duct dilatation; regional lymph nodes appeared normal. Given biliary obstruction, percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography with stent placement was performed, revealing a stricture of the lower common hepatic duct with proximal biliary dilatation.

A patient in early adolescence (female) presented to the emergency department with a 1-day history of nausea, right lower quadrant abdominal pain, and myalgias, accompanied by a low-grade fever (37.4°C). She denied cough, dyspnea, or skin rash. She had no significant past medical history. She tested positive on a rapid antigen test for a circulating respiratory virus at the time of presentation. Vital signs on admission: blood pressure 105/50 mmHg, heart rate 70/min, respiratory rate 14/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical examination was notable for right lower quadrant abdominal tenderness. Initial laboratory studies showed an elevated white blood cell count with neutrophilia (77.7% of total WBC), lymphopenia (12.5% of total WBC), and mild monocytosis (7.1% of total WBC). Serum creatinine, ALT, and blood glucose were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an 11-mm diameter, non-compressible, hypoechoic tubular structure in the right lower quadrant, with a small amount (5 mm) of free fluid between adjacent ileal loops.

An older adult male with no known past medical history presented to the emergency department with a 1-day history of abdominal pain. Initial vital signs showed mild hypertension (BP 134/76 mmHg), heart rate 76 bpm, afebrile, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Exam revealed a mildly distended abdomen with epigastric tenderness, no rebound, rigidity, or guarding. Labs showed elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL) and mild leukocytosis (11.7 x10/mm3). EKG showed normal sinus rhythm at ~118 bpm without ST/T changes. Abdominal/pelvic CT with contrast showed gallbladder distension with cholelithiasis and possible trace pericholecystic changes. Right upper quadrant ultrasound showed sludge/stones versus polyps, gallbladder only partially visualized. He was symptomatically managed and discharged with plans for outpatient elective gallbladder surgery evaluation. Two days later, at a routine visit for preoperative clearance, he was found to have an irregular rapid heart rhythm and was sent back to the ED. He reported ongoing epigastric pain and decreased oral intake. Vitals showed BP 156/91 mmHg, HR ~157 bpm, afebrile, saturation 99%. Labs showed mildly elevated troponin (39 pg/mL), mildly elevated BNP (111 pg/mL), rising total bilirubin (3.3 mg/dL), and leukocytosis (12.2 x10/mm3). EKG showed a rapid atrial arrhythmia with atrial rate ~300 bpm and ventricular rate ~150 bpm. Rate-control medication was given without adequate response, prompting transfer to a higher level of cardiac care. Echocardiography showed reduced ejection fraction and a small pericardial effusion. Further imaging during a transesophageal study prompted urgent additional cross-sectional vascular imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: An older adult male with a history of progressive, widely metastatic esophageal adenocarcinoma on immunotherapy (anti-PD-1 agent, most recent dose administered three weeks prior) presented to the emergency department with a one-week history of dyspnea, nausea, vomiting, and fatigue. He reported significant unintentional weight loss of approximately 14 kg over the preceding few months. He had no personal history of diabetes mellitus, no prior corticosteroid or SGLT2 inhibitor use, and no family history of diabetes or autoimmune/endocrine disease. On evaluation, vital signs were notable for tachypnea. Physical exam revealed signs of dehydration and generalized weakness, without focal findings. Initial laboratory studies showed markedly elevated blood glucose (30 mmol/L), elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate (9.6 mmol/L), arterial pH 7.2, bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, pCO2 58 mmHg, and an anion gap of 31.4 mEq/L. Initial serum potassium was 5.3 mEq/L. Hemoglobin A1c was 7.5%, notably elevated compared to a recent prior baseline of 5.7% obtained before initiation of current systemic therapy. Given the severity of metabolic derangement, the patient was admitted for further management including intravenous fluid resuscitation and continuous insulin infusion, with close monitoring of electrolytes and acid-base status.

An older adult man (early 80s) was brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious at home on a hot night, in a poorly ventilated room without any cooling measures in use. He had no history of infection or antibiotic use prior to this event. On arrival, he was comatose. Vital signs: temperature 41°C, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, pulse 112/min, respiratory rate 29/min. A small amount of wet rhonchi was heard bilaterally in the lungs. Neurologic exam showed absent tendon reflexes and bilateral positive pathologic reflex signs; other systems were unremarkable. Shortly after admission he developed worsening respiratory distress (respiratory rate 33/min, SpO2 88%), requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Labs showed WBC 13.16×10^9/L (90.6% neutrophils, 5.6% lymphocytes), platelets 165×10^9/L, RBC 5.02×10^12/L, hemoglobin 15.9 g/dL, markedly elevated serum myoglobin (1303 ng/mL), prolonged coagulation times (PT 16.40 s, aPTT 86.30 s), urea 10.7 mmol/L, creatinine 110.7 μmol/L, ALT 177.4 U/L, AST 244.3 U/L, procalcitonin 2.5 ng/mL, arterial pH 7.48, PaCO2 27 mmHg, PaO2 100 mmHg (FiO2 41%), and lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Urinalysis revealed reddish-brown urine. Cranial CT showed no hemorrhage or infarction; chest CT showed findings consistent with bronchitis.

A woman in her late 20s, in her first pregnancy, presented at 37 weeks gestation with severe hypertension. Blood pressure had been normal early in pregnancy, occasionally up to 140/99 mmHg, but by 37 weeks reached 175/112 mmHg. She had a history of resistant hypertension treated with three antihypertensive medications, along with hypothyroidism, asthma, and obesity (BMI 39). No features suggestive of a connective tissue disorder were present. At 39 weeks, cervical ripening with a balloon catheter was attempted; two induction attempts failed. During induction she reported pain radiating to the left scapula. Immediately before cesarean delivery, blood pressure rose to 230/130 mmHg with heart rate 89 bpm; spinal anesthesia was given, and the cesarean section proceeded without immediate complication, with a healthy newborn. Several hours postpartum she developed abdominal pain. Abdominal x-ray showed air-fluid levels suggesting ileus, and ultrasound raised concern for bowel obstruction; laparotomy revealed necrotic bowel from the ileum to the transverse colon. Within 24 hours she was transferred to a tertiary center in critical condition—unconscious, intubated, sedated, and hemodynamically unstable, with blood pressure 67/37 mmHg, pulse 67 bpm, oxygen saturation 90% on room air. Labs showed normal platelet count, low albumin (2.1 g/dL), markedly elevated amylase and lipase, elevated creatinine and urea, D-dimer >10,000 ng/mL, and markedly elevated transaminases. Arterial blood gas showed severe respiratory acidosis (pH 6.899, pCO2 53.8 mmHg). Contrast CT of the chest and abdomen was attempted but image quality was limited by extensive intra-abdominal free air.

Adult male in his 60s with a history of hepatitis B-related glomerulonephritis, end-stage renal disease requiring hemodialysis via a temporary femoral catheter, hepatitis B-related decompensated cirrhosis, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease presented with melena. Endoscopy identified upper gastrointestinal mucosal ulceration and erosive changes, and fecal occult blood testing was positive. Initial labs showed severe normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 53 g/L), platelets 106×10^9/L, elevated blood urea and creatinine consistent with known renal failure, and metabolic acidosis on blood gas. He was transfused and started on hemodialysis. Several days into admission, while dialyzing via the femoral catheter, he developed fever and rigors with a peak temperature of 40.5°C, without erythema, tenderness, or discharge at the catheter site. Blood cultures drawn simultaneously from the catheter and a peripheral vein grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and the catheter tip culture was also positive; the catheter was removed and intravenous antibiotics started. Despite resolution of fever, the patient then reported acute-onset pain and progressive vision loss in one eye, with visual acuity declining from counting-fingers to hand-motion-only over several days. Examination revealed conjunctival injection, keratic precipitates, a positive Tyndall phenomenon in the anterior chamber, posterior synechiae, lens opacity, and a fundus that was increasingly difficult to visualize. Intraocular pressure was 19 mmHg on the affected side versus 14 mmHg on the unaffected side, which was otherwise unremarkable. B-scan ultrasonography showed progressive vitreous opacity with an associated proliferative membrane.

A man in his mid-40s presented to an outpatient rehabilitation clinic with non-traumatic right shoulder weakness and pain lasting about one day. Past medical history included poorly controlled hypertension and gout, with no prior joint pain, infectious disease, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, hyperthyroidism, allergies, trauma, surgery, or transfusion. On exam, he was alert but agitated. Neurological assessment showed no focal deficits. Shoulder range of motion was normal without swelling, erythema, or warmth. Manual muscle testing showed mild proximal weakness (4+/5) in the right arm; resistance testing did not reproduce symptoms. Further history revealed the pain began as mild paresthesia in the shoulder, worsened after alcohol use (VAS 2/10). Chest was symmetrical with clear breath sounds; abdomen was soft and flat without organomegaly or tenderness. Pain localized initially to the right coracoid process area, later migrating to the right shoulder and chest, a shifting pattern raising concern for a non-musculoskeletal cause. During assessment, the patient developed tachycardia (133 bpm), hypertension (178/98 mmHg), and tachypnea (22/min), along with sudden severe tearing chest and upper abdominal pain, diaphoresis, a sense of impending doom, chest tightness, and dyspnea. Cardiac auscultation revealed a regular rhythm without murmurs; brachial pulses were symmetrical. ECG showed no abnormalities. Initial imaging was obtained emergently given hemodynamic changes and evolving pain pattern.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A woman in her 50s presented to the emergency department with a two-hour history of sudden-onset shortness of breath and palpitations, without chest pain, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, fever, cough, sore throat, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, or urinary symptoms. This was her first such episode. On examination, she appeared anxious, tachypneic, and in respiratory distress, using accessory muscles, with audible wheezing. Vital signs: blood pressure 130/71 mmHg, heart rate 130 bpm, respiratory rate 28/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, temperature 37°C. Random blood sugar was 186 mg/dL. Chest exam showed decreased bilateral air entry with no added sounds; cardiovascular exam was normal with no murmurs or extra sounds; abdomen was soft and non-tender; neurological exam was unremarkable. Initial venous blood gas showed respiratory alkalosis with hypoxemia (pH 7.484, pCO2 30.7 mmHg, pO2 25.6 mmHg, HCO3- 22.6 mmol/L). Co-oximetry showed total hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, oxyhemoglobin 51.2% (low), deoxyhemoglobin 48.0% (elevated). ECG showed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Bedside ultrasound showed good ejection fraction, no wall motion abnormalities, no pericardial effusion, no right ventricular strain, and a normal inferior vena cava. Labs showed creatinine 159 µmol/L, WBC 12.62 x10^9/L, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, lactate 2.77 mmol/L, normal troponin and CK-MB. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. She was treated empirically for presumed airway bronchospasm with bronchodilators, steroids, magnesium, and fluids, with partial improvement but persistent tachycardia. Hours later she developed heartburn and nausea; repeat cardiac markers and D-dimer were unremarkable. During observation, random blood glucose was found to be 500 mg/dL, and repeat venous blood gas revealed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.211, HCO3- 10.0 mmol/L, lactate 10.09 mmol/L).

A previously healthy male child (early school age) presented with a purpuric rash, polyarticular joint pain and swelling, testicular pain/swelling, and abdominal pain. He was initially evaluated and admitted to another facility; a throat culture grew Group A Streptococcus, treated with oral amoxicillin. Because abdominal pain worsened after several days, oral corticosteroid therapy was started and he was transferred for further management. On admission he was afebrile with normal vital signs. Exam showed a purpuric rash on the upper and lower extremities with non-pitting pedal edema, and diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound or rigidity. Abdominal ultrasound showed minimal ascites in the subhepatic and pelvic regions without intussusception; abdominal X-ray excluded obstruction or perforation. Labs on day two showed normal complete blood count, hemoglobin, platelets, renal function, total protein, albumin, electrolytes, complement levels, autoimmune serologies, and immunoglobulin levels. Mild elevation of CRP (10.4 mg/L) and ESR (41 mm/h), and elevated transaminases (AST 66 U/L, ALT 83 U/L) were noted. Urinalysis showed non-nephrotic-range proteinuria without hematuria, and fecal occult blood was positive. He was continued on corticosteroids, proton pump inhibitor, and acetaminophen, with intravenous morphine for pain. After initial improvement, on day nine he developed worsening abdominal pain with hematemesis and gross hematochezia, prompting repeat imaging showing bowel wall thickening and increased ascites without perforation or intussusception.

A woman in her 60s with a history of hypertension and remote smoking (cessation 30 years prior) presented to the emergency department with concern for a foreign body sensation after eating fish. She reported sore throat, dry cough, a foreign-body sensation in the throat, and mild difficulty swallowing. Examination showed erythema of the left posterior pharyngeal pillar; flexible laryngoscopy showed erythema of the ipsilateral arytenoid. She was treated symptomatically and discharged. She returned the next day with worsening throat pain on swallowing, drooling, and a sensation of neck swelling; neck palpation was unremarkable. Oropharyngeal erythema persisted, but repeat laryngoscopy now showed an erythematous, tense, swollen supraglottic structure with a Cormack-Lehane grade of 4, limiting view of the vocal cords. She was afebrile, heart rate 72/min, respiratory rate 17/min, oxygen saturation 96%. Blood tests showed WBC 12.36 (thousand/µL) with neutrophil predominance, glucose 116 mg/dL, and C-reactive protein 82.2 mg/L (normal 0-5). She was admitted for intravenous antibiotics, corticosteroids, noninvasive oxygen support, and nebulized budesonide under close airway monitoring. She improved over several days; by day 9 she was asymptomatic with normal vitals, WBC 6.47, CRP 52 mg/L, and procalcitonin 0.04 ng/mL, and was discharged on oral antibiotics and tapering steroids with outpatient follow-up.

A woman in her late 20s presented with acute onset of nausea and severe unilateral headache accompanied by ocular pain, blurred vision, and redness of the right eye. Symptoms began about one hour after starting a new psychiatric medication that had been added several days into treatment for a recently diagnosed depressive disorder; she had no prior psychiatric treatment history. She had no chronic medical conditions, no other medications, no history of eye disease, refractive error, or known predisposing ocular risk factors. Neurological examination was intact and vital signs were normal. Ophthalmology was consulted. Best corrected visual acuity was 8/10 in the right eye and 10/10 in the left. Intraocular pressure was 26 mmHg on the right and 12 mmHg on the left. Slit-lamp exam showed mild corneal edema and conjunctival injection of the right eye with a shallow anterior chamber; the left eye was normal. The right pupil was mid-dilated and unreactive to light. The anterior chamber angle on the right was closed 360 degrees on examination, while the left angle was open. There was no lens thickening, and fundus exam was unremarkable bilaterally. Central corneal thickness and axial length were similar between eyes. Intravenous osmotic therapy was administered and the new medication was discontinued, with rapid improvement in symptoms and normalization of eye pressure.

A woman in her early 30s presented with approximately a 2-month history of intermittent fever and night sweats. She had undergone cesarean delivery about 3 months earlier, with symptom onset within weeks of delivery. About a month before presentation she developed bilateral lower limb edema and dizziness, followed by general fatigue, chest pain, and dyspnea prompting transfer for higher-level care. She had no significant past medical history, no recent dental procedures, no animal exposure, no relevant travel, and no drug use. A prior echocardiogram at the time of delivery had shown no congenital heart disease. On presentation, temperature was 37.8°C, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and systolic blood pressure 70 mmHg. She had pale conjunctivae but no petechiae, Osler nodes, or Janeway lesions. Laboratory workup showed WBC 8.5 x10^9/L, hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, serum creatinine 0.83 mg/dL, and elevated CRP at 20.5 mg/dL. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a mobile 20 x 15 mm mass attached to the anterior mitral valve leaflet, with associated severe mitral regurgitation and clinical signs of worsening heart failure. Blood cultures were drawn on admission.

A man in his 50s with a history of HIV infection (well controlled on antiretroviral therapy), end-stage kidney disease maintained on peritoneal dialysis for approximately 2 years, uncontrolled hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, and non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction estimates ranging 38-55% on prior imaging) presented to the emergency department with 3 days of worsening orthopnea and exertional dyspnea. Initial vital signs: blood pressure 140/80 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, temperature 36.7°C, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Lung exam revealed bilateral rales; remainder of exam was unremarkable. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia and a prolonged corrected QT interval (530 ms). Chest x-ray showed mild pulmonary edema with normal aortic diameter. He was admitted for management of volume overload attributed to peritoneal dialysis failure and underwent diuresis and dialysis with a hypertonic dialysate solution, achieving net ultrafiltration of 1200 mL. The following morning, cardiac auscultation revealed a new loud grade III/IV diastolic murmur at the left parasternal border. An urgent echocardiogram was obtained and demonstrated severe aortic regurgitation, prompting further advanced cross-sectional imaging of the chest.

A one-year-old male infant was brought to the emergency department with redness of the right eye, eye rubbing, and decreased appetite that began the previous evening. Past ocular history was notable for lensectomy with wide anterior vitrectomy for congenital cataract in the same eye at six weeks of age, leaving the eye aphakic; he had been managed since with patching and a contact lens. On presentation the infant was lethargic. Examination of the right eye showed conjunctival injection, mild diffuse microcystic corneal edema, a centrally shallow anterior chamber with 360-degree iridocorneal touch peripherally, and a fixed, mid-dilated pupil. The globe was tense to palpation. Intraocular pressure by tonopen was 70 mmHg in the right eye versus 16 mmHg in the left, which was quiet with a deep anterior chamber. Topical dual-agent pressure-lowering therapy did not reduce the elevated pressure, and an attempt to pharmacologically constrict the pupil did not change pupil size or chamber depth. Given the lack of response to medical therapy and the severity of findings, urgent surgical evaluation was pursued.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her mid-40s with a history of menorrhagia due to uterine fibroids (on tranexamic acid and mefenamic acid as needed, used inconsistently) presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of central, nonradiating, pleuritic chest pain with intermittent exertional shortness of breath. She denied diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, cough, fever, or infective symptoms, and had no recent long-distance travel or other typical risk factors for venous thromboembolism. She had no prior history of blood clots, did not smoke or drink alcohol, had a normal body mass index, and used no contraception. Family history included type 2 diabetes and myocardial infarction in her mother; no family history of clotting disorders or cancer. On examination, she was tachycardic (heart rate 119/min) with otherwise normal vital signs and unremarkable physical findings. Chest x-ray and ECG were normal aside from sinus tachycardia. D-dimer was mildly elevated at 0.66 μg/ml (normal 0.05-0.50), troponin I was negative, and other labs including electrolytes, complete blood count, inflammatory markers, and clotting screen were normal. She was managed conservatively and discharged with analgesics and follow-up. She returned twice over the following months with recurrent similar pleuritic chest pain and, later, interscapular pain and exertional dyspnea, with intermittently elevated D-dimer, tachycardia, and otherwise normal repeat workups, prompting further risk-stratification and imaging.

A woman in her early-to-mid 50s with a history of diabetes presented to the Emergency Department with a 1-week history of pain and blurred vision in the right eye. She denied any family history of glaucoma, denied use of relevant medications, and had no history of ocular trauma. She was born after an uneventful full-term pregnancy with normal birth weight. Her ocular history was notable for longstanding myopia corrected with glasses. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/100 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 40 mmHg in the right eye (central corneal thickness 522 μm) and 16 mmHg in the left eye (central corneal thickness 518 μm). Anterior segment exam showed a quiet conjunctiva and clear cornea bilaterally, with the anterior chamber moderately deep centrally but shallow peripherally, mild lens nuclear changes in both eyes, and a mid-dilated, nonreactive pupil in the right eye, without phacodonesis or iridodonesis. Optic discs were tilted bilaterally with cup-disc ratios of 0.4 and 0.3, without optic neuropathy. Fundus exam revealed a tessellated, highly myopic appearance with peripapillary atrophy bilaterally. Gonioscopy revealed 360-degree appositional angle closure in both eyes. Biometry showed axial lengths of 25.34 mm (right) and 25.08 mm (left), with anterior chamber depths of 2.39 mm and 2.35 mm respectively.

A young adult male presented with shortness of breath and cough. Initial vital signs were BP 125/80 mmHg, HR 105 bpm, temperature 37.4°C, RR 32/min, SpO2 96%. He had no known underlying disease, no personal or family history of heart disease, and no history of inflammatory disease in himself or his family. BMI was within normal range. He reported a history of working in harsh conditions under high physical exertion/pressure. ECG on presentation was normal. Chest imaging and ultrasound demonstrated a right-sided pleural effusion. Given clinical suspicion, further cardiac imaging was obtained, including transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography, followed by an urgent CT angiogram of the aorta. Laboratory workup included complete blood count, antibody panel, rheumatoid factor, CRP, and IgG to evaluate for possible inflammatory or autoimmune contributions. Based on the imaging findings, the patient was taken emergently for open-heart surgery involving cardiopulmonary bypass, aortic root and ascending aorta replacement with a composite valve graft, and coronary artery reimplantation. Intraoperative findings included a markedly dilated aortic segment (approximately 7-8 cm) with abnormal wall architecture near the aortic annulus extending into the ascending aorta, with associated aortic valve dysfunction. Postoperatively he was monitored in the cardiac surgical ICU for hemodynamic stability, bleeding, and tamponade, with an uneventful recovery course, and was discharged about one week after surgery with preserved ventricular function (ejection fraction 55%) on follow-up.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis, unspecified with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A woman in her late 30s (G2P1, twin pregnancy) at approximately 35-36 weeks' gestation was brought to the operating room for cesarean delivery due to failure to progress in labor. Her medical history was notable for long-standing hyperthyroidism managed with an antithyroid medication for several years, continued throughout pregnancy, with free T4 levels previously documented in the normal-to-mildly-elevated range. She also had gestational hypertension diagnosed earlier in pregnancy, with blood pressures progressively rising over recent weeks; no proteinuria was noted. On arrival, she reported abdominal pain and mild nausea. Vital signs showed heart rate 124/min, blood pressure 210/117 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. During preparation for anesthesia, she developed dyspnea, with oxygen saturation dropping to 90% despite supplemental oxygen; arterial blood gas showed a partial pressure of oxygen of 58 mmHg, with normal electrolytes. Blood pressure rapidly rose to 240/120 mmHg and heart rate to 200/min, with the patient becoming irritable and having a disturbance in consciousness. Emergency airway management and cesarean delivery were performed, with delivery of two neonates in stable condition. Postoperatively, she developed fever, tachycardia, and diarrhea. Imaging showed bilateral pulmonary edema, and cardiac ultrasound revealed left ventricular concentric hypertrophy with decompensated heart failure and preserved ejection fraction.

A woman in her early 50s presented with a several-week history of non-productive cough, progressive dyspnea, and fatigue. Past medical history was notable for hypertension and end-stage kidney disease attributed to hypertensive nephropathy, managed with hemodialysis via an arteriovenous fistula. She had no prior known cardiac disease and had never had a cardiac ultrasound. Roughly one month earlier she had tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR and was treated with azithromycin, corticosteroids, zinc, and vitamin C, but her respiratory symptoms persisted, prompting referral. On admission, vital signs showed respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 88% on room air, heart rate 94 bpm, blood pressure 170/94 mmHg, and temperature 37.3°C. Exam revealed jugular venous distension, hepato-jugular reflux, a mitral systolic murmur on cardiac auscultation, and bilateral findings suggesting pleural effusion on pulmonary auscultation. ECG showed regular sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a mobile mass on the posterior mitral leaflet with prolapse, measuring approximately 12x8 mm. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed bilateral ground-glass opacities, a focal area of consolidation, and a filling defect in the right hypogastric arterial branch. Labs showed elevated ferritin (2080 ng/mL), lymphopenia (490/mm3), mild CRP elevation (37 mg/L), fibrinogen 4.2 g/L, and LDH 240 IU/L. Repeat SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative, with positive IgG serology. Blood cultures were negative.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute appendicitis with perforation, localized peritonitis, and gangrene, with abscess
train_cases.note: A man in his mid-40s presented to the Emergency Department after being referred from another hospital due to concern for bowel perforation following an abdominal paracentesis, during which purulent/feculent-appearing fluid was drained and imaging suggested free air in the abdomen. He reported approximately one week of abdominal pain and distension prior to the paracentesis, with intermittent nausea but no fever or chills. Past medical history included newly diagnosed liver cirrhosis (MELD 30, Child-Pugh class B), type 2 diabetes, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and prior deep vein thrombosis. Home medications included aspirin, apixaban, tamsulosin, amiodarone, insulin, and other agents. On presentation, vital signs were stable (BP 145/95 mmHg, pulse 99 bpm, temperature 38.1°C). He was an obese male in no acute distress; the abdomen was softly distended with mild tenderness in the right upper and lower quadrants, without rebound, rigidity, or guarding. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Labs showed lactic acid at the high end of normal (1.83 mmol/L), normal white blood cell count (5.4 K/cmm) and platelets (217 K/cmm), with prolonged PTT (46 sec), PT (27.3 sec), and elevated INR (2.46). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed free air and a large tube-like fluid collection with an air-fluid level extending across the abdomen, abutting the inferior tip of the right hepatic lobe, with uncertainty whether this represented a closed-loop obstruction or a large abscess.

A woman in her 40s presented to the emergency department with hematemesis and melena accompanied by symptoms of postural lightheadedness. She denied abdominal pain, fever, or jaundice. About one week earlier she had been diagnosed with an acute gallbladder inflammatory condition and managed conservatively with a course of antibiotics and anti-inflammatory analgesics. She had a history of hypertension on medical treatment. On examination she was tachycardic (heart rate 110/min) with blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. She appeared markedly pale without jaundice, and had tenderness in the right upper quadrant on deep palpation. Initial labs showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 4.5 g/dl), marked leukocytosis (32.4x10^3/cc), platelet count within normal range, mildly prolonged prothrombin time, elevated bilirubin (2.0 mg/dl), mildly elevated ALT, normal AST, and markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase (497 IU). She was resuscitated with intravenous fluids, blood transfusion, and parenteral proton pump inhibitors. Upper GI endoscopy showed a normal esophagus, blood and clots filling the stomach, and a deep ulcer with adherent clot on the posterior inferior wall of the first part of the duodenum; the second part of the duodenum was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed a thick-walled gallbladder with multiple calculi, a normal common bile duct and portal vein, and a rounded heteroechoic lesion with a central anechoic, Doppler-flow-positive component anterior to the portal vein.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A woman in her early twenties, first pregnancy, presented at approximately 36 weeks gestation with fetal tachycardia and rupture of membranes. She had no significant prior medical or family history and had received routine prenatal care elsewhere without documented thyroid testing. On admission, weight was 57.5 kg, height 158 cm, temperature 36.8°C, blood pressure 132/88 mmHg, and heart rate 118 beats/min. Fetal heart rate was elevated at 150-200 beats/min with regular uterine contractions; vaginal exam showed meconium-stained fluid, and ultrasound suggested growth lagging gestational age. Fetal distress was diagnosed and emergency cesarean section under general anesthesia was performed, with uneventful delivery of a live infant. Intraoperatively the patient had persistent tachycardia (110-130 beats/min) and blood pressure 115-145/75-100 mmHg. Postoperatively, despite analgesia, sedation, and intermittent esmolol, heart rate rose progressively to 160 beats/min, with respiratory rate 25/min, agitation, profuse sweating, and temperature 38.2°C, while remaining alert and denying chest pain or dyspnea. Palpation revealed a mildly enlarged, non-tender thyroid gland, and manipulation of the gland appeared to transiently worsen the tachycardia. Hydrocortisone and continuous esmolol infusion were started and the patient was transferred to intensive care for further evaluation and laboratory workup.

An older adult woman presented to the emergency department with unrelieved chest tightness, shortness of breath, and back pain of several hours' duration. Shortly before arrival she had been evaluated at another facility, where an acute anterior myocardial infarction was suspected and loading doses of aspirin and clopidogrel were given without symptom relief. Several days earlier she had experienced brief exertional chest tightness with shortness of breath that resolved with rest. Past history included prior pulmonary tuberculosis and a remote 40-year smoking history. Vital signs: blood pressure 100/76 mmHg, heart rate 82/min, respiratory rate 20/min. Cardiopulmonary exam was unremarkable without peripheral edema. Labs showed mildly elevated troponin I and CK-MB, with normal complete blood count and renal/liver function. ECG showed abnormal Q-waves and ST-segment elevation with biphasic and negative T-waves across multiple anterior/lateral leads. Initial echocardiogram showed an enlarged left ventricle with reduced ejection fraction (36%) and regional wall motion abnormality involving the anterior, anteroseptal, anterolateral, and apical segments, with mild tricuspid regurgitation and estimated pulmonary pressure elevation. Emergency coronary angiography revealed only stable, non-obstructive plaques without rupture or dissection. Further history-taking revealed longstanding right lower extremity pain, several months of bilateral lower limb weakness, and a recent 10-hour period of immobility during travel.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism with acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her late 50s presented to the emergency department with acute-onset chest pain and dyspnea, accompanied by a single episode of vomiting, fatigue, and dizziness. She had no significant past medical history. On initial assessment, vital signs were: temperature 37.3°C, blood pressure 120/68 mmHg, heart rate 95 bpm, respiratory rate 23/min, and oxygen saturation 84.3% on room air. Cardiac auscultation revealed a high-pitched P2; abdominal exam was unremarkable and there was no lower-extremity edema. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, white cell count 15.68x10^9/L with neutrophil predominance (74.8%), platelets 334x10^9/L, CK-MB 1.96 ng/mL, troponin T 0.046 ng/mL, myoglobin 21.23 ng/mL, and markedly elevated D-dimer (6.38 mg/L). ECG showed sinus rhythm with ST depression in II, III, aVF, and V4-V6. About six hours later she developed sudden syncope, with heart rate rising to 100-130 bpm, hypotension (BP 80-90/55-60 mmHg), and oxygen saturation 85-90% on nasal oxygen. Repeat ECG showed new ST elevation in aVR with worsening ST depression in the inferolateral leads. Repeat labs showed further rises in CK-MB, troponin T, myoglobin, and D-dimer. Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated right ventricular enlargement, flattened interventricular septum, an enlarged main pulmonary artery, and poor visualization of peripheral pulmonary vessels, without a large central filling defect. She subsequently developed bradycardia and cardiopulmonary arrest en route for further care, requiring resuscitation and mechanical ventilation.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A man in his mid-40s with no known medical or surgical history and on no medications presented to the emergency department with a 10-day history of intermittent subjective fever, diffuse abdominal pain, and repeated vomiting, with new-onset palpitations on the day of presentation. He denied altered mental status, loss of consciousness, syncope, chest pain, diarrhea, or constipation. On examination, heart rate was 140-150 bpm and respiratory rate 27 breaths per minute; other vitals were normal. He appeared acutely ill and in distress, but was alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Brisk carotid pulses and distended neck veins were noted. Chest exam was unremarkable. The abdomen was distended, soft, and lax, with mild right upper quadrant tenderness and hepatomegaly. Facial exam showed bilateral exophthalmos, otherwise unremarkable. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Bedside echocardiogram showed severely reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (~30%), global hypokinesis, impaired right ventricular function, dilated atria, a dilated inferior vena cava, and elevated filling pressures. Labs showed markedly elevated AST/ALT, elevated total and direct bilirubin, elevated alkaline phosphatase and LDH, prolonged PT with elevated INR, elevated lactic acid, elevated CRP, elevated intact PTH, suppressed TSH, and elevated free T3 and free T4. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative.

A man in his late 50s with a known history of schizophrenia presented to the emergency department reporting right eye pain and decreased vision for the past 3 days. He had been started by his psychiatrist approximately one week earlier on a low-dose atypical antipsychotic medication, taken once daily; he denied use of any other medications. There was no history of ocular trauma and no family history of eye disease. On examination, visual acuity was markedly reduced in the right eye and near-normal in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was significantly elevated in the right eye and within normal limits in the left eye. Slit lamp examination of the right eye showed conjunctival injection, microcystic corneal edema, a mid-dilated and non-reactive pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber with iris bombe configuration; the optic nerve appeared healthy. The left eye examination was unremarkable. Gonioscopy revealed an appositionally closed angle in the right eye and a narrow angle in the left eye. Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the right eye confirmed a shallow anterior chamber with circumferential angle narrowing/closure. No prior similar episodes were reported.

An adult male presented in respiratory distress with severe bronchospasm requiring emergency intubation. Chest CT at presentation was negative for pulmonary embolism. On transfer to intensive care he was profoundly hypoxic and hypotensive with absent bilateral breath sounds; bilateral chest drains were inserted for suspected tension pneumothoraces. He remained difficult to ventilate until an intravenous ketamine bolus was given. Over the following days he received infusions of aminophylline, adrenaline, magnesium and salbutamol, plus regular intravenous hydrocortisone, antibiotics and nebulised salbutamol; respiratory viral PCR was negative. Despite six days of intensive bronchodilator therapy he remained ventilated with persistent hypercapnic respiratory failure; an ECMO referral was declined as his pH remained above 7.2 and the underlying process was considered reversible. Sputum culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus, but Aspergillus PCR and precipitins were negative and a vasculitis screen was negative. Serum IgE was elevated at 270 kU/L; magnesium and theophylline levels were normal. Echocardiogram showed good biventricular function with a small pericardial effusion. Prior spirometry had shown an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.7 with a 37% rise in FEV1 after salbutamol. Eosinophilia persisted despite a week of corticosteroids, prompting escalation of steroid dosing. On day 10 he deteriorated further with rising pCO2 and hypoxemia, and repeat CT showed new bilateral lower lobe consolidation and pleural effusions.

Adult male, transferred to the emergency department after 3 days of care at another hospital for a febrile illness with altered mental status. Five days before that admission he had undergone a dental extraction. He had a long-standing history of diabetes mellitus managed with oral hypoglycemics. At the outside facility he was febrile, adynamic, anxious, and confused, with leukocytosis, elevated CRP, hyperglycemia, and elevated nitrogenous waste products; he was treated with IV ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin plus supportive care. On arrival at this facility, a SARS-CoV-2 PCR test was positive. Vitals: temperature 40°C, blood pressure 88/57 mmHg, heart rate 130-140 bpm (normal sinus rhythm), respiratory rate 35/min, peripheral oxygen saturation under 70% on non-invasive ventilation. He was somnolent, confused, oligoanuric (~200 mL concentrated urine), tachypneic with poor respiratory mechanics, and had lumbar tenderness on abdominal exam. Labs showed leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte disturbance, hyperglycemia, and markedly elevated renal retention parameters. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.5, pCO2 28 mmHg, pO2 60 mmHg, glucose 19.1 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, lactate 4 mmol/L, SO2 82%. Head CT was unremarkable. Renal ultrasound showed bilaterally enlarged, edematous kidneys with numerous hyperechoic foci suggesting intraparenchymal gas. Chest CT showed bilateral basal consolidation, atelectasis, and bilateral pleural effusions. Abdominal/pelvic CT showed bilaterally enlarged, heterogeneous, non-enhancing kidneys with foci of necrosis and irregular gas collections extending into perirenal and subfascial spaces, worse on the left, with features of acute renal failure.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A middle-aged adult woman with a five-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, previously on glimepiride, vildagliptin, and metformin, presented to the emergency department after a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor was added to her regimen by her primary care provider five days earlier. She reported two days of increasing lethargy and generalized weakness, without fever, cough, sore throat, chest pain, syncope, headache, vomiting, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms. She denied chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, thyroid disease, stroke, substance use, or recent travel, and reported recovery from a COVID-19 infection two weeks prior. She was a non-smoker and non-drinker with adequate oral intake. On examination she appeared pale, mildly drowsy but easily arousable, and dehydrated, without jaundice or lymphadenopathy. Vitals: heart rate 106 bpm regular, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg without postural drop, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 88% on room air, afebrile. Neurologic exam showed normal tone, power, and reflexes but bilaterally impaired vibration sense in the lower limbs; remaining systemic exam was unremarkable. Labs showed leukocytosis and elevated HbA1c. Arterial blood gas revealed low pH, low bicarbonate, low potassium, and low PCO2. Blood glucose was within normal limits, but there was an elevated anion gap with significant ketosis and urinary ketones. Chest X-ray was unremarkable. There was no history of methanol, ethanol, or paraldehyde ingestion.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A woman in her 40s, multiparous, at approximately 35 weeks gestation presented to the emergency department with altered mental status, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and fever (38.3°C). She had tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by nasopharyngeal PCR two days earlier, with associated sore throat. On arrival she required emergent endotracheal intubation for airway protection given respiratory compromise.
