Obstetric history was notable for one prior cesarean delivery two years earlier; the current pregnancy had been uncomplicated on prenatal visits, and there was no known history of chronic medical, autoimmune, or thyroid disease per family report. She denied tobacco, alcohol, or substance use, and there was no family history of autoimmune or thyroid disorders. Exam showed generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity with drooling and sustained upward eye deviation; pupils were reactive, symmetric, and consensual. Blood pressure was 121/71 mmHg, heart rate 115 beats/min. Labs showed elevated CRP (15.7 mg/L), elevated ESR (37 mm/h), and elevated D-dimer (2.7 µg/mL). Urinalysis showed no proteinuria; liver enzymes, electrolytes, glucose, BUN, and creatinine were normal. Thyroid function testing revealed a markedly suppressed TSH with elevated free T4 and total T3 relative to trimester-specific reference ranges. Noncontrast head CT showed no hemorrhage or focal lesion. Chest radiograph and ECG were unremarkable. Fetal ultrasound showed appropriate growth, normal heart rate and movement, and no contractions on tocometry. Given the seizures and altered consciousness, eclampsia was initially considered, though blood pressure was normal and there was no proteinuria, growth restriction, thrombocytopenia, or organ dysfunction.

A woman in her 90s with a history of hypertension and non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with progressive shortness of breath and right foot pain of three days' duration. She reported that the foot pain was triggered by minimal exertion and impaired her mobility, and she noted new blue discoloration of the right toes that had not been present before. Physical examination revealed bilaterally diminished breath sounds and cyanotic discoloration of the right toes. Oxygen saturation on room air was 84%, prompting supplemental oxygen. Initial labs showed a white blood cell count of 28.48 K/mcL, hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, lactic acid 4.7 mmol/L, D-dimer 11.3 μg/mL, mild transaminitis (ALT 91 U/L, AST 73 U/L), elevated alkaline phosphatase, C-reactive protein 16.8 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 56 mm/hr. A rapid test for a common respiratory pathogen returned positive. CT angiography of the chest showed bilateral ground-glass opacities without evidence of pulmonary embolism. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia without acute ischemic changes. Venous ultrasound of the lower extremities was negative for deep vein thrombosis; initial arterial ultrasound showed no focal occlusion, though a repeat arterial ultrasound of the right leg later showed predominantly monophasic waveforms below the knee. CTA of the lower extremities showed no hemodynamically significant occlusion, aneurysm, or vascular malformation. A repeat D-dimer was elevated at 12.6 μg/mL.

An adult female in her late 40s with a history of hypothyroidism (inconsistently treated with levothyroxine), prurigo nodularis, and depression presented to the emergency department with one day of gradually worsening sore throat, dysphagia, odynophagia, and chills. She described a distressing sensation of being unable to swallow her own saliva. She denied allergies, sick contacts, recent travel, or illicit drug use, and her immunizations were up to date. She owned two dogs but could not recall any bites, scratches, or mucosal contact with them. On initial exam she was non-toxic appearing, afebrile, with normal vital signs. Her voice and oropharyngeal exam were normal; external neck exam showed mild left submandibular lymphadenopathy, with the remainder of the exam unremarkable. After a dose of ketorolac and a period of observation, she became unable to tolerate oral liquids. Following topical lidocaine, flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy revealed a markedly reddened, swollen supraglottic structure with edema and erythema extending to the aryepiglottic folds and arytenoids, and mild pooling of secretions; the true vocal folds were symmetric and mobile without erythema or edema. She was treated with dexamethasone, IV antibiotics, diphenhydramine, and racemic epinephrine nebulizer. Complete blood count showed a white blood cell count of 22.6 (x10^3/µL) with 91% neutrophils, and blood cultures were obtained. ENT was consulted and recommended ICU admission. Several hours later her work of breathing increased, prompting an awake nasotracheal fiberoptic intubation in the operating room with surgical airway backup on standby.

A man in his 70s presented to the emergency department with atraumatic right shoulder pain that began abruptly overnight, transiently resolved, then recurred with increasing severity. He reported associated body aches and chills but remained afebrile throughout. He had played 18 holes of golf the day before symptom onset and denied any other inciting trauma. Past medical history included coronary artery disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, mitral regurgitation, left ventricular hypertrophy, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, polyneuropathy, benign prostatic hyperplasia, copper deficiency, and chronic low back pain following prior lumbar fusion. Home medications included aspirin, tamsulosin, topical diclofenac, amlodipine, and an as-needed opioid/acetaminophen combination for back pain. On presentation, vital signs were within normal limits and he was afebrile. Examination showed minimal tenderness over the right glenohumeral joint without erythema, swelling, fluctuance, induration, or skin lesions. Active range of motion was limited by pain, with reduced passive flexion, abduction, and rotation, and pain reproduced with axial loading. Shoulder radiographs showed only degenerative acromioclavicular changes without acute bony or soft tissue abnormality. Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 33,100/µL (reference 4800-10,800) and C-reactive protein of 11 mg/dL (reference 0-0.8). MRI demonstrated a rotator cuff tear with a joint effusion and thickened capsule. The following morning he developed new contralateral shoulder pain with a similar examination.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A woman in her early 20s presented to the emergency department in the second stage of labor at approximately 29 weeks gestation (second pregnancy, one prior birth, singleton, live intrauterine fetus). She had a history of untreated hyperthyroid disease for several years and poor antenatal care, with only one prior prenatal visit and no formal records; she reported being told her blood pressure was elevated but had not taken prescribed antihypertensive medication. She presented with regular uterine contractions beginning about 6 hours earlier. On arrival she was agitated with a Glasgow Coma Score of 12 (E3V4M5). Vital signs: blood pressure 220/120 mmHg, heart rate 156 bpm, temperature 38.4°C, respiratory rate 40/min, oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Exam revealed bilateral proptosis, a diffuse, non-bruited neck mass, a grade 3/6 murmur loudest at the apex, bilateral basal lung rales, warm extremities, and bilateral pitting edema. Obstetric exam showed fundal height 30 cm, frequent contractions, fetal heart rate 140 bpm, fully dilated cervix, and fetal feet palpable at station +2. Labs showed pH 7.455, bicarbonate 17.8 mmol/L, pCO2 25.1 mmHg, urine protein 2+ and blood 1+, sinus tachycardia on ECG, low TSH (<0.02 µIU/mL), elevated free T4 (3.75 ng/dL), and LDH 547 U/L. SARS-CoV-2 antigen testing was performed per hospital protocol.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis, unspecified with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A young adult male presented after an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with an initial rhythm of ventricular fibrillation, occurring in the setting of a preceding acute respiratory illness. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after approximately 60 minutes of resuscitation, including bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation and external defibrillation by paramedics. On arrival to the Emergency Department he was febrile (temperature 40.5°C), hypertensive (blood pressure 146/83 mmHg), and markedly tachycardic (heart rate 155 beats per minute). Glasgow Coma Scale was 3. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable, with no goiter appreciated. Collateral history from family described a two-month history of heat intolerance, unintentional weight loss, hand tremors, and palpitations, as well as a maternal history of an autoimmune thyroid condition. Initial investigations showed elevated inflammatory markers, mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis, an elevated troponin I, and normal serum electrolytes. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia. Chest radiograph demonstrated prominent pulmonary vasculature without focal consolidation. Point-of-care echocardiography showed impaired left ventricular systolic function, though marked tachycardia limited accurate ejection fraction estimation. CT brain was normal, urine toxicology screen was negative, and coronary angiography was normal. A provisional cardiac diagnosis was being considered pending further workup.

A man in his late 20s with a history of incompletely repaired congenital heart disease (Shone complex variant with prior coarctation repair, subaortic and pulmonic stenosis, ASD/VSD closure in infancy, and mechanical aortic and mitral valve replacements via a Konno procedure at age 1) and persistent atrial flutter presented with acute-onset, severe (10/10) sharp chest pain radiating to the back that began after a bowel movement. He was known to have a progressively enlarging thoracic aortic aneurysm on annual surveillance imaging, measuring 5.3 cm several years earlier and 5.8 cm on a scan obtained less than one month prior to this presentation; he had been counseled on surgical options but had not yet followed up, and he reported poor adherence to beta-blocker therapy along with ongoing heavy weightlifting. Outside-hospital cross-sectional imaging of the chest was obtained and the patient was transferred for a higher level of cardiac care. On arrival he was afebrile, with a systolic blood pressure in the low 90s, heart rate in the 70s with an irregular rhythm consistent with his known atrial flutter, and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. He was started on intravenous antihypertensive/rate-control infusions. He was alert and oriented with no focal motor or sensory deficits on exam.

A woman in her early 70s with a history of hypertension and metastatic colon cancer (with prior liver and lung involvement) on ongoing chemotherapy presented to the emergency department with fatigue, malaise, orbital headache, nausea, vomiting, mild abdominal pain, and chills. She reported that symptoms began hours after a chemotherapy infusion given about two days earlier, following a recent dose reduction after an episode of low white blood cell count. She also noted decreased urine output and darkening of her urine, and had developed jaundice with icteric sclera over the prior day. She was a never-smoker and took irbesartan/amlodipine and atenolol at home. Vitals: temperature 37.1°C, heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 167/72 mmHg, oxygen saturation 100%. Exam showed jaundice and scleral icterus. Cardiac workup excluded acute myocardial infarction. Labs showed platelet count 30 x10^3/mm3, hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, total bilirubin 6.4 mg/dL (indirect 3.3), AST 1725 IU/L, LDH 4866 IU/L, haptoglobin <0.1 g/L, creatinine rising from 0.9 to 5.5 mg/dL over the preceding week, BUN 78 mg/dL, and uric acid 10.6 mg/dL. Peripheral smear showed anisopoikilocytosis, hypochromia, ovalocytes, echinocytes, rare schistocytes and helmet cells, occasional teardrop cells and stomatocytes, and polychromasia. Antibody screening was negative and the coagulation panel was normal.

A woman in her mid-20s, gravida 2 para 1, previously healthy, presented at 28 weeks of gestation with sudden-onset severe chest pain radiating to her back. She had an uneventful vaginal delivery two years prior. Past medical history included subclinical hypothyroidism and gestational diabetes. She had no family history of aortic disease or sudden cardiac death. She was tall (168 cm) and weighed 80 kg. Vital signs on arrival: blood pressure 148/73 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats/min, respiratory rate 23 breaths/min, temperature 36.5°C. Cardiovascular exam revealed a diastolic murmur at the aortic valve area. General exam noted a tall, thin habitus with arachnodactyly, a funnel-shaped chest deformity, and lens displacement on eye exam, but no acute distress. Fetal heart rate was 155 beats/min with no signs of fetal distress, and no uterine contractions were noted. Laboratory studies showed an elevated D-dimer of 4.32 mg/L; cardiac troponin T was within normal limits. Given the pregnancy, contrast-enhanced CT angiography was deferred in favor of transthoracic echocardiography for further cardiovascular evaluation.

A toddler-aged male with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department with fever, vomiting, and progressive shortness of breath of acute onset. His caregiver denied any choking event or prior episodes of respiratory distress. On examination he was febrile, with nasal flaring, suprasternal and intercostal retractions, and low-pitched inspiratory stridor. There was no drooling or abnormal breath sounds, and cardiac and abdominal exams were normal. A slight hyperextension of the neck and an oral breathing pattern were noted. During observation he had recurrent non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting with signs of mild dehydration, treated with a normal saline bolus. Given concern for an upper airway process, he received IV dexamethasone and nebulized adrenaline, followed by high-flow nasal cannula support and nebulized budesonide, with initial but incomplete improvement. Labs showed leukocytosis with a predominant polymorphonuclear differential and mildly elevated C-reactive protein. A lateral neck radiograph was obtained. Due to worsening respiratory status in the ICU, nasotracheal intubation was performed; airway visualization revealed marked upper airway soft tissue swelling with purulent-appearing secretions. Blood and airway cultures were obtained and empiric antibiotics started. He improved over 48 hours, remained intubated for airway edema, was extubated after several days, and completed a 10-day antibiotic course before discharge.

A woman in her 60s with no known chronic systemic disease presented with several hours of headache, a sensation of fullness, and pain in the right eye, despite already using multiple topical pressure-lowering eye medications (a combined beta-blocker/carbonic-anhydrase-inhibitor, an alpha-agonist, and a prostaglandin analog). About one year earlier she had an episode of severe right eye pain with markedly elevated eye pressure that was treated emergently with intravenous osmotic therapy and a laser iridotomy procedure at two clock-hour positions of the iris, after which pressure normalized and she remained on chronic topical therapy. On this visit, right eye intraocular pressure was 41 mmHg (fellow eye 9 mmHg). Visual acuity was 0.3 (right eye, uncorrected/bare). Diffuse microcystic corneal edema was present. The anterior chamber was shallow with 4+ cells. Gonioscopy showed a 360-degree closed angle with invisible posterior trabecular meshwork (Shaffer grade 0). The iris showed scarring at the 10 and 12 o'clock positions from the prior laser site, an iris-bombe configuration, and a mid-dilated pupil with poor light reaction. Severe lens nuclear sclerosis was noted bilaterally. Fundus examination and optical coherence tomography showed a crowded optic disc with normal retinal nerve fiber layer thickness and a clear vitreous. Vital signs were otherwise unremarkable.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A teenage female with a history of type 1 diabetes managed on sensor-augmented insulin pump therapy presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of intractable vomiting, markedly decreased urine output progressing to no urine output, and a worsening level of consciousness. Her diabetes had been diagnosed several years earlier without prior severe metabolic decompensation, and recent glycemic control had been suboptimal. On arrival she was in a state of poor perfusion with altered mental status (Glasgow Coma Scale 12) and no focal neurological deficits, with pale skin and deep, labored breathing. Physical exam revealed weak, rapid distal pulses, cool extremities, and delayed capillary refill (>2 seconds); the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Point-of-care venous blood gas showed marked acidemia (pH 6.93) with very low bicarbonate and a large base deficit, an elevated anion gap, and elevated lactate. Blood glucose was markedly elevated with high calculated serum osmolality. Renal function was impaired with elevated creatinine, and serum potassium was elevated, with corresponding changes noted on electrocardiogram. Two isotonic saline boluses were given with improvement in perfusion parameters, and the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit for further correction of her metabolic and electrolyte derangements. A brain CT performed given her altered consciousness excluded cerebral edema.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism with acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her 70s with no known chronic illnesses presented to the emergency department with acute dyspnea and chest tightness. On examination she appeared cyanotic, particularly around the lips. Vital signs showed tachycardia (heart rate 102 bpm), tachypnea (respiratory rate 25/min), hypotension (blood pressure 88/51 mmHg), profound hypoxemia (oxygen saturation 61% by pulse oximetry), and a normal temperature (36.0°C). An electrocardiogram obtained on arrival showed sinus tachycardia, nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay, abnormal Q waves in leads III and V1, ST-segment depression in leads V2-V4, T-wave inversion in leads II, III, aVF, and V1-V4, and right-axis deviation. About 10 minutes after arrival she developed cardiac arrest, and high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation was started immediately. Blood testing during the resuscitation period showed a markedly elevated D-dimer level (8051 ng/mL). After 60 minutes of resuscitation, spontaneous circulation returned, and she was transferred to intensive care because of ongoing hemodynamic instability. Doppler ultrasonography of the lower extremities identified a small intermuscular vein thrombus (4.3 mm) in the right calf. Contrast-enhanced chest imaging showed a filling defect within the left lower pulmonary artery trunk along with additional small filling defects in more distal pulmonary artery branches.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis, unspecified with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A man in his 40s was brought to the emergency department for evaluation of a suspected perforated gastric ulcer. He reported a 4-day history of nausea, diffuse abdominal pain, general weakness, anorexia, and indigestion. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a thyroid condition, for which he had discontinued all medications approximately one year earlier. Family and personal history could not be obtained. On examination he had hypoactive bowel sounds and direct tenderness in the epigastric region. Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 12.5 x10^9/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 38 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 16.93 mg/dL. Thyroid function testing revealed free T4, total T3, and total T4 levels above the reference range with a thyroid-stimulating hormone level below the lower limit of detection. Computed tomography demonstrated peritonitis with findings concerning for a perforated gastric malignancy and possible peritoneal spread. He underwent emergent surgical repair and was admitted to the surgical intensive care unit. On the second postoperative day, he developed a fever peaking at 41.3C, tachycardia to 138 beats per minute, irritability, severe pain, and a reduced level of consciousness with eye opening only to speech, no verbal output, and localized response to painful stimuli.

train_cases.diagnosis: Malignant neoplasm of lower lobe, left bronchus or lung
train_cases.note: A man in his early 60s presented to respiratory clinic with a 6-month history of persistent cough, hemoptysis, and recurrent chest infections, accompanied by worsening breathlessness, mild hoarseness, fatigue, reduced appetite, and weight loss. Chest X-ray showed left-sided opacification with a small pleural effusion. CT thorax demonstrated a large (approximately 7 x 9 cm) complex, centrally necrotic mass in the left lower lobe with distal lung collapse and consolidation, associated with multiple enlarged bilateral hilar and supraclavicular lymph nodes and a thrombus within the left inferior pulmonary vein. Past medical history included osteoarthritis, hyperlipidemia, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He was an ex-smoker (25-30 cigarettes/day) who had recently quit. Approximately 6 months later, he presented acutely to vascular surgery with sudden-onset left leg pain. Examination revealed a cold, mottled, pale left leg with absent sensation but preserved toe movement, a palpable femoral pulse, and an absent popliteal pulse. He was started on intravenous heparin for suspected acute limb ischemia. CT angiogram revealed an occlusive thrombus in the mid superior mesenteric artery with patent inferior mesenteric and iliofemoral arteries, and delayed imaging showed a large popliteal artery occlusion at the bifurcation without distal run-off. Imaging also showed interval worsening of the left lower lobe mass extending along the pulmonary vein toward the left atrium, and infarction of the lower pole of the right kidney.

A woman in her mid-40s, an active smoker (approximately 25 pack-years), with no known drug allergies and no previously documented chronic respiratory diagnosis, presented with severe, rapidly progressive respiratory distress. Over the preceding six months she had monthly episodes of wheezing and chest tightness that resolved with inhaled short-acting bronchodilator use. One week prior to this presentation she had been treated at another facility for acute respiratory failure with intravenous corticosteroids, nebulized bronchodilator and steroid therapy, and supplemental oxygen, and was discharged on an oral corticosteroid taper plus a long-acting inhaled bronchodilator/antimuscarinic combination. After initial improvement she returned days later with recurrent severe dyspnea. On this presentation she had marked diffuse airway narrowing with hypoxic-hypercapnic respiratory failure and severe respiratory acidosis that did not respond to intravenous corticosteroids, magnesium, bronchodilators, or non-invasive ventilation, requiring emergent intubation and mechanical ventilation. Despite high-pressure invasive ventilation, worsening acidemia and ventilatory failure persisted, prompting initiation of veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Subsequent whole-body CT imaging showed pneumomediastinum with consolidation of the left upper lobe and lingula, and bronchoalveolar lavage testing returned positive for Influenza A.

A woman in her mid-70s with a history of stage IV poorly differentiated ovarian carcinoma on long-term palliative chemotherapy presented with a brief syncopal episode accompanied by lethargy, nausea, light-headedness, and increased watery ileostomy output following a chemotherapy session about a week earlier. Relevant history included prior bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and hysterectomy, ileostomy for small bowel obstruction with subsequent fistula formation, bilateral nephrostomy tubes for radiation-induced ureteric obstruction, recurrent urinary tract infections with prior colonization by a resistant organism, hypertension, prior pulmonary emboli on anticoagulation, and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. On initial exam she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, with an unremarkable general and neurological examination. Labs showed sodium 127 mmol/L, creatinine 145 (baseline lower), hemoglobin 87 g/L, white cell count 4.52, and lymphocyte count 0.7. On day 2 she developed fever to 38.5°C and was started empirically on broad-spectrum antibiotics; nephrostomy tubes were exchanged and an initial infectious workup was unrevealing. Fever persisted into the third week despite negative site cultures, prompting further imaging that incidentally showed an abnormal focal finding near a cardiac valve, later characterized as a small mobile mass on echocardiography. On day 17 she developed delirium with fluctuating consciousness, and brain imaging revealed a new focal enhancing lesion. Repeat blood cultures obtained around day 22, after prolonged incubation, grew an organism with unusual antimicrobial susceptibility. Targeted therapy was initiated, but given her overall condition she was managed palliatively and died several days later.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism with acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A man in his 90s with a history of hypertension (well-controlled on medication), prior stroke on clopidogrel for secondary prevention, asbestos-related lung disease with pleural calcification, rheumatoid arthritis with reduced mobility, and a remote history of deep venous thrombosis presented after an acute event. He had been in his usual state of health when, that morning, he developed sudden dizziness and weakness while dressing, fell backward onto his bed, and slid to the floor. There was no loss of consciousness, seizure activity, or incontinence. On EMS arrival he was lethargic with a heart rate of 18 beats/min and first-degree AV block; he responded to two doses of intravenous atropine with an increase in rate to 80 beats/min. In the emergency department he denied chest pain, dyspnea, or cough. Vitals: blood pressure 136/90 mmHg, pulse 73 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Cardiopulmonary and neurologic exams were unremarkable, without peripheral edema. Labs showed leukocytosis (11.6×10^9/L), creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, troponin 1.75 ng/mL, and pro-BNP 1829 pg/mL. ECG showed sinus bradycardia (48 bpm) with first-degree AV block. Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a dilated right ventricle with a hypokinetic free wall, preserved apical contraction, and leftward septal displacement. Further diagnostic workup for the etiology of these findings was initiated, limited in part by renal impairment.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism with acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her late 30s with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department with acute chest pain ongoing for about two hours. She reported no prior similar episodes and no personal or family history of coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, stroke, malignancy, or venous thromboembolism. On examination she was tachycardic with a regular pulse of 110 beats/min, blood pressure 100/65 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 95% on room air (improving to 99% with 2 L/min supplemental oxygen), and temperature 37°C. Cardiac auscultation was normal and there was no jugular venous distension. An initial electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with 2 mm ST-segment elevation in leads V2-V3 without other abnormalities. Given concern for an acute coronary event, antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy were started and she was transferred urgently for coronary angiography. About twenty minutes later, a repeat ECG showed a new right bundle branch block with resolution of the earlier ST-segment elevation. Coronary angiography subsequently demonstrated angiographically normal coronary arteries without stenosis. Transthoracic echocardiography showed right ventricular dilation and an elevated estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of approximately 60 mmHg. Further imaging and vascular studies were pursued to clarify the underlying cause of her presentation.

An adult male in his mid-30s with no significant past medical history, medication use, or alcohol use was transferred from another facility's emergency department for evaluation of one episode of massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding. On arrival, he demonstrated signs of hypovolemic shock, including pallor, diaphoresis, hypotension (blood pressure 100/50 mmHg), and tachycardia (heart rate 105 bpm). Laboratory testing showed acute anemia, with hemoglobin of 9.9 g/dL on initial measurement dropping to 8 g/dL on repeat testing shortly after. A previously placed nasogastric tube drained approximately 300 mL of blood. He was resuscitated with intravenous fluids, transfusion of one unit of packed red blood cells, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and intravenous proton pump inhibitor therapy. Emergent upper endoscopy was performed, revealing a non-pulsatile bulging lesion approximately 3 cm in diameter along the proximal greater curvature/posterior wall of the gastric corpus, with a small surface erosion and a visible vessel but no active bleeding at the time of examination; the gastric lumen contained a large amount of fresh blood. Endoscopic hemostatic therapy was performed at the site. No other upper gastrointestinal lesions were identified. Given the unusual endoscopic appearance in a young patient without prior illness, further cross-sectional imaging with contrast was pursued to characterize the lesion and surrounding vascular anatomy.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism with acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A middle-aged man was admitted for acute abdominal pain and diffuse peritonitis of several days' duration. He underwent emergency abdominal surgery; because of severe septic shock, a central venous catheter was placed via the right internal jugular vein to support rapid fluid resuscitation and vasoactive medication. His postoperative course was initially favorable: hemodynamics stabilized within two days, he began ambulating with spontaneous flatus by day three, vasoactive support was weaned by day five, low-dose oral intake and low-molecular-weight heparin prophylaxis were started around day seven (with parenteral nutrition via the central line), and by day fourteen he was tolerating a normal diet with parenteral nutrition discontinued. On day fifteen, while the central venous catheter was being removed, he abruptly lost consciousness and suffered cardiac arrest, requiring emergency cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Bedside ultrasound performed during resuscitation showed a mobile echogenic structure within the right jugular vein moving with blood flow. Focused echocardiography demonstrated reduced systolic excursion of the right atrium and ventricle, a dilated inferior vena cava fixed in caliber without respiratory variation, right ventricular outflow tract dilation with reduced left ventricular wall motion, ventricular septal flattening with a 'D'-shaped left ventricle, and an increased right-to-left ventricular ratio with diminished right ventricular contractility. Systemic thrombolytic therapy was administered empirically. Spontaneous circulation returned after about 20 minutes, but he remained hypotensive and comatose, developed multi-organ failure, and died approximately 50 hours later; confirmatory cross-sectional imaging could not be performed given his instability.

An adolescent/young adult female with a known history of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, currently under hematologic care, presented with 24 hours of abdominal pain. The pain was not associated with heartburn or vomiting. Vital signs on evaluation showed a temperature of 38.4°C, heart rate 85 beats per minute, blood pressure 115/71 mmHg, and respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute. Abdominal examination revealed a soft, non-distended abdomen with only mild tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.46 g/dL, white blood cell count 1.55 K/µL, platelets 58.8 K/µL, and C-reactive protein 1.35 U/L; liver and renal function tests and serum amylase were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography performed at presentation showed the appendix measuring 9 mm in diameter with hyperechoic mucosa and a small amount of free fluid surrounding the appendix. Given the clinical and imaging findings, surgical evaluation was pursued. The patient subsequently underwent an operative abdominal procedure via a right lower quadrant incision without intraoperative or postoperative complications, and was discharged in good condition on postoperative day 3 for continued hematology follow-up. Blood and peritoneal fluid cultures were obtained intraoperatively.

A young adult male with a history of cocaine use presented to the emergency department with a one-week history of fever, fatigue, and shortness of breath, without sore throat or cough. Past medical history was otherwise unremarkable, with no known cardiac disease or immunosuppression, and he denied intravenous drug use. Vaccination records were up to date. On examination he was febrile (38°C), hypoxemic (SpO2 85%), tachypneic (28/min), tachycardic (120 bpm), and severely hypotensive (80/40 mmHg). Auscultation revealed a grade III mitral systolic murmur and diffuse bilateral crackles. Exam also showed signs of acute arterial occlusion of the left lower limb. Labs showed marked leukocytosis (27,050/mm3) with neutrophilia (22,452/mm3), anemia (hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL), elevated creatinine (2.99 mg/dL), elevated arterial lactate (50 mg/dL), and markedly elevated C-reactive protein (320 mg/L). HIV serology was negative. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Chest x-ray showed findings compatible with pulmonary congestion, including Kerley B lines and bilateral reticular opacities. Vascular ultrasound of the left lower limb demonstrated occlusion of the proximal anterior tibial artery. Given the severity of presentation, the patient required emergent airway management, mechanical ventilation, vasoactive support, empiric antimicrobial therapy, and urgent endovascular thrombectomy of the occluded limb vessel. Blood cultures were obtained.

A woman in her early thirties, gravida 4 para 2, with an intrauterine pregnancy at 37 weeks 5 days, presented to the Emergency Department with fever and cough for 2 days. She reported decreased fetal movements over the prior day but denied contractions, fluid leakage, or vaginal bleeding. Past history included a prior cesarean section, prior excision of an anterior abdominal wall endometrioma, and a history of atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance on cervical screening. She denied tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drug use. Fever resolved after acetaminophen. Obstetric evaluation found the patient and pregnancy stable, and she was discharged on a course of oral azithromycin for possible community-acquired pneumonia, with outpatient follow-up arranged. She returned 5 days later in preterm labor with respiratory distress. Oxygen saturation was 75% on room air, deteriorating to 60%, requiring a nonrebreather mask; chest imaging showed bilateral infiltrates. She underwent emergent cesarean delivery under general anesthesia with a viable female infant delivered, and remained intubated postoperatively in the intensive care unit. On postoperative day 2 she developed fever of unclear source; cultures were drawn and broad-spectrum antibiotics started. Bedside cardiac ultrasound showed preserved contractility with a dilated, non-collapsing inferior vena cava. Her course was marked by worsening tachycardia, hypertension, ventilator dyssynchrony, need for maximal ventilatory support, barotrauma requiring chest tube placement, and markedly elevated D-dimer requiring therapeutic anticoagulation.

A man in his 40s presented with sore throat and odynophagia after receiving an intravenous dose of ceftriaxone for presumed acute pharyngitis, without symptomatic improvement. He had no significant past medical history and was a non-smoker. On presentation, vital signs were: temperature 37.1°C, heart rate 122 beats/min, blood pressure 138/88 mmHg, and peripheral oxygen saturation 99% on room air. External examination of the pharynx and neck showed no abnormalities. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed diffuse necrotic-appearing erosions throughout the larynx, with a red-to-white, coarsely roughened surface extending from the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis to the subglottis, and red, swollen, eroded mucosa involving the bilateral arytenoid regions; vocal cord mobility was preserved with no paralysis. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 10,580/µL and C-reactive protein of 14.075 mg/dL. Non-contrast chest CT showed no evidence of pneumonia. Given the extensive laryngeal findings and concern for airway compromise, the patient was admitted for close monitoring and further evaluation, including additional microbiologic and virologic testing.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A young adult man with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus on insulin therapy, and a long-standing autoimmune hyperthyroid condition diagnosed in adolescence (previously managed with antithyroid medication and potassium iodide, with inconsistent follow-up), presented to the emergency department with altered consciousness and nausea. He had multiple prior hospitalisations for similar hyperglycaemic episodes attributed to poor adherence with insulin therapy, most recently discharged about two months earlier. On arrival, vital signs showed blood pressure 130/64 mmHg, heart rate 220 beats per minute with an irregular rhythm (atrial fibrillation), respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and temperature 36.3°C. Glasgow Coma Scale was 10 (E2V3M5). He appeared restless, with tachycardia and signs suggestive of fluid overload/heart failure. Blood gas analysis revealed pH 7.036, glucose 736 mg/dL, base excess -24.4 mmol/L, lactate 26.0 mg/dL, bicarbonate 6.3 mmol/L, anion gap 27.5 mmol/L, sodium 125.6 mmol/L, potassium 5.15 mmol/L, with increased urine ketones; HbA1c was 12.2%. He was admitted to the intensive care unit and treated with intravenous fluids, continuous insulin infusion, and electrolyte correction, but showed little improvement in mental status despite metabolic correction, prompting further evaluation.

A man in his late 50s presented to the emergency department with acute-onset chest and back pain. His medical history was notable for hypertension (not on regular medication) and a prior emergency endovascular aortic repair procedure performed approximately 4 months earlier for an acute aortic syndrome involving the ascending aorta, at which time multiple stent-grafts had been placed with fenestrations to the carotid arteries; a follow-up scan roughly one month after that procedure had shown stable, well-remodeled aorta without complication. On this presentation, vital signs showed the patient was hemodynamically stable with controlled blood pressure and heart rate, though details were not specified as critical. Physical examination revealed no acute distress documented beyond chest and back pain; cardiac auscultation findings were not detailed. Electrocardiography and cardiac enzyme testing were performed to evaluate for acute coronary syndrome. Computed tomography angiography showed an intimal flap extending from the region of the proximal endograft proximally to involve the aortic root, with the aorta at this level measuring approximately 57 mm in maximal diameter. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated marked dilation of the aortic root and ascending aorta (aortic sinus ~43 mm, ascending aorta ~56 mm) with severe aortic regurgitation, but preserved left ventricular systolic function.

A woman in her late 50s presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of sharp, unremitting left upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back. She had been hospitalized three times in the past year for acute pancreatitis of undetermined cause and had undergone lithotripsy twice for bilateral kidney stones and a ureteral stone. Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus (on metformin) and hypertension (on bisoprolol and a combination irbesartan/hydrochlorothiazide tablet). She was a never-smoker and never-drinker. On exam, temperature was 36.2°C, blood pressure 93/60 mmHg, heart rate 65 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Bowel sounds were hypoactive; there was diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound, guarding, or ascites; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Labs showed WBC 9.44×10^3/µL (normal), hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL (normocytic anemia), creatinine 1.18 mg/dL (normal), and markedly elevated lipase at 1041 U/L, with normal liver enzymes, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild fatty liver and a dilated common bile duct (0.9 cm). MRCP revealed main pancreatic duct irregularities and pancreatic atrophy with two small pseudocysts in the tail. ANA, IgG4, and triglycerides were normal, but serum calcium was elevated at 11.9 mg/dL with normal albumin.

An adolescent male with a known history of rheumatic heart disease, previous tonsillectomy about a decade earlier, and antibiotic prophylaxis discontinued roughly 6 months prior, presented with yellowing of the eyes and skin and dark urine, without dysuria or urinary frequency. He had recent travel to a region with endemic mosquito-borne and viral hepatic illnesses. He then developed intermittent high-grade fever, headache, fatigue, myalgia, abdominal discomfort, nausea, vomiting, and poor appetite. He denied smoking, alcohol, or drug use. On initial examination he was febrile with scleral icterus and a rash over the trunk and upper limbs; bilateral basal lung crepitations, mild abdominal tenderness, and hepatomegaly were noted; cardiac exam was initially normal. Initial labs showed a mildly elevated white cell count with neutrophilia, markedly elevated CRP, transient thrombocytopenia, normocytic normochromic red cells, low albumin, urine positive for bilirubin without red cells or pus cells, elevated ALT, elevated direct bilirubin, and prolonged INR/PT. He was treated supportively and discharged, but five days later returned with persistent high fever unresponsive to antipyretics, nausea, vomiting, malaise, myalgia, and reduced appetite. Heart rate was 112/min and blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. Repeat labs showed further increased white cell count with neutrophilia and rising CRP. Examination now revealed a new grade 3 systolic murmur at the mitral area and sacral edema. Abdominal ultrasound later showed hepatomegaly and bilateral pleural effusion.

A 35-year-old male presented with an 11-year history of a chronic, relapsing, pruritic inflammatory skin condition affecting the face, trunk, and extremities. He reported numerous major flares over the preceding decade, several of which required tapering courses of systemic corticosteroids for control. Prior treatments included topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, and phototherapy, all with minimal sustained benefit. He was otherwise healthy with no other chronic medical conditions reported. On physical examination, there was marked erythema, scaling, and lichenification involving approximately 70% of body surface area, including the face, trunk, and extremities. Standardized severity scoring showed a high objective skin severity score (55) and a markedly elevated quality-of-life impairment score (26), indicating severe disease burden and functional impact. Vital signs were not remarkable. No lymphadenopathy, oozing, or crusting was noted at this initial presentation. Given the severity and treatment-refractory course, systemic therapy with methotrexate 15 mg orally weekly was initiated; this produced minimal clinical improvement and was associated with malaise, leading to discontinuation after an inadequate trial.

A man in his 40s presented with a long-standing skin disorder, ongoing for approximately 12 years. He reported recurrent, widespread erythematous plaques with overlying scale involving the trunk and extremities, occurring alongside recurrent painful nodules, abscess-like lesions, and draining sinus tracts affecting the trunk and scalp. Both components of the skin disease had followed a chronic, relapsing course over the preceding decade, substantially impairing quality of life. Prior treatment had included topical corticosteroid/vitamin D analogue combination therapy with limited benefit, followed by more than one year of an oral retinoid, which produced less than 50% improvement in standardized severity scoring. Past medical history was notable for chronic hepatitis B infection, managed with antiviral therapy for approximately 10 years with good virologic suppression, and a history of colorectal cancer with synchronous liver metastasis, surgically resected approximately 6 years earlier with no recurrence on long-term surveillance imaging. On examination, extensive scale-covered erythematous plaques covered a large proportion of the body surface, and multiple subcutaneous nodules with sinus tracts were noted on the trunk and scalp, with occasional drainage. Imaging of the chest wall showed subcutaneous soft-tissue nodules and mildly enlarged bilateral axillary lymph nodes. Baseline liver imaging showed post-surgical changes and fatty infiltration without new focal lesions, tumor marker levels were within normal limits, and viral load testing confirmed ongoing suppression on antiviral therapy.

A woman in her late 40s was evaluated for a 9-month history of bilateral lower extremity swelling, left leg pain, purplish striae over the abdomen, and abdominal distension. She had undergone a hysterectomy for uterine fibroids two years earlier and reported no other significant medical history, no prior radiotherapy. She was obese, weighing approximately 90 kg with a BMI near 33. On examination she had central obesity, a rounded facial appearance, fat deposition over the upper back, peripheral edema, thin and fragile skin, acne, and increased facial/body hair. Blood pressure was elevated at 146/115 mmHg. Routine biochemistry showed hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, and low serum potassium. Hormonal evaluation revealed markedly elevated morning and afternoon serum ACTH and cortisol concentrations with loss of the normal diurnal rhythm. Dynamic testing showed incomplete suppression of cortisol with low-dose dexamethasone administration but greater than 50% suppression with high-dose dexamethasone. Serum prolactin, gonadotropins, testosterone, and thyroid function studies were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed a small (~3 cm) extra-axial enhancing mass along the right frontal convexity with adjacent dural enhancement, as well as a separate small hypoenhancing focus within the sellar region with slight displacement of the pituitary stalk. Plain and contrast-enhanced adrenal CT imaging was unremarkable.

A man in his late twenties, with a several-year history of chronic viral hepatitis B infection first identified during an evaluation for fatigue, presented with a few days of febrile illness. He had previously shown fluctuating transaminase elevations, a rising liver stiffness measurement on elastography over three years, and a liver biopsy showing mild activity with moderate fibrosis. He had been started on an oral antiviral agent with initial virologic and biochemical improvement, but had discontinued this therapy prior to the current presentation. He now presented with headache, diffuse myalgia, and fever measured at 38.3°C, without cough, dyspnea, or gastrointestinal symptoms reported. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Complete blood count was within normal limits. Liver function tests were disturbed compared to his prior baseline, with alanine aminotransferase about 4.4 times the upper limit of normal, aspartate aminotransferase about 2 times the upper limit of normal, and mildly elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase. Chest computed tomography showed two small ground-glass density nodules in the right upper lobe, with minimal estimated parenchymal involvement (under 10%). Given the epidemiologic context and clinical picture, further evaluation for an infectious respiratory etiology was pursued, alongside resumption of antiviral therapy for his underlying chronic liver condition and close monitoring of hepatic function.

A man in his early 60s presented to the emergency department with a four-day history of abdominal pain radiating to the lower back, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and constipation. He described daily intermittent episodes of severe, sharp abdominal pain that worsened with leaning backward and improved with sitting forward. He tolerated clear liquids but vomited after eating solid food. He denied fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, dysuria, hematochezia, or melena. His history included long-standing intermittent abdominal pain of unclear cause previously evaluated, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, stage III chronic kidney disease, prior cholecystectomy and gastric bypass, and remote alcohol and cocaine use disorders, both in sustained remission (abstinent from alcohol for several months). He reported daily marijuana use and had recently increased his intake of caffeinated energy drinks, consuming two 16-oz servings on each of the two days before admission, which he felt worsened his pain. He denied a family history of pancreatic or autoimmune disease. Vital signs showed elevated blood pressure (176/102 mmHg) with normal temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation. Physical exam revealed tenderness to palpation over the left mid and lower abdomen radiating to the back, without rebound or rigidity, and a soft, nondistended abdomen. Laboratory testing showed a normal white blood cell count, lipase and amylase at the upper limit of normal to mildly elevated, and mildly elevated liver enzymes. Alcohol level and urine toxicology screen were negative, and triglycerides were normal. Abdominal CT imaging was unremarkable. Abdominal MRI showed mild dilation of the main pancreatic duct with no findings of an acute process.

A man in his 70s with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and chronic kidney disease presented with cardiorespiratory symptoms occurring within the fourth week after starting a new oral targeted anti-cancer therapy for recurrent lung adenocarcinoma. He had previously undergone lobectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy for early-stage disease roughly a decade earlier, with recurrence identified several years later. After initiation of the new agent, he was hospitalized twice, initially with acute kidney injury, and on the second admission developed decreased urine output, bilateral leg edema, dyspnea, and diarrhea. Despite temporarily withholding the medication, he showed minimal improvement, and approximately three weeks after starting the drug he developed acute desaturation and dyspnea at rest. Examination revealed bilateral lower-limb edema and signs of volume overload. Vital signs showed tachypnea and hypoxia. Laboratory testing showed a marked rise in NT-proBNP to above 10,000 ng/mL. Electrocardiography demonstrated new T-wave inversions in the lateral precordial leads and a partial left bundle branch block. Echocardiography showed an acute decline in left ventricular ejection fraction from a baseline of 55%-60% to 25% over four days. Standard heart failure therapy was initiated with only partial symptomatic improvement.

A man in his 50s, working in agriculture, presented with widespread scaly, itchy skin lesions involving the scalp, upper limbs, trunk, and lower legs. Symptoms had been present for approximately 14 years, beginning on the scalp and gradually spreading to the limbs and trunk over time, with periods of partial improvement followed by recurrence despite various oral and topical treatments tried at multiple health facilities. He had no history of hypertension, diabetes, or hypothyroidism, no prior hospitalizations, and no family history of a similar skin condition. Predisposing factors included long-standing dietary habits such as excessive curd intake and lying down soon after eating, present since childhood. Vital signs were within normal limits at presentation. On examination, skin lesions were smooth to touch with blackish-red discoloration. The scalp showed mild involvement with small keratotic patches over about 30% of the area. Generalized blackish keratotic patches with mild scaling covered roughly 50% of the upper limb surface area, and erythematous patches with minimal scaling covered about 40% of the trunk surface. The lower legs showed mildly indurated, non-uniformly distributed erythematous patches. No oozing or discharge was noted from any lesion. On specific testing, gentle scraping of a lesion elicited pinpoint bleeding, while induction of new lesions at sites of skin trauma was not observed. Tongue examination showed coating suggestive of digestive disturbance; stool habits were normal in consistency with occasional constipation.

train_cases.diagnosis: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia of B-cell type not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: A man in his mid-60s with a longstanding history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (previously treated with chlorambucil, currently off active therapy) and idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (approximately 25%) was evaluated for a suspected pocket-site process related to his single-chamber implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, which had been in place for several years. He reported a roughly 6-week history of painless erythema with marked pruritus overlying the device pocket, without fever. Vital signs were unremarkable, with temperature ranging 36.5-36.9°C. Examination revealed localized erythema and skin induration over the pocket site without purulence, drainage, or dehiscence. Laboratory studies showed mildly elevated C-reactive protein (17.3 mg/L; ULN <5), normal procalcitonin (0.2 ng/mL; ULN <0.5), and leukocytosis (29.0 ×10^9/L) with marked lymphocyte predominance (84%). Because the appearance of the pocket area was atypical for a straightforward infectious process, device extraction was deferred and an exploratory excisional biopsy of the indurated skin was performed instead. Aerobic and anaerobic cultures of the tissue were negative. Histopathologic examination of the excised skin revealed a dense lymphocytic infiltrate within the dermis, with further immunophenotypic characterization pending.

A teenage girl presented with intermittent chest tightness and dyspnea persisting for several months. She had been hospitalized twice previously for a left-sided pleural effusion, treated empirically with anti-parasitic medication and later with chest tube drainage after the effusion enlarged, with initial symptomatic improvement. Despite this, she continued to have intermittent chest tightness and dyspnea over the following two months and had lost approximately 5 kg over the preceding six months. On further questioning, she also reported intermittent, mild abdominal pain for more than a year that had not prompted prior evaluation because it was not severe. She denied tobacco or alcohol use, abdominal trauma, prior abdominal surgery, or known pancreaticobiliary disease. Family members were reportedly in good health. On examination, she was thin (height 165 cm, weight 36 kg). There was decreased vocal fremitus and breath sounds with dullness to percussion over the left hemithorax; the rest of the examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed mildly elevated serum amylase (193 IU/L) and lipase (536 IU/L), with markedly elevated pleural fluid amylase (>2400 IU/L). Chest imaging revealed a large left hydropneumothorax with atelectasis. Abdominal CT showed a small low-density lesion in the distal pancreas with an associated pseudocyst and dilation of the main pancreatic duct. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated an abnormal tubular tract extending from the pancreatic region along the spine into the pleural cavity.

A woman in her late 50s, left-handed, with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia was brought for evaluation after being witnessed to have involuntary leftward head turning with vocalization followed by a generalized tonic-clonic seizure and prolonged unresponsiveness, prompting treatment for status epilepticus with a benzodiazepine and an antiepileptic, after which she returned to baseline mental status. She reported a one-month history of mild, dull, constant bilateral temporal headache radiating to the jaw, without fever, chills, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, or photophobia. She had no prior seizure disorder and did not use alcohol. She had a remote history of hypothyroidism previously treated with thyroid hormone replacement, currently off therapy while euthyroid. Initial brain MRI and CT were unremarkable and spot EEG showed no epileptiform activity, but over the following days she developed new confusion, unusual behavior, and short-term memory impairment; ambulatory EEG showed right hemisphere focal slowing with quasi-periodic sharp waves. On re-presentation, vitals were BP 144/89 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, temperature 99.1°F. She was alert, oriented, and fluent, following multistep commands, but recalled only 2 of 6 words after nine minutes; cranial nerves, motor, sensory, coordination, and gait exams were normal. Repeat MRI showed subtle pial enhancement near the right frontal lobe. Infectious and rheumatologic serologies were negative. Lumbar puncture showed clear CSF, 71 WBC, 3 RBC, normal glucose, and elevated protein (51 mg/dL); meningitis/encephalitis panel and paraneoplastic antibodies were unremarkable. Chest/abdomen CT incidentally noted an enlarged, hypervascular thyroid gland.

An 87-year-old man, previously healthy, presented with a two-year history of progressive dyspnea and dysphagia. He had been managed for a chronic neuromuscular condition affecting respiratory and swallowing function, using home noninvasive ventilation to relieve breathlessness. As symptoms progressed, he developed respiratory failure requiring tracheostomy and invasive mechanical ventilation for two weeks, after which he was weaned and discharged; tracheostomy and nasogastric tubes were retained due to persistent dysphagia and aspiration risk. Attempts at intermittent noninvasive ventilation via oronasal mask were poorly tolerated because of prolonged daily use and concern about facial pressure injury. Three months later he was hospitalized again with acute worsening of breathlessness and generalized weakness, requiring two weeks of invasive ventilation. Once spontaneous breathing and hemodynamics stabilized, weaning was attempted; he tolerated a 60-minute spontaneous breathing trial but failed full ventilator disconnection on at least five occasions, each time becoming anxious, irritable, and reporting chest tightness. Arterial blood gas during a failed attempt showed PaO2 69 mmHg and PaCO2 48 mmHg, with no improvement on conventional oxygen therapy. Airway endoscopy and clinical review found no mechanical airway obstruction and no evidence of undertreated underlying illness. Despite psychological support and respiratory rehabilitation, weaning was unsuccessful, prompting consideration of respiratory muscle weakness and anxiety-related ventilator dependence as contributing factors.

A teenage boy presented with a 9-year history of recurrent, intensely itchy rash affecting the trunk and extremities. The eruption had a relapsing course, characterized by scattered lesions with redness, crusting, scaling, and areas of localized skin thickening consistent with chronic scratching. He reported longstanding constipation, with bowel movements occurring only 2-3 times per week and associated straining. Family history was notable for urticaria in his mother and eczema in his grandmother. He carried known allergies to milk, freshwater fish, sesame seeds, animal hair, and pollen. Prior to evaluation, he had been treated with multiple oral antihistamines and topical corticosteroid and calcineurin-inhibitor preparations, which produced only partial and transient improvement, with recurrence of symptoms within days to weeks after each course. On physical examination, several discrete skin lesions were noted in various stages, showing erythema, scaling, crusting, and lichenification. No acute systemic symptoms, fever, or signs of superinfection were described. The family sought further evaluation and alternative therapeutic options given the chronic, treatment-refractory nature of the skin condition. Baseline laboratory assessment prior to intervention included serum eosinophil ratio and inflammatory cytokine panel, and stool and skin swab samples were collected for microbial analysis as part of the diagnostic work-up.

A man in his early 30s presented with a several-year history of an itchy, well-circumscribed, erythematous, scaly plaque involving more than half of the surface area on both forearms, with a few additional lesions on the back. He reported that lesions flared during periods of psychological stress. There was no family history of a similar skin condition. He had previously been treated with an oral systemic immunomodulatory agent in two separate one-year courses (tapering weekly dosing schedules), which had achieved approximately 90% clearance of the lesions with a low residual disease-severity score at that time. Treatment had been discontinued for the past three years, during which he used only emollients, prior to the current relapse. At presentation he was on no topical or systemic therapy other than regular emollient use. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination showed thick, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with overlying silvery-white scale on the extensor forearms bilaterally and scattered smaller plaques on the back, without nail, scalp, or joint involvement noted. Dermoscopic examination of the plaques revealed red dots in a regular distribution admixed with white scale.

A school-age boy with a known inherited disorder of T-cell immune regulation, previously identified through family screening, presented for evaluation. His relevant history included mild chronic diarrhea that had not affected his growth, and a pre-existing neurodevelopmental diagnosis. Earlier laboratory work-up had shown no evidence of systemic inflammation, negative celiac serology, and mildly elevated fecal calprotectin, with normal white blood cell count, lymphocyte subsets, and immunoglobulin levels. Approximately six months later, he presented acutely with vomiting, headache, and intermittent double vision, followed by development of an unsteady gait with frequent falls. He had no fever, no recent illness, and no clinical signs of encephalopathy or seizures. His long-standing diarrhea had worsened, with rising fecal calprotectin and associated failure to thrive. Neurological examination revealed cerebellar gait ataxia, saccadic eye movement abnormalities, and nystagmus, without other focal deficits. Blood tests, including inflammatory markers and repeat immune screening, were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed normal opening pressure with a lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated total protein, and an elevated IgG index; routine microbiological studies, including a viral PCR panel, were negative, and CSF cytology showed no malignant cells. A chest CT performed to screen for an underlying occult process showed no mass lesion.

A teenage female presented for evaluation of progressive weight gain with truncal fat redistribution, a dorsal fat pad, and centripetal adiposity that had been noted over several months to years prior to work-up. She reported associated body image dissatisfaction, low self-esteem, and social withdrawal; no formal psychometric scales had been administered. Hormonal evaluation on repeated occasions showed markedly elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol, in the range of approximately 460-740 µg/24h (normal <50 µg/24h). No dynamic suppression or stimulation testing was performed. There was no clinical or biochemical evidence of adrenal insufficiency on follow-up. Thyroid function testing showed a mildly elevated TSH (4.28 µUI/mL; reference 0.27-4.20) with total and free T3 and T4 within normal limits, without clinical features of thyroid dysfunction. Pituitary imaging identified a small (4 x 3 mm) lesion within the anterior pituitary gland. She underwent transsphenoidal endonasal resection of the pituitary lesion, with initial clinical improvement. Several years later, recurrence of hypercortisolism was confirmed biochemically, and a second transsphenoidal resection was performed. Despite these interventions, persistent hypercortisolism led to progressive changes in body fat distribution, including centripetal truncal adiposity and a dorsal fat pad, which later required surgical contouring.

A woman in her early 70s was referred for endocrinological evaluation after her ophthalmologist noted coarse facial features—macroglossia and frontal bossing—during work-up for recent bilateral lens dislocation. She had experienced sudden-onset visual impairment developing spontaneously over the preceding days to weeks, without trauma; slit-lamp examination confirmed bilateral dislocation of the lenses into the vitreous cavity, subsequently managed surgically. There was no family history of pituitary or other endocrine tumors. Past medical history included long-standing essential hypertension, chronic heart failure attributed to dilated cardiomyopathy (echocardiography showed mild left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction), obstructive sleep apnoea with chronic pulmonary disease related to severe kyphoscoliosis, osteoporosis complicated by a recent low-energy femoral fracture, type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with basal insulin and a GLP-1 receptor agonist, intellectual disability, reduced mobility, and a prior colectomy with permanent colostomy for volvulus. On examination, coarse facial features and severe spinal deformity were noted. Initial hormonal work-up demonstrated markedly elevated growth hormone and IGF-1 concentrations, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and an indeterminate morning cortisol level prompting dynamic adrenal testing, which confirmed preserved adrenal function. Cross-sectional imaging of the sellar region (computed tomography, performed due to severe kyphoscoliosis precluding MRI) demonstrated a 15-mm expansile, slightly hyperdense, homogeneously enhancing lesion.

An 11-year-old boy presented with fever and generalized tonic-clonic seizures for seven days, occurring 2-3 times daily, each lasting 1-2 minutes with brief postictal unresponsiveness; between episodes he was alert with no headache or focal deficits. There was no cough, vomiting, diarrhea, ear discharge, head trauma, jaundice, urinary symptoms, or recent injections. He had a history of two brief similar seizure episodes in the preceding year, investigated elsewhere without available records. On examination he was afebrile-to-low-grade febrile (38.1C), tachycardic with low-volume pulse, blood pressure 82/54 mmHg, weight and height both below the 3rd centile, with mild pallor and generalized darkening of skin, oral mucosa, and nails; sexual maturity was prepubertal. Systemic and neurological examination was otherwise normal. Labs showed mild normocytic anemia, normal white cell count and CRP, no malaria parasites, marked hyponatremia (sodium 111 mEq/L) with normal potassium, low-normal blood glucose, normal renal function and blood gas, and mildly elevated liver transaminases. Urinalysis, cerebrospinal fluid studies, and blood/urine/CSF cultures were unremarkable; chest radiograph, abdominal ultrasound, and head CT were normal, tuberculin test negative, EEG normal. Endocrine testing showed low-normal morning cortisol and aldosterone with an attenuated cortisol rise on stimulation testing; thyroid and parathyroid studies were normal. Abdominal MRI showed small, non-calcified adrenal glands. Autoimmune markers and viral serologies were negative.

A man in his 40s presented with a 1-week history of persistent dull pain in the left upper abdomen, unrelated to meals or movement. He denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, chills, or fever, and had no history of chronic disease. He had smoked several cigarettes daily for over a decade and did not drink alcohol. Endoscopic examination revealed a submucosal mass in the upper gastric body with an obscure boundary and swollen overlying mucosa. On physical examination, the abdomen was soft and nontender with no palpable mass and normoactive bowel sounds; vital signs were normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the upper abdomen showed a hypodense focus in the gastric fundus, diffuse pancreatic swelling with partial atrophy, a small hyperdense focus in the pancreatic body, low attenuation of the peripancreatic area, and mild pancreatic duct dilation with a normal bile duct. Both kidneys showed multiple low-density parenchymal areas. Laboratory testing showed elevated fasting glucose, elevated amylase and lipase, a markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and elevated total IgG and IgG4 levels. Routine blood counts, liver and renal function, and tumor markers were normal. Viral hepatitis, HIV, tuberculosis, and autoantibody testing were negative. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a hypoechoic gastric fundic lesion with a non-enhancing central area, and a hyperechoic pancreatic body focus with duct dilation. Fine-needle aspiration of the pancreas showed inflammatory cells and spindle-shaped macrophages with scattered immunostaining for the elevated serum immunoglobulin subclass.

A woman in her early 60s, with a history of kidney transplantation two decades earlier for hypertensive nephrosclerosis and malignant hypertension, presented with rapidly progressive dyspnea and dry cough. She was maintained on antihypertensive agents, an immunosuppressive regimen (tacrolimus and low-dose corticosteroid), a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor, a statin, and a long-term antiarrhythmic agent for recurrent supraventricular tachyarrhythmia. On presentation she was afebrile (36.7°C) with tachypnea (respiratory rate 34/min), heart rate 66/min, blood pressure 131/48 mmHg, and severe hypoxemia (oxygen saturation 67%). Lung auscultation revealed bilateral basal crackles. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated C-reactive protein (375 mg/L), leukocytosis (24,720/µL), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (508 IU/L), and acute kidney injury (creatinine 4.49 mg/dL, above baseline). Arterial blood gas showed hypoxemia with mild respiratory alkalosis. Chest radiograph showed bilateral basal infiltrates; chest CT demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities with septal thickening. Because of rapidly worsening hypoxemia, the patient required intubation, mechanical ventilation, and temporary renal replacement therapy. Extensive microbiologic evaluation of respiratory secretions and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (neutrophil-predominant) was unrevealing for bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, parasitic, and viral pathogens, and screening for myositis-specific and other autoimmune antibodies was negative. Echocardiography showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aortic valve disease, preserved ejection fraction, and moderate-to-severe pulmonary hypertension.

A woman in her late twenties presented to the emergency department with an acute, severe headache that began the previous day, at the end of a work shift, without preceding trauma. Her past medical history included a congenital atrial septal defect and rheumatic fever in childhood. Obstetric history included an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery approximately two years earlier. Neuroimaging obtained because of the headache identified a sellar mass measuring approximately 20 x 17 x 13 mm, extending into the suprasellar cistern and compressing the optic chiasm, with a small area of peripheral T2 hyperintensity raising the possibility of a focal hemorrhage or cystic component. On further questioning, she reported roughly five months of absent menstrual periods, tightening of her rings, an increase in shoe size by two sizes, and gradual widening of her nasal bridge, none of which had previously prompted evaluation. Vital signs were unremarkable. Biochemical testing showed normal fasting glucose, prolactin, adrenal axis, and gonadal axis hormones, with calcium-phosphate metabolism also within reference range; however, a growth-hormone-axis marker (IGF-1) was elevated to 4.4 times the upper limit of the reference range. She was referred for neurosurgical evaluation.

A man in his 40s had a six-year history of migraine headaches that had not responded adequately to prophylactic trials of propranolol and amitriptyline. He was started on galcanezumab, a monoclonal antibody for migraine prevention, with improvement in headache frequency and severity over the following two months. He then began having episodes of binocular horizontal diplopia while at work, initially lasting about an hour and attributed to fatigue. The next day similar diplopia recurred, this time accompanied by neck pain and heaviness. Over the following days he developed increasing fatigue that was more pronounced later in the day, and he noticed mild drooping of the left eyelid on self-examination. He denied difficulty swallowing, denied weakness of the arms or legs, denied sensory symptoms in the extremities, and reported normal bowel and bladder function. On examination there was subtle, fatigable ptosis, more prominent on the right, and horizontal diplopia on sustained right lateral gaze. Motor examination of the upper and lower extremities was unremarkable, and sensory examination was inconclusive. Laboratory testing showed negative acetylcholine receptor antibodies and anti-MuSK antibodies, and normal thyroid function tests. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest showed normal thymic tissue and normal lung volumes.

A woman in her early 30s was admitted to a community hospital for worsening weakness related to a long-standing autoimmune neuromuscular disorder diagnosed approximately five years earlier. She reported progressive ambulatory dysfunction, requiring assistance to walk to the bathroom, and was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin during this admission. Her chronic maintenance regimen included a corticosteroid and an oral cholinergic medication dosed multiple times daily. She had previously undergone several therapeutic plasma exchange treatments, the most recent approximately three months prior to this admission. During hospitalization, a psychiatric consultation was requested for worsening depressive and anxiety symptoms. She described low mood, crying spells, anhedonia, fatigue, insomnia, and feelings of excessive guilt, along with pervasive worry and anxiety. There were no suicidal or homicidal ideations, and no manic or psychotic symptoms were present. She denied substance use. She identified her declining physical health and recent job loss as psychosocial stressors, and reported diminished self-esteem related to a 20-pound weight gain over the preceding year. She was maintained on mirtazapine, bupropion, and alprazolam, with supportive psychotherapy during admission. Past surgical history included thymus gland removal without malignancy, and postsurgical hypothyroidism following total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid cancer, managed with levothyroxine.

A man in his 70s with obesity (BMI ~31), longstanding myasthenia gravis (diagnosed roughly a decade earlier, previously treated with immunosuppressive therapy, with thymoma resection many years prior), ischemic heart disease status post percutaneous coronary intervention with stenting, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and a lipid metabolism disorder presented for management of persistently elevated cholesterol. Statin therapy had previously been avoided because of concerns related to his neuromuscular disease and the patient's personal preference. Routine labs showed elevated total and LDL cholesterol with low HDL and mildly elevated triglycerides; glucose, electrolytes, liver and renal function, cardiac markers, blood counts, and inflammatory markers were normal, and ECG showed sinus rhythm with rare ventricular ectopy. A PCSK9-inhibitor injection was started for dyslipidemia. According to family members, within 24 hours of the first injection the patient developed severe generalized muscle weakness, joint pain, fever, and malaise lasting several days; testing for a common respiratory viral illness was negative. Despite medical advice against it, a second identical dose was self-administered about two weeks later, followed within 24 hours by marked worsening of muscle weakness, unstable gait, and speech difficulty, prompting hospital admission. Examination showed inability to squat and gait instability. MRI of the neuraxis was unremarkable. Nerve conduction studies showed prolonged distal motor latencies in multiple limb nerves, reduced compound muscle action potential amplitudes, and increased F-wave latencies. High-dose corticosteroids produced no improvement; pregabalin and plasmapheresis were subsequently used with slow improvement.

A woman in her early 70s was admitted to a general medicine service for a 20-year history of intermittent cough and wheeze, recently worsened, with new generalized edema over the preceding week. For two decades she had recurrent winter episodes of dyspnea, cough, sputum, and wheeze, previously labeled as chronic bronchitis and treated with courses of antibiotics during flares. Nine days before admission, after a cold exposure, she developed worsening dyspnea, yellow-white sputum, and reduced exercise tolerance; outpatient treatment with antibiotics and inhaled steroid did not improve symptoms, and she became bed-bound with orthopnea, followed by progressive generalized edema and bilateral lower-limb weakness. Hypokalemia (potassium 2.48 mmol/L) was noted and weakness resolved with supplementation; there was no history of exogenous corticosteroid use. She had a 20-year history of hypertension, a 30-pack-year smoking history (quit), and longstanding exposure to smoke and soot while living in a region with severe winters. On exam: HR 92, BP 140/87, SpO2 89% on room air, BMI 33.9 with central obesity, supraclavicular and dorsocervical fat pads, thin skin, axillary hyperpigmentation, scattered ecchymoses, enlarged tongue without tremor, barrel chest, and biphasic expiratory wheeze; lower-limb strength was normal. Labs showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, mild anemia, elevated CRP and D-dimer, elevated HbA1c, and low CD4/CD8 counts. Chest CT showed hyperinflation, right middle lobe consolidation, bilateral patchy/cord opacities, and bronchial narrowing; CT angiography suggested a chronic pulmonary arterial filling defect. Spirometry showed an obstructive pattern with reduced diffusion capacity. Morning cortisol and ACTH were elevated, with markedly elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol not suppressed by low-dose dexamethasone. Vitamin D was low with elevated PTH and bone turnover markers; sex hormone levels were mildly abnormal for menopausal status.
