A man in his early 60s with a 10-year history of plaque psoriasis, previously mild and controlled with topical corticosteroids, presented for evaluation of a new, worsening skin eruption. He had no family history of psoriasis. He was undergoing systemic therapy (a platinum-fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy combination plus an anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor and an antiangiogenic agent) for pulmonary metastases following prior colon cancer resection. Approximately three weeks after starting the checkpoint inhibitor, he developed erythematous, scaly lesions first involving the medial feet and lateral lower legs, which progressively spread over the following weeks to involve the trunk and scalp, with thick, layered scaling. He denied fever or other systemic symptoms. On evaluation roughly five weeks after onset, examination showed extensive, coalescing deep-red plaques covering large body-surface areas, most pronounced on the trunk and lower extremities, almost entirely covered by thick, adherent, layered scale, with scalp involvement. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory testing, including liver and renal function panels, was unremarkable. Screening for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and latent tuberculosis was negative. Chest computed tomography showed stable known pulmonary nodules. A skin biopsy was obtained for further characterization of the eruption.

An adult in their mid-30s, with a longstanding history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis diagnosed in adolescence and previously treated with several disease-modifying therapies including interferon beta and dimethyl fumarate, was started on an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody after evidence of ongoing neurological disease activity. After approximately five months on this therapy, the patient developed pruritic, burning skin lesions in the perianal, genital, and groin regions, which subsequently spread to the scalp, retroauricular areas, and lower legs over several weeks. The anti-CD20 agent was discontinued at the onset of the eruption, with gradual improvement of the lesions. On examination, nails, oral mucosa, and joints were unremarkable; two viral warts were noted incidentally on the right hand. Routine blood work was unremarkable, without eosinophilia. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, and C, HIV, and Chlamydia trachomatis were negative, and mycological testing from the groin was negative. Skin biopsy showed acanthotic epidermal hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis, elongation of rete ridges, thinning of suprapapillary plates, a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in the upper-to-mid dermis, and dilated, tortuous papillary dermal vessels. Dermoscopy of the genital lesions showed a regular arrangement of red-dotted vessels on a light-red background. After a period of drug withdrawal the lesions partially improved but recurred upon reintroduction of the same therapy, prompting a switch to an alternative disease-modifying agent for the underlying neurological condition.

train_cases.diagnosis: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia of B-cell type not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: An 84-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of persistent, constant, non-colicky abdominal pain localized to the epigastric region and right upper quadrant, radiating to the right shoulder, unrelated to meals or bowel movements. He reported significant anorexia, nausea, and vomiting, initially of undigested food three times weekly, which after two weeks became clear fluid streaked with blood. There was no diarrhea, melena, or constipation. Past history included cirrhosis of unknown cause diagnosed two years earlier, managed with lactulose, propranolol, and spironolactone; cholecystectomy four years prior for choledocholithiasis; and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with inhaled corticosteroids. He had a 30 pack-year smoking history and daily oral opium use, without alcohol or other illicit drug use. On examination he was cachectic and ill-appearing with pallor and temporal wasting. Vitals showed hypotension (90/60 mmHg), pulse 72/min, tachypnea (25/min), fever (38.9°C), and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. Conjunctivae were pale; sclerae anicteric. Bilateral lower lobe crackles were heard. The liver was nodular and firm; the spleen was massively enlarged, extending beyond the point of palpation. Mild generalized weakness (motor strength 4/5) was noted. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with lymphocyte predominance, anemia, and thrombocytopenia; liver and renal panels, coagulation, electrolytes, and other studies were obtained. Abdominal ultrasound showed a nodular, cirrhotic-appearing liver, a dilated common bile duct (13 mm) despite normal bilirubin, mild perisplenic free fluid, and engorged mesenteric vessels. MRCP excluded ductal obstruction or mass. Endoscopy showed nonbleeding esophageal varices treated with band ligation, and a benign hyperplastic gastric polyp.

A man in his early 50s was hospitalized for myalgia persisting for more than one month. He had a long-standing history (over a decade) of chronic hepatitis B, previously untreated with antiviral therapy. Two years prior, he was diagnosed with hepatitis B and cirrhosis, with elevated viral load, and was started on an oral antiviral agent; viral load became undetectable but later rebounded, prompting a switch to combination antiviral therapy. After starting the combination regimen, he developed progressive muscle pain, most pronounced in both lower limbs after walking, along with hypoesthesia in the distal limbs, without fever, headache, abdominal pain, or altered consciousness. Symptoms worsened over the following weeks despite discontinuing and changing antiviral agents. Laboratory testing showed elevated transaminases, lactate dehydrogenase, and creatine phosphokinase, with normal bilirubin initially. Imaging showed cirrhosis and gallstones. Days before admission he developed chest tightness, dyspnea, markedly elevated blood lactate, and severe metabolic acidosis requiring bicarbonate therapy. On admission he had dark urine with reduced output, elevated bilirubin, markedly elevated myoglobin and lactate, normal electrolytes, elevated uric acid, and normal renal function and white cell count. Exam revealed swollen, tender extremities with grade 3/5 weakness in both lower limbs, without erythema or warmth. Electrodiagnostic and imaging studies suggested a peripheral neuromuscular process, and muscle biopsy showed myopathic changes with mitochondrial abnormalities.

A woman in her late 50s presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of sharp, unremitting left upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back. She had been hospitalized three times over the preceding year for episodes of abdominal pain of unclear etiology, and had undergone two sessions of extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy for bilateral kidney stones and a ureteral stone. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin, and hypertension treated with a beta-blocker and a combination angiotensin-receptor-blocker/thiazide diuretic. She did not smoke or drink alcohol. On examination she was afebrile, blood pressure 93/60 mmHg, heart rate 65/min, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Bowel sounds were hypoactive and there was diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound, guarding, or ascites; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Labs showed a normal white cell count, mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL), normal renal function, and markedly elevated lipase (1041 U/L) with normal liver enzymes and bilirubin. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild fatty liver and a mildly dilated common bile duct. Cross-sectional pancreatic imaging showed irregularity of the main pancreatic duct, pancreatic atrophy, and two small pseudocysts in the tail. Autoimmune and metabolic pancreatitis markers (ANA, IgG4, triglycerides) were normal. Serum calcium was elevated at 11.9 mg/dL with normal albumin, prompting further endocrine workup.

A teenage boy presented with two weeks of fever followed by one week of bilateral lower extremity swelling, productive cough, and dyspnea. He described generalized malaise, poor appetite, and facial swelling. In the days before presentation he noted decreased urine output with intermittent dark, tea-colored urine. There was no abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, night sweats, or weight loss. Vitals: temperature 36.7°C, heart rate 100/min, respiratory rate 19/min, blood pressure 120/90 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98%. Exam showed a midline chest surgical scar, a grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the right sternal border with regular rhythm, and bilateral ankle edema; neurologic exam was normal, with no rash or clubbing. Past history was notable for a complex congenital heart defect (mirror-image dextrocardia with double outlet right ventricle, ventricular septal defect, and pulmonic stenosis), surgically palliated in infancy with conduit revision in childhood; outpatient follow-up years earlier had shown conduit stenosis and a small proximal conduit aneurysm. He kept indoor/outdoor cats with no known bites or scratches. Labs showed BUN 92 mg/dL, creatinine 6 mg/dL, potassium 6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mg/dL, albumin 1.8 g/dL, normal CRP, markedly elevated BNP, low C3 and C4, hemoglobin 6 g/dL, platelets 76,000/µL without schistocytes, normal LDH, and anuria. Blood and urine cultures were negative; ANA, dsDNA, and ASO were negative. Echocardiography showed severely reduced biventricular function, conduit stenosis with an echodensity, and residual shunt. Imaging revealed hepatosplenomegaly, bilateral renal cortical cysts, pleural effusions, and subpleural opacities. Renal biopsy showed proliferative glomerulonephritis with full-house immunofluorescence staining and subendothelial deposits on electron microscopy, without crescents or necrosis.

A man in his mid-20s, of African-Canadian background with a darker skin phototype, presented to a dermatology clinic with worsening of a chronic skin condition along with new-onset chills, rigors, weight loss, and diffuse reactive lymphadenopathy. He had a history of a chronic inflammatory skin disorder first diagnosed in childhood, previously well controlled with topical therapy alone, with no prior hospitalizations or skin infections requiring systemic antibiotics. He was otherwise healthy, with a known allergy to tree nuts. Over recent weeks to months his skin disease had progressed to near-total body surface involvement, though the true extent of disease may have been under-recognized earlier given his skin phototype and less apparent erythema. On examination he had diffuse erythema and scaling involving nearly the entire body surface, with extensive lichenification and excoriation and a predominance over facial and flexural areas. Body surface area involvement was estimated at 95%, with severity indices in the very-severe range. Palpable lymphadenopathy was present in the bilateral cervical and axillary chains. Palms and soles were spared, and there was loss of eyebrow hair. Given the systemic symptoms and diffuse lymphadenopathy, skin biopsies were obtained to exclude a lymphoproliferative process, along with additional systemic laboratory work-up prior to consideration of immunosuppressive therapy.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other specified congenital malformation syndromes, not elsewhere classified
train_cases.note: A toddler-aged female child presented for further cardiac assessment after an incidental finding of pulmonary artery narrowing on echocardiogram performed in the neonatal period during an admission for meconium aspiration. Past medical history included a seizure disorder that had been treated with two anticonvulsant medications, discontinued approximately 8 months prior after prolonged seizure freedom. Family history was notable for parental consanguinity (first-cousin marriage) and a paternal-side cousin with a similar vascular anomaly requiring balloon dilatation, raising suspicion for a recessively inherited condition. On examination at age 2 years, the child had generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score 6), growth parameters showing weight at the 11th percentile, height at the 33rd percentile, and head circumference at the 4th percentile, and dysmorphic craniofacial features including an elongated face, prominent ears with a simplified helix, and mild micrognathia. A soft systolic murmur was audible at the left sternal border. Diagnostic catheterization showed a dilated main pulmonary artery with severe stenosis of tortuous bilateral branch pulmonary arteries and suprasystemic right ventricular pressure (136 mmHg, RVSP/LVSP ratio 1.2). Angiography demonstrated a diffusely tortuous aorta without focal stenosis. Echocardiography confirmed elevated gradients across both branch pulmonary arteries.

A man in his late 50s presented with 2 days of painless jaundice. His personal history included dyslipidemia and a glucose metabolism disturbance (prediabetes noted approximately 8 months earlier), managed with dietary modification. Physical examination revealed a mild productive morning cough, otherwise unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed elevated transaminases, markedly elevated gamma-glutamyltransferase, markedly elevated total bilirubin with a predominantly direct fraction, mildly elevated serum amylase, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate; tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, CA15-3, CA125) were within or near normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed diffuse enlargement of the pancreatic parenchyma, most pronounced in the head, with an ill-defined hypodense border, increased density of gallbladder content, peripancreatic inflammatory change, and dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts and common bile duct. MRI showed inflammatory change in the pancreatic head. MRCP demonstrated a focal lesion at the lower limit of the pancreatic head with low T1 signal, hypovascularity, and restricted diffusion, considered suspicious for malignancy, along with pancreatic duct dilation; abdominal lymph nodes appeared normal. Because of biliary obstruction, percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography was performed, revealing biliary tract dilation due to a stricture of the lower common hepatic duct, with successful stent placement and subsequent decrease in bilirubin.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute myeloblastic leukemia, not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: A preschool-age male child, born to consanguineous parents, developmentally normal and fully immunized, had a known history of a chronic hemoglobinopathy diagnosed in infancy via hemoglobin electrophoresis, for which he had been receiving regular blood transfusions—initially every six months, increasing in frequency to weekly over the preceding months. He had not undergone screening for iron overload and had never been started on iron chelation therapy. He presented with a two-week history of persistent low-grade fever (99-101°F), accompanied by abdominal pain and distention, cough, decreased appetite, and progressively worsening fatigue. On examination, he was vitally stable but appeared markedly pale, lethargic, and irritable, with a protuberant abdomen. Non-blanching bruising (approximately 2 x 4 cm) was noted on the anterior aspects of both legs. Abdominal examination revealed massive splenomegaly extending to the right iliac fossa, without hepatomegaly; the remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Initial blood work showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 5.3 g/dL), marked thrombocytopenia (platelets 16x10^9/L), and leukocytosis (total leukocyte count 33x10^9/L) with neutropenia, occasional myelocytes, and a markedly elevated blast percentage on differential, along with numerous nucleated red cells. Red cell morphology showed hypochromia, microcytosis, and occasional fragmentation. Serum ferritin was markedly elevated (>4,000 ng/mL). Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were subsequently pursued given the cytopenias, splenomegaly, and circulating blasts.

train_cases.diagnosis: Ankylosing spondylitis of unspecified sites in spine
train_cases.note: A man in his late 30s presented with a multi-decade history of sacroiliac and hip joint pain that began in early adolescence, characterized by stiffness, restricted mobility, and inability to squat, with morning stiffness improved by physical activity. There was no family history of inflammatory joint disease. He had a 15-year smoking history (approximately 2 cigarettes/day) without significant alcohol use. Height was 171 cm, weight 59 kg, BMI 20.2 kg/m². Over the following two decades he received multiple immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory therapies with only partial symptomatic benefit, interspersed with periods of self-discontinuation. In his late 30s he developed worsening low back and sacroiliac pain along with swelling of the left knee and both wrists. Examination revealed thoracic kyphosis, tenderness over both groins and greater trochanters, markedly restricted hip range of motion with inability to squat or ambulate without crutches, a positive left Thomas test, and an incomplete right Patrick's test; chest expansion and occiput-to-wall distance were reduced. Composite mobility and disease-activity indices were markedly abnormal, and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) were elevated. Sacroiliac joint CT demonstrated bilateral joint-space narrowing with osseous bridging. He subsequently required staged bilateral total hip arthroplasty for progressive hip joint destruction, with recurrent disease flares despite sequential biologic and targeted-synthetic immunosuppressive therapies.

A woman in her early 40s presented with a long-standing history of a chronic, intensely pruritic skin condition. Past medical history included allergic rhinitis, asthma, hypertension, and endometriosis (managed with oral contraceptives). She reported a maternal family history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and eczema. Her skin symptoms began in childhood, with eczematous changes affecting flexural regions, the neck, periocular areas, upper lip, wrists, thighs, and lower back, with notable worsening in hot weather. In early adulthood, her condition worsened substantially, with widespread erythematous, elevated, intensely pruritic lesions. She was treated initially with systemic corticosteroids for one month, then high-dose methotrexate, achieving control for approximately two years before relapsing after tapering. Thalidomide was trialed for 6-12 months without significant benefit. Cyclosporine was used for less than a year but discontinued due to worsening hypertension. She has since remained on methotrexate 15 mg weekly for about three years, with adverse effects of nausea and headache, plus antihistamines, but continues to have frequent flares. Biologic therapy is being considered given the extent and refractoriness of disease. Nocturnal itching significantly disrupts sleep and quality of life; heat and certain fabrics are identified triggers. On examination: dyshidrotic-pattern changes on the left hand, erythematous-scaly plaques over upper extremity flexures, generalized dryness, periorbital darkening, and lichenification of the neck and arms.

A woman in her late 60s with a 35-year history of primary adrenal insufficiency, maintained on stable low-dose oral glucocorticoid replacement therapy for the preceding 25 years without prior crises, was evaluated for chronic fatigue, diffuse myalgia, and back pain. Physical examination was unremarkable aside from thoracic kyphosis; neurological exam was normal. Baseline laboratory studies showed normal serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and C-reactive protein. Serum creatinine was mildly elevated at 1.51 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 32 mL/min/1.73 m². She was started on analgesia, vitamin D, calcium supplementation, and physical therapy. Because of long-standing corticosteroid exposure, bone density testing was performed and demonstrated osteoporosis (lumbar spine T-score -3.5, left femoral neck -2.4, left femoral total -1.6). Given her renal impairment, she was given a single subcutaneous dose of an antiresorptive agent, with no adjustment made to her usual glucocorticoid dose at that time. Approximately 24 hours later she developed progressive fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness, and skin darkening, presenting the following day with marked weakness and near-syncope. On examination she appeared acutely unwell, with blood pressure 80/50 mmHg, pulse 84/min, temperature 37.1°C, clinical dehydration, and peripheral coldness. Laboratory results showed sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 4.85 mmol/L, glucose 85 mg/dL, creatinine 1.73 mg/dL, and calcium 7.61 mg/dL. C-reactive protein was elevated at 101 mg/L with a normal white blood cell count. Blood and urine cultures, chest X-ray, ECG, and troponin were unremarkable. A morning cortisol level drawn prior to any steroid administration was low relative to the severity of her illness.

A male child, first-born to non-consanguineous parents, born at term, presented in infancy with severe generalized eczema first apparent at approximately 6 months of age. Over the following months he required several hospital admissions for severe skin flares, prolonged diarrhea, and pneumonia, and separately developed acute otitis media and an episode of bacteremia, all within the first year of life. There was no family history of immunodeficiency, early infant death, recurrent severe infections, chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, or skeletal abnormalities. He had received only the birth BCG vaccination with no other childhood immunizations and no vaccine-related complications. After the first year, no further severe infections requiring hospitalization occurred, but the skin disease persisted as a chronic, severely fluctuating condition with seasonal variation. In later childhood he developed asthma-like respiratory symptoms controlled with inhaled corticosteroids, and in adolescence the allergic skin phenotype intensified. A trial of systemic cyclosporine in later childhood gave limited benefit. At most recent evaluation (age ~11 years), he was alert and afebrile, with weight, height, and BMI near the 50th percentile; there was no edema, purpura, or hepatosplenomegaly, but diffuse xerosis, erythema, and generalized pruritic papules were present. Early labs showed leukocytosis, marked eosinophilia, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminemia, low total protein, and rapidly rising total IgE (into the thousands IU/mL) with otherwise near-normal immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets. Eosinophilia and markedly elevated IgE persisted into adolescence despite normalized albumin and stable immunoglobulins; abdominal imaging and viral studies were unremarkable.

A woman in her mid-30s, working full-time 12-hour night shifts in an intensive care setting, presented with a history of generalized weakness. Past medical history included eczema in adolescence, sickle cell trait, and two prior term pregnancies. Red blood cell indices showed slightly reduced mean corpuscular volume and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, without clinical anemia. Surgical history included a prior cesarean section, an abdominal wall repair, and breast implant surgery. She was a nonsmoker, did not drink alcohol, and had a normal body mass index. She was physically active, having played amateur basketball and later taken up running, though she reported abnormal weakness predating increased activity. She presented with right hand weakness affecting fine motor tasks (brushing teeth and hair, carrying light loads, cutting meat), a sensation of head heaviness, a nasal voice quality, drooping of the eyelid, double vision, difficulty swallowing, and difficulty chewing and articulating speech. On evaluation, serum autoantibodies against a neuromuscular junction receptor were markedly elevated, and electrodiagnostic testing with repetitive nerve stimulation showed significant decrement across multiple muscle groups including facial/bulbar muscles. A composite muscle strength score was moderately reduced. Thoracic imaging did not show a discrete anterior mediastinal mass but suggested thymic gland enlargement.

A woman in her late 50s, previously independent in activities of daily living and self-employed, presented with a progressive decline in cognitive function over approximately 10 years, manifesting as social withdrawal, inattentiveness, progressive memory impairment, inappropriate behaviour, urinary incontinence, and gait/balance difficulties. She also had episodes of emotional lability, alternating between depressive symptoms with psychomotor retardation and agitation with paranoid ideation, insomnia, and confusion. Her course was complicated by a spontaneous subdural haematoma treated surgically, a perioperative seizure, and a subsequent pulmonary embolism requiring temporary anticoagulation. Despite surgery, cognitive status continued to decline with recurrent delirium requiring frequent hospitalisations. Assessment showed impaired executive function, reasoning, and problem-solving; MMSE was 24/30. She required full-time assistance with personal care and daily activities, and was on antipsychotic/antidepressant medications. Barthel Index was 7/20. Past history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes, thyrotoxicosis treated with radioactive iodine, osteoporosis with a vertebral compression fracture, recurrent urinary tract infections requiring suprapubic catheterisation, and hyperandrogenism with onset after age 40. Examination showed a round face, central obesity, skin thinning, a dorsocervical fat pad, mild facial hirsutism, kyphosis without tenderness, and mild proximal myopathy. Labs showed elevated serum cortisol with normal ACTH, elevated 24-hour urine free cortisol, and non-suppressed cortisol on overnight low-dose dexamethasone testing. HIV and syphilis serology were negative. Brain MRI showed extensive white matter changes beyond expected for age with moderate cerebral atrophy; pituitary MRI showed a 2 mm lesion. Prolonged EEG showed no epileptiform activity.

train_cases.diagnosis: Ankylosing spondylitis of unspecified sites in spine
train_cases.note: A woman in her late 50s with end-stage renal disease due to chronic glomerulonephritis, status post kidney transplantation 25 years earlier with longstanding stable graft function, maintained on chronic immunosuppression (a calcineurin inhibitor, mycophenolate mofetil, and low-dose prednisone), was admitted with fever up to 39°C and a two-week history of sacroiliac region pain radiating to the left lower limb. She had no prior history of a connective tissue disease. Physical examination and vital signs were unremarkable. Labs showed markedly elevated CRP, normal white cell count, mild anemia, negative procalcitonin, and urinalysis with mild proteinuria and pyuria without hematuria. Graft function, liver enzymes, and immunosuppressant drug levels were within expected ranges; viral serologies and blood/urine cultures were negative. Cardiac imaging excluded endocarditis. During admission she developed left knee swelling and warmth; joint aspiration yielded turbid fluid, and gout was excluded. Doppler ultrasound incidentally revealed deep vein thrombosis, treated with anticoagulation. Additional infectious workup (mycobacterial, Lyme) was negative. On further questioning, she reported nearly two decades of inflammatory-type low back pain worsening with rest and improving with activity and NSAIDs, with prolonged morning stiffness. Examination showed markedly reduced spinal mobility in all planes and a positive provocative sacroiliac maneuver on the left, without other peripheral joint involvement. Inflammatory markers remained elevated with mildly worsening graft function.

A man in his mid-30s presented with a two-week history of generalized fatigue, poor appetite, nausea, and jaundice, accompanied by mild weakness and numbness in the limbs. He had a several-year history of schizophrenia maintained on antipsychotic therapy, and a known diagnosis of chronic hepatitis B infection made about two years earlier, previously treated with an oral antiviral for nearly a year before self-discontinuing once symptoms improved. He denied blood transfusions, injection drug use, high-risk sexual exposure, or recent travel. Outpatient labs had shown elevated transaminases and he was treated supportively without improvement; weakness progressed to difficulty climbing stairs, hand numbness, and reduced grip strength, prompting hospital transfer. On admission, vital signs were unremarkable; exam showed jaundice, mild tenderness over the liver, and no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Labs showed markedly elevated transaminases, low albumin, elevated bilirubin (direct and total), mildly elevated alpha-fetoprotein, and normal blood ammonia. Liver fibrosis testing suggested mild-to-moderate fibrosis and activity. Within days, limb weakness and numbness rapidly worsened, with inability to walk, proximal and distal weakness, reduced muscle tone, diffusely diminished deep tendon reflexes, and reduced distal pain/temperature sensation, without cranial nerve involvement or altered consciousness. Nerve conduction studies showed extensive demyelinating and axonal changes in peripheral sensorimotor nerves and roots. Cerebrospinal fluid showed a normal cell count with elevated protein. Imaging of the head and neck was unremarkable. Liver enzymes continued to rise sharply during this period, and abdominal ultrasound showed diffuse hepatic parenchymal changes and mild splenomegaly.

train_cases.diagnosis: Malignant neoplasm of lower lobe, left bronchus or lung
train_cases.note: A man in his mid-70s presented with a two-week history of dyspnea at rest, together with a worsening cough and increased respiratory secretions; he denied hemoptysis or chest pain. His background included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease diagnosed roughly nine years earlier, for which he used home oxygen therapy, and radiologically diagnosed pulmonary fibrosis identified about two years prior, treated with an antifibrotic agent with initial improvement in lung volumes and gas transfer, followed by only mild interval radiologic progression on subsequent imaging. He was a former smoker of 40 pack-years, with a history of hypertension and ischemic heart disease. On admission, oxygen saturation was 89% on room air; arterial blood gas showed pH 7.43, pCO2 44 mmHg, and pO2 48 mmHg. During the admission he tested positive on a respiratory viral antigen test; he had not been vaccinated against this virus. Chest CT demonstrated a new large infiltrative mass involving the lower lobe and part of the upper lobe of the left lung, with associated mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy that had not been present on imaging obtained roughly eleven months earlier, along with progressive fluid in the left pleural space and pericardium and narrowing of a lower lobe pulmonary artery branch. The underlying fibrotic lung changes were also noted to have progressed compared with prior studies.

A man in his 40s with a several-year history of chronic pancreatitis complicated by a pancreatic pseudocyst, and a two-decade history of ongoing alcohol use, presented with worsening blood in the stool and upper abdominal pain following prior symptomatic treatment and blood transfusion elsewhere. On examination, vital signs were stable; the abdomen was distended and tender. Laboratory studies showed an elevated white blood cell count, mildly low hemoglobin, elevated platelet count, elevated transaminases, and elevated total and direct bilirubin; amylase and lipase were within normal limits. Upper endoscopy revealed a large volume of blood in the stomach and a large clot in the duodenal bulb, without a clearly identified bleeding source. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a large retroperitoneal hematoma, a vascular outpouching arising from a hepatic artery branch, and mild dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts. Follow-up imaging over subsequent days showed the abnormal vascular structure to fluctuate in size, at one point appearing to resolve before being seen again as a smaller lesion in a fine arterial branch. The patient subsequently developed a duodenal fistula and evidence of retroperitoneal infection with gas, with an initially poor response to antibiotics and rising white cell count. There was no imaging evidence of an acute inflammatory flare of the underlying pancreatic disease.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her late 60s was acutely admitted to a psychiatric unit due to threatening behavior, marked irritability, and inability to care for herself. She had two prior psychiatric hospitalizations at the same facility. Past somatic history was notable only for a prior thyroid surgery. Her long-term outpatient medication was an antidepressant, which had reportedly not been taken for several weeks prior to admission. On initial assessment she displayed pressured speech, pronounced irritability, affective lability, disorganized and tangential thought process, and prominent delusional content. Given symptom severity and risk of self-harm, involuntary admission was initiated, and due to severe agitation she required rapid pharmacologic tranquilization with sequential antipsychotic, sedative, and benzodiazepine agents (oral and intravenous) over several hours because of insufficient response to initial treatment. Approximately two hours after the last dose, she acutely deteriorated: became soporous, with severe hypotension (blood pressure 40/24 mmHg), heart rate 90/min, and oxygen saturation of 90%. She was treated emergently with intravenous fluids and a reversal agent, with limited effect; hemodynamic parameters improved partially but hypoxemia persisted, with oxygen saturation around 85% on room air. Continuous monitoring subsequently showed intermittent episodes of tachycardia. Initial laboratory studies were largely unremarkable aside from mild leukocytosis (12 G/L) and elevated cholesterol. Repeated electrocardiograms showed no classic acute right heart strain pattern.

A woman in her mid-20s with functional quadriplegia due to cerebral palsy was brought to the emergency department by family members for evaluation. She was nonverbal at baseline, so history was obtained from family, who reported three days of right-sided abdominal discomfort with intermittent abdominal guarding and reduced oral intake. There was no reported fever, vomiting, or chills. Past medical history included cerebral palsy with quadriplegia, a seizure disorder, severe chronic constipation, and recurrent kidney stones with prior ureteral stent placements. On presentation she was tachycardic but otherwise hemodynamically stable. Examination showed tenderness in the right lower quadrant radiating toward the flank. Labs showed potassium 2.9 mEq/L, magnesium 1.6 mg/dL, and a white blood cell count within normal limits. Urinalysis showed positive nitrites, positive leukocyte esterase, and 3+ white blood cells. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed right perirenal and periureteral fat stranding, a small hypoenhancing focus in the anterior mid-right kidney, multiple right renal calculi (largest 0.7 cm), and a 1.1 cm right lower-pole lesion of higher-than-fluid attenuation, likely a complex cyst. No hydronephrosis or ureteral obstruction was seen. She was treated with intravenous fluids, empiric antibiotics, and electrolyte repletion, with symptomatic improvement before discharge.

An adolescent female (approximately 11 years old) presented with a several-year history of drooping eyelids, ongoing for about 4-5 years prior to evaluation. Over the two months before presentation, she developed progressive, fluctuating difficulty swallowing, voice changes/hoarseness, and generalized limb weakness that appeared to worsen with exertion and fluctuate through the day. There was no reported trauma, prior neurological illness, or relevant family history. On examination she had bilateral eyelid drooping, weakness of the limbs, and bulbar findings including hoarseness and swallowing difficulty; specific vital signs were not remarkable. A trial of a short-acting cholinesterase-inhibitor medication produced transient improvement in muscle strength. Electrodiagnostic testing with low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation demonstrated a decremental motor response on the affected muscles. Serologic testing showed an elevated titer of a circulating autoantibody directed against a neuromuscular junction antigen, above the laboratory reference range. Chest computed tomography showed no mediastinal or thymic mass or other abnormality. Using standardized functional and severity scoring instruments, her overall impairment was rated as moderate-to-severe, with meaningful limitation in daily activities related to swallowing, speech, and limb strength. No other systemic abnormalities were identified at the initial evaluation.

A man in his early twenties, previously a laboratory technician, was brought to care by a family member with acute-onset weakness of the right upper and lower limbs and inability to speak for two days. One month earlier he had an episode of sudden right-sided limb weakness and numbness that resolved completely within 24 hours; during that evaluation he was found to have non-oliguric renal impairment with elevated renal parameters. A similar transient weakness episode had occurred several months before that, for which no medical attention was sought. The current episode is acute, non-progressive, involving right hemiparesis with expressive aphasia, without seizures, loss of consciousness, headache, vomiting, or cranial nerve, bowel, or bladder involvement. There is no history of diabetes, hypertension, cardiac disease, or trauma. Family history is notable for a sibling who died at age 23 from renal failure and a stroke-like illness. On examination, the patient was alert with pallor, stable vitals, Broca's aphasia, flaccid paralysis (0/5 power) of the right limbs with extensor plantar response, and normal sensory and cerebellar exam. Labs showed hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL, platelets 32,000/mcL, LDH 734 U/L, creatinine 8.6 mg/dL, urea 132 mg/dL, elevated reticulocytes, negative Coombs test, and peripheral smear showing schistocytes. MRI brain showed an acute infarct with additional old infarct-like changes; MRA/MRV were normal.

A previously healthy woman in her early 20s presented with a one-week history of progressive behavioral changes, anxiety, insomnia, and mood lability, followed by the development of focal seizures, dysarthria, and fluctuating level of consciousness. She had no significant past medical history other than a known 2 cm ovarian cyst identified about 10 months earlier, managed conservatively with oral contraceptives under gynecologic follow-up. On emergency evaluation, she was awake but disoriented, with marked fluctuation in attention and incoherent, dysarthric speech. Vital signs showed tachycardia (131 bpm) and hypertension (149/91 mmHg). Cranial nerve exam revealed orofacial dyskinesias without clear focal deficits. Motor exam showed hyperreflexia, increased tone, and focal weakness of the right upper limb; sensory exam was limited by poor cooperation. Brain MRI (FLAIR and T2) showed no structural abnormalities, mass lesions, or abnormal signal. CSF analysis showed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (11 cells/mm3) with normal glucose (63 mg/dL) and protein (39.9 mg/dL); infectious CSF, blood, and urine cultures and PCR panel were negative. EEG showed diffuse theta-delta slowing with superimposed irritative activity. Leukocytosis (13.32 x10^3/uL) and marked hypofibrinogenemia were noted; ANA, anti-dsDNA, and lupus anticoagulant were negative. Pelvic MRI incidentally revealed an enlarged left ovarian mass (11x14x5.4 cm) with heterogeneous cystic and fatty components and a mural nodule; tumor markers (AFP, CA-125, CA19-9, CEA) were all within normal limits.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other ectopic pregnancy without intrauterine pregnancy
train_cases.note: A woman in her mid-20s (gravida 1, para 0) presented to the emergency department with a several-day history of left upper abdominal pain accompanied by intermittent nausea and vomiting. Her menstrual cycles were regular (28-30 days) and she was amenorrheic, with a positive home urine pregnancy test obtained shortly before presentation, consistent with early pregnancy. Approximately one week prior, she had presented to another facility with milder left upper abdominal pain; non-contrast imaging at that time showed a small indeterminate mass (~21x19x10 mm) in the left upper abdomen. She was treated empirically for a presumed gastrointestinal illness without symptom improvement. On the day of transfer, her pain acutely worsened with associated nausea and vomiting. Ultrasound showed no intrauterine gestational sac, endometrial thickness of 8 mm, and no adnexal abnormalities. Contrast-enhanced imaging demonstrated significant interval enlargement of the left upper abdominal mass (~46x40x56 mm), now hypervascular. On admission, vital signs were stable (BP 107/77 mmHg, pulse 89 bpm, temperature 36.7°C). Examination revealed localized left upper abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs elsewhere; pelvic exam showed normal external genitalia, no active bleeding, a closed cervix, and no cervical motion tenderness or adnexal mass. Serum beta-hCG was markedly elevated at 10,130 IU/L. She denied prior pelvic inflammatory disease, chronic illness, tobacco, or alcohol use. Given the clinical picture, surgical evaluation was pursued for further diagnosis and management.

train_cases.diagnosis: Benign neoplasm of left adrenal gland
train_cases.note: A woman in her 50s with a history of poorly controlled hypertension managed on a calcium channel blocker presented with acute-onset chest pain, dyspnea, and palpitations. She denied any recent emotional or physical stressor preceding the episode. On further questioning, she reported a longer-standing history of recurrent paroxysmal episodes of headache and palpitations occurring in the setting of labile, poorly controlled blood pressure. Initial ECG showed sinus rhythm with 1 mm ST-segment elevation in the anterior precordial leads without reciprocal changes, and cardiac biomarkers were elevated. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a regional wall motion abnormality with apical ballooning and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45%. Coronary angiography of the right and left coronary systems showed no significant obstructive lesions, and left ventriculography confirmed the apical ballooning pattern. During hospitalization, the patient developed a severe tachyarrhythmia with a rapid ventricular rate exceeding 150 bpm, resulting in acute hemodynamic instability with a nadir blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. This required emergent electrical cardioversion followed by antiarrhythmic therapy and admission to the intensive care unit for close monitoring. Given the combination of electrical instability, labile blood pressure, and the history of unexplained paroxysmal headache and palpitations, further evaluation for a secondary endocrine cause of hypertension was initiated.

A woman in her late twenties, gravida 4 para 2 with one prior pregnancy loss, presented at approximately 32 weeks' gestation with several days of fever, chills, myalgias, and dyspnoea. Her past medical history included bilateral nephrolithiasis complicated by obstructive uropathy requiring bilateral percutaneous nephrostomy tubes, recurrent urinary tract infections managed with chronic suppressive antibiotic therapy, and a prior hospitalization for a severe urinary tract infection related to kidney stones. On examination, she was febrile (101.4°F) and tachycardic (116 beats per minute), with a gravid uterus consistent with gestational age; there was no evidence of volume overload or peripheral embolic phenomena. Initial laboratory evaluation showed pyuria and bacteriuria, and blood cultures obtained on admission grew a gram-positive coccus (identified as Enterococcus faecalis) within 24 hours. Given her genitourinary history, an infection originating from the urinary tract was initially considered. Because of the bloodstream infection, cardiac imaging was pursued: transthoracic echocardiography showed a possible echodensity on one of the aortic valve cusps, and a subsequent transoesophageal study confirmed a mobile, small (1.1 × 0.4 cm) mass on one of the aortic valve leaflets with moderate aortic regurgitation, which progressed to severe on serial imaging, accompanied by progressive left ventricular dilation.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute leukemia of unspecified cell type not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: A boy in the early school-age range presented to the emergency department with fatigue and pallor of recent onset. No significant prior medical history was reported. On evaluation he was hemodynamically stable without signs of acute distress; physical examination revealed pallor consistent with anemia, without documented lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or bleeding. Initial laboratory testing showed a hemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL (low), a total white cell count of 4.2 x10^3/uL, with a reduced absolute neutrophil count and a reduced platelet count. A peripheral blood smear identified circulating blasts, prompting hospital admission for further evaluation. Bone marrow aspiration was performed; the sample was hemodiluted without marrow spicules, and morphologic examination on May-Grunwald Giemsa-stained smears showed a blast population resembling that seen in the peripheral blood. Multiparameter flow cytometry was subsequently performed, assessing a broad panel of markers spanning myeloid and lymphoid lineages, with blast gating based on CD45 expression and side scatter, in order to characterize the immunophenotype of the blast population and guide further diagnostic classification and treatment planning.

A woman in her mid-70s with a history of hypercholesterolaemia and a documented penicillin allergy, on no regular medications prior to admission, presented with a four-day history of worsening breathlessness and fever. Initial assessment revealed a marked systemic inflammatory response with very high inflammatory markers, together with unexpected neutropenia and leukopenia despite the severity of infection. Arterial blood gas confirmed type 1 respiratory failure. Chest radiography showed dense consolidation involving the right mid and lower zones, and CT pulmonary angiogram excluded pulmonary embolism. She required intensive care admission for hypoxic respiratory failure and was started on high-flow oxygen therapy with close monitoring. Blood cultures grew a gram-positive organism, and given her penicillin allergy she was commenced on an alternative intravenous antibiotic per local severe pneumonia protocol. Her neutrophil count normalised spontaneously within 48 hours, considered part of the acute infective process rather than drug-related. Approximately three days after starting this antibiotic, she developed sudden lip swelling. Over the next 48 hours this progressed to painful erythematous macules of the lips and perioral skin that evolved into flaccid blisters with epidermal sloughing and haemorrhagic crusting extending onto the nose and cheeks, with subsequent involvement of the oral mucosa and both conjunctivae. Extensive infectious and pharmacological causes were investigated and excluded. By day 10 of admission, the left eye was swollen shut with purulent discharge and markedly reduced visual acuity, while the right eye also showed reduced acuity.

A man in his late 60s with a history of hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic hepatitis C (previously partially treated, with antiviral therapy completed several months prior), and a remote (several years earlier) spinal hardware infection treated at that time, presented with a one-and-a-half-week history of progressive generalized weakness and shortness of breath. He reported chronic, stable back and hip pain dating back to his prior spinal infection. He denied intravenous drug use, recent skin infections, or recent dental procedures. Social history included light daily smoking and daily alcohol use. On presentation, temperature was 98.5°F. Initial labs showed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.1 x10^9/L). Physical exam revealed raised, erythematous, pruritic plaques on the lower extremities that began around the onset of malaise, had partially improved, and were beginning to recur; decreased breath sounds were noted on auscultation; there was no spinal tenderness. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without acute changes. Blood cultures were negative at five days and on repeat testing. CT angiogram of the chest showed multifocal bilateral peripheral nodular and mass-like pulmonary opacities. CT abdomen/pelvis was unremarkable. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography showed a prominent right atrial Chiari network with a small oscillating echodense structure attached to it (0.5 cm x 0.4 cm), new compared to prior imaging from several years earlier; ventricular function and heart valves were otherwise normal. Bronchoscopic cultures were negative. Workup for malignancy and autoimmune disease was unremarkable.

A man in his late 20s with a history of obesity and prediabetes presented with a painful right thigh abscess requiring incision and drainage; wound culture grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. He was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone followed by a 10-day course of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and cephalexin. Over the following weeks he returned multiple times for persistent leg pain, diagnosed as superficial thrombophlebitis and treated with apixaban. During one visit he reported right eye pain, but no ophthalmic examination was performed at that time. Approximately two and a half months after the abscess was drained, he presented with worsening right eye pain and decreased vision. Visual acuity in the right eye was 20/50, with conjunctival injection, corneal edema, and a large anterior chamber mass. Laboratory testing showed markedly elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >130 mm/hr, CRP 149 mg/L); infectious serologies were negative, and basic metabolic panel was unremarkable. Topical antibiotic and cycloplegic drops were started. The next day, vision declined further and intraocular pressure rose to 41 mmHg, with an enlarging hypopyon; topical corticosteroid and pressure-lowering drops were added. Over subsequent days, pain worsened, vision progressed to light-perception only, the anterior chamber filled with fibrin and hypopyon, and new nodular scleral thickening with early thinning developed. B-scan ultrasound showed no posterior segment involvement. Oral corticosteroid was started and increased, with an additional anti-inflammatory agent added. An anterior chamber sample was obtained for culture and PCR, and brain/orbital MRI was unremarkable.

A young adult male with no significant medical or surgical history presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of left lower abdominal pain and left inguinal swelling beginning approximately four hours prior to arrival. The pain was described as sudden, colicky, localized to the left inguinal region, severity 9/10, non-radiating and non-shifting. He denied nausea, vomiting, altered bowel habits, fever, recent heavy lifting, or trauma. A CT scan showed no abdominal wall defect but demonstrated a left-sided non-communicating hydrocele with engorgement of the left spermatic cord. On examination, vital signs were normal and he was afebrile. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with a tender, irreducible swelling measuring about 3 x 3 cm in the left groin. The right testicle appeared normal on exam; the left testicle was slightly elevated with a thickened, palpable spermatic cord at its base but no direct tenderness. Labs showed white blood cell count 10.8 x10^9/L, hemoglobin 16.2 g/dL, platelets 225 x10^9/L. Scrotal ultrasound showed the right testicle with homogeneous echogenicity and preserved vascularity. The left testicle was hypoechoic relative to the right, showed absent internal vascularity on color Doppler, and was abnormally oriented, with an associated hydrocele and a small epididymal tail cyst measuring 0.5 x 0.4 cm.

A woman in her early thirties presented with a several-day history of progressively worsening headache and behavioural change, evolving over about a week into agitation and impaired responsiveness. She subsequently developed epileptic seizures and was admitted for further evaluation. Cranial MRI showed a T2 hyperintensity in the right temporal lobe. Lumbar puncture demonstrated cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis (38 cells, lymphocytic predominance) without oligoclonal bands. Empirical anti-infective therapy was started but stopped after bacterial and viral studies were negative. Her clinical course deteriorated over the following days, with worsening confusion and recurrent seizures despite antiseizure medication, progressing to continuous seizure activity confirmed on EEG that proved refractory to benzodiazepines and multiple antiseizure drugs. A short course of high-dose glucocorticoids produced no improvement. Given the refractory course, she was transferred to a tertiary intensive care unit for escalation of therapy, including anaesthetic agents, intravenous immunoglobulin, and plasma exchange, with only transient EEG improvement. Systemic evaluation performed as part of an extended diagnostic work-up, including tumour screening, identified a mass in the right ovary, which was later surgically removed. Vital signs during acute decompensation reflected a critically ill, encephalopathic patient requiring intensive monitoring and airway support.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute appendicitis with perforation, localized peritonitis, and gangrene, with abscess
train_cases.note: A male in his late 30s presented to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of severe right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder, associated with nausea. He denied fevers, rectal bleeding, or change in bowel habits. His past medical history was notable for a bowel resection in childhood for an unspecified congenital abnormality. On assessment he was haemodynamically stable and afebrile. Examination revealed right upper quadrant tenderness with a negative Murphy's sign. Blood tests showed a marked inflammatory response with white cell count 24.4 x10^9/L with neutrophilia, C-reactive protein 323 mg/L, and mildly deranged liver function tests. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a thickened tubular structure in the right iliac fossa measuring 14 mm in diameter with surrounding fat stranding, and a small adjacent 10 mm fluid collection near the right psoas muscle. Additionally, multiple hypodense lesions were identified in the right lobe of the liver, the largest located in segment 8 measuring 55 mm in diameter, in keeping with fluid collections. He was commenced empirically on intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics for further management and source control.

A six-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of right testicular pain, swelling, and erythema. The pain was sudden in onset, severe, persistent, and progressively worsening. There was no history of trauma, no haematuria, and no voiding difficulty. He had no significant past medical history and was up to date with immunisations. Approximately one week earlier he had been hospitalised with fever, intermittent periumbilical abdominal pain, and a non-blanching purpuric rash over the lower extremities. At that time vital signs were stable, the abdomen was soft and non-tender, and palpable purpura was noted on the lower limbs. Urinalysis showed trace protein only, with no haematuria, nitrites, or leucocytes; complete blood count, renal function, and clotting profile were normal. He improved with supportive care and was discharged for outpatient follow-up. Five days later he developed acute scrotal pain. On examination he was afebrile with stable vital signs but uncomfortable. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. The right testis was tender, swollen, and erythematous, raising concern for testicular torsion; the left testis was normal. A palpable purpuric rash persisted over the buttocks and legs. Blood tests and urinalysis were unremarkable. Ultrasound was unavailable, prompting urgent surgical exploration, which revealed a swollen, oedematous epididymis and testis with reactive hydrocele and vascular congestion, without torsion.

A man in his early 30s with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department with a two-day history of left-sided abdominal pain accompanied by nausea, several episodes of vomiting, and anorexia. He denied fever or constipation. The pain reportedly began in the periumbilical region and subsequently migrated to and localized in the left lower quadrant. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness and guarding localized to the left lower quadrant. Initial laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count within the normal range but marked neutrophilia (90%), a markedly elevated C-reactive protein (140 mg/L), normal hemoglobin, and a mildly elevated platelet count consistent with a reactive process. Given the atypical left-sided presentation, differential considerations included diverticulitis and ureteric colic. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen was obtained to further evaluate. Imaging demonstrated a mirror-image arrangement of the abdominal and thoracic organs, with a tubular structure in the left lower quadrant measuring approximately 11 mm in diameter showing mural thickening and hyperenhancement, adjacent fat stranding, and a small amount of free fluid. The cecum showed mild reactive wall thickening and edema, with several enlarged reactive lymph nodes nearby. No free intraperitoneal air was seen. A chest radiograph showed the cardiac apex positioned on the right side.

train_cases.diagnosis: Benign neoplasm of left adrenal gland
train_cases.note: A man in his late 50s of Turkish origin was referred to endocrinology for evaluation of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, present for approximately 10 years. He denied episodic headache, palpitations, diaphoresis, anxiety attacks, or other paroxysmal symptoms, and reported no history of hypertensive episodes. There was no family history of endocrine tumors or similar skin findings. Past surgical history was unremarkable for adrenal or endocrine disease. On examination, blood pressure was persistently low, averaging approximately 90/50 mmHg on repeated measurements, with heart rate within normal limits. Dermatologic examination revealed multiple café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, numerous cutaneous neurofibromas, and a large plexiform neurofibroma (approximately 10 cm) over the right hip. Ophthalmologic examination demonstrated bilateral Lisch nodules of the iris. Given the persistent unexplained hypotension in this setting, biochemical screening for an adrenal medullary process was pursued. Plasma renin activity was 0.38 ng/mL/h and aldosterone was 4 ng/dL, with serum cortisol appropriately suppressed on a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test. Catecholamine analysis showed isolated elevation of plasma metanephrine (393.8 ng/L; reference 0-90 ng/L), with normetanephrine, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine within normal limits. Twenty-four-hour urinary metanephrine was similarly elevated (1698 µg/day; reference 44-261 µg/day), while other urinary catecholamines were normal. Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography demonstrated a 3.7×3.7×4.0 cm mass in the left adrenal gland with central hypodense areas, appearing hypervascular without features typical of a lipid-rich lesion.

A woman in her 60s presented with a 7-day history of fever and progressively worsening right-sided flank pain. She additionally reported a 1-day history of dysuria, increased urinary frequency, and urgency. Her medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus with chronically poorly controlled blood glucose levels. Prior to this presentation, she had been treated at an outside facility with an unspecified oral antibiotic without symptomatic improvement. On presentation, vital signs were: temperature 37.5°C, respiratory rate 25 breaths/min (tachypneic), pulse 90 beats/min, and blood pressure 103/52 mm Hg. She was awake but appeared slightly lethargic. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable except for tenderness to percussion over the right costovertebral angle. Initial laboratory and imaging evaluation were pending at the time of this assessment.

A woman in her mid-40s presented with dyspnoea. She had no significant past medical or family history and took no regular medications, with no smoking history. She reported a productive cough beginning approximately two weeks earlier, followed by the onset of orthopnoea one day prior to presentation. She denied chest pain or back pain. On examination, temperature was 37.7°C, blood pressure 123/54 mmHg, heart rate 103/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. She was 165 cm tall and weighed 62.4 kg (BMI 22.9 kg/m2). Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade II/VI diastolic murmur at the left third intercostal space, and bilateral wet rales were heard at the lung bases; no musculoskeletal abnormalities were noted. Laboratory studies showed an elevated D-dimer of 3.60 μg/dL (reference 0-1.0) and elevated brain natriuretic peptide of 611.1 pg/mL (reference ≤20); she had no dyslipidaemia or diabetes. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated marked dilation of the right coronary sinus (50 mm) with a mobile linear structure and severe aortic regurgitation. Contrast-enhanced chest CT confirmed marked aortic root dilation (51 mm) and bilateral pleural effusions. Cardiac-gated CT with 3D reconstruction revealed flap-like structures near the ostia of both coronary arteries, forming a spiral pattern extending from the right coronary ostium toward the left coronary ostium and the sinotubular junction.

A man in his late 30s presented for evaluation after an incidental finding of a pituitary mass detected during workup for chronic headaches. He reported a several-year history of progressive coarsening of facial features, mandibular enlargement, and macroglossia, along with gradual enlargement of the hands and feet, having changed shoe size from a European 42 to 44 over the preceding three years and having removed his wedding ring due to increased finger size. He described a long-standing headache accompanied by progressively diminished peripheral vision, low libido, and erectile dysfunction. No other significant past medical history was reported. On examination, blood pressure was 141/83 mmHg with normal temperature and heart rate. He had coarse facial features, mandibular prognathism, macroglossia, a mild diffuse non-nodular goiter, and enlarged, bulky hands. Confrontation visual field testing and formal perimetry both demonstrated bitemporal hemianopia. Initial laboratory testing showed insulin-like growth factor-1 of 742 ng/mL, growth hormone 22.7 ng/mL, prolactin 440 ng/mL, TSH 2.1 µIU/mL, cortisol 8.9 µg/dL, ACTH 39 pg/mL, low-normal LH and FSH, low free T4 of 0.6 µg/mL, and total testosterone approximately 180 ng/dL on two morning samples (reference range 246-836 ng/dL). HbA1c was 6.4% and fasting glucose 115 mg/dL. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild left ventricular hypertrophy with preserved ejection fraction and no valve disease. MRI of the pituitary gland demonstrated a large sellar mass measuring 48 × 38 × 29 mm with hemorrhagic components, displacing the optic chiasm superiorly and laterally invading both cavernous sinuses.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection, unspecified
train_cases.note: A 12-month-old female infant, previously healthy with no prior hospitalizations, chronic medications, or known allergies, presented to the emergency department with acute-onset vomiting and vigorous crying that began earlier the same day. The crying was sudden and intense, interpreted as abdominal discomfort, followed by five episodes of non-projectile, non-bilious, non-bloody vomiting (initially larger volume, then smaller), with subsequent decreased appetite. The caregiver reported difficulty breathing since onset, though no cyanosis or desaturation was observed. There was no fever, diarrhea, constipation, jaundice, rash, trauma, toxin/medication ingestion, recent travel, or sick contacts, and no prior similar episodes or family history of pancreatic, lipid, or autoimmune disease. Birth history was unremarkable (term, cesarean delivery, birth weight 3 kg, no NICU stay), and vaccinations were up to date, with a routine immunization received several days prior to presentation. On examination, vitals were stable (temperature 36.2°C, heart rate 125/min, respiratory rate 38/min, SpO2 100% on room air), and she was alert and well-perfused. Epigastric tenderness was noted initially, improving with antiemetic treatment; later exam showed a soft, non-tender, non-distended abdomen with normal bowel sounds. Growth parameters were age-appropriate with no dysmorphism; the remainder of the exam was normal. Capillary blood gas showed mild metabolic acidosis (pH 7.31, HCO3- 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L). Abdominal X-ray was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed a bulky pancreas with peripancreatic fluid and minimal free fluid, prominent common bile duct, and gallbladder sludge without obstruction. Serum lipase and amylase were markedly elevated, trending downward over the following days. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated. Viral serologies for cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus were negative; other viral studies were not performed. She improved with supportive care over several days and remained well on follow-up over the subsequent year.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A woman in her early 30s (gravida 3, para 2) with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy presented at approximately 22 weeks of gestation with resolved postcoital vaginal bleeding that had occurred two days earlier. She had a known short cervix on transvaginal ultrasound identified several weeks prior, for which vaginal progesterone had been prescribed but not yet initiated. Her history included untreated chronic hypertension and a hyperthyroid condition diagnosed several months before conception, with poor adherence to antithyroid medications throughout pregnancy due to side effects and persistently suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone on outpatient labs. On presentation, vitals showed systolic blood pressures in the 150s mmHg (peak 161), tachycardia up to 109 bpm, and normal oxygen saturation; she was afebrile. Exam revealed a fine tremor but was otherwise unremarkable. Initial evaluation for a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy was reassuring after repeat testing. Thyroid function testing showed markedly elevated free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine with an undetectable thyroid-stimulating hormone level. Hours later she acutely developed headache, agitation, tremor, diaphoresis, and worsening tachycardia (120-130 bpm) with severe, wide-pulse-pressure hypertension refractory to intravenous antihypertensives, prompting transfer to intensive care. Over the following days she developed preterm labor, required plasmapheresis for medication-refractory hormonal decompensation, delivered preterm twins, and ultimately underwent surgical management after failing maximal medical therapy.

A 57-year-old woman was referred to endocrinology for evaluation of persistent elevated serum calcium noted incidentally on routine laboratory testing over the preceding 2 years. Review of systems was notable for fatigue and night sweats; she denied nephrolithiasis or fragility fractures. Past medical history included hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and breast cancer diagnosed one year earlier, treated with lumpectomy, with no evidence of recurrent disease at last follow-up. Family history included osteoporosis and hypertension in her mother, and skin and colon cancer in her father; there was no family history of calcium or parathyroid disorders. Medications were ezetimibe 10 mg daily and metoprolol 25 mg daily; she denied use of thiazide diuretics, lithium, loop diuretics, acetazolamide, or over-the-counter supplements including high-dose biotin. Dietary calcium intake was reported as adequate. Physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory testing showed a corrected total serum calcium of 10.6 mg/dL (reference 8.6-10.0) and ionized calcium of 5.5 mg/dL (reference 4.7-5.4), with serum phosphorus, creatinine, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D within normal limits. Serum parathyroid hormone was 27 pg/mL (reference 15-65), not suppressed despite the elevated calcium. A 24-hour urine collection showed calcium excretion of 399 mg/24h (reference <200), with normal urine creatinine and volume. Given mild abnormalities and lack of definitive symptoms, short-interval observation with repeat testing was initially pursued.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A man in his late 50s was evaluated preoperatively prior to scheduled surgical repair of a right knee injury sustained after trauma. During routine preoperative assessment, incidental hypoxemia was noted, with oxygen saturation of 85% on room air; the patient reported no chest pain, dyspnea, or other cardiopulmonary symptoms. Physical examination revealed marked bradycardia with a heart rate of 42 beats per minute, and swelling of the right lower extremity was noted, with no clearly documented duration of onset. Laboratory evaluation showed an elevated D-dimer level of 1,200 µg/L. Point-of-care ultrasonography of the lower extremity venous system demonstrated echogenic material within the right gastrocnemius muscular vein and the popliteal vein, consistent with venous thrombus formation. There was no reported history of prior venous thromboembolism, malignancy, prolonged immobilization, or known coagulopathy. The patient had been otherwise asymptomatic from a cardiopulmonary standpoint prior to this incidental finding. Further diagnostic imaging of the chest was pursued to determine the cause of the hypoxemia in the context of the lower extremity findings.

A man in his 70s presented for evaluation of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and headaches that had been progressively worsening over several months. His medical history included hypertension of five years' duration, well controlled on treatment, and severe obstructive sleep apnea managed with continuous positive airway pressure. He had been diagnosed with diabetes mellitus 10 years earlier; despite good adherence to metformin and glimepiride along with lifestyle modifications, glycemic control had remained poor. On examination he weighed 78 kg with a body mass index of 28 kg/m². He had a firm goiter and several dysmorphic features, including thickened lips, coarse facial traits, a widened nasal base, prominent frontal wrinkles and bossing, and enlarged extremities, with a reported increase in shoe size over recent years. Blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg. Ophthalmologic assessment showed no retinopathy or visual field defects. Laboratory testing revealed a hemoglobin A1c of 10%. Additional hormonal work-up showed a serum insulin-like growth factor 1 level markedly above the upper limit of normal, with insufficient suppression of growth hormone during an oral glucose tolerance test. Brain imaging identified a right temporoparietal extra-axial mass exerting mass effect on the adjacent ventricle, with no pituitary lesion identified on any sequence. Further evaluation including whole-body imaging, thyroid ultrasound, and receptor-based scintigraphy was pursued to search for the source of the hormonal abnormality.

A woman in her mid-70s with a history of atrial fibrillation on rivaroxaban (no valvular disease), hypertension, hypothyroidism, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and colonic tubular adenoma presented with several hours of sudden-onset, severe generalized headache accompanied by chills, photophobia, nausea, and vomiting; symptoms began while traveling. On arrival she was afebrile (36.7°C), severely hypertensive (225/94 mmHg), heart rate 60 bpm, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, alert and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15 and no focal neurologic deficit, though she appeared slow to respond. Neck was supple without rigidity; cardiac exam showed regular rate and rhythm without murmurs; no peripheral stigmata of systemic infection were noted. She denied visual blurring or projectile vomiting. Labs showed leukocytosis (16x10^3/uL) with neutrophilic predominance (13.52x10^3/uL); comprehensive metabolic panel, urinalysis, and troponin were unremarkable; respiratory viral PCR panel was negative. CT head and chest X-ray showed no acute abnormality. She was admitted for hypertensive urgency and reactive leukocytosis of unknown cause and started on empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics. Within 24 hours she became lethargic and confused while remaining afebrile and hemodynamically stable, with serum lactate rising from 2.5 to 4.6 mmol/L. Blood cultures obtained on admission grew a viridans-group streptococcal organism. Lumbar puncture showed cerebrospinal fluid leukocytosis with neutrophilic predominance, elevated protein, and low-normal glucose; CSF gram stain and culture were negative, as were meningitis pathogen panel and herpes PCR. Brain MRI showed small foci of diffusion restriction with subtle enhancement in the right cerebral hemisphere and right occipital horn. CT angiography incidentally revealed a small saccular anterior communicating artery aneurysm.

A man in his late 70s with a history of hypertension and bladder cancer, and prior endovascular repair of an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (originally 58 mm) performed 12 years earlier, presented to the emergency department with acute low back pain. Surveillance imaging obtained annually had shown no endoleak, with gradual shrinkage of the aneurysm sac to 41 mm. On initial presentation he was hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL and D-dimer 6.4 μg/mL, unchanged from a recent outpatient baseline. Non-contrast CT at that visit showed no acute findings, and he was discharged. He returned the next morning with similar back pain, was treated symptomatically, and again discharged after no interval change was noted. Approximately four hours later he presented a third time with worsening back pain and new vomiting. Vital signs showed blood pressure 126/77 mmHg and heart rate 100 bpm (sinus tachycardia). Repeat labs showed hemoglobin decreased to 9.6 g/dL and D-dimer markedly increased to 53.6 μg/mL compared with prior testing. Given the acute worsening of symptoms, hemoglobin drop, and marked rise in D-dimer, further contrast-enhanced imaging was pursued to evaluate for an acute aortic process.

train_cases.diagnosis: Malignant neoplasm of lower lobe, left bronchus or lung
train_cases.note: A 41-year-old male, non-smoker, presented with a several-week history of swelling and pain involving multiple limb joints. Physical examination revealed limited mobility of the lower limb joints without visible deformity. Laboratory evaluation showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 87 mm/h, a markedly elevated rheumatoid factor of 370 IU/ml, and a positive anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody of 34.5 RU/ml, findings consistent with an inflammatory polyarthritis. As part of pre-treatment evaluation prior to consideration of biologic therapy for the joint disease, a chest CT scan was obtained. This incidentally revealed an irregular mass in the right lower lobe measuring approximately 3.5 cm x 2.8 cm, with ill-defined borders abutting the diaphragm and heterogeneous contrast enhancement, along with multiple small nodules along the right interlobar pleura. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed no evidence of intracranial lesions. A CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of the lung mass was subsequently performed for further characterization, with pathology results pending at the time of this evaluation. The patient had no prior history of malignancy and no other significant chronic illnesses noted.

A man in his 70s with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia presented to the emergency department with a 48-hour history of high fever, progressive confusion, and decreased level of consciousness. There was no recent trauma, seizure activity, or focal neurological deficit prior to admission. On examination, temperature was 39°C, and he was disoriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 10 (eye opening to verbal stimuli, incomprehensible speech, localizing to pain). Neurological exam showed no focal cranial nerve deficits or limb weakness, with symmetric reflexes. Cardiovascular exam initially revealed a regular rhythm without murmurs; other systems were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (WBC 15,800/µL), elevated C-reactive protein (185 mg/L), and elevated procalcitonin (12 ng/mL). Given fever and altered mentation, blood cultures were drawn and lumbar puncture performed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 680 WBC/µL (90% neutrophils), glucose 28 mg/dL, and protein 185 mg/dL. Gram stain of CSF showed small gram-positive rods. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and adjunctive corticosteroid were started. Despite therapy, mental status remained depressed. Echocardiography was pursued given persistent fever. Brain MRI showed multiple small areas of acute infarction thought to be embolic, plus chronic age-appropriate white matter changes; MR angiography showed no large-vessel occlusion or aneurysm. Abdominal imaging showed a splenic infarct, an incidental infrarenal aortic aneurysm, and multiple small hepatic lesions with peripheral rim enhancement suggestive of microabscesses.

A woman in her late twenties, previously reported as healthy, presented with several days of fever and malaise before being admitted to a local hospital. Initial laboratory testing showed an elevated neutrophil count. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an abnormality of aortic valve morphology with associated regurgitation. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy was started, but fever persisted over the following two months, with peak temperatures up to 39.4°C despite treatment. Due to the prolonged, unresponsive febrile illness, she was transferred to a tertiary referral center for further evaluation. Blood cultures obtained at the referral center grew a hemolytic streptococcal organism. Transesophageal echocardiography and cardiac CT were performed for further anatomic characterization, showing an abnormal communication tract in the region of the left ventricular outflow tract adjacent to the aortic and mitral valve apparatus, in addition to the previously noted aortic valve malformation and regurgitation. No prior cardiac diagnoses, procedures, or hospitalizations were reported. A multidisciplinary team evaluated the patient for possible surgical management given the persistent bacteremia, structural cardiac abnormality, and lack of response to medical therapy alone.

An 84-year-old man presented with left-sided weakness and impaired consciousness.
