He had sustained a head injury after a fall approximately two days prior; a head CT performed shortly afterward at another facility was unremarkable, and he was discharged home. He returned emergently after acute onset of left-sided weakness. Brain MRI demonstrated an acute infarct in the right parietal lobe, and MR angiography showed no significant large-vessel occlusion. He was started on dual antiplatelet therapy for acute ischemic stroke. His neurological status subsequently stabilized and rehabilitation was initiated. On hospital day six, routine electrocardiography incidentally revealed diffuse ST-segment elevation without chest pain. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated akinesis of the mid-to-apical left ventricular segments with compensatory hyperkinesis of the basal segments, a pattern not corresponding to a single coronary artery territory. Coronary angiography showed approximately 75% stenosis of the proximal right coronary artery and approximately 75% stenosis of the left anterior descending artery, neither considered flow-limiting. Laboratory testing showed marked elevation of troponin I and brain natriuretic peptide on day six compared with admission, with a mild increase in C-reactive protein; white cell count, renal function, and coagulation parameters were largely unchanged. Several hours later, the patient developed sudden bradycardia followed by pulseless electrical activity and cardiac arrest. Bedside echocardiography during resuscitation showed a new pericardial effusion with echogenic material adjacent to the left ventricular free wall. Despite resuscitative efforts, the patient died.

A man in his early 40s presented to the emergency department with a two-day history of generalised malaise, agitation, confusion, and progressively worsening drowsiness. He also reported recent onset of an erythematous rash across the nasal bridge and forehead. He described intermittent intranasal use of street-obtained cocaine over the preceding three months, with no other illicit drug use and no prior documented substance-use history. He denied recent trauma, seizures, excessive exertion, or alcohol intake. Past medical history included obstructive sleep apnoea managed with CPAP, and depression treated with sertraline 100 mg daily. On examination, he had an altered mental status with drowsiness, and an erythematous rash was noted over the nasal bridge and forehead; no vital sign abnormalities were documented. Initial investigations showed creatine kinase 18,753 U/L (reference 40–320), alanine aminotransferase 240 U/L (reference 0–45), creatinine 152 µmol/L (reference 59–104), white cell count 11.03 ×10⁹/L, and C-reactive protein 155 mg/L. Serial arterial blood gases showed persistently normal lactate. Blood and urine cultures were sterile, and viral screening was negative. CT brain and chest X-ray were unremarkable, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis via lumbar puncture was normal. He was admitted for observation, given aggressive intravenous hydration with monitoring of renal function and electrolytes, and his mental status and laboratory abnormalities improved progressively over the following 72 hours without need for renal replacement therapy.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A man in his 30s with no prior history of liver or thyroid disease and no regular medications presented with a 2-day history of fatigue, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations. At the initial evaluation, laboratory testing showed markedly elevated free triiodothyronine and free thyroxine levels with a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone level, consistent with severe thyrotoxicosis. Liver function tests showed elevated transaminases and marked hyperbilirubinemia. White blood cell count was within normal limits. Given tachycardia (heart rate 111 bpm) and prominent gastrointestinal symptoms including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and jaundice, the patient was treated empirically with an antithyroid medication, potassium iodide, a beta-blocker, and intravenous corticosteroids, then transferred two days later to a tertiary center for further endocrine and hepatology evaluation. On arrival, vital signs were: temperature 36.8°C, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min. Exam showed conjunctival icterus without palpable goiter, exophthalmos, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, or pretibial edema; cardiovascular and respiratory exams were unremarkable. Repeat labs showed persistent thyrotoxicosis (though improved from initial values), continued hyperbilirubinemia, and elevated transaminases. Serial monitoring of thyroid and liver parameters was planned during ongoing treatment.

A woman in her late 60s, with a decades-long history of systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus nephritis (diagnosed in her twenties, previously with a skin rash and proteinuria; renal function had remained stable at baseline with normal urinalysis), was maintained on prednisolone, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, hydroxychloroquine, plus a proton pump inhibitor, iron supplementation, and a bisphosphonate. Five days before this admission she developed lower back pain and difficulty ambulating. Three days before admission she developed altered consciousness and was taken to another hospital, where imaging showed a right ureteral stone with hydronephrosis and perinephric fat stranding; a ureteral stent was placed and antibiotics started. On transfer, vital signs were: blood pressure 137/80 mmHg, heart rate 82/min, temperature 38.4°C, SpO2 95% on 2 L/min oxygen. She was febrile with depressed consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale E2V2M4). Brain MRI showed multiple acute infarcts involving the bilateral centrum semiovale, bilateral temporal lobes, basal ganglia, and right cerebellar peduncle. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia (platelets ~10.5×10^4/µL), elevated LDH, markedly elevated BUN and creatinine, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, elevated CRP, mildly low complement C3/C4, and borderline anti-dsDNA antibody titer. Urinalysis showed marked proteinuria, numerous red blood cells, and pyuria.

A woman in her 60s presented for neurological evaluation. She had a history of stage IIIB2 uterine carcinosarcoma treated with hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, followed by chemotherapy and an immune checkpoint inhibitor, the latter continued as maintenance therapy for approximately 10 months prior to presentation. Other history included a resected left cavernous sinus meningioma with residual left sixth cranial nerve palsy, deep vein thrombosis, depression, chronic low back pain, and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. She reported two months of progressively worsening fatigue, generalized weakness, lightheadedness, and gait instability. Vital signs showed blood pressure 156/85 mmHg; she was afebrile, non-tachycardic, with oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She was alert, oriented, and cognitively intact, without dysarthria or aphasia. Cranial nerve exam was notable only for the known chronic left sixth nerve palsy. Strength was full (5/5) in all extremities, with reduced pinprick sensation (about 70%) distal to the bilateral mid-shins, a positive Romberg sign, symmetric 2+ reflexes, negative Hoffmann's sign, and an ataxic, short-stepped gait without limb dysmetria. The neck was supple with negative meningeal signs. Initial labs (complete blood count, metabolic panel, CRP, CK, aldolase, procalcitonin, ANA, copper, ammonia, B12, TSH, cortisol, ACTH) were unremarkable aside from mildly elevated ESR and lactic acid. CT, CT angiography, and MRI of the head/neck and spine showed no acute abnormality. Lumbar puncture showed lymphocytic pleocytosis and oligoclonal bands with normal opening pressure, protein, and glucose. Additional serum and CSF studies were sent to an outside laboratory for further evaluation.

A two-month-old female infant presented to the emergency department with poor feeding, lethargy, irritability, and failure to thrive over the preceding one month. She was born at term via normal vaginal delivery after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with a birth weight of 3.1 kg. She was exclusively breastfed and received vitamin D supplementation at 400 IU daily. She also received oral calcium supplementation for one week at one month of age, which was then discontinued, with no further calcium given. Elevated serum calcium and low serum phosphate were noted on routine testing, prompting referral for further evaluation. On examination, length was 54 cm and weight 3.1 kg, both below expected norms for age. She appeared lethargic and dehydrated, with decreased skin turgor and dry mucous membranes; no dysmorphic facial features were noted. Blood pressure was 88/52 mmHg (50th centile for age). Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed markedly elevated serum calcium (3.59 mmol/L; normal 2.17-2.82) and low serum phosphate (1.39 mmol/L; normal 1.68-2.71), with normal renal function, normal arterial blood gas pH, and suppressed intact parathyroid hormone. 25-hydroxyvitamin D was normal, while 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D was markedly elevated. Spot urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio was elevated, and tubular phosphate reabsorption was reduced. Inflammatory markers, serum ACE, and parathyroid hormone-related peptide were normal. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis; echocardiogram was normal.

A woman in her mid-30s with a history of papillary thyroid carcinoma (previously treated with total thyroidectomy and radioiodine ablation) and a prior right ovarian mature cystic teratoma (surgically removed) was previously well until she developed fever and rapidly progressive confusion. Over the following days she exhibited abnormal behavior, disorientation, and autonomic instability, progressing to markedly decreased level of consciousness. Serum and cerebrospinal fluid studies were obtained. She was managed in the intensive care unit with sequential immunotherapy, including high-dose corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and plasma exchange, followed by additional immunosuppressive agents given an incomplete response. She remained comatose and required prolonged mechanical ventilation via tracheostomy. Several months into her ICU course, abdominal imaging revealed a newly developed left adnexal cystic lesion; after surgical removal, pathology showed a benign mature cystic teratoma. Her neurologic status gradually stabilized over an extended period. Approximately 20 months after symptom onset, she remained tracheostomy-dependent with severe deconditioning and minimal responsiveness, but met safety criteria for initiating intensive rehabilitation, including stable hemodynamics, stable ventilation via a secure airway, and absence of uncontrolled seizures, severe dysautonomia, or active infection. At baseline she had no measurable functional mobility, cognitive responsiveness, or communication ability on standardized assessments.

A woman in her early 40s with a known history of cutaneous and articular systemic lupus erythematosus, treated with hydroxychloroquine for one year, presented with acute febrile encephalopathy. She reported jaundice, asthenia, and progressively altered mental status developing over a short period. On examination she was febrile (38°C), hemodynamically stable, with a fluctuating Glasgow Coma Score of 9-12. Generalized jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly were noted. Initial laboratory studies showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL) with macrocytosis, reticulocytosis, schistocytes on peripheral smear, markedly elevated LDH, and undetectable haptoglobin, findings consistent with microangiopathic hemolysis. There was profound thrombocytopenia (platelets 8,000/uL) and leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance, along with elevated CRP. Direct Coombs test was negative. Mild transaminitis and elevated indirect bilirubin were present; renal function, electrolytes, and calcium were within normal limits. Vitamin B12 was low-normal and folate slightly low. Hepatitis A and HIV serologies were negative. Transthoracic echocardiography was unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement and periventricular white matter hyperintensities with contrast enhancement. Autoimmune workup was negative for antiphospholipid antibodies, anti-dsDNA, and lupus anticoagulant, with normal complement C3.

A woman in her 60s with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency department after two days of abdominal pain and nausea, followed by new-onset confusion and difficulty speaking. Family reported that she appeared disoriented and was unable to recognize familiar people or her surroundings. A stroke response was activated on arrival. Her initial NIH Stroke Scale score was 2, attributable to inability to state the correct month and her age. On examination, Glasgow Coma Scale was 13; she was alert but disoriented to time and place. Cranial nerve testing revealed horizontal nystagmus without facial weakness, and motor strength was preserved in all extremities. CT of the head and CT angiography of the head and neck showed no hemorrhage and no large vessel occlusion. Laboratory studies showed severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count 8 x10^3/uL) and anemia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL), with elevated lactate dehydrogenase (1536 IU/L), undetectable haptoglobin (<10 mg/dL), and elevated total bilirubin (4.8 mg/dL, predominantly indirect). Renal function was mildly impaired (BUN 43 mg/dL, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL). White count was mildly elevated at 11.26 x10^3/uL. Additional specialized hematologic testing was pending at the time of initial evaluation.

A 40-year-old male manual laborer presented with a 2-week history of high-grade, intermittent fever and worsening breathlessness. He had reported exertional dyspnea (baseline NYHA class II) for one week prior, which progressed to dyspnea at rest (NYHA class IV) over the following two weeks. There was no chest pain, palpitations, cough, expectoration, or pedal edema at symptom onset. He had no history of rheumatic fever, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, or known structural heart disease. He was a non-smoker, did not consume alcohol, had no identifiable cardiovascular risk factors, and denied intravenous drug use. On examination he was dyspneic at rest; pulse 100/min, blood pressure 140/60 mmHg (right arm), temperature 100.4°F, respiratory rate 18/min. He appeared pale with bilateral pitting pedal edema. Jugular venous pulse was just visible at the root of the neck. The apex beat was displaced to the sixth intercostal space, 2 cm lateral to the midclavicular line, without a palpable thrill. Auscultation revealed a grade 3/6 early diastolic murmur at the aortic area, accentuated on expiration, and a grade 3/6 pansystolic murmur at the apex. No peripheral stigmata were noted. Bilateral basal crepitations were heard. Abdominal and neurological examinations were unremarkable. Labs showed hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, leukocyte count 16,400/mm³ with 88% neutrophils, lymphocytes 10%, ESR 76 mm/hr, CRP 70 mg/L, and procalcitonin 2 ng/mL. Renal and liver function were normal; a vasculitis panel was negative. Multiple blood cultures were sterile, and serologic testing for atypical organisms was negative. ECG showed sinus rhythm at 100/min with normal PR interval. Chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly. Echocardiography revealed an echolucent space posterior to the aorta bulging into the left atrium, a mitral regurgitation jet, an echodense mobile density on the anterior mitral leaflet, and a bicuspid aortic valve. CT angiography showed multiple blood-filled cavities posterior to the aortic root, one communicating with the aortic root via a 4.3 mm neck, another communicating with the left ventricular outflow tract via an 8 mm neck, and a heavily calcified aortic valve.

A woman in her 60s, African American, presented with a two-week history of progressive, painful oral ulcers involving the buccal mucosa and sublingual region, accompanied by fever, chills, sore throat, dyspnea, dry cough, palpitations, and anorexia. She denied recent sexual activity, medication changes, or toxic exposures. Past medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, psoriasis, COPD not requiring home oxygen, and lumbar spinal stenosis, with prior multiple joint replacements. Home medications included losartan, levothyroxine, liraglutide, metformin, albuterol, fluticasone, weekly low-dose methotrexate (2.5 mg, stable dose for years), and folic acid. She had quit smoking one month prior and denied alcohol or illicit drug use. Vital signs: blood pressure 119/72 mmHg, heart rate 107 bpm, temperature 37.8°C, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Exam showed multiple aphthous ulcers on the perioral mucosa, bilateral buccal mucosa, and sublingual surface with hard palate erythema and diffuse oral mucosal dryness; lungs were clear without distress; no lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, petechiae, or ecchymoses. Labs revealed leukopenia (WBC 1.7×10⁹/L), neutropenia (ANC 0.7×10⁹/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 36×10⁹/L), mild anemia with microcytosis (Hgb 12.9 g/dL, MCV 76.4 fL), elevated CRP (156.8 mg/L) and ESR (50 mm/h), ferritin 466.4 ng/mL, LDH 325 U/L, haptoglobin 484 mg/dL, troponin 20 ng/L, and D-dimer 1.54 µg/mL. ECG showed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Chest radiograph was unremarkable; CT angiography excluded pulmonary embolism but showed right middle lobe atelectasis and bilateral patchy parenchymal opacities. By hospital day 4, she developed hypoxia (SpO2 85%) and recurrent fevers to 39.4°C, with worsening cytopenias (WBC 0.9, ANC 0.2, platelets 16×10⁹/L) and new bilateral infiltrates with vascular congestion on repeat imaging; blood cultures remained negative throughout.

A woman in her early 50s with a history of hypertension and thyroid cancer (status post thyroidectomy) presented acutely with bilateral flank pain, fever, and myalgias, prompting hospital admission. She denied hematuria, unintentional weight loss, or a palpable mass. On examination she was febrile with bilateral flank tenderness. Laboratory testing showed leukocytosis; urinalysis findings were consistent with a urinary tract infection, and urine cultures grew Escherichia coli, susceptible to empiric antibiotic therapy. Given symptom severity, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained, showing a bulky right upper pole with surrounding perinephric fat stranding and background cortical scarring, without a clearly defined mass; the region was hypoenhancing (92 HU) relative to adjacent cortex (115 HU). The left kidney was atrophic with cortical scarring. Follow-up contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 3.5 × 4.4 × 4.0 cm well-circumscribed, predominantly endophytic right upper pole lesion, T2 isointense, with diffusion restriction, arterial-phase hypoenhancement, near-isointensity on the venous phase, and progressive washout on delayed imaging; no necrosis, hemorrhage, or fat was seen. Given diagnostic uncertainty, CT-guided core needle biopsy of the right kidney was performed. Histopathology showed chronic vascular nephrosclerotic changes with no evidence of malignancy, prompting close interval imaging follow-up.

A previously healthy man in his mid-20s presented to the emergency department with a three-day history of progressive chest pain and dyspnea. Several days earlier he had been evaluated elsewhere and treated for presumed pneumonia and pleuritis. The chest pain was left-sided, sharp, radiating to the jaw, pleuritic and positional, worsening when supine or lying on the left side and improving with sitting forward. He denied prior similar episodes, alcohol, or recreational drug use, though collateral history revealed use of vape pens and nicotine salts. Medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable. Vitals: heart rate 101 bpm, temperature 36.9°C, blood pressure 119/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Electrocardiogram showed diffuse ST-segment elevations with reciprocal ST depression in lead aVR. Labs showed markedly elevated high-sensitivity troponin I (31,097 ng/L), leukocytosis (16.5 ×10³/µL), elevated CRP and ESR, mildly elevated AST/ALT, and elevated BNP. Chest radiograph showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates; CT angiography excluded pulmonary embolism but showed patchy bilateral infiltrates, dependent atelectasis, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Initial infectious workup was unrevealing. While awaiting admission, he developed rapid deterioration with hypoxia, hypotension (91/49 mmHg), and tachycardia (140 bpm). Echocardiography showed mildly reduced left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 43%) with global hypokinesis, markedly reduced global longitudinal strain, and a trivial pericardial effusion without tamponade. Lactate rose from 1.6 to 3.3 mmol/L. Coronary angiography showed non-obstructive coronary arteries.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A woman in her early 30s, recently started on an antithyroid medication (carbimazole 40 mg daily) three weeks prior for a newly diagnosed overactive thyroid condition, presented with several days of fever, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain, together with palpitations and diarrhea that had prompted the initial thyroid diagnosis weeks earlier. On admission, vital signs showed blood pressure 121/90 mmHg, heart rate 92 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and temperature 37°C. Physical examination was unremarkable, with no palpable goiter. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, white cell count 4.2×10^9/L, platelets 153×10^9/L, elevated free thyroxine with suppressed TSH, and a cholestatic pattern of liver enzyme derangement (elevated ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, and total bilirubin). Imaging performed two weeks earlier for unexplained liver enzyme elevation had shown gallbladder wall thickening and surrounding inflammatory changes without gallstones or biliary dilatation. Over the following days in hospital, the patient developed a marked drop in white cell and neutrophil counts with low-grade fever, followed by high-grade fever up to 40.8°C, persistent vomiting, worsening hypotension and tachycardia, bibasal lung crackles, and progressively worsening liver function with coagulopathy, despite negative blood cultures and a low procalcitonin level.

A man in his mid-30s, employed as a laborer, presented after being found unconscious following several hours of continuous outdoor manual work during a period of extreme ambient heat. He was brought to the hospital acutely comatose. On arrival, he was unresponsive with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 3 (eye 1, verbal 1, motor 1). Vital signs showed core temperature 41.9°C, heart rate 98 bpm, respiratory rate 40/min, and blood pressure 71/35 mmHg. Pupils were 3.0 mm bilaterally with sluggish reactivity. Pulmonary auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds without rales; cardiac exam was unremarkable. Muscle tone was normal but strength could not be assessed given the level of consciousness. Skin was dry without petechiae, and Babinski signs were absent bilaterally. Electrocardiogram showed nonspecific ST-segment changes. Initial noncontrast cranial CT was unremarkable. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates with pleural thickening and effusion. Initial laboratory studies revealed elevated AST 96 U/L, ALT 139 U/L, creatinine 169 μmol/L, lactate 7.7 mmol/L, procalcitonin 5.92, and markedly elevated LDH 1,643 U/L, with hemoglobin 96 g/L and platelets 128×10^9/L. The patient was admitted to intensive care and treated with rapid physical cooling, fluid resuscitation, mechanical ventilation, infection control, and organ-protective supportive care.

A woman in her early twenties was admitted for sudden-onset behavioral change, including social withdrawal, absence of verbal communication, and unusual orofacial grimacing, occurring after a single day of profuse vomiting. On admission she was awake but markedly uncooperative, with progressively worsening psychomotor agitation and apparent perceptual disturbance (continuous scanning of surroundings); verbal contact and formal mental status testing were not possible. History was notable for past recreational marijuana use, with a positive urine screen for THC on this admission. After parenteral haloperidol was given for agitation, she developed acute dystonic reactions with oculogyric crises, which resolved with biperiden; antipsychotic therapy was changed. Over subsequent days she had fluctuating severe agitation, orofacial dyskinesias, involuntary tongue movements, and active resistance behaviors (forceful eyelid closure). Autonomic instability was noted, with tachycardia, hypertension, and fever up to 38°C. Labs showed leukocytosis (12.26×10^9/L), markedly elevated creatine kinase (6023 U/L), elevated CRP (42.1 mg/L), and elevated AST/ALT (183/91 U/L). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed pleocytosis (38×10^6/L). Brain MRI showed only a mildly prominent right parieto-occipital perivascular space, without other structural abnormality. EEG showed diffuse theta/delta slowing without epileptiform discharges, indicating diffuse cortical dysfunction. Mild anisocoria (smaller left pupil) was also noted.

A woman in her 70s was brought to the hospital with a chief complaint of sudden onset of sharp back pain. She reported no associated syncope, limb weakness, or lower extremity ischemic symptoms. On arrival she was alert and hemodynamically stable. Blood pressure was 180/92 mmHg with no inter-arm difference, and heart rate was 92 beats per minute. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no significant valvular disease, with only mild left ventricular hypertrophy. Laboratory testing showed no evidence of hepatic or renal dysfunction. She was obese, with a height of 143 cm and weight of 80 kg. Her past medical history was notable for hypertension, treated with olmesartan 40 mg daily. She had no family history of aortic disease. Given the acute, severe nature of the back pain and her cardiovascular risk factors, urgent contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging of the chest was obtained for further evaluation and to guide emergency management planning.

A woman in her early 60s with no smoking history and a prior diagnosis of resected lung adenocarcinoma (stage IIB, harboring an EGFR exon 21 L858R mutation, no ALK/ROS1 alterations) had been receiving adjuvant osimertinib (an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor) 80 mg daily for approximately three months when she developed dyspnea and chest tightness that progressed over this interval, without fever, cough, sputum production, or other infectious symptoms. On examination she was afebrile with bibasilar inspiratory crackles on auscultation; the remainder of the cardiopulmonary exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 6.8×10^9/L, C-reactive protein 5 mg/L, and procalcitonin <0.05 ng/mL, arguing against an infectious process. Serum B-type natriuretic peptide was 35.4 pg/mL (normal <100), and cardiac enzymes and troponin I were within normal limits. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes or arrhythmia. High-resolution chest CT demonstrated new bilateral, diffuse ground-glass opacities with fine reticulation, predominantly in the peripheral and basal lung zones, without lymphadenopathy or effusion described. There was no clinical or radiographic evidence of recurrent malignancy, cardiac decompensation, or infection to account for the findings.

A woman in her mid-40s presented to the emergency department with a cough and worsening dyspnea beginning approximately six weeks after a high-speed motor vehicle collision, at which time she had been diagnosed with multiple left-sided rib fractures managed conservatively. She reported a subacute course with development of a semi-productive cough and progressive dyspnea on minimal exertion. She denied chest pain, fever, hemoptysis, interval trauma, or lower extremity swelling, and had no prior cardiopulmonary risk factors or disease. Vital signs showed heart rate 126 bpm, respiratory rate 27/min, blood pressure 151/71 mmHg, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and temperature 36.7°C. Exam revealed decreased breath sounds on the left with tenderness along the lower left chest wall. Labs showed hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL (low), high-sensitivity troponin-T <2.6 ng/L (normal), and D-dimer 1,249 ng/mL (elevated). Chest radiography showed complete opacification of the left hemithorax with mediastinal shift; CT chest confirmed subacute fractures of the left sixth through eighth posterior ribs and a trace pericardial effusion. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with poor R-wave progression anteriorly, no ST changes. A chest tube was placed, draining nearly two liters of serosanguinous fluid; afterward new ST-segment changes appeared on the monitor and the patient developed transient hypoxia (SpO2 83% on room air, improving to 93% on non-rebreather), without chest pain. CT angiography excluded pulmonary embolism, vascular injury, or active bleeding, showing lung re-expansion with diffuse alveolar infiltrate. The chest tube tip lay near the cardiac apex. ECG changes resolved spontaneously within two hours. High-sensitivity troponin-T peaked at 5,956 ng/L. Coronary catheterization showed no significant coronary disease; left ventriculography showed anterior apical akinesis, and echocardiography showed severe anteroapical hypokinesis with ejection fraction 40-45%.

A male infant in the 10-month age range, with a known congenital multisystem disorder involving cardiovascular and connective-tissue features confirmed by genetic testing in early infancy, was admitted for evaluation of markedly elevated serum calcium levels. He was the first child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents, born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with birth weight and length in the low-average percentile range and a normal Apgar score. At birth, dysmorphic facial features, a cardiac murmur, and a right-sided inguinoscrotal hernia were noted. Echocardiography performed in infancy identified supravalvular aortic stenosis. He has since been enrolled in a multidisciplinary follow-up program. At four months of age, routine nephrology follow-up demonstrated right-sided pyelectasis on renal imaging and hypercalciuria on urine studies, with serum calcium documented as normal at that time. He has received routine vitamin D supplementation (400 IU/day) since the first month of life. On the current admission, laboratory testing revealed markedly elevated serum calcium levels, prompting further inpatient evaluation to determine the cause and guide management of the elevated calcium level.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute leukemia of unspecified cell type not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: A young adult woman (early 20s), with no known toxic exposures, presented with a one-month history of progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, and anterior chest pressure that acutely worsened over the 48 hours before admission. She was afebrile, with Grade II obesity, jugular venous distension, tachypnea (respiratory rate 36/min), and tachycardia (heart rate 130 bpm); blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg with muffled heart sounds and diminished breath sounds with prolonged expiration on lung auscultation. No hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Oxygen saturation was 89% on room air, with arterial blood gas showing hypoxemia and hypercapnia. Complete blood count showed WBC 5340/mm3 (88% neutrophils, 8% lymphocytes, 4% monocytes), hemoglobin 12 g/dL, platelets 330,000/mm3, and a peripheral smear without atypical cells. Inflammatory markers and coagulation studies were unremarkable; tumor markers were negative. ALT was mildly elevated (81 U/L) with otherwise normal liver, renal, and uric acid studies. Echocardiography showed preserved ejection fraction, mild septal thickening, and a large circumferential pericardial effusion without diastolic collapse. Chest CT demonstrated extensive mediastinal lymphadenopathy encasing mediastinal vessels and a large circumferential pericardial effusion, with clear lungs and no abdominal lymphadenopathy. Given hemodynamic compromise, surgical debulking with pericardiectomy was performed; pericardial fluid cytology showed low-cellularity smears with small-to-medium lymphoid cells, some with prominent nucleoli. A subsequent bone marrow aspirate revealed a hypercellular marrow with 43% blasts—medium-to-large cells with high nucleocytoplasmic ratio, lobulated or indented nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and scant agranular cytoplasm—with reduced granulocytic maturation and preserved megakaryopoiesis.

A man in his 50s was admitted after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure followed by a reduced level of consciousness. He had a body mass index of 19.5 kg/m² (height 165 cm, weight 56 kg) and no history of chronic kidney disease. There was no reported prolonged immobilization, excessive exertion, trauma, illicit drug use, or exposure to known myotoxic agents. On admission he was hemodynamically stable. Initial laboratory testing showed serum creatinine 108 µmol/L, urea 2.4 mmol/L, and estimated GFR 67 mL/min/1.73 m²; creatine kinase was not measured at that time. Over the following three days, renal function deteriorated rapidly: creatinine rose to 482 µmol/L, urea to 11.8 mmol/L, and eGFR fell to 11 mL/min/1.73 m². Creatine kinase, checked at this stage, was markedly elevated at 89,345 U/L. On day four, creatinine was 314 µmol/L, urea 11.9 mmol/L, eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73 m², and creatine kinase remained elevated at 88,808 U/L. From day five onward, with intravenous fluid therapy, renal parameters improved progressively while creatine kinase declined more slowly, falling to 65,983 U/L (day five), 26,828 U/L (day six), and 9,905 U/L (day seven), alongside normalization of creatinine, urea, and eGFR. Complement C3/C4, antinuclear antibody, anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody, proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase antibodies, serum protein electrophoresis, and antistreptolysin O titer were unremarkable aside from a low IgG; these findings argued against an immune, vasculitic, or paraprotein-related cause of renal impairment.

A woman in her early 50s, right-handed, presented to the emergency department with three days of generalized fatigue and headache, accompanied by mild diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, and decreased appetite. She subsequently noted heaviness in all four limbs, initially attributed to fatigue. About ten days before presentation she had experienced burning on urination and was treated empirically at a primary care clinic with a five-day course of ciprofloxacin, without further investigation. She had no history of recent vaccination, viral illness, or other medication use. Past medical history was unremarkable; she led an athletic lifestyle, did not smoke, and did not drink alcohol. Initial vital signs and physical and neurologic examination were normal. Laboratory testing showed elevated liver enzymes (alkaline phosphatase 151 U/L, ALT 521 U/L, AST 249 U/L) with normal bilirubin and ammonia, prompting admission for further work-up. On the second hospital day she reported worsening lower-limb heaviness and could no longer walk unassisted. Examination revealed right nasolabial flattening, tongue deviation to the right on protrusion, motor power 4+/5 in the upper limbs and 4-/5 in the lower limbs, reduced upper-limb reflexes, absent knee and ankle reflexes bilaterally, flexor plantar responses, and normal sensory and cerebellar findings. Liver enzymes had stabilized, but she developed acute hyponatremia, sodium falling from 133 to 122 mmol/L. Brain imaging showed bilateral parieto-occipital white-matter signal changes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed mild albuminocytologic dissociation with elevated protein and IgG index. Over the following days her weakness progressed to near-complete quadriplegia with respiratory failure requiring intubation, followed by gradual improvement, extubation after three weeks, and normalization of liver enzymes and sodium.

A man in his mid-50s was admitted with a three-week history of cough and expectoration that had worsened over the preceding week with fever. He had a six-month history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes and a 20-year smoking history; hypertension, avian exposure, and recent travel were denied. On admission, temperature was 38.7°C, respiratory rate 25/min, pulse 89/min, and blood pressure 120/80 mmHg; physical examination was unremarkable. Initial labs showed leukocytosis (14.52×10^9/L, 79.7% neutrophils), CRP 141.46 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.21 ng/mL, and ESR 110 mm/h; tuberculosis, fungal, and autoimmune markers were negative, and sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage cultures grew a Gram-negative bacillus. Imaging showed a cavitary consolidation in the right upper lung. He was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, airway clearance measures, and glucose control, with clinical and radiologic improvement by day 8. On day 9, following a sharp rise in ambient temperature and a period of outdoor activity, he developed recurrent high fever (up to 40.9°C), dizziness, fatigue, diffuse myalgia, and nausea with vomiting after drinking cold water, though warm beverages were tolerated. Over subsequent days, despite antipyretics and physical cooling, he remained persistently febrile with fluctuating white cell counts, thrombocytopenia, markedly rising transaminases, LDH, creatine kinase, and creatinine, and coagulopathy (D-dimer >16 mg/L), while repeat blood and sputum cultures and multiple infectious/parasitic panels remained negative. He subsequently developed a hypertensive emergency (blood pressure 220/120 mmHg) without focal findings on vascular imaging.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A man in his 20s with no prior medical history presented with a one-month history of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and 5-kg weight loss beginning after a viral respiratory illness, without fever. Abdominal imaging showed narrowing of the duodenum between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery with proximal gastric dilatation. Initial laboratory studies were unremarkable, and upper and lower endoscopy showed no abnormalities. He was treated with nasogastric tube feeding and improved, but symptoms recurred with low-grade fever within days of discharge, prompting readmission. Repeat imaging showed resolution of the earlier findings. Nasogastric feeding was resumed but symptoms did not improve, and his body temperature and heart rate progressively increased. Thyroid function testing revealed markedly elevated free T3 and free T4 with a suppressed TSH. There was no family history of thyroid disease. On transfer for further evaluation, vital signs showed tachycardia (142 beats/min) and hypotension (88/50 mmHg). Physical examination revealed a goiter. Thyroid ultrasonography showed diffuse enlargement of the gland with increased vascularity. Laboratory studies at that time showed mildly elevated transaminases, elevated BUN and creatinine, and an elevated white blood cell count, with normal CRP. He subsequently developed atrial fibrillation that progressed to ventricular tachycardia and cardiac arrest, followed by shock and multiorgan failure requiring intubation, mechanical ventilation, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.

train_cases.diagnosis: Benign neoplasm of left adrenal gland
train_cases.note: A man in his 40s presented with a 15-day history of burning micturition and dull, aching left flank pain radiating to the groin, without associated vomiting, hematuria, or lithuria. He had known hypertension and diabetes mellitus, one episode of hypertensive crisis five months earlier, a cerebrovascular accident one year prior with full recovery, a history of recurrent renal calculi, and prior percutaneous coronary intervention of the left circumflex artery one year earlier. There was no history of purplish striae, cushingoid features, or stigmata of neurocutaneous syndromes. Laboratory testing showed low hemoglobin and hematocrit, low blood urea, low serum sodium and magnesium, mildly elevated serum phosphorus, and an elevated procalcitonin level. Plasma and 24-hour urinary metanephrine and normetanephrine levels were within normal limits. Ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic lesion in the left suprarenal region, with the left adrenal gland not separately identified. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, thick-walled, peripherally enhancing cystic lesion in the left suprarenal region, without calcification, septations, solid component, or hemorrhage, with maintained fat planes relative to adjacent structures. The lesion compressed the left renal vein anteroinferiorly and abutted the left renal artery posteroinferiorly, without vascular invasion or thrombosis. Surgical excision of the mass was planned.

A man in his mid-40s with a known history of an advanced hepatobiliary malignancy with hepatic and adrenal involvement, previously treated with a programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) inhibitor-based immunotherapy regimen combined with chemotherapy and subsequently maintained on the same immunotherapy agent plus an oral antiangiogenic drug, presented approximately nine months after starting this treatment with sudden-onset chest tightness of one day's duration. He denied limb weakness. On examination, blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg and heart rate was 115 beats per minute. Electrocardiogram showed a wide-complex tachycardia with two alternating QRS morphologies, regular RR intervals, 1:1 atrioventricular conduction, and marked upwardly convex ST-segment elevation in the inferior and anteroseptal leads. A single oral dose of metoprolol did not terminate the arrhythmia. Laboratory testing revealed markedly elevated cardiac troponin I, creatine kinase-MB, myoglobin, and B-type natriuretic peptide, along with elevated transaminases, creatinine, and blood urea nitrogen. Intravenous amiodarone converted the rhythm to sinus with frequent bigeminal premature ventricular contractions. Bedside echocardiography the following day showed localized segmental wall motion abnormalities with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 59%. Over the next several days, recurrent tachyarrhythmia episodes occurred without persistent hypoperfusion, requiring repeated antiarrhythmic therapy and electrical cardioversion. Liver and kidney function progressively worsened over six days while cardiac injury markers trended downward. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was subsequently obtained for further evaluation.

A man in his early 60s with a history of decompensated alcoholic liver cirrhosis with ascites, hepatocellular carcinoma, and coronary artery disease status post triple-vessel coronary artery bypass graft presented with abdominal distention, generalized weakness, proximal muscle pain, and dark urine. His symptoms began approximately two weeks earlier, shortly after rifaximin and lactulose were started for hepatic encephalopathy, with progressive worsening of muscle pain and weakness over that interval. On presentation he was alert and in no acute distress, hemodynamically stable with blood pressure 150/80 mmHg, pulse 68 beats per minute, temperature 36°C, and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute. The abdomen was distended with ascites. He had diffuse muscle tenderness, motor strength 5/5 in all extremities, no asterixis, and normal reflexes and tone. Complete blood count showed white cell count 5.0×10^9/L, hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, and platelet count 108×10^9/L. Basic metabolic panel showed sodium 137 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, and creatinine 1.33 mg/dL. Initial creatine kinase was markedly elevated at 29,000 U/L. An autoimmune myositis panel (anti-smooth muscle, anti-ribonucleoprotein, anti-Scl-70, anti-histone, anti-Jo-1, and anti-HMG-CoA reductase antibodies) was negative. He had been on a statin for coronary artery disease, which was discontinued on admission, and he was started on aggressive intravenous fluids and monitoring given the markedly elevated muscle enzyme level and rising creatinine.

A man in his 70s presented with a five-day history of reddish-brown discolouration of urine, followed by progressively worsening bilateral lower limb weakness that had rendered him bedbound, and bilateral upper limb weakness with inability to raise his arms above shoulder level for three days, accompanied by diffuse muscle aching. His medical history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and single-vessel coronary artery disease treated with coronary angioplasty two months earlier, after which he was started on a statin, a P2Y12 inhibitor, and aspirin for secondary prevention. There was no recent febrile illness, respiratory or gastrointestinal infection, and no other medications known to affect muscle were being taken concurrently. On examination he was alert and oriented with stable vital signs. Neurological examination revealed symmetrical proximal weakness in all four limbs, more pronounced in the lower limbs (power 1/5) than the upper limbs (power 3/5), with equivocal plantar responses, diminished sensation in a glove-and-stocking distribution, and globally reduced deep tendon reflexes. Bilateral pitting oedema was present. Bulbar and cranial nerve function were intact, with no dysarthria, dysphagia, or respiratory compromise. Mild tenderness was noted in the right upper abdomen. Urine appeared dark red-brown. Initial laboratory studies showed markedly elevated creatine kinase and urine myoglobin, elevated inflammatory markers, elevated transaminases (AST greater than ALT) with low albumin, mild hyponatremia, normal renal function, and vitamin D deficiency. Nerve conduction studies showed a demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy, while electromyography showed a myopathic pattern.

A 63-year-old male with a history of depression, bipolar disorder, anxiety, GERD, hypothyroidism, tobacco use disorder, alcohol use disorder, and recent chronic diarrhea was brought to the emergency department unresponsive and tachycardic after being dropped off by a work colleague, who reported the patient had been working outdoors on a very hot day during an active heat wave warning; no further history was available as the colleague left immediately. On arrival, temperature was 105.4°F temporal and 107.5°F rectal, blood pressure 83/55 mmHg (left arm) and 87/51 mmHg (right arm), with sinus tachycardia. The patient was incontinent of stool, unresponsive to pain, and unable to follow commands, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6 (eye 1, verbal 1, motor 4), though he began improving shortly after arrival. He was protecting his airway with end-tidal CO2 of 36-38 mmHg. Skin was warm to touch without diaphoresis. A bruise was noted on the upper chest and an abrasion on the posterior left shoulder; peripheral pulses were 2+ and equal bilaterally. Labs showed BUN 2.4 mg/dL, creatinine 2.64 mg/dL, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 2.4 mmol/L, anion gap 16, eGFR 26, WBC 12.3 thou/cmm, urine protein 100 mg/dL, and trace urine ketones; creatine kinase and glucose were normal. CT head, cervical spine, and chest/abdomen/pelvis were unremarkable. Four liters of normal saline and IV naloxone produced no improvement. Drug screen and alcohol level were later negative.

A man in his late 60s, with a remote history of surgically treated and irradiated hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (approximately a decade earlier), was found to have a locally recurrent pharyngeal mass several months ago, confirmed on biopsy and staged as recurrent disease without distant metastasis. He was treated with combination chemotherapy (a platinum agent plus a taxane) and a PD-1 inhibitor every three weeks for six cycles, achieving a partial radiologic response. During this course he experienced mild, self-limited pruritic maculopapular rashes on the trunk after treatment cycles, along with grade 2 leukopenia and mild nausea, all managed conservatively. He continued on maintenance PD-1 inhibitor therapy, again developing recurrent mild trunk rashes after each cycle. Several weeks later, because of these recurring mild cutaneous reactions, the maintenance agent was switched to a different PD-1 inhibitor without a washout period. Within 48 hours of the new infusion, he developed rapidly progressive dark-red confluent macules on the face, trunk, and extremities, evolving into flaccid blisters with epidermal detachment and erosion covering nearly the entire body surface area. Nikolsky's sign was positive. Mucosal involvement included conjunctival erosion, oral ulceration, and genital erosion. Skin biopsy from the lower limb showed full-thickness epidermal necrosis with subepidermal clefting; immunohistochemistry showed negative PD-1 and moderate-to-strong PD-L1 expression in keratinocytes, with dense CD4+ and CD8+ T-lymphocyte infiltration at the dermal-epidermal junction.

A man in his 50s with a history of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presented to a local hospital with acute-onset back pain, accompanied by several days of general fatigue and decreased appetite; no urinary symptoms were reported. Initial vital signs showed tachycardia (heart rate 114 bpm), hypotension (86/54 mmHg), respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 36.8°C, and SpO2 98% on room air. Plain CT at the outside hospital showed extensive gas formation in the left renal pelvis, renal parenchyma, and perirenal space extending into the retroperitoneum. Laboratory testing showed acute kidney injury and an HbA1c of 12.8%. He was transferred for further management. On arrival, heart rate was 106 bpm, blood pressure 113/81 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min, temperature 36.9°C, and SpO2 97% on 2 L/min supplemental oxygen. Physical examination revealed left costovertebral angle tenderness without signs of peritoneal irritation. Laboratory findings showed white blood cell count 11,600/μL, platelet count 99,000/μL, C-reactive protein 28.22 mg/dL, serum creatinine 2.62 mg/dL, sodium 118 mEq/L, and potassium 4.5 mEq/L. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.47, pCO2 31 mmHg, pO2 127 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, and lactate 1.7 mmol/L, with a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 530.8. Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score was 9. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated extensive gas in the left kidney and perirenal space extending to the contralateral perirenal region, and multiple low-density lesions with internal septations in the prostate gland. No urinary tract obstruction was observed. Blood and urine cultures subsequently grew Klebsiella pneumoniae.

A woman in her 40s presented to the emergency department with severe lower back pain, progressive bilateral lower limb weakness, and acute left-sided facial asymmetry. She had previously been fully independent and mobile. Past history included anxiety, depression, and thyroid cancer treated with total thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine roughly a decade earlier, resulting in hypothyroidism managed with levothyroxine. She had recently stopped several supplements on specialist advice after abnormal thyroid function tests. Following this, she developed flu-like symptoms with fever, myalgia, lethargy, and diarrhoea. Days later she developed sharp lower back pain and paraesthesia in the hands and feet, progressing over subsequent days to gait instability, inability to stand unaided, severe leg pain, urinary incontinence, and constipation. Approximately 24 hours before presentation, family noted new left facial droop and slurred speech. On examination she had normal sensation, a left lower motor neuron facial palsy, limb power 4/5 with normal tone, diminished bilateral ankle and knee reflexes with normal upper limb reflexes, and reduced anal tone. Thyroid function showed markedly elevated TSH with low-normal free T4; other routine bloods were largely unremarkable. Imaging of the brain, whole spine, and torso showed no acute abnormality. Within 24 hours she developed worsening limb weakness, dysphagia, worsening speech, hypotonia with diminished-to-absent reflexes in all limbs, external ophthalmoplegia, and declining respiratory reserve, prompting cerebrospinal fluid analysis, which showed markedly elevated protein with a normal white cell count and negative cultures.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A man in his late 40s, of North African descent, with a history of smoking and substance use disorder, presented to the emergency department following an episode of prolonged generalized convulsive activity lasting about 30 minutes. Family members described a one-year history of progressive lethargy, excessive urination and thirst, along with unexplained weight loss and increased appetite. On arrival he was obtunded with ongoing generalized tonic-clonic movements requiring airway support and intravenous anticonvulsant therapy. Initial testing showed markedly elevated capillary glucose (500 mg/dL), large ketonuria (+4), and a low serum bicarbonate (9 mmol/L) consistent with significant metabolic acidosis. After seizure control, he regained consciousness without focal neurological deficits, though post-ictal confusion persisted for several hours. Non-contrast brain CT was unremarkable. Brain MRI showed multiple bilateral white-matter hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR sequences in subcortical and periventricular regions with scattered microbleeds on susceptibility-weighted imaging. EEG performed after seizure control showed a normal background rhythm without epileptiform activity. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed elevated glucose with normal cell counts and negative cultures. Extended laboratory work-up revealed HbA1c of 15.2%, mild hyponatremia (130 mmol/L), low corrected calcium, elevated CRP (84 mg/L) with normal procalcitonin, elevated INR (1.5), and normal thyroid, adrenal, and viral hepatitis/syphilis serologies. There was no family history of seizure disorders or diabetes.

A woman in her late teens with a known history of bronchial asthma, not on regular controller inhaler therapy and with no prior hospital admissions for asthma, presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe shortness of breath that began shortly after eating seafood. On arrival she was in severe respiratory distress, dyspneic, tachypneic, tachycardic, and cyanosed, with oxygen saturation of 64% on room air and blood pressure 120/70 mmHg. Chest examination revealed bilateral diffuse wheezing with markedly reduced air entry. Initial arterial blood gas showed acute hypercapnic respiratory failure with respiratory acidosis (pH 7.23, PaCO2 68 mmHg, PaO2 50 mmHg, HCO3- 28 mEq/L, lactate 3.0 mmol/L). Chest radiography showed diffuse bilateral air-space opacities without focal consolidation or pneumothorax. Despite repeated nebulized bronchodilators, high-dose intravenous corticosteroids, and intravenous magnesium sulfate, her respiratory status progressively worsened with persistent hypoxemia and respiratory acidosis, requiring intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation. Post-intubation gases remained severely deranged. During ventilation she developed extensive subcutaneous emphysema and pneumomediastinum from dynamic hyperinflation. Blood gases continued to deteriorate to pH 7.00, PaCO2 115 mmHg, HCO3- 34 mEq/L, and lactate 14 mmol/L despite maximal ventilatory support, prompting escalation to extracorporeal life support.

train_cases.diagnosis: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia of B-cell type not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: A man in his 60s with a history of rheumatoid arthritis (not on disease-modifying agents) and Raynaud's phenomenon presented with several days of new, raised skin lesions on both palms that progressively ulcerated and spread to the elbows, accompanied by diffuse body-wide joint aches and worsening of his baseline chronic joint pain. One year prior, he had been diagnosed with a tick-borne rickettsial illness with a similar skin presentation and was treated with a prolonged course of doxycycline; at that time he had marked leukocytosis. Further history revealed an unintentional 40-pound weight loss over the preceding three months. On examination, skin lesions ranged from nodules to large erythematous, macular lesions with central necrosis. There was no history of incarceration but this was considered given endemic exposure concerns. Vital signs were not significantly abnormal. Laboratory studies showed marked leukocytosis (white blood cell count 135.4 x10^3/uL, compared with 24 x10^3/uL roughly a year earlier), with a lymphocytic predominance and no atypical lymphocytes or bandemia noted, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, and platelets 161 x10^3/uL. Computed tomography showed hepatosplenomegaly with evidence of portal hypertension, retroperitoneal and pelvic lymphadenopathy, and numerous small nodules in the lung bases. Initial differential considerations included recurrent rickettsial infection, pyoderma gangrenosum, vasculitis, and cutaneous mycobacterial infection. Empiric doxycycline was restarted while further diagnostic workup was pursued, including peripheral blood studies and a skin biopsy.

A 21-month-old male toddler was brought to the emergency department with pain and swelling of the left scrotum for the past 18 hours. The parents reported a preceding fall from a height of approximately 1 foot with trauma to the perineal region. The pain was sudden in onset and progressive, associated with scrotal swelling. There was no history of hematuria, nausea, vomiting, or fever, and no other significant past medical history. On examination, the right testis appeared normal, while the left testis was edematous and tender to palpation. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated findings suggestive of a testicular fracture with a loculated collection and no demonstrable vascularity in the left testis. Given the clinical picture, emergency scrotal exploration was planned.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis, unspecified with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A woman in her late 20s presented to the emergency department with chest discomfort, palpitations, sweating, left arm paraesthesia, weakness, and exhaustion. She reported a one-month history of episodic focal seizure activity predominantly affecting her left arm, followed by post-ictal drowsiness; she had experienced six such episodes over the month, four affecting the left side, with increasing frequency. She also described several weeks of fatigue, palpitations, and unintentional weight loss. Past medical history included hypothyroidism previously treated with levothyroxine (discontinued a few years earlier), type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin and an SGLT2 inhibitor, mixed anxiety-depressive disorder, and polycystic ovarian syndrome. There was no history of alcohol excess or illicit drug use. On initial examination she appeared clinically stable; blood pressure was 131/64 mmHg, pulse 94 bpm, temperature 37.1°C, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on air. Laboratory testing showed a markedly suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (<0.01 µU/mL; reference 0.27-4.20) with markedly elevated free thyroxine (>100 pmol/L; reference 11.3-21.6). Plasma ketones were elevated at 6.2 mmol/L with normal blood glucose (8.1 mmol/L) and venous pH 7.29. Alternative causes of the metabolic derangement, including recent seizures, infection, reduced oral intake, alcohol, and drug overdose, were considered. An initial brain CT showed extensive dense falx calcification, unusual for her age, along with frontal lobe hypodensities.

A woman in her late 20s presented to the emergency department with a four-day history of severe abdominal pain, nausea, fever, and muscle pain. She had recently started a new injectable medication for obesity treatment and related the onset of symptoms to this. She had a history of depressive disorder treated with two psychiatric medications. On examination, there was tenderness in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen with a positive Blumberg's sign in that area. No other symptoms were present at admission. Point-of-care ultrasonography showed thickening of the gallbladder wall and slight enlargement of the right kidney without evidence of urine stasis. A formal ultrasound confirmed gallbladder wall thickening up to 5 mm with pericholecystic oedema, no gallstones, deposits, or bile duct dilatation, and liver enlargement up to 18 cm. Blood tests showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, markedly elevated C-reactive protein and procalcitonin, mildly elevated creatinine, and normal bilirubin and GGTP. Urinalysis showed increased erythrocytes and leukocytes per high-power field. About four hours later, on surgical consultation, a positive Goldflam's sign (costovertebral angle tenderness) developed on the right side. A CT scan revealed liver enlargement up to 20 cm, periportal and perivesicular edema, marked enlargement of the right kidney with numerous wedge-shaped areas of poor contrast enhancement predominantly in the arterial phase, perinephric fluid, and small amounts of fluid in the peritoneal and both pleural cavities.

A 44-year-old woman with no known drug allergies was admitted for evaluation of symptomatic anemia and systemic illness. She reported several days of progressive fatigue prior to admission, prompting inpatient work-up. During hospitalization her hematologic status evolved rapidly, with worsening anemia, leukocytosis, and fluctuating platelet counts requiring close monitoring. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 6.5 g/dL (later improving to 9.9 g/dL), hematocrit 21%, RBC 1.97 x10^6/uL, elevated MCV (106.6 fL) and RDW (30.5%), and marked reticulocytosis (16.2%). Platelet count was markedly reduced at 26 x10^3/uL with subsequent recovery. WBC count was elevated at 13.5-18.5 x10^3/uL with neutrophil predominance. Lactate dehydrogenase was markedly elevated (996 U/L) with low haptoglobin (<20 mg/dL) and indirect hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL, direct 1.0 mg/dL). AST and ALT were mildly to moderately elevated; renal function (creatinine, BUN) was normal. Troponin I was mildly elevated and rose during the course. Coagulation studies showed mild PT/INR prolongation with normal aPTT and preserved fibrinogen. Peripheral smear showed numerous schistocytes with anisocytosis and polychromasia. Direct antiglobulin test was negative. Infectious workup (HIV, hepatitis C, syphilis) was negative; hepatitis B serology reflected prior immunization. Urinalysis showed mild proteinuria and hematuria. CT brain, chest imaging, echocardiography, abdominal ultrasound, and lower extremity venous ultrasound were all unremarkable.

A man in his mid-50s with hepatitis B-related cirrhosis, well-controlled type 2 diabetes, and hypertension presented for evaluation of cardiac abnormalities. He had undergone resection of a hepatic mass approximately four months earlier and had since received two cycles of an anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody, with the most recent dose given about two months prior to presentation. He had remained asymptomatic after the first infusion. An ECG obtained before the second infusion showed a new complete left bundle branch block with QRS widening (152 ms) and QTc prolongation (493 ms), compared with a baseline tracing that had shown only nonspecific ST-segment changes and poor R-wave progression. Approximately three weeks before admission he developed an upper respiratory illness with transient chest tightness and dyspnea, which resolved with symptomatic care; no pathogen was identified. Coronary angiography performed at that time showed only mild (40%) proximal left anterior descending stenosis. On admission, BNP was mildly elevated (117.2 pg/mL) with normal high-sensitivity troponin I. ECG showed further QRS widening (167 ms) and QTc prolongation (487 ms). Echocardiography showed a mildly enlarged left ventricle with reduced ejection fraction (45%). Cardiac MRI showed septal hypokinesia, mild wall thickening, bilateral pleural effusions, diffusely elevated T2 and native T1 values, elevated extracellular volume, and no late gadolinium enhancement. Endomyocardial biopsy showed myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial edema, and sparse lymphocytic infiltrate with predominant CD3+/CD4+ T cells and CD68+ macrophages, with negative CD8 and CD20 staining.

A man in his late 40s presented to the emergency department with a several-day history of progressive generalized weakness, diffuse extremity pain, and dizziness, culminating in a fall with a laceration to the left parietal scalp. He was hemodynamically stable on arrival. His past medical history included arterial hypertension, tobacco use, hyperlipidemia, non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, a prior myocardial infarction treated with coronary stenting, and depressive episodes managed with an antidepressant; he also reported chronic heavy alcohol use. Home medications included an SSRI antidepressant, ezetimibe, and a statin. Surgical evaluation determined the scalp laceration did not require repair, and cranial CT excluded acute hemorrhage, ischemia, or a space-occupying lesion. Venous blood gas showed metabolic acidosis (base excess -13 mmol/L) and hyperkalemia (potassium 7.5 mmol/L). Laboratory testing revealed markedly elevated renal retention parameters and strikingly elevated creatine kinase (92,047 µg/L) and myoglobin (136,554 µg/L). The patient became oligo-anuric with evidence of fluid overload. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for further evaluation and management, and conservative measures to promote renal clearance were not feasible given the severity of his metabolic derangement and urine output failure.

A previously healthy man in his early twenties presented with sudden-onset weakness of the right side of the body. Initial brain MRI showed a focal area of restricted diffusion in the left basal ganglia, with no vascular abnormality on magnetic resonance angiography and no abnormal contrast enhancement. He was managed empirically for a presumed acute cerebrovascular event and made a complete recovery. Approximately two months later he developed a second episode with acute weakness of the opposite (left) side and slurred speech. Repeat MRI demonstrated bilateral basal ganglia signal changes on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted imaging that did not conform to any single vascular territory, with only minimal reduction on apparent diffusion coefficient mapping. Contrast-enhanced imaging additionally showed a new pattern of thin, linear enhancement radiating outward from the ventricular margins, which had not been present on the earlier study. Further diagnostic evaluation was initiated. Empiric high-dose intravenous corticosteroid therapy was given, with complete neurological recovery and resolution of the periventricular enhancement on follow-up imaging three months later. When steroids were subsequently tapered, the patient relapsed with dysesthesia of the right limbs and was found to have elevated cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure. A steroid-sparing immunosuppressive agent was added, achieving durable remission over subsequent follow-up.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A young adult male with no prior medical history presented to the emergency department with a five-day history of progressive left-sided facial swelling and high fever, followed by three days of shortness of breath and a rapid heart rate. Vital signs showed blood pressure 130/85 mmHg, heart rate 118 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Examination revealed marked edema of the left face involving the lips and submandibular region, with erythema and tenderness. Superficial ultrasound of the face showed diffuse soft tissue edema, inflammatory changes, and multiple microabscesses in the left facial and submandibular region. Labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 20.56×10^9/L), CRP 316.9 mg/L, mildly elevated AST/ALT, low albumin (32 g/L), hyponatremia (131 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (6.31 mmol/L), low corrected calcium, low uric acid, hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, and platelets 237×10^9/L. Blood cultures were drawn and empiric antibiotics started. Several days later the patient developed worsening dyspnea and hypoxia; chest CT showed multiple peripherally distributed pulmonary nodules, some with a feeding vessel sign and cavitation, plus wedge-shaped subpleural lesions. Echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations. Blood cultures later grew Staphylococcus aureus, sensitive to vancomycin, clindamycin, and meropenem, and targeted therapy was adjusted. The hospital course was complicated by bilateral pneumothoraces requiring chest tube placement, with subsequent resolution and discharge in stable condition.

A woman in her late 50s presented to the emergency department with a two-day history of severe throat pain, painful swallowing, subjective shortness of breath, and chills. Her past medical history included breast cancer previously treated with chemotherapy, radiation, and mastectomy, as well as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, peripheral neuropathy, and a remote history of tobacco use. On the first day of symptoms she could still tolerate oral intake, but she subsequently developed difficulty managing oral secretions and a muffled voice noted by a family member. Review of systems was otherwise negative, with no recent travel or known sick contacts. On examination she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable (temperature 37.0°C, heart rate 92 bpm, respiratory rate 17, blood pressure 140/96 mmHg, oxygen saturation 95% on room air). She appeared uncomfortable, with bilateral anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, post-nasal drip, an erythematous posterior oropharynx, edematous tonsils without exudate, a muffled voice, pain with tracheal rocking, and anterior neck pain on full neck extension. Laboratory workup showed leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance, elevated ESR, and elevated CRP, with procalcitonin, metabolic panel, urinalysis, blood cultures, rapid strep test, mononucleosis screen, and an extended respiratory pathogen panel all unremarkable or negative. Chest radiograph showed no acute pathology. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck showed a small amount of retropharyngeal soft tissue edema extending over several cervical vertebral levels, without discrete abscess. Given the nonspecific imaging findings, further direct airway visualization was pursued.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other specified congenital malformation syndromes, not elsewhere classified
train_cases.note: A woman in her early 30s presented with a 2-day history of sudden-onset, persistent non-rotatory dizziness and bilateral blurred vision, worse on left gaze, beginning immediately upon waking. She denied nausea, vomiting, hearing changes, dysphagia, dysarthria, headache, or dyspnea. She had no history of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, or smoking, and denied oral contraceptive use, illicit drug use, or ergot derivative exposure. Family history was notable for a father with aortic dissection who had undergone surgical repair. Vital signs were normal (blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, heart rate 72/min). Physical examination showed increased distance between the eyes and mild flattening of the cheekbones, without joint hypermobility (Beighton score 2/9), bifid uvula, long/thin fingers, chest wall deformity, or abnormal skin texture; cardiovascular, skeletal, and skin examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Neurological examination revealed a left homonymous hemianopia on confrontation visual field testing and mild decreased sensation on the left side, with normal cranial nerve, motor, cerebellar, and gait findings; NIHSS score was 3. Vascular imaging demonstrated tortuosity of the bilateral internal carotid and posterior cerebral arteries, an aberrant right subclavian artery with aneurysmal dilation (maximum 15 mm), and aneurysmal dilation of the right vertebral artery V1 segment. Aortic root diameter and echocardiography were normal, and CT angiography of the thorax and abdomen showed no dissection.

A man in his early 30s with a history of recurrent obstructive episodes suggestive of small bowel obstruction—at least five prior episodes managed conservatively at outside facilities without a definitive etiological diagnosis—presented to the emergency department with a five-day history of progressively worsening colicky abdominal pain. The current episode was associated with marked abdominal distension, nausea, multiple episodes of non-bilious vomiting, and absence of bowel movements and flatus. On initial evaluation he appeared mildly dehydrated but was hemodynamically stable. Abdominal examination revealed significant distension, decreased bowel sounds, and generalized tympany, with diffuse tenderness to deep palpation but no signs of peritoneal irritation. Hernial orifices were intact, with no evidence of external hernias or prior surgical scars. Laboratory evaluation showed hyponatremia (129 mmol/L) and hypochloremia (86 mmol/L), with normal potassium (3.74 mmol/L); white blood cell count and C-reactive protein were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated dilated small bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels and a well-defined transition point in the distal ileum. A blind-ending, sac-like outpouching arising from the antimesenteric border of the ileum was identified, containing intraluminal material and associated with a prominent feeding vessel. Given persistence of obstructive symptoms and imaging findings consistent with mechanical small bowel obstruction, the patient was taken for urgent exploratory laparotomy.

A 75-year-old man with a history of myasthenia gravis maintained on azathioprine and pyridostigmine, and generalized anxiety disorder treated with escitalopram and as-needed hydroxyzine, was transferred from an extended care facility to the emergency department with altered mental status and generalized weakness, occurring one day after discharge from a recent hospitalization for a urinary tract infection. Emergency medical services documented multiple episodes of wide- and narrow-complex tachyarrhythmia; on arrival he was noted to be in a supraventricular tachycardia that spontaneously converted to sinus rhythm, with blood pressure remaining stable throughout. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring and respiratory support after developing acute hypercapnic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation; treatment included intravenous immunoglobulin, intravenous corticosteroids, and continuation of home immunosuppressive therapy. Electrocardiography on hospital day two showed a markedly prolonged corrected QT interval of 563 ms with associated ventricular ectopy on telemetry; escitalopram and hydroxyzine were discontinued, and the QTc improved to 531 ms by day three. Admission labs showed sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, anion gap 14, and mildly elevated creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL, which normalized on repeat testing. There was no evidence of worsening generalized weakness during the hospitalization.

A man in his late 60s with well-controlled diabetes mellitus presented with a three-day history of binocular double vision, without headache, ocular pain, or antecedent infectious illness. Examination showed restricted adduction of the left eye and diplopia on lateral gaze; there was no dysarthria, dysphagia, dyspnea, limb weakness, or sensory disturbance. Thyroid function was normal, and glycated hemoglobin was 6.2%. Antibody testing showed an elevated acetylcholine receptor antibody titer (12 nmol/L); antibodies against GQ1b, nuclear antigens, myeloperoxidase, proteinase 3, and SS-A/SS-B were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed no aneurysm or structural lesion, and contrast-enhanced chest CT showed no mediastinal mass. Repetitive nerve stimulation of facial muscles showed a decremental response on low-frequency stimulation in some muscles but not others. Symptoms resolved with high-dose corticosteroid therapy but recurred twice over the following four months, each time responding to further steroid courses, with the antibody titer remaining stable. Seven months after onset, the patient developed worsening double vision and eyelid drooping, followed the next day by dyspnea, with oxygen saturation of 85% on room air. Examination then showed near-complete limitation of eye movements, ptosis, nasal speech, and mild weakness of eye-closure muscles, without limb weakness or swallowing difficulty. The antibody titer had risen to 81 nmol/L, while cardiac and chest imaging were unremarkable.

A man in his 40s with no prior medical conditions presented after a 2-hour course of rapidly worsening difficulty breathing. He worked as a plumber and had experienced a choking sensation at a new worksite that day, but denied throat pain, diarrhea, or accidental ingestion. He reported a 2-year history of rash and itchiness triggered by cold exposure. His child had a mild cough the preceding week. He had no known allergies, took no medications, and his immunization history was unclear. On arrival, respiratory rate was 30/min, SpO2 100% on 10 L/min supplemental oxygen, blood pressure 178/114 mmHg, and temperature 39.0°C. He was alert but in severe respiratory distress with marked stridor, unable to speak or lie flat; no oral pseudomembrane was seen. Given rapidly worsening obstruction, he was emergently intubated; bronchoscopy showed severe pharyngeal and laryngeal edema. There was no rash, generalized edema, or abdominal pain at that time. Labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 10.5×10^9/L, neutrophils 9.3×10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.84×10^9/L, eosinophils 0.021×10^9/L) and mildly elevated CRP (0.17 mg/dL); liver and kidney function were normal. SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. A respiratory antigen test was positive with a significantly elevated serologic titer, though PCR on tracheal aspirate was negative; blood cultures were negative and tracheal aspirate culture showed normal flora. CT showed marked pharyngeal and laryngeal swelling without tumor, abscess, or pneumonia, with near-complete airway obstruction.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection, unspecified
train_cases.note: A teenage female presented with a three-day history of epigastric pain, persistent vomiting (more than 10 episodes), and inability to tolerate oral intake. On admission, vital signs were stable (blood pressure 110/72 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm, temperature 37.2ºC). She appeared mildly dehydrated and had epigastric tenderness on examination without signs of peritonitis. Laboratory testing showed markedly elevated amylase (1097 U/L), normal hemoglobin, leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), and elevated liver enzymes (ALT, AST, GGT, alkaline phosphatase) with normal total bilirubin. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated pancreatic enlargement with altered echogenicity and free abdominal fluid, though bowel gas limited full visualization. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed diffuse pancreatic enlargement with decreased T1 signal, heterogeneous enhancement, mild T2 hyperintensity, ascites, and biliary sludge, without evidence of ductal obstruction. Given imaging findings suggesting a biliary etiology, laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed. Intraoperatively, widespread small (<5 mm) whitish peritoneal implants were noted, raising concern for a neoplastic process.
