Post-operative cross-sectional imaging confirmed persistent pancreatic inflammatory changes with abdominopelvic free fluid, extensive peritoneal and mesenteric micronodules, and reactive mesenteric lymphadenopathy, without a discrete mass lesion. Peritoneal biopsy was obtained given concern for possible malignant seeding. The patient was managed medically and improved clinically prior to discharge.

A toddler-aged boy presented with a three-day history of right-sided knee pain, swelling, and reduced ability to bear weight. Approximately one week prior, he had experienced a febrile illness with lower respiratory symptoms, which resolved after treatment with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. He had no known drug allergies and no history of trauma. On initial examination he was afebrile, active, and playful, with mild swelling of the right knee and reduced range of motion limited by pain; no rash or other systemic findings were noted. Ultrasound of the knee showed mild periarticular fluid with subcutaneous edema, without joint effusion or collection. He was managed conservatively with analgesia and observation. Two days later, he developed an erythematous maculopapular rash over the lower limbs with subtle early petechial-type change, along with new swelling and pain of the right elbow, and intermittent abdominal pain without vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, or distension. Abdominal ultrasound excluded intussusception and showed mesenteric lymphadenitis. Over the following days the rash increased in density with partial coalescence, progressing to nonblanching palpable lesions over the lower limbs. He remained systemically stable throughout, with normal blood pressure. Laboratory testing showed mild leukocytosis, reactive thrombocytosis, and mildly elevated inflammatory markers, with preserved renal function. Serial urinalysis showed no hematuria or proteinuria. Corticosteroids were not given, and he was managed supportively with close monitoring.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other specified congenital malformation syndromes, not elsewhere classified
train_cases.note: A male infant was born preterm at 34 weeks' gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery to a mother in a consanguineous marriage; this was her third pregnancy and third delivery. Birth weight was 2300 g, with Apgar scores of 7 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes. On examination the neonate had multiple dysmorphic craniofacial features: a round facial appearance, depressed nasal bridge, anteverted nostrils, low-set ears with simplified auricular folds, a small mouth with relative macroglossia, long philtrum, and micrognathia. Extremity findings included bilateral camptodactyly and persistently clenched fists. Within hours of birth the infant developed recurrent paroxysmal episodes of marked hypertonia, opisthotonic posturing, generalized tremors, and involuntary facial/oropharyngeal muscle contractions, consistently triggered by crying or painful procedures and resolving after removal of the stimulus and supplemental oxygen. After a period of partial stabilization, the infant was re-hospitalized at 1 month 20 days of age in critical condition with severe respiratory distress, cardiac rhythm disturbance, lethargy, complete absence of the swallowing reflex, and recurrent non-epileptic spastic episodes (EEG showed no epileptiform discharges). Laboratory testing showed leukocytosis, progressively worsening anemia, thrombocytopenia, and rising CRP and procalcitonin. Blood cultures grew a gram-negative organism. Serial chest radiographs showed bilateral infiltrates progressing to diffuse bilateral opacification; abdominal radiography showed intestinal gaseous distension without free air, and ultrasound showed mild splenomegaly.

A previously healthy adolescent male with recent international relocation approximately 80 days prior presented to the emergency department after two days of fever and sore throat. He had been evaluated the prior day at an urgent care clinic, where influenza and rapid streptococcal testing were negative, and he was discharged with a diagnosis of viral pharyngitis. Overnight, he developed persistent high-grade fevers and new difficulty swallowing, prompting emergency evaluation. On arrival, vital signs showed temperature 39.4°C, heart rate 143 bpm, blood pressure 123/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Initial examination revealed mild neck swelling. Over the following hours he rapidly deteriorated, developing shortness of breath, a muffled voice, and biphasic stridor, requiring supplemental oxygen and urgent airway management. Initial laboratory studies revealed severe leukopenia (WBC 0.21 x10^3/mcL) with an absolute neutrophil count of 0, markedly elevated C-reactive protein (34.6 mg/dL), and mild anemia (hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL). Blood cultures were obtained prior to antibiotic initiation. Imaging of the neck demonstrated extensive inflammatory soft-tissue changes with cellulitis, swelling of the epiglottis and prevertebral soft tissue, diffuse edema, mild upper airway narrowing, and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy with tiny foci of necrosis without frank abscess formation. He was started on broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and subsequently required intensive care admission for hemodynamic instability and airway support.

A 70-year-old male presented with right temporomandibular joint (TMJ) pain, initially evaluated at a dental clinic and referred for further assessment. On examination there was tenderness and swelling in the right preauricular region, with palpable dislocation of the right TMJ, inability to achieve normal occlusion, and deviation of the mandible to the left. He had a single remaining tooth (left mandibular canine) with no pathology and no evidence of odontogenic infection. Panoramic and TMJ-specific imaging showed dislocation of the right TMJ with flattening of the mandibular condyle and osteophyte formation. Cross-sectional imaging showed irregular resorption of the right mandibular condyle with surrounding sclerosis and osteophyte formation, relatively preserved articular fossa and eminence, and thickened soft tissue around the right condyle, raising concern for longstanding joint instability or prior undiagnosed dislocations. MRI showed bilateral anterior disc displacement (without reduction on the right) and a well-defined fluid collection with joint effusion in the right TMJ, without abscess or surrounding tissue infiltration. Manual reduction of the dislocation was unsuccessful due to pain, and reduction under general anesthesia was planned. Laboratory testing showed markedly elevated C-reactive protein (16.22 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.668 ng/mL). A fluctuant area over the right cheek was aspirated under local anesthesia, yielding yellow fluid sent for bacterial analysis. Admission was advised but initially deferred at the patient's request.

A woman in her late 20s, gravida 2 para 1, at 34 weeks of gestation, presented with one week of severe fatigue, headache, and a petechial rash over the lower extremities. She denied visual disturbances or abdominal pain. Her prior pregnancy was uncomplicated, and the current pregnancy had been uneventful until this presentation. Family history was non-contributory for hematologic or thrombotic disorders. On examination she appeared fatigued but was alert and oriented, with stable vital signs. Petechiae were noted over the lower extremities, and mild splenomegaly was palpable on abdominal exam. There was no jaundice, mucosal bleeding, or other skin lesions. There was no hypertension or proteinuria. Initial laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 8.5 g/dl (reference 12-16), platelet count 45,000/μl (reference 150-450 x10^3/μl), lactate dehydrogenase 450 U/l (reference 140-280), indirect bilirubin 1.5 mg/dl (reference 0.2-1.2), and normal serum creatinine at 0.9 mg/dl, with otherwise normal liver and renal function. Peripheral blood smear showed schistocytes. Coagulation parameters and urinalysis were obtained. Given the acute onset of thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, and absence of hypertension or elevated liver enzymes, further specialized hematologic testing was pursued to clarify the underlying cause of this microangiopathic process in pregnancy.

A woman in her late 20s with a history of autoimmune thyroiditis (on levothyroxine) and major depressive disorder (on sertraline) presented with a five-day history of left-sided headache, followed by intermittent episodes of confusion and paranoia. Shortly before admission she experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure with loss of consciousness for approximately one hour; she received intravenous diazepam during transport. On arrival she was alert, oriented, and had no focal neurological deficits. Initial complete blood count, metabolic panel, and inflammatory markers were within normal limits. During hospitalization she developed recurrent seizures progressing to refractory status epilepticus, requiring ICU transfer, endotracheal intubation, and intravenous phenytoin. EEG showed generalized slowing with sparse epileptiform discharges. Brain MRI showed no acute infarction, hemorrhage, or mass effect, no diffusion restriction, and no abnormal enhancement; scattered T2/FLAIR hyperintensities were noted in subcortical white matter of the centrum semiovale and corona radiata bilaterally, sparing juxtacortical fibers. Cerebrospinal fluid cultures, a multiplex meningitis/encephalitis PCR panel, and an autoimmune encephalitis antibody panel (including neuronal surface antibodies) were negative, as were syphilis and HIV serologies. Thyroid antibody testing showed elevated anti-thyroglobulin and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies with normal TSH and free T4. Antinuclear antibody was positive at low titer with speckled pattern; extractable nuclear antigen panel and complement levels were normal.

train_cases.diagnosis: Malignant neoplasm of lower lobe, left bronchus or lung
train_cases.note: A man in his 50s presented with a six-month history of cough productive of whitish, mucoid sputum, together with progressively worsening exertional dyspnea (functional class II) that had intensified over the preceding 15-20 days. There was no fever, hemoptysis, or significant weight loss. He was a lifelong non-smoker with no history of diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, or occupational exposure to dust or carcinogens. On examination, vital signs were stable and oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Complete blood count and liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. Chest radiography showed persistent bilateral heterogeneous opacities, more pronounced in the left lower zone, without significant change despite several weeks of empirical antitubercular therapy given on clinicoradiological grounds. Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and nucleic acid amplification testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative. Sputum Gram stain showed gram-positive cocci in chains, felt to represent colonization given lack of clinical response. Flexible bronchoscopy showed inflamed airway mucosa without an endobronchial mass; bronchoalveolar lavage cytology was negative for malignant cells. High-resolution CT of the thorax revealed dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms, perilymphatic nodularity, and interlobular septal thickening. PET-CT demonstrated a metabolically active left lower lobe lesion, bilateral mediastinal lymphadenopathy, septal thickening with nodularity, a small pleural effusion, and an incidental right adrenal lesion.

A man in his 60s of South Asian descent, with a history of Alzheimer’s disease, coronary artery disease status post bypass surgery, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension, presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of fever and altered sensorium. He had a 15-year history of chronic alcohol use, with the last drinking episode about 10 days earlier, and a history of tobacco sniffing. There was no history of seizures, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, neck pain, dysuria, cough, head trauma, ear pain or discharge, skin rash, recent travel, or vaccination, and no recent respiratory or gastrointestinal illness. On examination he was drowsy, with a pulse of 150/min, blood pressure 80/60 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air; he was intubated for poor sensorium (Glasgow Coma Scale E1V2M1). Neck stiffness was absent, and Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs were negative; no rash, eschar, or lymphadenopathy was noted. The oculocephalic reflex was absent. Motor examination revealed 0/5 power in all four limbs with reduced tone, hyporeflexia, and bilaterally absent plantar reflexes; sensory and cerebellar testing were not assessable due to poor sensorium. Laboratory studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, acute kidney injury, and a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, with arterial blood gas findings consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis. A tropical fever panel (dengue, scrub typhus, malaria, leptospirosis) and urine toxicology screen were negative. He subsequently had two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed no pleocytosis, normal protein, and elevated glucose, with negative infectious and autoimmune studies. Brain CT and MRI were normal. Electrophysiological studies showed absent motor and sensory nerve responses in all four limbs.

A woman in her 60s presented to the emergency department with a five-day history of right lower limb pain and progressive inability to stand. Her medical history included hypertension, managed with regular medication for the past three months. She had no other past medical or surgical history. She reported a sudden onset of severe, electric shock-like pain originating in her right flank, shooting down her right leg and radiating distally, lasting approximately 15 minutes before resolving spontaneously. The pain was immediately followed by persistent numbness and significant generalized weakness, leaving her unable to stand on both lower limbs, though she denied frank paralysis. She had no fever, chest pain, abdominal pain, or history of trauma. On examination, she was conscious, oriented, cooperative, and hemodynamically stable (blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, heart rate 88 bpm). Cardiovascular and respiratory exams were unremarkable. Both lower limbs showed normal color, no hair loss, no dilated veins, no muscle atrophy, no swelling, ulceration, or gangrene, with normal capillary refill, no tenderness, and palpable distal pulses bilaterally. Neurological exam showed symmetrical reduction in motor strength (4/5) in both lower limbs without focal myotomal distribution, preserved and symmetrical deep tendon reflexes, and subjective paresthesia without a dermatomal pattern or sensory level. There was no saddle anesthesia, bowel or bladder dysfunction, and anal tone and bulbocavernosus reflex were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no proximal aortic involvement or cardiac source of emboli. Further cross-sectional vascular imaging of the abdomen was obtained to clarify the etiology.

A man in his late 60s with a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented with several days of generalized weakness. Vital signs on admission were stable. Neurological examination at that time showed normal strength, intact sensation, and preserved deep tendon reflexes without focal deficits. Initial labs showed serum sodium 123 mmol/L (corrected 127 mmol/L given glucose 365 mg/dL), mild acute kidney injury, and microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, MCV 72 fL). Renal function and hemoglobin trends were evaluated; gastrointestinal bleeding was excluded by negative occult blood testing and unremarkable endoscopy. Despite fluid management, serum sodium remained persistently low (fluctuating 116-128 mmol/L over the following week). Serum osmolality was low with inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality 476 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 140 mmol/L), thyroid and adrenal function were normal, and the patient remained clinically euvolemic without diuretic exposure. Over the subsequent days, the patient developed progressive, ascending bilateral lower then upper extremity weakness with generalized hypotonia and loss of deep tendon reflexes, followed by dysphagia and respiratory muscle weakness (negative inspiratory force -25 cm H2O) requiring intensive care admission. Head CT was unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed protein 95 mg/dL with white blood cells 19 cells/mm3, normal glucose, negative oligoclonal bands, and negative infectious studies.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute myeloblastic leukemia, not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: A previously healthy man in his early 60s presented to the emergency department after recent travel, reporting about two weeks of progressive fatigue, weakness, poor appetite, dizziness, and intermittent fever with chills. On the day of presentation he had six generalized tonic-clonic seizures associated with head trauma. He appeared pale and lethargic. Vital signs showed temperature 99.9°F, heart rate 158 bpm, blood pressure 102/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on nasal cannula. Exam showed marked pallor, mild facial swelling, and a maculopapular rash over both lower extremities, without lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Neurologically he was alert, oriented, and without focal deficits. Labs revealed marked leukocytosis (WBC 132.9x10^9/L), severe anemia (hemoglobin 5.4 g/dL), severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 11x10^9/L), hyperlactatemia, hyperuricemia, acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.1 mg/dL), and markedly elevated LDH with mild AST elevation. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive. Peripheral smear showed circulating immature myeloid cells. Non-contrast head CT was unremarkable; lumbar puncture was deferred given severe thrombocytopenia. Chest CT angiography showed mild ground-glass opacities and small pleural effusions, and chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly with left basilar opacities.

A woman in her 70s presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of vomiting, diarrhoea, and poor oral intake. Her medical history included a mechanical mitral valve replacement performed several years earlier for rheumatic valve disease, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. She had a history of recurrent falls with a prior intracranial haemorrhage while on warfarin, and epilepsy. She had no recent travel, no exposure to fresh water or hiking, and did not use intravenous drugs. She was anticoagulated with therapeutic-dose low-molecular-weight heparin, as she could not tolerate warfarin, and was not on immunosuppressive therapy. An echocardiogram performed several months earlier had shown a well-functioning prosthetic mitral valve and mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction. On arrival she was hypotensive (84/50 mmHg), tachycardic (126 bpm), febrile (38.9°C), and drowsy; physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. She required noradrenaline for haemodynamic support and was admitted to intensive care. Blood tests showed a CRP of 197 mg/L and white-cell count of 16x10^9/L. Chest radiograph showed low lung volumes and old bilateral humeral fractures, without focal consolidation. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Blood cultures grew gram-negative bacilli, later identified as Yersinia pseudotuberculosis; stool and urine cultures were negative. A transoesophageal echocardiogram performed once stabilized showed mobile echo-densities on the atrial surface of the mitral valve leaflets and annulus, without valve dysfunction or abscess formation.

A woman in her late 50s with no significant past medical or surgical history presented to the emergency department with sharp abdominal pain localized to the right iliac fossa, with two days of progressive worsening. She reported nausea without vomiting and low-grade fever. On examination there was abdominal distension with decreased bowel sounds, positive rebound tenderness, a positive psoas sign, and positive Rovsing's and Blumberg's signs. Initial laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated white blood cell count (12.19 x10^9/L) with elevated absolute neutrophils (8.55 x10^9/L), hemoglobin 15.10 g/dL, hematocrit 44.80%, and alkaline phosphatase 100 U/L. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels and normal colonic fecal loading. In the right iliac fossa, a thick-walled loop measuring up to 21 mm in diameter with 5 mm wall thickness was noted, with associated periappendiceal fat stranding and a small amount of free fluid and free air; other solid organs were unremarkable. No target sign or other feature of bowel telescoping was identified. The imaging was read as suggestive of a complicated inflammatory process in the right lower quadrant, with mechanical obstruction from an alternate underlying cause not excluded. Given clinical status, the patient was started on antibiotics and analgesics and taken for emergency surgical exploration.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A woman in her mid-30s with a history of Graves' disease, hypertension, and depression presented after being found in cardiac arrest. Home medications included methimazole and a beta-blocker, though outpatient adherence was uncertain; she had not been taking any psychotropic medications or other agents known to prolong the QT interval. Over the preceding year, following her Graves' disease diagnosis, she had unintentionally lost approximately 27 kg (60 lb). The evening before presentation she developed chest pain radiating to the left arm, which intensified over the following day. While being transported to the hospital, she developed seizure activity and collapsed. Emergency medical services found her pulseless, in ventricular fibrillation. After prolonged resuscitation efforts, return of spontaneous circulation was achieved, though she required a second round of cardiopulmonary resuscitation for recurrent ventricular fibrillation. She was subsequently intubated, sedated, and admitted to the intensive care unit for further management.

train_cases.diagnosis: Benign neoplasm of unspecified adrenal gland
train_cases.note: A man in his mid-30s presented with a 24-year history of painful, recurrent ulcerations and necrosis affecting both lower limbs. Symptoms began in early adulthood with erythema and pain in the left foot following exposure to alternating heat and cold, then progressively extended to both legs and feet with recurrent ulceration over subsequent months and years. Multiple courses of antimicrobial therapy produced a poor response. Skin biopsy performed early in the course showed leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics, and vasodilators produced only transient improvement, with exacerbations recurring one to two times yearly, typically after cold exposure and during spring and autumn, each leaving residual hyperpigmentation and atrophic scarring. He was a long-term smoker with no family history of similar illness and no other systemic symptoms. On examination there was atrophic scarring and hyperpigmentation of both lower extremities with irreversible necrosis of the tip of the left second toe. Complete blood count, vasculitis screen, and autoimmune panel were unremarkable, without evidence of coagulopathy. Repeat skin biopsy after admission showed nonspecific vasculitis. Duplex ultrasound and CT angiography of the lower-limb vessels were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed an adrenal mass measuring approximately 4.8 x 3.7 cm. Plasma norepinephrine, dopamine, and normetanephrine were markedly elevated, as was 24-hour urinary norepinephrine excretion; levels fluctuated with symptom severity, peaking during episodes of acute pain and limb swelling. ACTH, sex hormones, and parathyroid hormone were normal. The patient later noted transient symmetrical cyanosis of the trunk and limbs after cold exposure, and denied palpitations, sweating, dizziness, or headache.

A man in his mid-40s presented with a two-day history of fever, confusion, and worsening pain in the left upper arm. His history included type 1 diabetes mellitus (recent HbA1c 78 mmol/mol), hypertension, a previous ischemic stroke, and a permanent dual-chamber pacemaker implanted several years earlier for complete heart block. He had also recently sustained a nonoperatively managed fracture of the left proximal humerus. He used a flash glucose monitoring sensor on the left upper arm, and the skin at the insertion site showed extensive erythema, ulceration, and purulent discharge, with tenderness extending to the shoulder. On admission, blood tests showed white cell count 9.8x10^9/L (normal 4.0-11.0), CRP markedly elevated at 421 mg/L (normal <5), pH 7.3, lactate 3.5 mmol/L, glucose >24 mmol/L, and ketones 2 mmol/L. Blood cultures taken on admission grew Staphylococcus aureus in all four bottles. Intravenous antibiotics were changed from piperacillin-tazobactam to flucloxacillin, but repeat blood cultures over the following week continued to grow the same organism, with the first negative culture obtained after about ten days. Imaging of the left shoulder showed gas within the joint space. Further whole-body imaging demonstrated a large glenohumeral joint effusion with increased metabolic uptake in surrounding soft tissue. A transthoracic echocardiogram performed six days after admission showed no valve or lead abnormality. Because bacteremia persisted, surgical washout of the shoulder was performed roughly four weeks after admission, with cultures again growing Staphylococcus aureus.

A woman in her late 70s presented to the emergency department with chest pain and exertional dyspnea (NYHA class III) that had progressively worsened over the preceding week, accompanied by marked fatigue and diaphoresis. Her medical history included severe aortic valve stenosis diagnosed several years earlier, previously asymptomatic; a stress test performed a few months prior had been unremarkable, and a conservative watchful-waiting approach had been adopted. On arrival, she was found to have a low-grade fever (37.8°C), tachycardia (110 bpm), and normal blood pressure, with clinical signs of acute decompensated heart failure including pulmonary crackles and peripheral edema. A loud systolic murmur was noted on auscultation. Laboratory studies showed an elevated C-reactive protein (134 mg/L), elevated troponin (259 ng/L), and markedly elevated NT-proBNP (26,317 ng/L). Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy but no acute ischemic changes. Transthoracic echocardiography showed two mobile, friable, supracentimetric masses attached to the tricuspid valve, one on the atrial side and one on the ventricular side, along with thickening of the anterior aortic annulus. The aortic valve was severely calcified and stenotic, with a peak velocity of 4.5 m/s and a valve area of 0.7 cm². A high-velocity flow signal (>5 m/s) was detected near the interventricular septum, adjacent to the ventricular mass. Blood cultures were obtained for further evaluation.

A 39-year-old Middle Eastern male with a history of hypertension (managed with a three-drug combination antihypertensive regimen), obesity, heavy smoking, and lumbar disc prolapse presented to the emergency department with progressively worsening shortness of breath and cough. He reported recent exposure to a respiratory illness among family members. On examination he was conscious and alert but hypoxic (oxygen saturation 85% on room air), tachycardic, and hypertensive. Chest examination revealed decreased air entry at both lung bases with fine bibasilar crepitations; the remainder of the examination, including cardiac auscultation, was unremarkable, and no Marfanoid features or stigmata of connective tissue disease were noted. Oxygen supplementation improved saturation to 95%. Given the acute hypoxic presentation, pulmonary embolism was suspected and CT pulmonary angiography was performed; this excluded embolism but showed bilateral patchy ground-glass opacities suggestive of an infectious or inflammatory process, along with an incidental markedly dilated ascending aorta suggestive of a large aneurysm. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia with non-specific changes. Troponin was normal, renal function was preserved, and C-reactive protein was mildly elevated. Echocardiography demonstrated preserved ventricular function with severe aortic regurgitation and marked aortic root dilation. He subsequently developed worsening hypoxia requiring escalation to high-flow oxygen therapy, and empiric antibiotics, corticosteroids, and strict blood pressure control were started.

A man in his 20s presented with a one-week history of headache, fever, and progressive memory decline. He had no prior neuropsychiatric history and no relevant family history. Approximately two weeks before admission, he developed intermittent fever (up to 39°C) and headache following an upper respiratory tract infection. A cranial CT scan performed early in the illness showed no significant abnormalities. He was treated empirically with an antibiotic and a corticosteroid, which improved the headache, but low-grade intermittent fevers persisted. About ten days after symptom onset, he developed new memory impairment, behavioral abnormalities, and personality changes, prompting further neurological evaluation; a Mini-Mental State Examination performed at that time scored 13/30, indicating significant cognitive impairment. Given this abrupt clinical evolution, he was referred for inpatient assessment. On admission, laboratory testing showed peripheral leukocytosis (18.27 × 10^9/L). Routine biochemistry, antinuclear antibody panel, and thyroid function studies were within normal limits. HIV and syphilis (rapid plasma reagin) screening were non-reactive. Chest CT and abdominal ultrasound, performed to screen for an occult malignancy, showed no masses or suspicious lesions.

An older adult presents to the hospital with symptoms leading to further cardiac evaluation. The patient has a history of malignancy for which systemic immunotherapy was initiated approximately two months prior to this presentation. One year before this admission, a routine electrocardiogram had incidentally shown an atypical atrial arrhythmia with variable conduction, without associated symptoms. Approximately one week before admission, a repeat electrocardiogram again showed an atypical atrial arrhythmia, this time with a new right bundle branch block pattern. On the day of admission, the patient was found to have a slow, regular heart rate and was admitted for further workup. Physical examination revealed a distressed-appearing patient with regular but bradycardic pulse. Cardiac evaluation on admission revealed sinus rhythm with complete heart block and ventricular escape rhythm. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, markedly elevated liver transaminases and alkaline phosphatase, elevated lactate, and substantially elevated cardiac biomarkers including troponin, creatine kinase-MB, and total creatine phosphokinase. Coronary angiography showed no obstructive coronary artery disease. Echocardiography after temporary pacemaker placement showed preserved left ventricular ejection fraction with a severely dilated left atrium and reduced cardiac index. Cardiac PET imaging showed no abnormal myocardial glucose uptake. A skeletal muscle biopsy was performed and demonstrated active inflammatory changes with clusters of muscle fiber necrosis and dense lymphocytic and macrophage infiltration.

A man in his late 60s presented to hospital with acute-onset chest pain. Contrast-enhanced computed tomographic angiography of the chest and abdomen demonstrated an intimal flap originating near the distal aortic arch, creating two flow channels (true and false lumina) that extended down to the level of the celiac artery takeoff. The abdominal visceral branches (celiac, superior mesenteric, and both renal arteries) arose from the true lumen. Initial management was conservative, consisting of analgesia and blood pressure control, with no intervention performed at that time. Approximately 18 days into the hospital course, the patient developed sudden oliguria with worsening renal function. Repeat CT angiography showed further distal extension of the false lumen with compression of both renal arteries, and reduced early-phase renal parenchymal enhancement was noted, consistent with impaired renal perfusion; no ischaemia was identified in other abdominal organs. Continuous haemodiafiltration was started for acute renal failure. Detailed ECG-gated CT analysis localized the primary intimal defect to a point less than 20 mm distal to the left subclavian artery origin, along the greater curvature of the distal aortic arch. No fever, no prior cardiac history, and no other past medical history were specified. Vital signs and detailed physical examination findings beyond the presenting chest pain were not described in the available record.

A man in his 30s with class III obesity (BMI 51 kg/m²) and no other significant past medical history presented with three days of severe right flank pain radiating to the groin. The pain began suddenly approximately one hour into yard work (mowing the lawn) on a warm day, progressing from 7/10 to 10/10 in severity, and was accompanied by one episode of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis and generalized weakness. He denied alcohol use, recreational or intravenous drug use, statin therapy, recent new medications, travel, prolonged immobilization, and any personal or family history of muscle disease or exercise intolerance. On arrival, temperature was 39.1°C, heart rate 120 bpm, blood pressure 165/98 mmHg, with dry mucous membranes and marked right costovertebral angle tenderness. Later examination revealed focal tenderness over the right anterior thigh without swelling, induration, or neurovascular compromise. Initial labs showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, normal creatinine, and markedly elevated AST with a lesser elevation in ALT, normal alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin; urine dipstick was strongly positive for blood but microscopy showed few red blood cells. Lipase and calcium were mildly low. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast showed a small extraluminal calcification near the left ureterovesical junction, with no hydronephrosis or obstructing stone. Right upper quadrant ultrasound showed hepatic steatosis with mild common bile duct dilation. Creatine kinase, checked after admission, was found to be markedly elevated, with subsequent decline in both CK and AST over several days; creatinine remained normal throughout. MRCP and viral hepatitis serologies were unremarkable.

A man in his 70s, a retired physician, with a 26-year history of hypertension treated with an ACE inhibitor, a 26-year history of type 2 diabetes managed with insulin, and long-standing atrial fibrillation managed with an antiarrhythmic but no anticoagulation, was brought to the emergency department by family. He also reported chronic heavy daily alcohol use since childhood. Five days before admission he developed behavioral changes, difficulty communicating, poor eye contact, and fluctuating inattention at home; head trauma was ruled out and the family initially attributed this to alcohol intoxication. Over the following four days his agitation and language difficulty progressively worsened, but care was not sought until day five due to lack of improvement. On arrival, vital signs were blood pressure 139/74 mmHg, heart rate 95 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air; history was obtained from his daughter due to impaired communication. Neurological exam showed disorientation, impaired attention and short-term memory, disorganized nonfluent speech with paraphasic errors and neologisms, intact naming and repetition, normal cranial nerves, normal strength and tone, symmetric reflexes, intact coordination, finger agnosia, acalculia, dysgraphia, and right-left disorientation. NIH Stroke Scale score was 5. Routine labs were within normal limits and ethanol level was zero. Electrocardiogram showed an irregular rhythm without discernible P waves. Cranial MRI revealed focal signal abnormalities with sulcal effacement in the left temporal and right temporoparietal lobes.

A man in his 40s presented with a 3-day history of fever and breathlessness. His past medical history included diabetes mellitus and dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease. On examination, he was tachycardic, tachypneic, and febrile. Transthoracic echocardiography and computed tomography of the chest revealed a large vegetation on the aortic valve in the left ventricular outflow tract with associated significant aortic regurgitation. He was electively intubated for respiratory support and scheduled for urgent cardiac surgery given the size of the vegetation. Blood cultures were drawn and empiric antibacterial therapy with ceftriaxone and vancomycin was started. Cultures flagged positive after approximately 34 hours of incubation, and a preliminary direct smear from the culture broth showed yeast-like cells and pseudohyphae, prompting addition of an antifungal agent. Serum antigen testing showed an elevated beta-D-glucan level and a positive galactomannan assay. He proceeded to surgical aortic valve replacement, where a large vegetation was found attached to the right coronary cusp without involvement of adjacent structures; the vegetation was sent for microbiological and histopathological analysis. Postoperatively he remained poorly responsive on the ventilator, developed high fevers, and required escalating vasopressor support with rising serum lactate over the following days.

A woman in her 80s, postmenopausal, presented with a one-year history of progressive muscle weakness and easy fatigability. Symptoms began insidiously with left eyelid drooping that gradually progressed over subsequent weeks to involve the right eyelid, without diplopia or blurred vision. She subsequently developed fatigable jaw and facial muscles, with difficulty chewing that worsened toward the end of meals, and her family noted slurred speech late in prolonged conversations, with frequent pauses. Four to five months before presentation she developed proximal upper limb weakness affecting overhead activities such as combing hair, followed by progressive proximal lower limb weakness with difficulty rising from a seated position and climbing stairs, later progressing to knee buckling and unsteady gait, with subjective truncal weakness. The weakness fluctuated, characteristically worsening with sustained activity and improving with rest. There were no sensory symptoms, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, or bowel/bladder dysfunction. Functional decline progressed from instrumental activities (household and outdoor tasks) to basic activities of daily living including bathing, dressing, and mobility. She had previously been evaluated by other primary care providers for these symptoms without significant improvement. On examination she appeared frail and undernourished, with patches of depigmentation on the face and around the eyes. Vital signs: blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, pulse 90/min, respiratory rate 24/min, oxygen saturation 94% on room air. She was alert and oriented. Examination revealed bilateral symmetric eyelid drooping without ophthalmoplegia, proximal upper limb weakness (3/5), mild distal upper and lower limb weakness (4/5), normal muscle tone, preserved symmetric deep tendon reflexes, bilateral flexor plantar responses, and unremarkable sensory and cerebellar examination. Initial laboratory studies showed mild normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL) with otherwise normal renal, hepatic, thyroid, and electrolyte panels, and negative viral serologies and antinuclear antibody testing.

A man in his late 50s with a history of hypertension (with reported medication non-adherence), hyperlipidemia, a known abdominal aortic aneurysm, obesity status post bariatric sleeve surgery, and arthritis presented after an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. He had been swimming and collapsed suddenly upon exiting the pool, with no preceding chest pain, dyspnea, or neurologic symptoms; he had attended a routine cardiology appointment earlier that same day. Bystander CPR was performed with return of spontaneous circulation achieved after two rounds of resuscitation; an advanced airway was placed in the field and later exchanged for an endotracheal tube. On arrival roughly 45 minutes after collapse, heart rate was 118 bpm and blood pressure 112/78 mmHg, which then fell to 72/48 mmHg, requiring norepinephrine for undifferentiated shock. He remained unresponsive with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 3 without sedation. Exam showed weak but symmetric radial pulses, dilated non-reactive pupils, absent gag reflex, and right thigh swelling. Point-of-care ultrasound of the neck vessels showed abnormal arterial wall findings bilaterally. Labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 16.5 x10^3/uL), mildly elevated creatinine (1.5 mg/dL from a baseline of 1.11), elevated AST, and normal troponin, lactate, and pH. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block. Cross-sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated extensive abnormal wall changes extending from the aortic root through the thoracic and abdominal aorta into both iliac systems, involving major arch and visceral branch vessels, with dilation of the proximal aorta. Brain MRI showed extensive acute multi-territory infarcts with loss of flow signal in several major cerebral and posterior circulation vessels.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other ectopic pregnancy without intrauterine pregnancy
train_cases.note: A woman in her mid-30s, gravida 2 para 1, presented at approximately 9 weeks' gestation with heavy vaginal bleeding. The pregnancy had been conceived spontaneously during a hormonal downregulation cycle preceding planned in vitro fertilisation for secondary infertility. Past history included a prior term vaginal delivery, previously treated chlamydial infection, adenomyosis, and bilateral tubal occlusion demonstrated on prior imaging. Initial serum hCG rose sub-optimally over 48 hours. Transvaginal ultrasound did not demonstrate a definite intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy, showing only a small avascular cystic structure of uncertain significance. She was managed expectantly with serial hCG measurement given the desired pregnancy and inconclusive imaging. Several days later she developed right iliac fossa pain; hCG continued to rise and repeat ultrasound raised the possibility of an early pregnancy sac, though findings remained equivocal. She remained haemodynamically stable throughout and was followed as a pregnancy of unknown location. Over the following two weeks, hCG rose progressively into the tens of thousands. A subsequent specialist ultrasound identified diffuse cystic changes within the myometrium alongside a discrete sac-like structure containing a fetal pole with no cardiac activity, located near the uterine cornu and not communicating with the endometrial cavity. Vital signs remained within normal limits and she had no fever.

A man in his mid-50s with known coronary artery disease, severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, hypertension, dyslipidemia, mild chronic kidney disease, and active smoking history had recently undergone implantation of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for primary prevention. Ten days after the procedure, he presented with malaise, low-grade fever, and mild erythema over the device pocket, without discharge or swelling. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, or symptoms of heart failure. On admission he was febrile (38.2°C) but hemodynamically stable. Cardiac auscultation revealed no murmurs, and there were no peripheral stigmata of systemic infection. Initial laboratory testing showed leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance, markedly elevated C-reactive protein, mildly elevated creatinine, and elevated NT-proBNP; procalcitonin, coagulation studies, and liver enzymes were near normal. Blood cultures obtained on admission grew a gram-positive organism identified as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. He was started on intravenous antibiotics, and the transvenous leads were extracted early in the admission without complication. A transesophageal echocardiogram performed two days after lead extraction showed a large, highly mobile echodense structure attached near the tricuspid annulus extending into the right atrium, along with an additional mass in the right atrial appendage.

An 80-year-old woman with a history of sarcoidosis, complete atrioventricular block treated with a dual-chamber permanent pacemaker, hypertension, and dyslipidemia presented with several months of worsening exertional dyspnea and dizziness. Evaluation identified severe aortic valve stenosis with associated heart failure symptoms (functional class II-III). Transthoracic echocardiography showed a heavily calcified aortic valve with peak velocity 4.1 m/s, mean transvalvular gradient 37 mmHg, stroke volume index 47 mL/m2, and valve area 0.51 cm2; left ventricular ejection fraction was preserved at 60%. Coronary CT angiography showed no significant coronary stenosis and favorable vascular access, but a steep aortic root angulation of 59 degrees with a sharp curvature into the proximal ascending aorta and minimal sinotubular junction calcification. Sinus of Valsalva diameters were 25.6 mm, 27.9 mm, and 27.9 mm. Given age and comorbidities, surgical risk was assessed as elevated, and after multidisciplinary review a transcatheter valve procedure was planned. During valve deployment, a transient device pop-out occurred, requiring recapture and deeper redeployment; the procedure was then completed. Immediately afterward, transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a new mobile flap-like structure in the aorta distal to the implanted valve, with acoustic shadowing limiting assessment near the valve frame. The patient remained hemodynamically stable with no pericardial effusion, and further cross-sectional imaging was obtained for characterization.

A man in his late 60s, originally from South Asia, was referred to an outpatient specialty clinic for evaluation of hypercalcemia identified incidentally on routine laboratory screening shortly after relocating to a new country; no prior calcium values were available for comparison. His past medical history included coronary artery disease with bypass surgery approximately a decade prior, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. He denied prior kidney stones, peptic ulcer disease, or thyroid disease, and had no known family history of calcium disorders or nephrolithiasis. He was a non-smoker. Current medications included low-dose aspirin, a beta-blocker, a statin, and an ACE inhibitor. He described chronic fatigue and mild diffuse musculoskeletal pain persisting for several years, previously attributed to aging, along with exertional shortness of breath. He also reported mild constipation and occasional mood lability, but denied excessive thirst, increased urination, confusion, or memory changes. On examination, he was an elderly-appearing man with a body mass index of 31.7 kg/m^2. The remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable aside from bilateral pitting edema of the lower extremities. Vital signs were not otherwise noted as abnormal. Further laboratory and imaging workup was pursued to evaluate the etiology of the elevated calcium level.

A man in his 60s presented to the emergency department with persistent chest pain lasting 3 days. Cross-sectional angiographic imaging of the aorta revealed a widened aortic contour with an intimal flap separating a true and false lumen, extending from the aortic root through the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta to the left external iliac artery, with involvement of the origins of the brachiocephalic trunk and left subclavian artery. Cardiac ultrasound (transesophageal and transthoracic) measured the aortic root diameter at 52 mm and demonstrated moderate regurgitant flow across the aortic valve, attributed to dilation of the valve annulus and interference of a mobile intraluminal flap with normal leaflet coaptation. No pericardial fluid collection was identified on initial cross-sectional imaging or echocardiography. Past medical history was notable for approximately 10 years of poorly controlled hypertension, with systolic blood pressure typically ranging 160-180 mmHg, and a cerebrovascular event 2 years earlier without residual neurologic deficit. No physical examination findings, vital signs at presentation, or laboratory results beyond the imaging and echocardiographic descriptions above were reported.

A man in his late 70s with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease, and recently diagnosed metastatic renal cell carcinoma on cabozantinib presented after transfer from an outside facility for evaluation of an elevated troponin. He reported several days of chest pain, back pain, progressive exertional dyspnea, and orthopnea. He had been given aspirin prior to transfer. On arrival, vital signs showed normal temperature, blood pressure 162/79 mmHg, heart rate 62 bpm, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Exam was notable for obesity, bilateral lower extremity edema, and venous stasis changes. EKG showed sinus rhythm, low voltage, left-axis deviation, and Q-waves in anterior precordial leads. Labs showed elevated high-sensitivity troponin (rising into the thousands ng/L), mildly elevated BNP, elevated CRP and ESR, unremarkable metabolic panel, and mild normocytic anemia. Chest X-ray showed mild cardiomegaly. He was admitted for decompensated heart failure and possible acute coronary syndrome and started on heparin. Creatine kinase returned markedly elevated, prompting discontinuation of statin therapy. Over the following days he developed worsening proximal muscle weakness, right-sided ptosis, right facial asymmetry, and escalating hypoxia requiring progressively higher respiratory support, with a reduced negative inspiratory force. CT chest showed no pulmonary pathology. Aldolase was elevated. Antibody panels and electrodiagnostic studies were pending at this stage of evaluation.

train_cases.diagnosis: Benign neoplasm of left adrenal gland
train_cases.note: A school-age male child (approximately 9 years old) with a known history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency presented to an eye clinic with blurred vision. Fundoscopic examination showed papilledema, prompting referral to the emergency department, where he was found to have markedly elevated blood pressure (190/130 mmHg) and was admitted to a pediatric intensive care unit for a hypertensive crisis, requiring a continuous intravenous antihypertensive infusion. History from the caregiver revealed recurrent, sudden-onset episodes of headache and profuse sweating occurring intermittently over the preceding two years, each lasting several minutes and resolving spontaneously without prior medical evaluation. On examination he was alert and in no acute distress, with normal heart sounds, well-perfused extremities, clear lungs, a soft non-tender abdomen without palpable masses, and a non-focal neurological exam. Serial blood pressure monitoring showed systolic values generally 128-160 mmHg and diastolic 80-98 mmHg, with heart rates 90-125 bpm, punctuated by two brief severe hypertensive/tachycardic episodes. Laboratory testing showed normal complete blood count and renal function, with mild, stable elevations in potassium and alanine aminotransferase. Urinary catecholamine metabolite levels were substantially elevated. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a well-defined, oval left adrenal mass (5.2 x 3.5 x 5.5 cm) with intense arterial-phase enhancement, a large central non-enhancing area containing hyperdense foci suggestive of vascular structures, adjacent mild fat stranding, and mild compression of the upper pole of the left kidney without invasion. Echocardiography showed mild-to-moderate concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with preserved systolic function. Brain imaging was unremarkable.

A woman in her 70s with a history of a cardiomyopathy diagnosed approximately a decade earlier, subclinical hyperthyroidism on low-dose antithyroid therapy, multinodular goiter, hyperlipidemia, and benign colonic polyps presented to the emergency department with a two-day history of worsening malaise, subjective fever, headache, nonproductive cough, generalized body aches, anosmia, and decreased appetite. She denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, or syncope. Vital signs on arrival: blood pressure 150/89 mmHg, heart rate 82 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 98.4°F, oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Initial labs revealed a mildly elevated high-sensitivity troponin, markedly elevated pro-BNP, elevated C-reactive protein, and mildly elevated ferritin; D-dimer, procalcitonin, LDH, and CPK were normal, and complete blood count and basic metabolic panel were unremarkable. A respiratory viral PCR was positive for a common seasonal pathogen. Initial electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with a nonspecific T-wave abnormality, most pronounced as inversion in the inferior leads, with QTc 452 ms. Chest radiograph showed bilateral lower-lobe atelectatic changes, and head CT showed age-related atrophy without acute findings. She was admitted for telemetry monitoring; a repeat troponin several hours later increased further, and a repeat EKG showed new, more extensive T-wave inversions in the inferior and lateral leads. She remained free of chest pain but had one episode of vomiting. Given concern for an acute cardiac process, she was started on antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy and transferred to a tertiary center for further evaluation.

A woman in her 40s with a history of depression presented to the intensive care unit with extensive skin lesions and epidermal loss involving the face, scalp, neck, torso, pubic region, and portions of the upper extremities. She reported a 2-3 week history of skin lesions that had progressively developed and worsened, with the face being the most severely affected area. She had been taking an anticonvulsant medication prescribed for management of her depression. No prior treatment for the skin findings had been administered before this admission. On evaluation, physical examination showed widespread epidermal detachment and denuded skin surfaces over the affected regions described above. Given the extent and appearance of the skin involvement, an acute infectious process was suspected, and wound cultures were obtained; a subsequent culture swab returned positive for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The patient was admitted for intensive supportive care, including systemic antibiotic therapy, intravenous immunoglobulin, anticoagulation prophylaxis, and nutritional support with attention to protein balance and vitamin supplementation, while a staged wound care plan was developed beginning with the most severely affected facial region.

A man in his mid-30s with no prior neurological history presented with a 3-day history of progressive left-sided weakness and numbness. Approximately 2 days before the onset of these neurological symptoms, he developed burning discomfort on the left side of the neck radiating to the shoulder and upper arm, along with a pruritic vesicular rash in a cervical dermatomal distribution. He was started on antiviral therapy for a presumed dermatomal viral rash, but despite this treatment his neurological symptoms progressed. He denied visual symptoms, balance disturbance, or cognitive changes, fever, recent travel, toxin exposure, or vaccination. There was no family history of neurological or autoimmune disease, no chronic medical conditions, and no tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drug use. He was previously independent in all activities of daily living. On examination, vital signs were normal and he was afebrile. Cranial nerves were intact with no meningeal signs. A pruritic vesicular rash with erythematous papules was present over the left lower neck extending to the mid-back. Neurological examination showed left-sided hemiparesis (4/5 strength in upper and lower limbs), reduced light touch and pinprick sensation over the left hemibody, mild dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing, and an ataxic gait with leftward veering. Blood counts, inflammatory markers, and HIV testing were unremarkable. Non-contrast CT of the brain showed a 3.5 cm hypodense right frontal white matter lesion without hemorrhage or midline shift. MRI demonstrated a ring-enhancing right frontal lesion with heterogeneous, focally thickened enhancement and surrounding edema but limited mass effect. Spinal MRI showed an enhancing intramedullary lesion at C2-C3. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed mildly elevated protein, oligoclonal bands, and normal cell count and glucose; viral PCR of CSF was negative.

A man in his late 60s presented with a one-week history of right-sided facial weakness, progressive difficulty swallowing, and bilateral lower limb weakness with associated decreased sensation. Approximately one month after admission, he developed sudden respiratory arrest requiring emergency intubation and mechanical ventilation. Nerve conduction studies/electromyography demonstrated extensive involvement of peripheral nerves in all four limbs, affecting both sensory and motor fibers. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed an elevated protein level with a normal cell count. Contrast-enhanced spinal MRI demonstrated abnormal enhancing foci within the spinal canal at the T11-L2 level with associated spinal cord compression and edema. Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT, performed to evaluate for occult malignancy or infection, showed increased tracer uptake along the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar nerve roots, as well as diffuse, heterogeneous hypermetabolism over the cerebral cortex, cerebellum, hypothalamic region, and dorsal medulla, with corresponding signal abnormalities on MRI. The patient also reported difficulty urinating. Color Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum revealed diffuse thickening of the scrotal wall with inflammatory changes of the right epididymis, testis, and spermatic cord, and areas of epididymal liquefaction; PET/CT showed intense hypermetabolism in the right prostate and testis. Biopsy of the testicular lesion showed inflammatory infiltration with a mixed population of T- and B-lymphocytes, partial CD5 co-expression, scattered plasma cells, and a Ki-67 proliferation index of 20%.

A woman in her late 40s, previously healthy, presented with acute onset of high fever (39°C), chills, severe headache, and myalgia. Molecular testing performed at symptom onset confirmed an arboviral infection, while dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and Mayaro virus infections were excluded by molecular and serologic testing. Fever and systemic symptoms persisted for about two weeks, after which she developed paresthesia in the lower limbs that progressively evolved into ascending weakness involving both upper and lower limbs, accompanied by bilateral facial weakness and progressive bilateral visual loss. A brief course of oral corticosteroids produced minimal improvement, and she was referred to a tertiary hospital approximately one month after symptom onset. On admission she had flaccid weakness of all four limbs, bilateral facial weakness, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Routine blood tests were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a normal cell count with markedly elevated protein. Electrophysiologic studies showed absent sensory nerve responses, mildly prolonged motor latencies, reduced motor amplitudes, delayed or absent F-waves, bilaterally absent H-reflexes, and reduced recruitment with increased motor unit activity on voluntary effort. Brain MRI showed bilateral facial nerve swelling; spinal MRI showed edema of lumbar nerve roots; orbital MRI was unremarkable. Ophthalmologic evaluation about three weeks after symptom onset showed visual acuity of 20/50 bilaterally, impaired pupillary light reflexes, red color desaturation, and mild optic disc edema without macular involvement. Infectious and autoimmune work-up, including HIV, hepatitis B/C, syphilis, tuberculosis, antinuclear antibody, aquaporin-4, and MOG antibody testing, was negative.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A woman in her mid-20s with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus (recent HbA1c 11.9%) presented to the emergency department with progressively worsening right flank pain and generalized body aches, similar to an episode of pyelonephritis diagnosed about three weeks earlier. She denied dysuria, urgency, or frequency. On examination she was febrile (38.5°C), tachycardic (116 bpm), and hypertensive (154/89 mmHg), with bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis was negative for leukocyte esterase and nitrites; complete blood count showed marked leukocytosis with a left shift. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 3.6 cm focal hypodense region in the left renal parenchyma without rim enhancement or fluid collection, and subtle inflammatory changes in the contralateral kidney. Past history was notable for angioedema and urticaria after ceftriaxone during the prior episode three weeks ago; because of this, oral levofloxacin 750 mg daily was started. During admission she developed nausea, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat labs showed hyponatremia, hypochloremia, low bicarbonate, an elevated anion gap, ketonuria, marked glucosuria, and a serum glucose within the normal range.

A man in his mid-60s with a history of laparoscopic surgery for gastroesophageal reflux disease (fully resolved) and no other chronic illnesses presented after 3 months of progressively worsening unresponsiveness and behavioral change. Those around him reported slowed responsiveness, urinary and fecal incontinence, apraxia with dressing, and disorientation. During the illness course he had a single generalized tonic-clonic seizure with loss of consciousness lasting about 10 minutes, and lost 5 kg of body weight. Cognitive assessment was limited by his mental state; a structured encephalopathy severity scale was markedly abnormal and functional status was severely impaired (Barthel Index 40). Routine cerebrospinal fluid cell counts and glucose were normal, though protein was mildly elevated (485.6 mg/L). A 24-hour EEG showed no epileptiform discharges. Cranial MRI demonstrated mild bilateral hippocampal and mesial temporal lobe volume loss. Whole-body 18F-FDG-PET-CT showed mild hypermetabolism at the gastroesophageal junction; subsequent upper endoscopy revealed no neoplastic lesion, and no other abnormal metabolic foci were identified. Testicular ultrasound incidentally revealed a small calcified lesion in the right epididymal tail. Peripheral blood lymphocyte subset analysis showed CD19+ and CD20+ B-cell percentages of 12.59% and 12.58%, respectively.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A woman in her early 30s with a 22-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus, previously well controlled, along with thyroid nodules and a left breast desmoid tumor (diagnosed after biopsy confirmed rapid enlargement of a previously stable mass), presented for evaluation of progressively worsening glycemic control. She had recently begun an investigational systemic therapy trial for her desmoid tumor. Within the first weeks of starting this therapy, she developed marked hyperglycemia, with blood glucose values documented above 250 mg/dL. She was subsequently hospitalized for acute metabolic decompensation despite reported adherence to a premixed 70/30 insulin regimen, which she had been using due to cost-related limitations after losing insurance coverage. No infectious source or pregnancy was identified as a precipitant. After hospitalization, her glycemic control remained difficult, with home blood glucose readings ranging from 180-300 mg/dL despite insulin dose escalation. She declined continuous glucose monitoring and insulin pump therapy. She was later transitioned to a basal-bolus insulin regimen with ongoing dose adjustments due to glycemic variability, including symptomatic hypoglycemic episodes. Hemoglobin A1c during this period ranged from 7.9% to 8.3%. Physical examination and additional vital signs were not detailed beyond the above findings.

A woman in her 70s with a long-standing history of thymoma-associated generalized myasthenia gravis (diagnosed roughly 15 years earlier, following resection of an invasive thymoma decades prior) presented with rapidly progressive memory impairment evolving over about 10 days. Her myasthenia had been clinically stable on a maintenance regimen including a complement/FcRn-targeted biologic infusion, low-dose oral corticosteroid, a calcineurin inhibitor, and pyridostigmine. She also had a history of chronic empyema; family history was unremarkable and she had no history of smoking or alcohol use. Over the preceding days she developed difficulty recognizing cohabiting family members' names, followed by progressive disorientation and difficulty navigating familiar routes. On admission, neurological examination showed mild disturbance of consciousness and marked impairment on standardized cognitive testing, particularly affecting orientation, delayed recall, calculation, and object memory. Cranial nerve examination was normal; there was mild neck flexor and extensor weakness without ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, dysarthria, or dysphagia. Sensory, cerebellar, and autonomic examinations were normal, and no seizures or abnormal movements were observed. Routine labs were normal aside from mildly reduced serum IgG; serum sodium was normal, and no metabolic derangement, hypoglycemia, hypotension, or hypoxia was identified. Brain MRI showed bilateral medial temporal (hippocampal/amygdalar) hyperintensity on FLAIR, T2, and diffusion-weighted sequences. Electroencephalography showed diffuse theta-alpha slowing without epileptiform discharges. Cerebrospinal fluid showed a mildly elevated cell count with normal protein and IgG index; infectious studies were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT showed progressive pleural dissemination of the known thymoma.

train_cases.diagnosis: Benign neoplasm of unspecified adrenal gland
train_cases.note: A woman in her mid-20s presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of sudden-onset diffuse abdominal pain, more than ten episodes of vomiting, pleuritic chest pain, and a new productive cough. She denied fever, diarrhea, urinary symptoms, weight loss, or sick contacts. She had a history of hypothyroidism with poor compliance to low-dose levothyroxine. There was no history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, thromboembolic events, or allergies. On presentation she was mildly hypoxemic (SpO2 90% on room air), tachycardic (HR 124/min), and tachypneic (RR 30/min), with normal blood pressure. Exam showed reduced air entry with crackles on the left hemithorax and generalized abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs; bedside ultrasound showed minimal pelvic free fluid. Neurological exam was unremarkable. Labs showed marked leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis with severe hyperlactatemia, acute kidney injury, transaminitis, markedly elevated troponin and creatine kinase, elevated inflammatory markers, elevated TSH, and low free T4. Chest radiograph showed left-sided consolidation with bilateral patchy opacities. She became hypotensic and was treated for presumed pneumonia with septic shock; blood cultures grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. She rapidly deteriorated with extreme tachycardia, required intubation and vasopressors, and sustained a cardiac arrest with return of circulation after resuscitation. Echocardiography showed severe global left ventricular systolic dysfunction (EF 20-25%) with a collapsed inferior vena cava. In the ICU she developed acute left lower-limb ischemia after femoral arterial catheterization; CT angiography showed complete occlusion of multiple left lower-extremity arteries and incidentally revealed a 4x4 cm left adrenal mass with peripheral arterial-phase enhancement and a central heterogeneous cystic component.

A 94-year-old male with a history of prostate cancer, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, bilateral knee osteoarthritis, left eye blindness, prior toe amputation for osteomyelitis, and longstanding movement disorder with baseline mild asymmetric resting tremor (left greater than right), chronic cognitive impairment limited to orientation, dysarthric speech, generalized weakness, and wheelchair dependence, presented after being found with acute left facial droop and inability to transfer from bed upon awakening. He had not been on any specific therapy for his baseline movement disorder. On admission, examination showed right upper and lower extremity strength 5/5, left lower extremity 4/5, and left upper extremity 3/5 with an associated resting tremor. Deep tendon reflexes were normal bilaterally without pathologic reflexes. Sensation was intact throughout. Muscle tone was normal without spasticity. Cranial nerve exam showed known impaired visual acuity in the left eye; other cranial nerves were intact. Speech was dysarthric with preserved comprehension. He had poor static and dynamic balance in sitting and standing. Initial non-contrast CT head showed no acute intracranial abnormality. MRI brain subsequently revealed multiple areas of acute signal abnormality involving the right frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes and the right insula. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for further workup and management, with subsequent significant decline in mobility, balance, and activities of daily living requiring inpatient rehabilitation.

A previously healthy adolescent male (early-to-mid teens) presented after the sudden onset of severe, one-sided scrotal pain while at home. He recalled a similar, self-limited episode of scrotal discomfort several weeks earlier that had resolved without evaluation. On this occasion the pain was severe and persistent, prompting him to seek help from a family member, and he was brought to the emergency department within approximately two hours of symptom onset. He rated the pain 9/10 and reported associated nausea. There was no history of trauma, fever, or urinary symptoms, and no other significant past medical history. On examination, the affected testis was noted to lie higher than the contralateral side with a horizontal (transverse) orientation. There was marked tenderness to palpation, erythema of the overlying scrotal skin, and the cremasteric reflex could not be elicited on the affected side. The contralateral testis appeared normal. Scrotal Doppler ultrasonography performed prior to intervention showed absent intratesticular arterial blood flow on the symptomatic side, with normal flow on the contralateral side.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A man in his 50s presented with a one-week history of polyuria, polydipsia, and dry mouth. A routine health check three months earlier had shown normal blood glucose. He denied excessive intake of sugar-sweetened beverages and had not experienced weight loss. On the day of presentation, urinalysis obtained at an outpatient clinic showed ketone bodies (3+) and glucose (3+), prompting referral for further evaluation. On admission, vital signs were: height 170 cm, weight 70 kg, temperature 36.8°C, blood pressure 112/72 mmHg, pulse 70/min, respiratory rate 16/min. He was fully alert with no other acute findings on examination. Initial laboratory results showed plasma glucose 720 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 8.0%. Arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.23, pCO2 15.8 mmHg, and bicarbonate 15.9 mEq/L, with an anion gap of 16 mEq/L. Serum ketone analysis showed acetoacetate 758 μmol/L and β-hydroxybutyrate 3493 μmol/L. Plasma osmolality was 301 mOsm/kg H2O. Serum sodium was 128 mEq/L (corrected 138 mEq/L) and potassium 5.1 mEq/L. Immunoreactive insulin was 1.02 μU/mL and C-peptide reactivity 0.05 ng/mL, both low relative to the degree of hyperglycemia. Anti-GAD, anti-insulin, and anti-IA-2 antibodies were all within normal limits. White blood cell count, renal function, and pancreatic enzymes were unremarkable. He was admitted for further management of severe hyperglycemia with metabolic acidosis.

A woman in her late 40s with a history of uncontrolled hypertension, active tobacco use, dyslipidemia, newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus, and nephrolithiasis presented after a 10-year history of recurrent episodes of headache, diaphoresis, and palpitations, previously attributed to panic attacks. Family history was unremarkable. She presented to the emergency department after sudden-onset oppressive chest pain that awoke her early in the morning, radiating to the left upper limb and associated with an episode of vomiting. On admission she was hypertensive (165/87 mmHg). Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm at 81 bpm with ST-segment elevation in leads aVR and V1 and diffuse ST-segment depression, maximal (2 mm) in the inferolateral leads. Emergency transthoracic echocardiography showed left ventricular systolic function at the lower limit of normal, with akinesia of the basal and mid segments of the anterior, anterolateral, and inferolateral walls and hypercontractility of the apex. Intravenous isosorbide dinitrate normalized blood pressure but did not relieve the chest pain. She received a loading dose of aspirin and ticagrelor, unfractionated heparin, and rosuvastatin. Emergency coronary angiography showed no epicardial coronary artery disease. Ventriculography confirmed akinesia of the basal and mid segments of all ventricular walls with apical hypercontractility.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: An 82-year-old man presented to an outpatient clinic with several days of chest pain and feeling generally unwell, accompanied by generalized weakness, shortness of breath, and nausea. He had no prior history of diabetes, though his mother and sister had type 2 diabetes. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and a stable chronic lower-extremity deep vein thrombosis on long-term anticoagulation. He denied tobacco or alcohol use and had not recently used corticosteroids. Medications included amlodipine, atorvastatin, lisinopril, and warfarin. In clinic, blood pressure was 97/69 mmHg and oxygen saturation was 89% on room air, prompting referral to the emergency department. There he was afebrile, normotensive, and not in respiratory distress; BMI was 26.07. He was alert and oriented with no focal neurologic deficits, well-nourished, with moist mucous membranes and capillary refill under 2 seconds. Labs showed sodium 118 mmol/L (corrected 130), potassium 5.4 mmol/L, chloride 83 mmol/L, CO2 21 mmol/L, glucose 880 mg/dL, BUN 56 mg/dL, creatinine 1.61 mg/dL (baseline ~0.9), calcium 11.1 mg/dL, anion gap 14, elevated calculated osmolality, mild transaminase and bilirubin elevation, beta-hydroxybutyrate 2.37 mmol/L, and leukocytosis. Troponins were serially negative; chest X-ray and ECG were unremarkable. A respiratory viral swab was positive for SARS-CoV-2. Hemoglobin A1c was subsequently found to be markedly elevated.

A woman in her seventh decade presented with a gradually progressive history of symptoms and clinical features suggestive of chronic excess cortisol production, evolving over a period of time prior to evaluation. No other significant past medical history was noted. Specific vital signs were not detailed in the available record. Physical examination was reported to show features consistent with a long-standing hypercortisolism-type phenotype, though granular exam findings were not specified. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated biochemical evidence of elevated cortisol secretion together with a plasma ACTH concentration in a range suggestive of an ACTH-dependent process rather than an adrenal source. Magnetic resonance imaging of the sellar region identified a cystic mass within the pituitary gland measuring approximately 15 mm in maximal diameter, consistent with a macroadenoma. Given the imaging and biochemical findings, surgical resection via a transsphenoidal approach was offered, but the patient declined operative intervention and elected to pursue medical management instead.

A 65-year-old male with age-related macular degeneration on ongoing intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy presented for a scheduled injection. Baseline best corrected visual acuity was 7/10 in the right eye and 1/10 in the affected eye, with mild bilateral lens sclerosis and known choroidal neovascularization and subretinal fluid in the affected eye. The injection was performed under topical anesthesia with povidone-iodine surface antisepsis and standard sterile technique, followed by a topical antibiotic drop. On the first day after the procedure, the patient returned with markedly decreased vision and ocular pain in the injected eye; visual acuity had dropped to hand motions. Slit-lamp examination revealed lid swelling, diffuse conjunctival injection, a ring-shaped corneal infiltrate, anterior chamber cells, vitreous haze, and a blunted red reflex, without hypopyon. B-scan ultrasonography showed dense vitreous opacity with an attached retina. The patient was afebrile with no systemic symptoms, denied ocular trauma, but reported a tooth extraction the day before the injection and ongoing dental implant treatment; he had not taken systemic antibiotics. A diagnostic vitreous sample was obtained; gram staining showed numerous gram-positive cocci, and empiric intravitreal and topical antibiotics along with oral antibiotics were started. Despite treatment, the corneal infiltrate progressed to complete corneal opacification, prompting combined vitrectomy and corneal transplantation.

A man in his 60s presented with generalized weakness, diffuse body pains, low back discomfort, and intermittent left-sided flank pain. He had a five-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with oral antidiabetic agents. There was no history of kidney stones, fragility fractures, proximal muscle weakness, or neuropsychiatric symptoms, and no significant family history was reported. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable with a pulse of 88 bpm and blood pressure 130/80 mmHg. General and systemic examination, including neurological assessment, was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed persistent elevation of serum calcium (11.6-12.2 mg/dL on two occasions one month apart) with elevated ionized calcium (1.44 mmol/L) and an intact PTH level that was inappropriately normal-to-mildly elevated (76 pg/mL). Serum phosphorus, magnesium, albumin, and vitamin D levels were within normal limits. Renal function, liver enzymes, and electrolytes were normal; HbA1c was 8.8%, reflecting suboptimal glycemic control. Serum protein electrophoresis showed no monoclonal peak. Spot and 24-hour urine studies showed relatively low urinary calcium excretion (96 mg/day) with a markedly reduced fractional excretion of calcium.
