Neck ultrasonography and a parathyroid scintigraphy study did not demonstrate a discrete parathyroid lesion. Bone densitometry showed osteopenia at several sites without frank osteoporosis. Further evaluation, including genetic testing, was pursued to determine the underlying cause of the calcium-PTH abnormality.

A woman in her early twenties presented with a high-grade fever that had persisted for 6 days prior to admission. She had self-administered acetaminophen without improvement. Two days before admission she was seen at an outside clinic and started on an oral fluoroquinolone antibiotic and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug. Laboratory testing at that visit showed markedly elevated C-reactive protein and serum creatinine, prompting referral and hospital admission. Body mass index was 17.6. On admission, temperature was 38.0°C, pulse 117 bpm, blood pressure 112/72 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18/min. Examination showed no nuchal rigidity, jolt accentuation, conjunctival injection, jaundice, cervical lymphadenopathy, peripheral edema, or skin rash; pharyngeal erythema was present. Laboratory studies revealed marked leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance, thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia, elevated blood urea nitrogen and creatinine consistent with severe acute kidney injury, and markedly elevated C-reactive protein. Urinalysis showed proteinuria, glycosuria, hematuria, bacteriuria, and pyuria, with markedly elevated urinary tubular injury markers. Total IgE was elevated; antinuclear and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Urine and blood cultures were negative, possibly due to prior antibiotic exposure. Non-contrast and subsequent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed bilateral renal enlargement (right greater than left), perirenal fat stranding, mild left renal pelvic dilation, and multiple poorly enhancing renal parenchymal areas. Renal biopsy on hospital day 2 showed 18 glomeruli without sclerosis, crescents, or adhesions, with white blood cell casts in tubules and dense neutrophil-predominant interstitial inflammatory infiltrate with scant eosinophils.

An 8-year-old boy with no history of prior abdominal surgery presented with one week of progressively worsening abdominal pain, more pronounced over the preceding 2-3 days, accompanied by several episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting. He had no significant past medical or surgical history. On arrival he was hemodynamically stable, with mild abdominal distension and tenderness in the lower abdomen; no peritoneal signs were documented. Laboratory evaluation showed mild leukocytosis without electrolyte or metabolic derangement. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis, obtained at an outside facility prior to transfer, demonstrated distended loops of distal small bowel measuring up to 2.8 cm with fecalization and a swirled appearance of the adjacent mesentery, raising concern for a high-grade, closed-loop small bowel obstruction; the appendix was not dilated. Given these findings, he was transferred for further surgical evaluation and management, and urgent operative assessment was planned given concern for closed-loop obstruction.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute myeloblastic leukemia, not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: A woman in her 50s with a history of intravenous drug use and chronic hepatitis C infection presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of progressive swelling and calf pain in the right lower extremity, without preceding trauma. She also had an erythematous rash with ill-defined borders on the anterior and lateral aspects of the right leg. On admission she was afebrile, normotensive, and had a normal heart rate. Laboratory testing showed an elevated C-reactive protein (16.51 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (100 mm/hr). Complete blood count revealed anemia (hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL) and mild thrombocytopenia (platelets 150,000/uL). CT of the right leg showed extensive edema; venous ultrasound of the leg was negative for deep vein thrombosis. Because of her history of intravenous drug use, an echocardiogram was obtained and showed a vegetation on the aortic valve; blood cultures remained negative throughout admission. She was treated empirically with intravenous antibiotics for suspected endocarditis and for the leg findings. During admission, her hemoglobin and platelet counts continued to decline despite antibiotic adjustments, with no splenomegaly or evidence of hemolysis to account for the cytopenias, and stable hepatitis C viral loads. Over the following weeks the leg rash evolved into an indurated plaque with well-defined borders, and by around day 30 her platelet count had fallen to 20,000/uL and hemoglobin to 5.6 g/dL. Skin and bone marrow biopsies were obtained for further evaluation.

A woman in her mid-70s with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, mitral valve prolapse, ischemic colitis, macrocytosis, diverticulitis, and external hemorrhoids presented to the emergency department with a diffuse rash of five days' duration. The rash began as a single small red macule on the right thigh and rapidly spread over the following day to the trunk, back, bilateral arms, and upper thighs, accompanied by constant moderate-to-severe itching and a burning sensation. She also reported sweating, fatigue, sore throat, and generalized weakness. Approximately two weeks earlier she had been treated by her primary care physician for a sore throat and chest congestion with azithromycin and an intramuscular steroid injection; due to lack of improvement she was switched to doxycycline. The rash began after completion of both antibiotic courses. On examination she had a diffuse erythematous, blanching maculopapular rash over the bilateral upper extremities, trunk, back, and upper lower extremities, with minimal involvement below the knees, and areas of bluish discoloration on the back. She was also noted to have oral candidiasis. Labs showed markedly elevated CRP (152.3 mg/dL) and ESR (80 mm/h), leukocytosis (WBC 17.2 x10^9/L) with neutrophilia (91.8%) and lymphopenia (2.4%), no eosinophilia (2.6%), and hyponatremia. Over the following days the rash progressed to involve the face and lower extremities below the knees, with persistent pruritus and burning, before gradually improving with corticosteroid and topical treatment. An autoimmune antibody panel (RF, JO-1, scleroderma antibody, SSA/SSB, SM, RNP) was negative, and a skin biopsy showed nonspecific mild perivascular chronic inflammation.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism with acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her early 70s presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset dyspnea. Her medical history included moderate Alzheimer's disease, a depressive disorder, hypertension, and hypothyroidism. On arrival, she was severely hypoxemic (oxygen saturation 71% on room air), hypertensive (182/103 mmHg), and tachycardic (174 bpm), with normal breath sounds on auscultation. Arterial blood gas analysis showed respiratory alkalosis with partial respiratory failure (pH 7.43, pCO2 23.7 mmHg, pO2 43.7 mmHg, bicarbonate 15.4 mmol/L, lactate 5.4 mmol/L). Electrocardiogram showed narrow-complex tachycardia (heart rate 116 bpm, QTc 530 ms). Within hours, her condition deteriorated with progressive respiratory distress, altered mental status, hypotension, and signs of peripheral hypoperfusion (mottling, prolonged capillary refill time >5 seconds). Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated right ventricular enlargement (RV/LV ratio >0.9), D-shaped interventricular septum, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 80 mmHg. Laboratory testing revealed a markedly elevated D-dimer (5493 ng/mL), elevated NT-proBNP (9481 pg/mL), mildly elevated troponin (99 pg/mL), and elevated C-reactive protein (5.0 mg/dL), with normal hemoglobin and platelet counts. Contrast-enhanced chest CT angiography showed extensive bilateral filling defects in the main pulmonary arteries with near-complete occlusion of segmental branches, right ventricular dilation, and interventricular septal flattening.

A man in his late 60s with a history of type II diabetes mellitus and hypertension presented to the emergency department with left thigh pain and swelling accompanied by lower back pain. He was obtunded and unable to give a reliable history. Family/records indicated that symptoms began approximately three months earlier after a mechanical fall (a seated fall from stairs, no loss of consciousness), with gradual worsening despite an outpatient analgesic injection from an orthopedic provider. On arrival, vital signs showed temperature 97.9°F, blood pressure 78/47 mmHg, heart rate 125/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and SpO2 86% on 6 L/min nasal cannula. He was oriented to person and time but not place. Exam revealed gangrenous change over the left medial and posterior thigh with large areas of black eschar interspersed with dusky violaceous discoloration, epidermal sloughing, and malodorous necrotic tissue with irregular, advancing margins. There was diffuse tenderness from the left hip to the leg with erythema and induration extending toward the groin, and reduced range of motion of the hip and leg due to pain. Labs showed WBC 22.7 ×10^3/µL, hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, lactate 2.9 mmol/L, and CRP 236.2 mg/L. Thigh X-ray showed soft tissue gas and edema tracking within the psoas muscle and thigh with abscess formation; abdominal/pelvic CT showed gas and edema along the iliopsoas plane, extensive gas within adductor muscles, and gas within the renal parenchyma, collecting system, and retroperitoneum extending to the perirenal space, with a large perirenal fluid collection.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute leukemia of unspecified cell type not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: A man in his 60s presented with fever up to 38°C, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea beginning approximately 20 days after a preceding upper respiratory illness. Chest imaging obtained around presentation showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, prompting admission to a hematology service for further evaluation. Past medical history included hypertension for 6 years and resection of a left frontoparietal hemangioma 3 years earlier. On examination, temperature was 36.8°C, pulse 84/min, respirations 21/min, and blood pressure 140/89 mmHg. He appeared pale, with scattered petechiae and ecchymoses on the skin; no lymphadenopathy was palpable. Sternal tenderness was present, and bilateral coarse breath sounds were noted. The abdomen was soft and non-tender without hepatosplenomegaly, and there was no lower extremity edema. Complete blood count showed red blood cells 2.23×10^12/L, hemoglobin 79 g/L, platelets 18×10^9/L, and white blood cells 189.3×10^9/L, with a differential showing 54% blast forms and 13% cells with basophilic precursor morphology. Peripheral smear confirmed numerous agranular blast cells and basophilic precursor forms with coarse granules. Blood chemistry revealed lactate dehydrogenase 3121 U/L, ALT 110.2 U/L, and AST 153.5 U/L. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed for further diagnostic workup prior to initiating therapy.

A woman in her mid-60s presented with a subacute febrile respiratory illness and acute progressive left eye symptoms. She had a 12-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin, without regular glucose monitoring; HbA1c on admission was markedly elevated at 10.8%. She had known diabetic peripheral neuropathy with decreased sensation in both lower extremities, without nephropathy or retinopathy. She reported a 14-day history of productive cough with yellow purulent sputum and 5 days of intermittent fever, with a peak temperature of 39.6°C. About a week into the illness, she developed rapidly progressive visual loss in the left eye, declining from an acuity of 0.3 to hand-motion vision over several days, accompanied by severe ocular pain (7/10), eyelid swelling, conjunctival redness and edema, and purulent discharge, worse with eye movement. On examination she was alert and cooperative, tachycardic (112 bpm), tachypneic (22/min), normothermic (37.0°C), with blood pressure 127/90 mmHg, without jaundice, respiratory distress, or peripheral edema. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams were unremarkable; neurological exam was nonfocal. Ophthalmic examination of the left eye showed corneal edema and opacity, a 2 mm layer of exudate in the anterior chamber, and marked opacification of the vitreous. Laboratory tests showed marked leukocytosis (16.22×10^9/L), elevated CRP (151.51 mg/L), elevated procalcitonin (7.73 ng/mL), and elevated ESR (86 mm/h), consistent with systemic inflammation.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis, unspecified with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A 20-year-old male was admitted to intensive care following a motor vehicle accident with multiple traumatic injuries, including blunt abdominal trauma requiring exploratory laparotomy and splenectomy, and a right forearm fracture treated surgically. He required intubation and mechanical ventilation and had a complicated hospital course over several weeks, including transfusion-related lung injury, ventilator-associated pneumonia, septic shock, diffuse axonal brain injury, and episodes of atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, managed with supportive care, antibiotics, and antiarrhythmic medication. On admission he was intubated with oxygen saturation 97%, in hypovolemic shock that stabilized with resuscitation; initial Glasgow Coma Scale was 3/15, improving after resuscitation. Several weeks into admission he developed a persistently depressed level of consciousness together with persistent tachycardia and high fever up to 40.8°C despite standard trauma management. Thyroid function testing showed markedly suppressed TSH (0.012 and 0.005 mIU/L, reference 0.40-5.0), elevated free thyroxine (45.5 and 40.13 pmol/L, reference 12-22), and elevated triiodothyronine (9.25 and 9.51 pmol/L, reference 3.1-6.8). Thyroid ultrasound showed two normal-sized lobes without nodules, calcifications, or lymphadenopathy, with a homogeneous echo pattern and increased parenchymal vascularity (peak systolic velocity approximately 43 cm/s). Biochemistry showed mild hyponatremia (132 mmol/L) with normal potassium, calcium, PTH, and vitamin D. Hematology showed normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL), leukocytosis (15.91x10^9/L) with neutrophilia and left shift, thrombocytosis (759x10^9/L), and mildly prolonged PT and PTT.

A woman in her mid-20s with a history of post-traumatic seizures managed with long-term antiepileptic therapy since childhood presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of fever and rapidly progressive skin eruption. The eruption was characterized by scattered maculopapular lesions, atypical flat target lesions, and bullae formation, involving approximately 5% to 10% of total body surface area, accompanied by erosions of the oral and genital mucosa. She also reported bilateral ocular irritation of similar onset. On examination, the described mucocutaneous lesions were confirmed, and ophthalmologic assessment revealed bilateral eyelid margin erosion with conjunctival epithelial defects and pseudomembrane formation; the corneas remained clear without epithelial defects at this stage. Vital signs and systemic examination were otherwise unremarkable. No confirmatory skin biopsy, culture, or other diagnostic study results were available at the time of initial presentation, and the patient was referred for urgent dermatologic and ophthalmologic evaluation given the acute, extensive mucocutaneous involvement.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A man in his 40s was transferred from a psychiatric inpatient unit to the acute medical service with a 2-day history of abdominal pain and vomiting. He denied fever, cough, sputum production, diarrhoea or dysuria. Per the psychiatric team, he had refused food and medications for approximately one week due to ongoing psychiatric symptoms. Past history included type 2 diabetes mellitus (previously managed with metformin and alogliptin, HbA1c 102 mmol/mol, recently started on subcutaneous insulin), bipolar disorder and schizophrenia treated with valproic acid. On arrival he appeared drowsy but was alert and oriented to time, place and person, Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Heart rate was 123 bpm, blood pressure 166/94 mmHg, temperature 37.0°C, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation normal on room air. Chest auscultation was clear bilaterally. Abdominal examination showed a soft, non-tender abdomen without distension, guarding or organomegaly, with active bowel sounds. No joint swelling, rash, peripheral oedema or focal neurological deficit was noted. Initial investigations showed blood glucose 26 mmol/L, serum ketones >7 mmol/L, arterial pH 7.25, bicarbonate 14.3 mmol/L, lactate 7.3 mmol/L, white cell count 24.7×10^9/L, CRP 6 mg/L and procalcitonin 0.13 ng/mL. Blood cultures, urine cultures and a viral swab were negative; chest X-ray showed no infiltrates and urinalysis was unremarkable.

A woman in her 70s presented to the emergency department with acute-onset chest and back pain. The pain began suddenly and was severe from onset, with no preceding trauma reported. No history of a similar prior episode was noted, and past medical history was not otherwise significant per available records. On arrival, vital signs were within normal limits and the patient was hemodynamically stable, without signs of shock. Physical examination did not reveal focal neurological deficits, pulse deficits, or signs suggestive of end-organ malperfusion. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated an intimal flap creating two separate flow channels extending from the proximal ascending aorta through the aortic arch and thoracoabdominal aorta down to both common iliac arteries. One channel remained widely patent along its entire course. Both renal arteries originated from the other channel, and there was no imaging evidence of visceral, renal, or limb malperfusion at presentation. Given the extensive involvement of the proximal aorta and arch, urgent surgical evaluation and intervention were pursued.

A man in his late 40s with untreated hypertension presented with progressive bilateral lower-extremity weakness. He had been well until several days prior, when he developed heaviness and weakness in both feet that progressed proximally over 48 hours, impairing ambulation. The next day he developed hand weakness affecting fine motor tasks. He denied pain, paresthesias, sensory loss, bowel or bladder dysfunction, fever, chills, recent gastrointestinal illness, or respiratory symptoms, though he had received influenza and COVID-19 vaccinations about three months earlier. He was initially discharged from an outside emergency department after basic labs; outpatient nerve conduction studies later showed absent bilateral peroneal and tibial motor responses with acute denervation in the lower extremities and paraspinal muscles, prompting referral for further work-up. On admission he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, with blood pressure 176/101 mmHg improving to 149/92 mmHg without treatment, heart rate 89 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was alert with intact cranial nerves. Motor exam showed distal-predominant upper-extremity weakness (shoulders 4+/5, wrists 4/5, fingers 3/5) and severe distal lower-extremity weakness (ankle movements 0/5) with relatively preserved proximal strength. Reflexes were diffusely diminished to absent, including absent ankle jerks. Sensation and coordination were intact. Labs showed mild hyperkalemia (peak 5.8 mmol/L, since resolved), mildly elevated creatine kinase (327 U/L), and elevated inflammatory markers (ESR 55 mm/hr, CRP 5.7 mg/L). Cerebrospinal fluid showed elevated protein (44 mg/dL) with 0 white cells and normal glucose. Contrast spine MRI showed lumbar nerve root enhancement without compressive pathology. Respiratory viral panel detected human coronavirus 229E; SARS-CoV-2 was negative. Serial respiratory function testing remained reassuring.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute leukemia of unspecified cell type not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: A man in his late 50s was referred to the hospital after routine bloodwork obtained by his primary care provider revealed a markedly elevated white blood cell count. He reported an acute, rapidly progressive course over the preceding two weeks, including a 10-pound unintentional weight loss, shortness of breath, and night sweats. Physical examination on admission was unremarkable, with no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly noted. Initial laboratory studies showed WBC 60.55 K/mcL (reference 4-11), RBC 2.64 million/mcL, hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, hematocrit 27%, MCV 102.3 fL, MCH 35.2 pg, MCHC 34.4 g/dL, and RDW 15.3%. The differential revealed markedly decreased neutrophils (1%, absolute 0.61 K/mcL) and a markedly elevated lymphocyte fraction (41%, absolute 58.13 K/mcL) with 55% atypical lymphocytes, along with mildly elevated absolute eosinophils (0.61 K/mcL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen, chest, and pelvis demonstrated a small fatty umbilical hernia and cholelithiasis, without splenomegaly or adenopathy. Flow cytometry of the peripheral blood identified a large population (~92%) of abnormal cells co-expressing markers associated with more than one hematopoietic lineage, including TdT, CD34, cytoplasmic CD3, CD117, CD2, CD7, and CD13, with partial CD33 expression; markers for mature T- and B-lymphocyte lineages and monocytic differentiation were negative. A bone marrow biopsy was hypercellular with a similarly expanded population of the same abnormal cells, positive for CD34, CD3, CD200, and HLA-DR, with partial CD2 and CD7 expression. Molecular testing identified an FLT3-ITD mutation.

A man in his late 30s with a background of advanced alcohol-related liver disease complicated by portal hypertension (gastropathy, esophageal varices, ascites) presented with lethargy and difficulty mobilizing after a fall with a seven-hour long lie. He reported four days of poor sleep, delirium, and auditory and visual hallucinations. He had been discharged from hospital one week earlier and had resumed alcohol intake for 48 hours before again abstaining. Over the preceding year he had multiple admissions for gastrointestinal bleeding, alcohol withdrawal, hepatic encephalopathy, low mood, and suicidal ideation, and over nine months had developed progressive peripheral and scrotal edema with a phimosis abnormality. Bilirubin had been persistently elevated for over a year. On examination he was oriented, jaundiced, without liver flap, abdomen soft without clinical ascites, with lower-limb edema extending to the mid-abdomen; he was hemodynamically stable with normal heart sounds. Hepatic encephalopathy was graded 1-2. Labs showed bilirubin 168 micromol/L, albumin 37 g/L, and prolonged prothrombin time of 23.7 seconds. Chest X-ray showed no consolidation but perihilar fluid overload. Diuretics were adjusted and coagulopathy corrected. He subsequently developed acute kidney injury, then became febrile to 39.4°C with tachycardia, non-productive cough, and dyspnea; a septic screen including blood cultures and ascitic tap was performed and empiric antibiotics started. Blood cultures grew an unusual gram-negative organism; ascitic fluid analysis was unremarkable. Days later he developed recurrent fever with scrotal pain and edema.

A 79-year-old man with a history of metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (low-volume by imaging criteria, Gleason 5+5=10 adenocarcinoma, markedly elevated baseline PSA) treated with combined androgen deprivation therapy, an androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor, and cytotoxic chemotherapy presented after his fifth chemotherapy cycle with low-grade fever and exertional dyspnea. He had no history of smoking, prior lung disease, thoracic radiation, autoimmune disease, or chronic cardiac or renal disease, and was not taking any medication known to cause pulmonary toxicity. On admission, oxygen saturation was 91% on room air, with bilateral fine crackles on auscultation; there was no peripheral edema or jugular venous distension. Chest CT showed newly developed diffuse, non-segmental ground-glass opacities in both lungs, in contrast to a normal scan obtained shortly before symptom onset. Laboratory testing showed elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein 11.46 mg/dL, LDH 310 U/L). Brain natriuretic peptide was normal. Echocardiography showed trivial mitral regurgitation, mild-to-moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and estimated right ventricular systolic pressure of 51 mmHg, without evidence of left-sided heart failure. Autoimmune serologic workup was largely unremarkable. Beta-D-glucan and Pneumocystis jirovecii PCR were negative, and blood cultures, viral PCR (including SARS-CoV-2), and routine bacterial cultures were negative. Two serum biomarkers associated with lung injury were elevated. Symptoms and radiologic findings developed acutely over the days following the most recent chemotherapy cycle in a patient with no prior respiratory or cardiac disease.

A woman in her late 60s with no significant past medical history was diagnosed with a generalized neuromuscular disorder several years prior, initially presenting with drooping eyelids, double vision, and slurred speech. Serologic autoantibody testing was performed, and imaging did not show a thymic mass. Symptoms were initially controlled with oral corticosteroids and a cholinesterase inhibitor, without severe respiratory compromise; however, self-discontinuation of corticosteroids due to concern about side effects led to clinical worsening. After an initial period of stable symptom control, she was hospitalized approximately ten months later for worsening eyelid drooping and double vision. During hospitalization, high-dose intravenous corticosteroid therapy produced a transient exacerbation followed by improvement, and she was discharged on an increased oral corticosteroid dose with the cholinesterase inhibitor discontinued. Over the following months to years, she received several courses of intravenous and subcutaneous biologic infusion therapy targeting neonatal Fc receptor recycling, each producing rapid but short-lived symptomatic improvement followed by relapse within weeks, prompting escalation to a complement-pathway-targeted subcutaneous therapy. Vital signs were unremarkable throughout. Examination during exacerbations showed ptosis, extraocular movement limitation, and dysarthria without evidence of respiratory distress. Functional and quality-of-life symptom scales were used serially to track disease severity.

A man in his early 50s presented with a multi-year history of progressive enlargement of the hands and feet, coarsening of facial features, and gradual deepening of his voice, first noticed around age 44. He required progressively larger shoe and glove sizes, and a ring he had worn no longer fit. He reported easy fatigability without headache, excessive sweating, fever, or weight gain, and had not previously seen a specialist. Over the next several years he developed progressive exertional breathlessness, orthopnea, frequent nocturnal breathlessness relieved by sitting upright, poor sleep quality, excessive daytime sleepiness, and irritability, without cough, chest pain, or palpitations. On examination several years after symptom onset he had coarse facial features, a prominent nose, widened interdental spacing, poor dentition, enlarged hands and feet, an asymmetrically enlarged thyroid gland, and distended neck veins. Laboratory testing included an oral glucose tolerance test showing failure of growth hormone suppression (growth hormone remaining elevated around 62.5 ng/ml at 1 and 2 hours) and a markedly elevated insulin-like growth factor-1 level (about 2.3-fold above the upper limit of normal); hemoglobin A1c was mildly elevated. Pituitary MRI demonstrated a roughly 19x17x16 mm mass in the right anterior pituitary gland. Thyroid function testing showed a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone with markedly elevated free T4. Thyroid ultrasound showed an enlarged gland with a large nodule, and cross-sectional chest imaging revealed a large thyroid mass extending into the chest, compressing the superior vena cava and displacing the trachea. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the thyroid showed follicular epithelial cells in a colloid-rich background with scattered hemosiderin-laden macrophages.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A young adult man was brought to the emergency department after convulsions lasting over 9 hours. Family reported limb twitching, foaming at the mouth, upward eye deviation, and loss of consciousness for about 10 minutes prior to arrival. On admission he was irritable, diaphoretic, vomited a large volume of stomach contents, and had involuntary limb movements. Vital signs: temperature 39.3°C, pulse 168 bpm, blood pressure 94/38 mmHg, oxygen saturation 94%, respiratory rate 35/min with shallow breathing. History included a diagnosis of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency at birth, a febrile convulsive episode in infancy, and a diagnosis of a thyroid condition years earlier for which he had been prescribed antithyroid medication and a beta-blocker, self-discontinued two months prior. No family history of thyroid, cardiac, or neurologic disease; no smoking or alcohol use. Exam showed coma (Glasgow Coma Scale 6), profuse sweating, an enlarged soft goiter with audible vascular murmur, coarse breath sounds with scattered crackles, tachycardia with accentuated first heart sound, and cool extremities. Labs showed metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, markedly elevated inflammatory markers, elevated cardiac and muscle enzymes, elevated brain natriuretic peptide, and abnormal thyroid function tests. Imaging showed bilateral pneumonia and mild cerebral atrophy; echocardiogram showed mildly reduced ejection fraction.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism with acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her mid-30s, a former smoker, presented in the early postpartum period following her second delivery. She initially developed acute onset of left lower limb swelling and pain, and was admitted to another facility where she was found to have extensive left iliofemoral venous thrombosis; anticoagulation with a low-molecular-weight heparin was started (platelet count before treatment was 124,000/µL). Several days later, despite ongoing anticoagulation, she developed acute respiratory distress. Cross-sectional pulmonary vascular imaging demonstrated extensive filling defects within the right and left pulmonary arterial branches. Anticoagulation was escalated to a continuous intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion. She subsequently developed hemodynamic instability with hypotension requiring vasopressor support and was transferred for higher-level care. On arrival she appeared severely unwell, with tachypnea and room-air oxygen saturation of 89%. Cardiac exam revealed a regular rhythm with a grade II/VI systolic murmur at the tricuspid area; lungs were clear. The left leg showed marked edema with local inflammatory signs. ECG showed sinus tachycardia (105 bpm), right axis deviation, and an S1Q3T3 pattern. Labs showed hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, platelets 53,000/µL, ESR 25 mm/h, WBC 11,340/µL with neutrophilia, high-sensitivity troponin I 31.3 ng/mL, and D-dimer 7650 ng/mL. Echocardiography showed right heart chamber dilation exceeding left-sided dimensions, reduced right ventricular systolic function, estimated pulmonary artery pressure of 60 mmHg, and severe tricuspid regurgitation, with normal left ventricular size and function.

A man in his 40s presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset left testicular and left lower abdominal pain that began two hours before arrival. He denied trauma, hematuria, or dysuria, but reported pain and perceived swelling of the left testicle. He had no significant past medical history and no family history of kidney stones. On examination he appeared uncomfortable, with tenderness in the left lower quadrant and left testicle; no visible scrotal swelling was noted. Vital signs: blood pressure 101/58 mmHg, heart rate 84 bpm, temperature 98.7°F. Labs showed WBC 13.2 K/μL, hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, glucose 114 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.3 mg/dL. Testicular ultrasound with Doppler showed decreased blood flow to the left testicle compared to the right. Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed no renal stones but incidental calcification within the aortic wall. He underwent surgical scrotal exploration, which was unremarkable, and was discharged. Two days later he returned with worsening left lower abdominal pain radiating to his back, described as sharp and tearing. He denied urinary symptoms or drug use. Vital signs: blood pressure 243/143 mmHg, heart rate 103 bpm, temperature 98.2°F. Labs showed WBC 14.0 K/μL, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, glucose 115 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. Further imaging was obtained and additional management was pursued.

train_cases.diagnosis: Malignant neoplasm of lower lobe, left bronchus or lung
train_cases.note: A 68-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension presented with progressive exertional dyspnea, intermittent low-grade evening fevers, anorexia, and unintentional weight loss over a three-month period. He had a modest smoking history of five pack-years. On examination, air entry was reduced over the left lower lung zone. Chest radiograph showed left lower lobe consolidation. He was treated with two courses of antibiotics and bronchodilators for presumed infective exacerbation of chronic lung disease, but symptoms and radiographic findings persisted after four weeks of therapy. Laboratory testing showed a markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (132 mm/hr), mild anemia (hemoglobin 11 g/dL), and a white cell count at the upper limit of normal. Corrected serum calcium was elevated at 2.92 mmol/L with a suppressed intact parathyroid hormone level (10 pg/mL); alkaline phosphatase, phosphate, renal and liver function were normal. Repeated sputum smears and molecular testing for tuberculosis were negative, and screening studies for plasma cell dyscrasia and granulomatous disease were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing left lower lobe mass with endobronchial extension. Bronchoscopy showed near-complete obstruction of the left main bronchus by a polypoidal, friable endobronchial mass with necrotic debris; biopsy was obtained.

A man in his 40s with no known past medical history was found unresponsive outdoors, febrile, with bilateral bulging eyes and minor facial abrasions. Paramedics recorded an initial temperature of 40°C; he was intubated in the field and transported for further care. On arrival, he was unresponsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 3/15), with a temperature of 42°C, heart rate 190 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 110/57 mmHg maintained on noradrenaline, and oxygen saturation 98% on mechanical ventilation with 100% FiO2. He had continuous watery diarrhea with loss of sphincter control. Examination showed shivering, bilateral exophthalmos with pinpoint, non-reactive pupils, a clear chest, and a soft abdomen without lower limb edema. Point-of-care cardiac ultrasound showed an ejection fraction of 40% with a collapsed inferior vena cava; a trauma ultrasound exam was negative. Active cooling measures were started, with rapid normalization of temperature within about an hour, accompanied by decreasing hemodynamic and ventilatory support requirements. Initial labs revealed leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/INR, elevated D-dimer, hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, markedly elevated liver transaminases, elevated LDH and creatine kinase, elevated lactate, elevated procalcitonin, and elevated troponin and myoglobin. Head CT and initial chest x-ray were unremarkable; a repeat chest x-ray several hours later showed new patchy opacities and mild pleural effusion. Blood, urine, and stool cultures were negative; a lower respiratory culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter cloacae. Toxicology screening was unremarkable.

A woman in her late 70s with a history of hypertension, radiculopathy, and gastroesophageal reflux disease presented to the emergency department with acute-onset substernal chest pressure that awoke her from sleep. She described the pain as severe and sudden, likening it to a heavy weight on her chest, and denied any prior similar episodes. Aspirin and nitroglycerin were given prehospital, reducing her pain from 10/10 to 6/10. On arrival, vital signs showed blood pressure 127/73 mmHg, heart rate 60 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and she was afebrile. Electrocardiography showed sinus bradycardia with premature atrial complexes and no ischemic changes. Serial troponin levels were normal. Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.1-13.0 ×10³/µL), mildly elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (194 pg/mL), and mildly reduced renal function with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 58 mL/min/1.73 m². Chest radiography showed apparent widening of the mediastinum on a portable anteroposterior film. Given her age, the abruptness of symptom onset, and persistent clinical concern, cross-sectional vascular imaging was obtained. This demonstrated crescentic thickening of the wall of the ascending aorta extending into the descending thoracic aorta, without contrast enhancement within the thickened segment and without an identifiable intimal flap or separate lumens; possible involvement of the brachiocephalic artery and proximal right common carotid artery was also noted. A specialty surgical service was consulted emergently, and intravenous anti-impulse therapy was initiated with titration to heart rate and blood pressure goals.

A man in his late 60s with a history of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, prior cataract surgery in one eye, bilateral radial keratotomy, long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus (approximately 25 years, insulin-treated), hypertension, dyslipidemia, and atrial fibrillation underwent uncomplicated combined cataract extraction and glaucoma drainage device implantation in the eye with advanced, medically uncontrolled neovascular glaucoma. Postoperative day 0 examination was unremarkable, with a well-positioned tube shunt, an adherent scleral graft, and an intact, stable conjunctival closure; routine topical antibiotic, corticosteroid, and anti-inflammatory drops were initiated. Four days after surgery, he presented to the emergency department with a two-day history of fever and confusion, along with progressive periocular pain, swelling, forward protrusion of the eye, eyelid drooping, conjunctival swelling, and purulent discharge from the operated eye. He was febrile (40.1°C), tachycardic, and hypotensive. Laboratory testing showed leukocytosis (white blood cell count 13.25x10^9/L, absolute neutrophil count 12.33x10^9/L) and an elevated lactate of 7.1 mmol/L. Non-contrast head CT demonstrated exophthalmos of the affected eye with hyperdense orbital material, periocular soft tissue swelling with fat stranding, a taut optic nerve, and thickening of the lateral rectus muscle. Ophthalmologic examination revealed vision limited to light perception, a relative afferent pupillary defect, markedly restricted eye movements, a small layered hypopyon, and severe vitreous haze obscuring the posterior view, with a possible choroidal detachment on bedside ultrasound.

An elderly male presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset right testicular swelling and pain persisting for three days. The pain was described as a heavy, dragging sensation that progressively worsened and was exacerbated by movement. He denied trauma, dysuria, fever, or prior episodes. His past medical history included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and prior lung volume reduction surgery. He had no known drug allergies. On physical examination, the right hemiscrotum was swollen, erythematous, and tender. The testicle appeared elevated and transversely orientated, with a surrounding hydrocele. The cremasteric reflex was diminished, and Prehn's sign was negative. No palpable masses were found. Laboratory investigations revealed an elevated C-reactive protein of 40 mg/L (reference <5 mg/L) and a white blood cell count of 15,000/µL (reference 4,000-11,000/µL). Urinalysis was negative for nitrites and leukocytes. Serum urea and electrolytes were within normal limits. Scrotal Doppler ultrasound of the right testis demonstrated absent vascularity within the affected testis, with findings suggestive of early ischemic change.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute leukemia of unspecified cell type not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: An elderly woman in her late 70s had a history of a surgically resected intraventricular meningioma (WHO grade I), with several subsequent local recurrences over the following years treated with staged stereotactic radiotherapy to lesions in the resection cavity, midbrain surface, temporal lobe, and frontal lobe. During routine follow-up imaging several years after the original surgery, two small new enhancing lesions were identified in the frontal lobe. After low-dose radiotherapy to these lesions, follow-up imaging two months later showed complete resolution, a response unusually rapid for her known tumor type, prompting further systemic evaluation. Whole-body PET/CT demonstrated diffuse increased glucose uptake throughout the bone marrow. She had no prior history of hematologic abnormality and remained clinically asymptomatic. She was referred for hematologic evaluation. Laboratory testing revealed severe pancytopenia: white blood cell count 2560/uL with 19% circulating blasts, hemoglobin 4.2 g/dL, and platelet count 26,000/uL. Bone marrow aspirate showed approximately 56% blastoid cells with marked suppression of normal trilineage hematopoiesis; a myeloid peroxidase-type cytochemical stain was positive in a small subset of blasts. Immunophenotyping showed blasts co-expressing markers of more than one hematopoietic lineage, positive for CD34, CD117, CD10, CD19, CD22, CD13, CD33, cyCD79a, cyTdT, and HLA-DR, with CD20 and CD3 negative. Cytogenetic analysis revealed a reciprocal translocation involving chromosomes 9 and 22 in all examined metaphases, with markedly elevated fusion transcript levels detected in peripheral blood.

A woman in her mid-40s with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department with a two-month history of progressive fatigue, new-onset petechiae on the limbs, and gastrointestinal symptoms including vomiting and constipation. Laboratory studies revealed anemia (hemoglobin 89 g/L), severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count 12 × 10^9/L), mild lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 1.25 × 10^9/L), and slightly elevated serum creatinine (1.43 mg/dL). Lactate dehydrogenase was markedly elevated (1082 IU/L), total bilirubin was mildly increased (1.3 mg/dL), haptoglobin was undetectable, and schistocytes were noted on the peripheral blood smear. Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen) were within normal limits. Physical examination was notable for longstanding molluscum contagiosum-type skin lesions in the groin and on the limbs, without lymphadenopathy or organomegaly reported. Cross-sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, brain MRI, breast imaging, and ophthalmologic examination did not identify an underlying malignancy, structural lesion, or end-organ damage. Autoimmune serologies, including antinuclear antibody, extractable nuclear antigen panel, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulant, and anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, were unremarkable.

A teenage male from a dengue-endemic region, previously healthy with no known congenital, structural, rheumatic, or familial cardiac disease, presented with a one-month history of febrile illness. Symptoms began with high-grade fever, malaise, myalgia, and headache; dengue serology was positive at that time, and he was managed conservatively as an outpatient. Over the following weeks he developed progressive clinical deterioration with anemia, thrombocytopenia, marked lymphopenia, monocytopenia, orthopnea, and new neurological symptoms, prompting hospital admission for further evaluation. On admission, imaging identified septic-appearing emboli involving the brain and abdominal organs; abdominal ultrasound showed wedge-shaped infarcts in the kidneys, liver, and spleen. Echocardiography demonstrated a mobile mass measuring 1.3 x 0.8 cm attached to the mitral valve with mild-to-moderate mitral regurgitation; left ventricular systolic function was preserved (ejection fraction 66%), and the remaining valves were structurally normal. Neurological imaging initially showed an intracerebral hemorrhage; a repeat scan about a week later revealed an ischemic infarct with an associated abscess, and MRI confirmed multiple abscesses. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8 g/dL, platelets 80x10^9/L, marked lymphopenia (7%), and normal renal function (creatinine 0.4 mg/dL). Repeat dengue serology showed positive IgM and negative IgG. Malaria testing and other viral markers were negative. Blood cultures, drawn after empirical antibiotics had been started, were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid was colorless with alkaline pH, glucose 61 mg/dL, LDH 40 U/L, protein 1105 mg/dL, and total WBC 32 cells/cmm. Empirical intravenous antibiotics and supportive care were initiated.

A man in his sixties presented with new-onset confusion. He had a history of a bicuspid aortic valve with aortic root dilatation, treated with an aortic root graft and tissue aortic valve replacement approximately a decade earlier, followed by a valve-in-valve transcatheter aortic valve implantation for severe aortic regurgitation three years prior. He had been on lifelong apixaban after thrombi were identified on the prosthetic valve leaflets two years earlier. Imaging on admission demonstrated multiple acute bilateral ischemic strokes involving both anterior and posterior circulation territories, including cerebral and cerebellar regions. He had fluctuating cognition and attention without signs of meningism. On examination, a pre-existing cardiac murmur and finger clubbing were noted. During admission he developed recurrent fevers above 38°C on separate occasions several weeks apart, with negative respiratory viral swabs and urine cultures each time. Four blood cultures obtained over the first month of admission grew Staphylococcus haemolyticus. Extensive investigations for vasculitis, autoimmune disease, chronic infection, lymphoma, myeloma, and antiphospholipid syndrome were largely unremarkable, though rheumatoid factor and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were markedly elevated. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed elevated protein with matched oligoclonal bands in serum and CSF, without pleocytosis or organisms seen. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography and an FDG-PET/CT scan showed no valve vegetations or focal source of infection. CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute myeloblastic leukemia, not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: An 11-year-old female presented with new-onset neurological symptoms, including mild weakness of one side of the face. There was no reported history of trauma, fever, or preceding infection specified. On evaluation, brain MRI demonstrated thickening of the meninges. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed an elevated white blood cell count with atypical-appearing cells noted on cytologic review. A peripheral blood smear revealed a markedly increased proportion of abnormal blast-like cells, estimated at approximately 70% of the cell population. Immunophenotyping of these cells showed expression of myeloid-associated surface markers (myeloperoxidase, CD33, CD13), along with weak expression of the B-lymphoid marker CD19. A subset of the abnormal cells also expressed monocytic-associated markers (CD64, CD15). No additional vital sign abnormalities, prior hematologic history, or comorbid conditions were reported. Physical examination was otherwise notable only for the facial nerve finding. Further diagnostic workup, including bone marrow evaluation, was pending at the time of this presentation to characterize the hematologic abnormality and central nervous system involvement.

A 65-year-old man with a history of hypertension and a prior stroke several years earlier without residual weakness presented with abdominal pain persisting for four months. He was clinically suspected of having gallstone disease and was admitted for further evaluation and planning of laparoscopic gallbladder surgery. Abdominal ultrasound showed a distended gallbladder containing multiple stones. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen confirmed cholelithiasis and incidentally revealed an abnormality of the descending thoracic aorta. Subsequent CT angiography showed diffuse soft plaque throughout the descending thoracic aorta, with a linear intraluminal flap beginning just distal to the origin of a major aortic arch branch and extending down to the origin of the left common iliac artery; maximum aortic diameter measured 35 mm. Coronary angiography demonstrated 60% ostial stenosis of the left anterior descending artery and, in a dominant right coronary system, 70% ostial stenosis of the posterior descending branch. Echocardiogram was normal. Electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia with first-degree atrioventricular block and a heart rate of 51 beats per minute. Other biochemical and hematological studies were unremarkable. He was asymptomatic, denying chest pain, syncope, palpitations, or exertional dyspnea. Home medications included amlodipine/valsartan, a statin, and aspirin.

An 80s-year-old male presented to the eye emergency department with pain and decreased vision in the left eye. He had a history of neovascular age-related macular degeneration treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections at regular 8-week intervals; he had received an injection in that eye the day prior to presentation, at which time visual acuity had been recorded as relatively preserved. Past medical history included diabetes mellitus with a recent hemoglobin A1c of 6.3%, and cataract surgery with lens implantation performed 6 years earlier. There was no history of eyelid margin disease, ectropion, entropion, or meibomian gland dysfunction. On presentation, best-corrected visual acuity in the affected eye was light perception, and intraocular pressure was elevated at 28 mmHg. Anterior segment examination revealed conjunctival injection, microcystic corneal edema, hypopyon, fibrin in the anterior chamber, pupillary membrane formation, and posterior synechiae in the setting of a posterior chamber intraocular lens. There was no view to the posterior segment. B-scan ultrasonography showed vitreous opacities and membrane formation with a shallow choroidal detachment. The fellow eye was uninvolved.

A previously healthy man in his late 40s presented with a 3-day history of nasal congestion and rhinorrhea, followed by low-grade fever and the acute onset (within the preceding 24 hours) of neuropsychiatric symptoms including lethargy, incoherent speech, agitation, shouting, and disrobing. He had no history of hypertension, diabetes, epilepsy, allergies, prior surgery, smoking, or alcohol use, and no family history of psychiatric illness. On admission, vital signs were stable (temperature 36.8°C, pulse 95 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 139/92 mmHg, SpO2 99% on room air). No jaundice or lymphadenopathy was noted; cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams were unremarkable. He was conscious but only partially coherent, uncooperative, and showed impaired higher cortical function. Pupils were equal and reactive with normal eye movements; limb strength was full (5/5); neck was supple; plantar response was extensor on the right and flexor on the left. Emergency cranial CT was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture showed elevated opening pressure (200 mmH2O) and CSF pleocytosis (WBC 60×10^6/L) with normal glucose, chloride, and protein; CSF AFB smear and India ink stain were negative. Blood tests showed mild anemia, elevated neutrophil percentage and CRP, and elevated D-dimer and fibrinogen. Serum cytomegalovirus IgG was positive with negative IgM and negative serum CMV-DNA PCR, while CSF metagenomic sequencing detected cytomegalovirus DNA. Brain MRI showed T2-FLAIR/T2 hyperintensities in the left frontal and temporal cortices. EEG showed diffuse slowing with loss of posterior dominant rhythm and delta activity. Chest/abdominal CT was unremarkable.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A woman in her early 20s with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with a five-day history of headache, nausea, vomiting, polyuria, and polydipsia. She reported having run out of her usual insulin supply several weeks earlier due to an insurance-related coverage change affecting both her long-acting and rapid-acting insulin prescriptions. She described confusion regarding which of her newly dispensed insulins was long-acting versus rapid-acting, and endorsed using a long-acting insulin multiple times daily before meals in place of a rapid-acting insulin, in addition to her prescribed long-acting insulin twice daily. She had been unable to obtain a rapid-acting insulin refill in the days preceding admission. On examination she was alert and oriented, with blood pressure 109/64 mmHg, heart rate 96 beats per minute, dry mucous membranes, and decreased skin turgor. Initial laboratory testing showed a random serum glucose of 576 mg/dL (32 mmol/L; reference less than 200 mg/dL), elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate of 6.56 mmol/L (reference less than 0.28), bicarbonate of 18 mmol/L (reference 21-31), and an anion gap of 22 (reference 7-15). She was admitted to the intensive care unit for further management.

A man in his 30s with a history of congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency, on chronic maintenance dexamethasone and fludrocortisone since childhood, presented to the emergency department with one day of nausea, several episodes of loose stools, decreased oral intake, and a single episode of non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting. He denied abdominal pain, fever, chills, anorexia, dysuria, or right lower quadrant discomfort. He reported feeling well the day prior, with no recent travel, sick contacts, or new medications. On arrival, vital signs were within normal limits and he appeared comfortable, in no acute distress. Abdominal examination showed a soft, non-distended, easily compressible abdomen without tenderness on light or deep palpation, and no guarding, rebound, rigidity, or percussion tenderness. McBurney's point tenderness, Rovsing's sign, psoas sign, obturator sign, and heel-drop test were all negative on repeated examinations by multiple clinicians, with the patient consistently denying pain. Laboratory evaluation showed hyponatremia (sodium 126 mmol/L), elevated blood urea nitrogen (35 mg/dL), and acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.0 mg/dL), with normal potassium and glucose. These findings were initially attributed to volume depletion from poor oral intake and gastrointestinal losses; the absence of hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia, or hemodynamic instability argued against acute adrenal crisis. Further imaging was pursued given the combination of gastrointestinal symptoms and metabolic derangement despite the benign abdominal exam.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A man in his mid-50s presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of vomiting, generalized weakness, polyuria, and polydipsia. He had a nine-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin and an SGLT2 inhibitor, along with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 41 mL/min/1.73m2). He also had long-standing hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Family history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and autoimmune thyroid disease in first-degree relatives. He reported light alcohol use and minimal tobacco exposure, with no illicit drug use. He denied fever, infectious symptoms, recent medication changes, steroid use, chest pain, dyspnea, or prior ketosis episodes. On examination he appeared dehydrated and unwell, alert but disoriented to time, place, person, and situation. Heart rate was 112 bpm, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min with deep breathing, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 36.8°C; BMI was 24 kg/m2. Mucous membranes were dry with reduced skin turgor and a noticeable breath odor. Mild epigastric tenderness was noted without guarding or rigidity. Cardiorespiratory exam was unremarkable. Initial labs showed blood glucose 186 mg/dL, HbA1c 7.2%, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, chloride 96 mmol/L, anion gap 24 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 4.8 mmol/L, serum osmolality 295 mOsm/kg, BUN 42 mg/dL, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.18, pCO2 24 mmHg, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, base excess -14. Urinalysis showed large ketones, moderate glucose, trace protein, specific gravity 1.030, and no active sediment.

A woman in her late 30s, gravida 5 para 1, at 19 weeks' gestation, was transferred from another hospital for hypertension and progressive generalized weakness, having initially sought care for lower abdominal pain and concern about fetal well-being. She has a history of a chronic autoimmune neuromuscular condition for which she takes an immunosuppressant, a corticosteroid, and a cholinesterase-inhibiting medication, though she reports not taking these recently due to lack of insurance access. At the outside hospital, obstetric ultrasonography confirmed a viable intrauterine pregnancy consistent with dating. She was noted to have elevated blood pressures (systolic >160 mmHg, diastolic >100 mmHg) with proteinuria and received IV magnesium sulfate for presumed preeclampsia; urinalysis suggested a urinary tract infection, treated with IV ceftriaxone. She reports that dysphagia began immediately after the magnesium sulfate infusion. On arrival, she reported headache; blood pressure was 156/94 mmHg. Examination showed bilateral ptosis and dysphagia; she was alert, spoke in full sentences, and had a strong cough. Negative inspiratory force ranged from -15 to -25 cm H2O, indicating notable respiratory muscle weakness without overt respiratory distress or hypoxemia. Fetal heart rate was 158 bpm. Labs showed normal renal function, liver enzymes, platelets, and coagulation studies; thyroid studies and cortisol were normal. Urinalysis showed turbid urine with positive nitrites, marked leukocyte esterase, and numerous bacteria, WBCs, and RBCs. She denied vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, chest pain, dyspnea, or urinary symptoms.

A woman in her 50s, employed as a physician, with no significant past medical history or comorbidities, presented after a household contact was diagnosed with an acute respiratory viral illness. As a close contact, she underwent nasopharyngeal PCR testing for the suspected pathogen, which returned positive. She had a mild sore throat and, wishing for rapid symptom resolution, was started on an antiviral medication the same day. Her sore throat improved by the next day, and after completing a five-day course, her symptoms had fully resolved, confirmed at a follow-up visit on day six; a quantitative viral antigen test at that time showed a low value. She was scheduled to return to work the following day. However, she returned for re-evaluation one day later due to recurrence of sore throat, along with new low-grade fever and cough that had begun that morning. On examination: temperature 37.9°C, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, blood pressure 114/64 mmHg, pulse 80/min, and mild pharyngeal erythema. Laboratory testing showed white blood cell count 7,000/μL with normal differential, LDH 171 IU/L, mildly elevated CRP (0.6 mg/dL), and a repeat quantitative viral antigen level markedly increased compared with the prior test. Chest radiography showed no evidence of pneumonia. She had no history suggestive of immunodeficiency.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other specified congenital malformation syndromes, not elsewhere classified
train_cases.note: A woman in her late 30s presented to the emergency department with several days of progressive fatigue, altered consciousness, nausea, vomiting, excessive thirst, muscle weakness, and decreased urine output, occurring against a background of known chronic kidney disease with lapsed nephrology follow-up. Relevant history included an endocrine disorder causing low calcium levels identified in early childhood (with an associated episode of tetanic convulsion at that time), for which she received calcium and active vitamin D supplementation that was inconsistently continued into adulthood; ongoing oral calcium carbonate (~2400 mg/day elemental calcium), vitamin D3, and calcitriol were reported prior to this presentation. She also had childhood-onset sensorineural hearing loss, treated with a cochlear implant with limited benefit and subsequently a hearing aid. There was no family consanguinity, though her young son had intellectual disability, speech delay, and epilepsy of undetermined cause. On examination she was somnolent with limited cooperation; blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, heart rate 115/min, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 36.5°C, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She had decreased skin turgor and dry mucous membranes, reduced proximal muscle strength, and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Initial labs showed serum calcium 20.7 mg/dL, phosphorus 4.3 mg/dL, creatinine 2.98 mg/dL (baseline ~1.3 mg/dL), eGFR 19 mL/min/1.73m² (baseline ~52), sodium 125 mmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 214 U/L. Renal ultrasound showed small-normal kidneys with increased parenchymal echogenicity, loss of corticomedullary differentiation, and bilateral parapelvic cysts, without calculi or dilation.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other ectopic pregnancy without intrauterine pregnancy
train_cases.note: A woman in her late twenties, gravida 4 para 3 with two prior cesarean deliveries, presented with intermittent vaginal bleeding of two weeks' duration at approximately 12 weeks' gestation by reliable dating. She had initially been evaluated elsewhere for a two-day history of bleeding; ultrasound at that time showed a viable pregnancy and she was managed conservatively with pelvic rest. A follow-up scan noted an area of echogenic tissue near the pregnancy. Because of persistent bleeding she was referred for further evaluation, and around that time reportedly passed clots and a piece of tissue. On presentation, vital signs were blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 37°C, with conjunctival pallor noted on exam. Abdominal exam showed only a well-healed low midline surgical scar. Pelvic exam revealed minimal cervical oozing with the os admitting one fingertip; the uterus was bimanually estimated at 10 weeks' size without adnexal tenderness or mass. Ultrasound showed an echogenic mass approximately 4-5 cm in the lower uterine segment with internal hypoechoic areas, prominent Doppler vascularity, apparent extension into the adjacent muscular wall, and a thin fluid rim along its superior margin. Labs showed hemoglobin 7 g/dL, platelets 432,000/µL, WBC 9,600/µL, serum β-hCG 22,000 mIU/mL, and normal coagulation studies. An attempted uterine evacuation procedure was aborted due to brisk bleeding that then stopped spontaneously. She was transfused with two units of blood and given a single intramuscular dose of methotrexate; β-hCG declined over the following days, though repeat imaging showed no reduction in lesion size. On day 12 after treatment she developed sudden profuse vaginal bleeding with blood pressure 85/60 mmHg, heart rate 114 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min, and temperature 36.8°C, prompting emergency surgical intervention.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other ectopic pregnancy without intrauterine pregnancy
train_cases.note: A woman in her early 30s, gravida 1 para 0, was transferred from an outside facility for evaluation and management of a suspected pregnancy located outside the endometrial cavity. She had no significant past medical history. A copper intrauterine device had been in place for approximately 2 years at the time conception was discovered. Given the elevated risk of extrauterine implantation with a device in place, she had been followed with serial serum β-hCG levels and ultrasound over several weeks. Initial β-hCG was low but rose appropriately for the expected doubling time; however, transvaginal ultrasound did not demonstrate an intrauterine gestation or an adnexal mass. About a week later, repeat ultrasound identified an adnexal finding with cardiac activity, and she underwent laparoscopic surgery with removal of adnexal structures. Surgical pathology did not identify any pregnancy tissue. Approximately one week after surgery, β-hCG was found to be markedly elevated compared with prior values, and repeat ultrasound again demonstrated a gestation with cardiac activity, prompting transfer for further care. On presentation, she was well-appearing with normal vital signs, no abdominal tenderness, no vaginal bleeding, and no palpable pelvic masses. Hemoglobin was 13.6 g/dL and β-hCG was markedly elevated. Ultrasound demonstrated a tubular adnexal structure extending toward the uterus with an adjacent gestational sac containing a yolk sac and fetal pole with cardiac activity, sized consistent with about 7 weeks; no free fluid was noted.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute appendicitis with perforation, localized peritonitis, and gangrene, with abscess
train_cases.note: An 84-year-old woman with a history of dementia requiring full-time assistance with activities of daily living, prior cerebral infarction, multiple lumbar compression fractures, a healed right femoral neck fracture, and a long-standing untreated right inguinal hernia presented with a palpable left breast lump. Core biopsy confirmed a malignant breast tumor, and she underwent mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy. Twenty-eight days before surgery, laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 11,300/µL. Preoperative whole-body CT incidentally showed a small amount of fluid around the appendix, which was not considered clinically significant at the time, and surgery proceeded as planned. On postoperative day four, a progressively enlarging mass developed in the right groin. Abdominal CT demonstrated fluid collections in the right groin and around the cecum, with no evidence of communication with adjacent bowel. Aspiration of the groin collection yielded purulent fluid. She had a mild fever and a white blood cell count of 12,860/µL, without pain localized to the cecal region. A drainage tube was placed and antibiotic therapy started, with resolution of the swelling and gradual normalization of laboratory findings; she was discharged 19 days later. She returned 31 days afterward with several days of decreased oral intake. Repeat abdominal CT again showed fluid collection around the cecum without demonstrable communication with the intestinal tract on contrast imaging. Despite conservative management, intestinal fluid began draining from the area after two days, and her condition failed to improve, prompting consideration of surgical exploration.

A 70-year-old man presented with recurrent episodes of staring and unresponsiveness, each lasting 2-3 minutes and resolving spontaneously, followed by headache and short-term memory difficulty. No convulsions, jaw clenching, oral frothing, or incontinence were noted during events. Personal and past medical history were unremarkable. Family history included a brother who died of coronary artery disease, another brother with Parkinson's disease, and a mother with diabetes mellitus. Initial brain MRI and EEG were normal; neuropsychological testing showed mild anxiety symptoms with mildly reduced cognitive screening scores. Despite antiseizure therapy, episodes recurred over the following weeks, and repeat EEG showed generalized slow-wave activity while imaging remained normal. Several months later the episodes worsened in duration and frequency, occurring in clusters and accompanied by abnormal repetitive behaviors; examination revealed action tremor and unsteady tandem gait, with other neurologic findings unremarkable. Repeat brain MRI showed new T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the left frontal and parietal lobes, and EEG showed diffuse background slowing most prominent over the left hemisphere. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed elevated protein with normal cell count, glucose, and chloride; infectious studies and connective-tissue disease screening were negative. Seizures became refractory to escalating antiseizure medication regimens, increasing caregiver burden and injury risk.

A previously healthy young child (approximately 6 years old, male) with no relevant past medical or family history presented with acute onset of high fever (up to 40°C), conjunctivitis, and a diffuse rash. There was no family history of allergic or drug-related reactions. He was initially started on an oral antibiotic for a suspected bacterial throat infection, but his condition worsened over the following days despite treatment. He was then treated with aspirin and intravenous immunoglobulin for a suspected systemic inflammatory vasculitic condition. Shortly afterward, he developed rapidly progressive skin sloughing and blistering affecting a large body surface area. Additional immunosuppressive therapy (a calcineurin inhibitor and corticosteroids) was started, but he developed respiratory failure within 3 days of the skin findings. A thorough review of his medication history did not identify a clear causative drug. By day 7 of illness he required endotracheal intubation for respiratory failure, and by day 11 his condition had progressed to the point of requiring transfer to a specialized intensive care/ECMO center. Physical examination at presentation showed mucocutaneous involvement including conjunctival injection and extensive epidermal detachment.

A teenage male with no known past medical or family history presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset left upper-extremity weakness of 12 hours' duration. There was no preceding trauma, vigorous exertion, crying or laughing episodes, recent infection, or neck manipulation. The weakness was painless and non-numb, more pronounced distally than proximally. His mother reported he had been unusually sleepy beforehand. There was no headache, vomiting, fever, neck pain, visual disturbance, seizure, or loss of consciousness. He took no medications and had no substance use history. On assessment he was alert and fully oriented, with normal vital signs (pulse 72/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, temperature 36.5°C, oxygen saturation 97% on room air). Neurological exam showed isolated left upper-extremity weakness with normal bulk and tone: proximal strength 4/5 at shoulder and elbow, distal strength 3/5 at wrist and fingers. Reflexes were mildly brisk on the left compared to the right, plantar responses flexor bilaterally. Sensory exam, gait, and cranial nerves were normal. Echocardiogram and ECG were normal. Baseline hematology, coagulation studies, renal and liver panels, and electrolytes were unremarkable; extended thrombophilia and autoimmune testing could not be performed. Brain MRI obtained about 13 hours after onset showed a focal T1-hypointense, T2-heterogeneously hyperintense lesion in the basal ganglia region with diffusion restriction and no hemorrhage. MR angiography showed absent visualization of the right distal internal carotid and anterior cerebral arteries, narrowing of the proximal right middle cerebral artery, and enlarged collateral vessels with compensatory enlargement of the contralateral anterior cerebral artery.

An 81-year-old male with a history of hypertension, congestive heart failure, stage 3A chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, and benign prostatic hyperplasia (status post transurethral resection of the prostate one month earlier without immediate complications) was transferred to a tertiary hospital after a two-day hospitalization elsewhere for a four-day history of unquantified fever and generalized weakness. On examination he was disoriented, Glasgow Coma Scale 14/15 (E4,M6,V4). Vitals: blood pressure 154/85 mmHg, heart rate 69 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 37.1°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiopulmonary exam was unremarkable. The abdomen was soft, non-tender, non-distended with normal bowel sounds; a reducible right inguinal hernia was present. Skin and extremities showed no signs of infection. Labs showed leukocytosis (14,610/µL, 80.4% neutrophils), hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, hematocrit 34%, platelets 249,000/µL, creatinine 1.50 mg/dL, NT-proBNP 8224 pg/mL, and procalcitonin 1.55 ng/mL. Urinalysis showed blood (++), 57.3 RBC/HPF, 506.5 WBC/HPF, and yeast (2.1/HPF). He was started on empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected complicated urinary infection but did not improve, developing chills, tremors, tachycardia, and tachypnea. Blood cultures grew Enterococcus faecalis resistant to fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides but sensitive to ampicillin and vancomycin; antibiotics were adjusted accordingly. Repeat urine culture showed no growth at 48 hours, raising doubt about a urinary source. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed no intra-abdominal collection or abscess, confirmed the inguinal hernia, and revealed an enlarged prostate (6.3×5.6×5.0 cm, ~97 g), along with incidental cardiomegaly, small pericardial effusion, bilateral pleural effusions, and basal atelectasis.

A man in his mid-60s presented to the emergency department with sore throat and painful swallowing that had begun three days earlier, accompanied by fever. He denied cough, rhinorrhea, shortness of breath, or chest pain. His medical history included type 2 diabetes managed with oral medications; he had no known drug allergies and no prior airway disease. He had been seen twice previously at another facility for the same complaint and treated with oral and then intravenous antibiotics and antipyretics without improvement, and was also given corticosteroids at a subsequent visit with an outside impression of pharyngitis. He returned with worsening painful swallowing and new difficulty swallowing tablets. On examination he appeared well but had a low-grade fever (37.6-38°C) and mild tachycardia (103-107 bpm), with normal blood pressure, no tachypnea, no drooling, no stridor, and normal oxygen saturation on room air; he tolerated lying supine comfortably. His voice was raspy. Throat exam showed mild pharyngeal congestion with normal-appearing tonsils. Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 14.1×10^9/L and markedly elevated C-reactive protein of 256.9 mg/L, with normal renal function and electrolytes. A lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph showed an enlarged, edematous structure projecting into the airway column. Further imaging with contrast was obtained to characterize the finding and assess for a localized fluid collection and airway compromise.

A man in his 40s presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of throat pain. He reported taking a dose of azithromycin the day before symptom onset, after which he developed generalized throat discomfort and soreness that worsened with swallowing and speaking. Review of systems was otherwise negative, and past medical and surgical history was non-contributory. On examination, there was severe bilateral throat tenderness to palpation accompanied by trismus; no lymphadenopathy was noted, and the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Neck imaging with CT and plain X-ray showed a swollen, rounded, thumb-like soft tissue prominence at the base of the tongue with associated narrowing of the airway lumen. Given concern for impending airway compromise, the patient was emergently intubated and admitted to the intensive care unit. An otolaryngology consultation was obtained, intravenous antibiotics were initiated, and the patient was later discharged on oral antibiotics with a tapered corticosteroid course.

An adult male presented with a sudden onset of painful skin blistering and widespread skin peeling. On dermatologic examination, multiple tender flaccid blisters, vesicles, and erythematous dusky-red plaques with erosions were noted, involving approximately 40% of the body surface area. Nikolsky sign was positive. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed eyelid edema and hyperemia of the bulbar and tarsal conjunctivae bilaterally. Erosive lesions with mucosal detachment were also present in the oral and genital mucosa. The patient reported recent initiation of a new oral medication shortly before symptom onset. Vital signs on admission showed tachycardia (heart rate 106 bpm) and intermittent fever ranging from 39.2°C to 40°C. He was alert and oriented. Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.458, PaCO2 32.5 mmHg, PaO2 75.4 mmHg, glucose 6.8 mmol/L, base excess −0.5 mmol/L, oxygen saturation 95.59%, total hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, and lactate 3.1 mmol/L. Complete blood count was within normal limits. High-sensitivity C-reactive protein was elevated at 28.1 mg/L (normal 0–10 mg/L). Chest computed tomography was unremarkable. Skin biopsy was not performed due to patient refusal. The presentation was acute, with rapid progression of skin and mucosal involvement over a short period preceding admission.

A young adult male presented to the emergency department with a four-day history of right-sided lower abdominal pain, associated with vomiting and fever. On examination, there was tenderness in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. Laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis with a total white cell count of 14,370/cumm (normal range 4,000-10,000/cumm) and an elevated CRP of 15.39 mg/L (normal range <6 mg/L). Ultrasound imaging of the abdomen revealed an irregularly shaped isoechoic lesion measuring 2.5x2.0 cm in the right iliac fossa; the appendix could not be visualized. Given clinical concern for an acute intra-abdominal process, the patient underwent diagnostic laparoscopy. Intraoperative findings and subsequent surgical management were pursued based on the operative findings. A specimen was sent for histopathological examination. Following surgery, imaging of the scrotum was performed, which showed a normally descended, unremarkable contralateral testis and an empty ipsilateral hemiscrotum. The patient had an uncomplicated postoperative recovery and was discharged home the following day.
