A woman in her early thirties with no prior medical or psychiatric history presented with a several-week history of headache, low-grade fever, and generalized weakness, accompanied by behavioral changes including social withdrawal, anhedonia, reduced responsiveness to her environment, sleep disturbance, and auditory hallucinations. Within days of symptom onset she experienced a generalized tonic-clonic seizure with frothing at the mouth. There was no history of substance use, recent infection, or prior neuropsychiatric illness. She was started on multiple antiseizure medications for recurrent generalized tonic-clonic seizures but continued to have seizures along with progressively worsening cognition, including impaired attention and concentration, short-term memory loss, slowed processing speed, and difficulty following conversations, prompting hospital admission for further evaluation. On admission she was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. Neurological examination showed global aphasia and cognitive impairment (Montreal Cognitive Assessment score 18/30), with deficits in attention, executive function, eye contact, and responsiveness. Cranial nerve examination was unremarkable. Motor strength was preserved, deep tendon reflexes were normal, and plantar responses were bilaterally flexor, with no signs of meningeal irritation. Antiseizure therapy was intensified to improve seizure control.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute leukemia of unspecified cell type not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: A woman in her late 60s with a history of hypertension and a remote, conservatively managed subdural hematoma presented with a three-week history of enlarging cervical lymph nodes, exertional fatigue, and easy bruising. On examination she had palpable cervical lymphadenopathy and scattered bruising; no other findings were specified. Initial laboratory evaluation revealed pancytopenia with hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 15.97x10^9/L with 80% circulating blasts, absolute neutrophil count 0.6x10^9/L, and platelets 18x10^9/L. Lactate dehydrogenase was elevated at 297 U/L and ferritin markedly elevated at 9986 ng/mL. Uric acid, creatinine, liver enzymes, and bilirubin were within normal limits. Coagulation studies showed a mildly prolonged PT/INR (15.7 s/1.15) with normal aPTT. Serologic screening for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV was negative. Peripheral blood flow cytometry demonstrated a population of blasts expressing cytoplasmic CD3, CD7, CD34, CD117, and HLA-DR, without myeloperoxidase expression. Bone marrow aspirate obtained the same week showed an 80% cellular marrow with 80% blasts. Conventional karyotyping revealed a hypodiploid clone, 45,XX,dic(7;12)(p11.2;p13). Targeted molecular sequencing identified an IDH2 R140Q mutation, with FLT3-ITD/TKD and IDH1 mutations negative. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 70% with moderate tricuspid regurgitation.

A male in his early 20s presented to the emergency department with a four-day history of fever, chills, bilateral eye redness, and reduced oral intake, occurring in the setting of a 10-day illness that began with sore throat, rhinorrhea, and fatigue and progressively worsened. He had been evaluated as an outpatient and prescribed an antiviral and an antifungal mouth rinse, which he was unable to tolerate due to severe pain with swallowing. In the days before presentation he developed chest pain, shortness of breath, and a productive cough with persistent chills. Vital signs showed a respiratory rate of 14/min, heart rate of 118/min, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Chest imaging showed multifocal infiltrates, prompting initiation of an antibiotic and a corticosteroid. Within days of starting the antibiotic he developed extensive oral ulcerations, worsening difficulty swallowing, and persistent chest pain, and he reported painful genital lesions without an associated skin rash. Examination revealed severe ulceration of the hard and soft palate and tonsils, conjunctival injection, and genital mucosal lesions, without cutaneous involvement. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance and lymphopenia, elevated CRP and ESR, and normal renal and hepatic function. An extensive infectious workup (HIV, EBV, CMV, COVID-19, influenza, blood/sputum/urine cultures) was negative. Repeat chest CT showed resolving pneumonia. Upper endoscopy revealed diffuse whitish plaques with surrounding erythema in the oropharynx and esophagus and a small hiatal hernia, with negative fungal special stains.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A man in his late 60s with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and long-standing poor glycemic control (recent HbA1c 8.47%), maintained on multiple anti-hyperglycemic agents including basal insulin, a sulfonylurea, an SGLT2 inhibitor, metformin, and a DPP-4 inhibitor, underwent elective right-sided colon resection with bowel anastomosis for a colonic malignancy. The perioperative course was uneventful. Starting on postoperative day 3, he developed lethargy and nausea. By postoperative day 5, he had become drowsy, was afebrile, tachypneic (respiratory rate 24 breaths/min) with oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and hypotensive (blood pressure 90/60 mmHg). Systemic examination was otherwise unremarkable. Random blood glucose was 203 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed profound acidosis (pH 6.99) with markedly reduced bicarbonate (1.4 mmol/L) and an elevated anion gap (28.2 mmol/L). Urine ketones were strongly positive, and serum beta-hydroxybutyrate was markedly elevated (5.84 mmol/L). Electrocardiography, serum cardiac enzyme levels, and two-dimensional echocardiography showed no acute abnormalities. White blood cell count was elevated at 15,400/mm3, and empiric antibiotics were escalated. Renal function and electrolytes were being closely monitored given the acute metabolic derangement.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism with acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her mid-60s with a history of coronary artery disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with inconsistent use of prescribed anticoagulation, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and type 2 diabetes presented with fever, cough, palpitations, and generalized weakness of recent onset. Examination showed mild tachypnea and tachycardia. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (14,000/mm3), with normal platelet count and hemoglobin. Chest radiograph showed a right mid-lung consolidation. She was treated empirically with antibiotics and discharged after clinical improvement. Approximately ten days later, she returned with rapid functional decline and worsening cough. She was tachycardic (heart rate 125), hypoxic (oxygen saturation 85% on 3 L supplemental oxygen), and had an elevated serum lactate of 5.2 mmol/L. Repeat chest radiograph showed a new smooth-walled cavitary lesion in the same region as the prior consolidation. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a partial filling defect within the right main pulmonary artery extending into a right lower lobe branch, along with a cavitary lesion containing an air-fluid level in the right middle lobe abutting the pleura. Echocardiography showed no evidence of right ventricular strain. She was started on therapeutic anticoagulation and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics. Due to lack of clinical improvement, she underwent surgical resection of the affected lung tissue, which revealed a large abscess cavity. Her postoperative course was complicated by sudden hemodynamic collapse and cardiac arrest.

A 10-year-old boy presented with a six-month history of progressive left eye vision loss, now reduced to light perception only, accompanied by recurrent episodes of vertigo. Past medical history was notable for nephrotic syndrome at age 4, treated with corticosteroids with remission achieved by age 5. There was no family history of neurologic or autoimmune disease. Birth history and developmental milestones were normal. On neurological examination, he was alert with age-appropriate cognition. Cranial nerve assessment showed left optic nerve dysfunction with divergent strabismus. Motor examination showed normal tone and 5/5 strength bilaterally; sensory examination, reflexes, coordination, and gait were normal. Ophthalmological evaluation showed right eye visual acuity of 10/10 and left eye light perception only, with a left relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy showed right papillary hyperemia and complete left optic atrophy. Brain and cervical spine MRI showed extensive T2/FLAIR hyperintensity throughout the left retrobulbar optic nerve extending to the chiasm without gadolinium enhancement, along with periventricular white matter lesions, including one at the left posterior internal capsule showing a central vein sign and paramagnetic rim, and additional lesions in the left thalamus and left pons. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed type 2 oligoclonal bands (CSF-positive, serum-negative), IgG index 0.577, mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, and normal protein. Serum antibody studies, complete blood count, metabolic panel, and rheumatologic studies were unremarkable.

A woman in her late 70s with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and stage IV serous endometrial carcinoma, status post total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy approximately two months earlier, presented from an oncology infusion center with several days of generalized weakness and persistent fatigue. She had completed her first cycle of combination chemoimmunotherapy about three to four weeks prior. She also reported new right eyelid drooping that began one day before presentation, preceded a few days earlier by transient visual spots and diplopia that was worse on rightward gaze and had since resolved. She denied headache, focal limb weakness, speech difficulty, chest pain, abdominal pain, bloating, vaginal bleeding, nausea, or vomiting; appetite was fair. She reported palpitations, night sweats, and about 10 pounds of unintentional weight loss since starting treatment. She had no known drug allergies and denied tobacco, illicit drug, or significant alcohol use. Home medications included amlodipine, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and cetirizine. On presentation she was tachycardic and tachypneic. Initial labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 15.0×10^9/L), markedly elevated transaminases (AST 1242 IU/L, ALT 758 IU/L), and mild acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.19 mg/dL). Hemoglobin and platelets were stable. Blood cultures were negative. CT angiography of the chest showed a left lower lobe consolidation without pulmonary embolism; abdominal/pelvic CT and liver appearance were unremarkable. Thyroid studies showed suppressed TSH with elevated free T4; TSH-receptor and thyroid peroxidase antibodies were negative. Creatine kinase was markedly elevated (13,000 IU/L) and high-sensitivity troponin I peaked at 15,000 ng/L. Electrocardiography showed new right bundle branch block with intermittent high-degree atrioventricular block. Neurologic examination revealed complete ptosis and bilateral ophthalmoplegia, with reduced single-breath count and vital capacity. Echocardiography showed a new decline in ejection fraction from a prior baseline.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A woman in her late 30s, with a background of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis previously treated with alemtuzumab, presented acutely with palpitations, chest tightness, dizziness, and light-headedness. On examination she was clinically symptomatic with marked sinus tachycardia (heart rate 160 beats per minute); other vital signs were otherwise unremarkable and she was afebrile at the time of the recorded temperature. Laboratory investigations revealed a markedly elevated free T4 (>100 pmol/L; reference 12-22 pmol/L) with a suppressed TSH (<0.01 mU/L; reference 0.4-4.0 mU/L). Troponin was mildly elevated at 71 ng/L (reference <14 ng/L), thought to reflect cardiac strain from tachycardia rather than primary ischemia. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Despite escalating doses of an antithyroid medication and a beta-blocker titrated for rate control, she remained markedly tachycardic (heart rate persistently above 130 bpm) with no biochemical improvement in thyroid function tests. Echocardiography excluded structural cardiac disease or regional wall motion abnormalities. Given the severity and apparent treatment-refractory nature of her biochemical and clinical thyroid dysfunction, further specialist endocrine assessment and consideration of more intensive medical and surgical management was pursued.

A woman in her late twenties, gravida 3 para 1, at 31 weeks and 6 days gestation presented with hypogastric pain that began the day before admission, worsening with movement, eating, and drinking, following a week of nausea and vomiting, including a recent self-limited episode of vomiting. She denied headache, visual disturbance, fever, rash, bleeding, bruising, vaginal loss, or pelvic pain, and was not taking anticoagulants. Her obstetric history included a prior pregnancy complicated by gestational diabetes with a spontaneous preterm vaginal delivery without complications, and a prior first-trimester pregnancy loss managed surgically. The current pregnancy was under specialist antenatal monitoring due to a body mass index of 40.6 kg/m²; earlier prenatal blood tests and glucose tolerance testing had been normal, with appropriate fetal growth. On admission, vital signs were normal, including heart rate 62 beats/minute, blood pressure 119/78 mmHg, temperature 37°C, and normal deep tendon reflexes. The abdomen was soft with mild hypogastric tenderness; the uterus was relaxed and non-tender. Fetal monitoring was reassuring. Laboratory testing showed a fall in hemoglobin from 120 to 86 g/L and platelet count from 220 to 9 x10^9/L, with normal white cell count, amylase, renal function, liver enzymes, and coagulation profile. Bilirubin was mildly elevated, urine dipstick showed heavy proteinuria, and the urine protein-creatinine ratio was elevated. A repeat blood count showed further decline in platelet count. Reticulocyte count and lactate dehydrogenase were subsequently found to be elevated, suggestive of an ongoing hemolytic process.

A man in his early 60s presented to the emergency department at night with acute right upper quadrant abdominal pain and a 5-day history of fever, peaking at 38.0°C. He reported an upper respiratory illness treated with routine medication about one month earlier, since resolved. He had no history of jaundice, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, or diabetes, no recent vaccination, occasional smoking and alcohol use, and no relevant family history. On examination he had right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy's sign and diminished bowel sounds; lungs were clear. Labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 12.13×10^9/L), elevated CRP (24.55 mg/L), and elevated liver enzymes (ALT 119.1 U/L, AST 103.2 U/L, GGT 107.4 U/L, ALP 138.5 U/L, total bilirubin 36.6 µmol/L) with mild hyperglycemia (8.1 mmol/L); electrolytes, renal, pancreatic, and thyroid studies, cardiac enzymes, troponin, and myoglobin were normal. ECG showed ST-segment changes, a prolonged QT interval, and abnormal Q waves. Abdominal ultrasound, CT, and MRI showed gallbladder wall thickening and edema, increased intraluminal density, and pericholecystic fluid, without gallstones or evidence of portal hypertension or cirrhosis. He was managed with bowel rest, IV fluids, and antibiotics, with surgery planned. Over the following 24-48 hours he developed rapidly progressive, ascending limb weakness worse in the lower limbs, paresthesia of the hands and feet, diminishing then absent tendon reflexes, dysphagia with choking on liquids, chest tightness, and worsening respiratory status. Brain and spine MRI showed no acute ischemic or compressive lesion.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other ectopic pregnancy without intrauterine pregnancy
train_cases.note: A woman in her late twenties presented to the emergency department with a 16-day history of abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, which she had initially attributed to her menstrual period. She had undergone a lower uterine segment cesarean section approximately three months earlier, with resolution of post-surgical bleeding about two months prior to this presentation. Her obstetric history included six prior pregnancies: three term births (two vaginal, one cesarean), and two prior pregnancy losses. Her last reported menstrual period was about one month before presentation. She had no chronic medical conditions and was not taking any medications. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits (blood pressure 119/74 mmHg, temperature 37°C). General physical exam was unremarkable except for suprapubic and left lower quadrant abdominal tenderness. Initial serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) was markedly elevated at 9,623 IU/mL (reference <5 IU/L); a repeat level 48 hours later rose to 16,587 IU/mL, an increase exceeding 66%. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated an empty uterine cavity with a cystic-appearing structure near the endometrium in the region of the prior cesarean incision, raising concern for an abnormally located early pregnancy.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A woman in her early 30s with no known history of thyroid disease presented to the emergency department with acute-onset generalized abdominal pain and palpitations. She denied recent upper respiratory infection, fever, or other systemic illness prior to onset. She reported intermittent cocaine use over the preceding week, with her most recent use approximately two days before presentation. On examination she appeared anxious and restless. She was febrile at 38 °C, with marked tachycardia (heart rate 145 bpm), tachypnea (respiratory rate 28/min), and elevated blood pressure (155/65 mmHg); oxygen saturation was 99% on room air. She was mildly diaphoretic with a fine tremor of the outstretched hands. The thyroid gland was not palpably enlarged. Abdominal exam was benign without tenderness, guarding, or peritoneal signs. She was alert but markedly agitated. Initial labs showed bicarbonate 14 mmol/L with an anion gap of 17, WBC 14.4x10^3/uL with neutrophilia (ANC 10.91x10^3/uL), MCV 72.6 fL, normal troponin, and NT-proBNP 982 pg/mL. Additional endocrine studies were obtained showing TSH 0.015 uIU/mL, free T3 10.69 pg/mL, free T4 4.02 ng/dL, TPO antibodies >1000 IU/mL, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin 340%, and TBII 16.41 IU/L. A clinical scoring tool for a hyperadrenergic syndrome was calculated. She was started on antithyroid medication, corticosteroid, and beta-blockade with supportive care, with subsequent improvement in heart rate, abdominal pain, anxiety, and tremor, and was discharged after ICU admission and clinical stabilization.

A man in his late 40s presented to the emergency department with a 7-day history of abdominal pain, predominantly localized to the right lower quadrant. On examination, he had tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (white blood cell count 19,600/µL; reference 4,000-11,000/µL) with neutrophilia (absolute neutrophil count 16,500/µL; reference 2,000-6,900/µL) and an elevated C-reactive protein of 18.4 mg/dL (reference <1.0 mg/dL). Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT with arterial and portal venous phases showed a dilated appendix with mural wall thickening and adjacent periappendiceal inflammatory fat stranding; no signs of perforation or bowel ischemia were seen. The same CT also revealed an intraluminal filling defect within the superior mesenteric vein with extension into mesenteric venous branches, without portal vein involvement at that time. One day later, the patient underwent diagnostic laparoscopy converted to open surgery for source control, followed by initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics and anticoagulation. A follow-up CT 10 days after surgery showed persistent mesenteric venous thrombosis and a new rim-enhancing fluid collection in the surgical bed. A subsequent CT 5 days later showed decreased size of the fluid collection but progression of the thrombus to the origin of the portal vein. Conservative management and serial imaging follow-up continued.

A man in his late 60s with a history of chronic alcohol misuse presented with sudden-onset weakness in his left leg that began abruptly and worsened over several hours. He denied facial droop, speech disturbance, visual symptoms, or upper-limb involvement, and had no headache, seizure activity, or loss of consciousness. On initial examination he was alert and oriented, cranial nerves were intact, upper-limb strength was normal, and the only abnormality was left lower-limb weakness; reflexes were not assessed at that time. Over the following four days his condition deteriorated, with weakness progressing to involve both lower limbs, accompanied by worsening gait ataxia and stocking-like sensory loss. On more detailed assessment five days after initial presentation, he reported a recent hospitalisation for an acute diarrhoeal illness several days before the onset of weakness. Examination now revealed bilateral lower-motor-neuron pattern weakness, glove-and-stocking sensory loss, diffuse areflexia, and normal cranial nerve and cerebellar findings. Shallow breathing and reduced respiratory effort were also noted. Blood chemistry and full blood count were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed elevated protein (4.3 g/L; normal 0.15-0.45) with a normal white cell count (1 cell/µL) and mildly elevated lactate (2.5 mmol/L). Brain MRI was normal with no evidence of acute infarction, haemorrhage, or mass lesion. Nerve conduction studies showed markedly prolonged distal motor latencies, reduced motor amplitudes, slowed conduction velocities, and absent sensory responses in upper-limb nerves, with electromyography showing reduced recruitment in multiple limb muscles without spontaneous activity.

A woman in her mid-30s, para 3, presented 40 days after an unsupervised vaginal delivery at home; she had not received regular antenatal care during the pregnancy. On the 5th postpartum day she developed a severe headache and fever unresponsive to over-the-counter medications. One day later she developed shortness of breath, palpitations, and increased sweating, prompting evaluation at a local hospital about 9 days postpartum. Examination there revealed bilateral basal crackles and a parasternal heave with thrill. Laboratory testing showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 5.2 g/dl), thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and a positive scrub typhus IgG; ECG showed T-wave inversion in leads V1-V4. She received potassium replacement, blood transfusion, and diuretic therapy, then was discharged before further workup due to financial constraints. Two weeks later, on postpartum day 40, she returned with 3 days of high-grade fever (up to 103°F) with chills, rigors, and sweating, progressively worsening exertional dyspnea, palpitations, orthopnea, a non-diurnal dry cough, and a pulsating frontotemporal headache without nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia. There was no history of intravenous drug use, childhood cardiac disease, or recent dental procedures. Repeat labs showed Hb 7.26 g/dl, WBC 11,210 with neutrophil predominance, ESR 40, procalcitonin 2.44, and NT-proBNP 1740. Serologic tests for brucella, dengue, scrub typhus, and leptospira were negative, as was AFB stain and blood culture. Chest X-ray showed wedge-shaped consolidation in the right lung. Echocardiography revealed a 32×9 mm oscillating structure attached to the pulmonary valve, severe pulmonary regurgitation, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and dilated right heart chambers. Contrast CT chest showed filling defects in right pulmonary artery branches with associated wedge-shaped consolidations.

A 78-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a three-week history of progressive dyspnea, palpitations, and bilateral lower extremity swelling. Symptoms began shortly after a dental extraction performed for acute tooth pain; she did not receive antibiotic prophylaxis prior to the procedure, as she denied any known cardiac disease. On admission she was afebrile (98.8°F), tachycardic (HR 115/min), hypotensive (BP 96/62 mmHg), and saturating 97% on room air without respiratory distress. Examination revealed confusion, diffuse pulmonary crackles, a grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, and 3+ pitting edema, without focal neurologic deficits or skin lesions. Labs showed leukocytosis (17.1 x10^3/µL) with neutrophilia (15.03 x10^3/µL), markedly elevated proBNP (22,598 pg/mL), elevated D-dimer (1.88 mg/L), and elevated CRP (8.0 mg/dL). Blood cultures drawn on admission grew a pansensitive gram-positive organism typically found as an oral commensal. Chest CT showed a filling defect in the right middle lobe pulmonary artery consistent with embolism, interstitial edema, bilateral pleural effusions, and cardiomegaly. Abdominal CT showed a wedge-shaped defect in the left kidney, with normal renal function and an unremarkable urinalysis. Mental status acutely worsened, and brain MRI showed a small area of restricted diffusion in the right frontal lobe consistent with an acute infarct. Echocardiography showed left ventricular ejection fraction 25-30%, a mildly dilated and hypokinetic right ventricle, moderately enlarged left atrium, severely enlarged right atrium, moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation, severe aortic valve stenosis with partial outflow obstruction, multiple mobile masses on the aortic valve, and a 1.5 x 0.9 cm mobile mass attached to the Eustachian valve.

A previously healthy preschool-aged male with no recent immunizations or medication use presented with a 1-week history of intermittent fever, green mucopurulent ocular discharge, rhinorrhea, and a dry cough. Approximately 48 hours after symptom onset, an erythematous papular rash appeared on the face and rapidly generalized. He was started on oral antibiotics for a presumed exanthematous illness, but the rash progressed within a day to painful blistering lesions with epidermal detachment, prompting transfer to a tertiary center. On examination he was hemodynamically stable without respiratory distress. Skin findings involved approximately 68% of body surface area, with a positive Nikolsky sign, diffuse dusky erythematous and violaceous patches, epidermal detachment, and denuded areas on the palms. Mucosal involvement included erosions of the lips and perioral mucosa. A skin biopsy from the edge of an early blister showed extensive keratinocyte necrosis, subepidermal cleft formation, basal layer vacuolization, and a sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. Infectious workup: respiratory PCR panel positive for adenovirus, negative for other respiratory viruses and atypical bacteria; viral loads negative for EBV, CMV, HHV-6/7, and KSHV; blood and stool cultures negative. Laboratory studies showed no hepatic or renal dysfunction.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A man in his late 50s with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department with a one-week history of progressive dyspnea on exertion. He reported having been diagnosed with influenza approximately one week before the onset of these symptoms. On initial evaluation he was hemodynamically stable, with blood pressure 113/78 mmHg, heart rate 83 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Laboratory testing showed a markedly elevated high-sensitivity troponin of approximately 2600 ng/L. Electrocardiogram showed ST-segment deviations in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) and precordial leads (V3-V4), with reciprocal ST depression in aVL, an S1Q3T3 pattern, and widespread T-wave inversions in the inferolateral leads. He was treated empirically with heparin and aspirin and taken for urgent coronary angiography, which showed nonobstructive coronary disease (less than 10% stenosis in all major vessels) and a preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 55% with an elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure of 13 mmHg. Given the discordance between the clinical/ECG picture and angiographic findings, the differential was broadened. Additional history revealed an 11-hour car trip shortly before symptom onset. Further labs showed TSH 1.18 uIU/mL, triglycerides 126 mg/dL, LDL 46 mg/dL, HDL 30 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1c 7.9%. Chest imaging was pending further evaluation.

train_cases.diagnosis: Benign neoplasm of unspecified adrenal gland
train_cases.note: A 51-year-old man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and dyslipidemia presented with headaches and palpitations. Symptom duration and onset were not otherwise specified, but the presentation prompted outpatient imaging. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a well-defined 7-cm mass in the right adrenal gland. Biochemical work-up showed markedly elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrine (24.6 mg/day; reference 0.04-0.19) and normetanephrine (13.1 mg/day; reference 0.09-0.33), along with markedly elevated plasma epinephrine (5,225 pg/mL; reference 0-100), plasma norepinephrine (8,032 pg/mL; reference 100-450), and mildly elevated plasma dopamine (23 pg/mL; reference 0-20). Blood pressure was suboptimally controlled on doxazosin 16 mg/day and nifedipine 20 mg/day, with associated tachycardia. Diabetes was managed with dapagliflozin and teneligliptin (HbA1c 7.8%). The patient was referred for surgical evaluation. Height was 169 cm and weight 78 kg. He was admitted for preoperative optimization, including uptitration of nifedipine, initiation of a beta-blocker for tachycardia, and intravenous volume expansion with saline prior to planned surgery. No other focal neurological, cardiac, or abdominal examination abnormalities were reported preoperatively.

A man in his late 60s with a history of tobacco use, essential hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with acute-onset hoarseness and rapidly progressive difficulty swallowing over the course of one day, beginning with trouble swallowing pills in the morning and progressing to significant swelling of the mouth and throat by later that day. He reported pain and swelling of the mouth and throat but was tolerating oral secretions and maintaining his airway at initial evaluation. Home medications included an oral anticoagulant, an antiarrhythmic, an ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, a statin, metformin, and a proton pump inhibitor; he had no known food or drug allergies. On examination he was afebrile and hemodynamically stable without respiratory distress. There was marked edema of the floor of the mouth and sublingual tissues with elevation of the tongue, limiting visualization of the posterior pharynx, and he was unable to fully close his mouth. Laboratory testing showed leukocytosis (16.8 k/uL, normal 3.5-11.3) and markedly elevated C-reactive protein (148 mg/dL, normal 0.0-5.0). Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck soft tissues showed edema involving the epiglottis, the left aryepiglottic fold, and the left lateral oropharyngeal mucosa, with associated edema of the floor of the mouth. Faint scratch marks were later noted on his left forearm, and family reported pet cats at home. Blood cultures obtained at presentation subsequently grew a gram-negative coccobacillus.

A man in his 40s with a history of ulcerative colitis on chronic immunosuppressive therapy, and a history of a high-grade pleomorphic sarcoma of the chest wall with subsequent pulmonary metastases status post multiple thoracic surgeries, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy, presented to the emergency department with acute onset of hypoxia and dyspnea. He had recently started a new systemic oral anticancer agent after prior chemotherapy regimens were discontinued for disease progression and toxicity, and developed worsening dyspnea, fever, and tachycardia within 72 hours of the first dose. Imaging obtained shortly before starting this medication had shown stable chronic fibrotic changes and pleural scarring in one lung, with the other lung clear aside from a solitary nodule. On arrival, he was profoundly hypoxic with oxygen saturation in the low 70s on room air and was admitted to the intensive care unit for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. Temperature was 38.1°C. Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Lung auscultation revealed dry crackles over one lung field and diminished breath sounds over the other, consistent with known chronic fibrosis. Chest imaging demonstrated new diffuse reticular and ground-glass opacities in the previously clear lung, with stable chronic changes on the other side. Laboratory evaluation showed leukocytosis (16.7 K/µL) with markedly elevated ESR (86 mm/hr) and CRP (192 mg/L); autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA, RF, anti-CCP) were negative. Blood cultures and infectious/respiratory viral panels, including SARS-CoV-2, were negative.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A man in his 50s with a history of hypertension treated with valsartan presented to the emergency department with acute onset of severe chest pain, palpitations, and profuse sweating over the preceding four hours. He also reported a one-week history of fever (up to 38.7°C), diarrhea, and recurrent vomiting prior to admission. On examination he had signs of volume overload with bilateral basal crackles and mild bilateral leg edema. Ocular examination showed no proptosis, lid lag, or other signs of orbital inflammation. Initial ECG showed ST depressions in the lateral leads with nonspecific ST-T changes. Troponin I was elevated at 1.2 ng/mL. Laboratory studies showed mild hyponatremia (134 mmol/L), leukocytosis (11.2x10^9/L), and elevated C-reactive protein (45 mg/L); renal function and liver enzymes were near normal. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a hyperdynamic left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 65%, grade I diastolic dysfunction, mild left atrial enlargement, and no regional wall motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography showed no significant obstructive disease. Shortly afterward, the patient developed marked sinus tachycardia (130-140 bpm) and rapidly declining consciousness, becoming obtunded (Glasgow Coma Scale 8), requiring intubation for airway protection. Additional testing revealed a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone level with markedly elevated free T4 and total T3, elevated thyroid autoantibody titers, elevated NT-proBNP (2500 pg/mL), mild transaminitis, mild lactic acidosis, and elevated serum cortisol.

A man in his mid-50s with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and chronic alcohol use presented to the emergency department with acute confusion and low blood pressure developing over a short period. On arrival he was febrile (39.4°C), tachycardic, and hypotensive, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12/15. Examination revealed suprapubic tenderness. Initial laboratory studies showed a marked inflammatory response, acute kidney injury, severe hyperglycemia, and elevated lactate. Urinalysis showed pyuria, positive nitrites, and bacteriuria; blood and urine cultures subsequently grew a multidrug-resistant strain of Escherichia coli. Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT showed bilaterally enlarged kidneys with multiple gas locules within the right collecting system, associated with patchy renal parenchymal hypoenhancement and perirenal fat stranding. The bladder wall was diffusely thickened with intraluminal and intramural gas foci along the anterior and posterior walls. A gas-containing fluid collection was seen in the rectovesical pouch. Two periurethral collections around the prostatic urethra demonstrated peripheral wall enhancement without internal gas. Delayed post-contrast images showed absent opacification of the excretory pathways. The patient was admitted to intensive care and started on fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics adjusted to culture results, vasopressor support, and glycemic control, with subsequent interventional drainage of the pelvic collection.

A man in his mid-30s with end-stage renal disease on maintenance hemodialysis via a left thigh arteriovenous graft, chronic anemia, a history of prior renal transplant rejection, and poorly controlled hypertension presented with worsening dyspnea and hypoxia. Over the preceding several weeks he had persistent symptomatic anemia, with hemoglobin values of 6-7 g/dL despite multiple red blood cell transfusions, intravenous iron, and high-dose erythropoietin, raising concern for anemia beyond his baseline renal disease. On the day of presentation, pre-dialysis hemoglobin had fallen to 5.4 g/dL, prompting transfusion and brief emergency department evaluation before discharge; he returned shortly afterward with worsening dyspnea, tachypnea, and tachycardia requiring admission. On presentation he was febrile (38.1°C) and hypertensive (185/100 mmHg). Exam revealed diffuse crackles and a new grade II/VI systolic murmur, without peripheral stigmata of infective disease, scleral icterus, or jaundice. Chest radiography showed a right perihilar opacity concerning for infection. Initial labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 20.1, 81% neutrophils), hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, hematocrit 22%, platelets 127, elevated reticulocytes (4.7%), elevated lactic acid and LDH, low haptoglobin (<8), mildly elevated total bilirubin, normal-to-low iron studies with markedly elevated ferritin, and elevated vitamin B12. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly.

A young adult male presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain of two days' duration and multiple episodes of bilious vomiting over the preceding day. The pain was insidious in onset, intermittent, and gradually progressive, without clear aggravating or relieving factors. He also reported an inability to pass stool or flatus for one day. There was no fever, chills, diarrhea, or history of abdominal trauma. He had no known comorbidities and no prior abdominal surgery. On examination, he was conscious, alert, and fully oriented. Vital signs were stable: blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The abdomen was soft but tender in the right iliac fossa, right lumbar region, and hypogastrium, with guarding in the right iliac fossa. Bowel sounds were sluggish. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (16,900/cumm) with neutrophilia (85%); renal and liver function tests were normal. Arterial blood gas was within normal limits, including lactate. An erect abdominal X-ray showed multiple dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed clustering of small bowel loops medial to the caecum with features suggesting a closed-loop obstruction of mid-ileal loops, and preserved bowel wall enhancement.

A woman in her mid-40s with a history of anxiety and depression presented with three weeks of progressively worsening cognitive decline, followed by new-onset agitation and confusion. Initial brain MRI showed scattered T2-hyperintense white matter lesions, including periventricular foci. Repeat imaging several days later showed interval development of new supratentorial and infratentorial lesions, some with contrast enhancement. MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine demonstrated several non-enhancing intramedullary lesions. Vital signs were within normal limits. Neurologic examination revealed confusion and impaired short-term memory without focal motor or sensory deficits reported. Extensive serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing was largely unremarkable; CSF analysis showed a lymphocyte-predominant pleocytosis (43 WBC/µL, 95% lymphocytes), mildly elevated protein (69.4 mg/dL), and unpaired oligoclonal bands (3 bands) with a normal IgG index. Serum and CSF autoimmune, infectious, and antibody panels (including antinuclear antibody, HIV, syphilis, Lyme, herpes/varicella, West Nile, cryptococcal antigen, ACE, aquaporin-4, and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies) were negative, and CSF cytology showed no malignant cells. Despite five days of high-dose corticosteroids, five sessions of plasmapheresis, and five days of intravenous immunoglobulin, the lesions continued to enlarge on follow-up imaging. Given lack of clinical or radiologic improvement, a brain biopsy was performed, showing diffuse macrophage-rich white matter injury with reactive astrocytosis, a predominantly T-cell (CD3+) inflammatory infiltrate with a minor CD20+ B-cell component, preserved axons, and extensive myelin loss with only sparse residual myelinated fibers; special staining for JC virus was negative.

A woman in her early 30s with an established history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (diagnosed roughly one year prior, previously with optic neuritis, characteristic white-matter lesions on MRI, and oligoclonal bands in cerebrospinal fluid) presented with a several-day history of sudden, painful contractions of the left upper limb. She was on a maintenance immunotherapy infusion regimen but had missed her most recent scheduled dose before symptom onset. Baseline neurological status had been stable, with only mild paresthesias and no functional disability on prior evaluation months earlier. Four days before presentation, she began having brief, forceful spasms of the left arm with abnormal posturing, occasionally causing falls; episodes lasted 10-20 seconds and occurred up to ten times daily, causing significant distress. Between episodes, strength, reflexes, and sensation were normal, with no new deficits. Brain MRI showed a new hyperintense lesion in the right lateral cerebral peduncle, anatomically consistent with the side and pattern of the spasms, along with stable chronic white-matter lesions compared to prior imaging. Spinal MRI showed no new lesions. Electroencephalogram was normal, without epileptiform activity. An initial anticonvulsant trial caused intolerable nausea and vomiting and was discontinued; a second anticonvulsant produced marked improvement, eliminating the spasms.

A man in his late 50s with a history of mitral valve prolapse with mild thickening of the posterior leaflet, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and former tobacco use presented to the emergency department with four days of nausea and vomiting. His spouse noted he had undergone a dental extraction approximately four weeks earlier. On arrival he was hemodynamically stable, with a late systolic murmur and a mid-systolic click on auscultation. Initial labs showed elevated troponin (512 ng/L, rising to 965 ng/L), markedly elevated C-reactive protein (280 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (53 mm/hr), elevated procalcitonin (4.89 ng/mL), transaminitis (AST 270 U/L, ALT 145 U/L), elevated total and direct bilirubin (5.6 and 3.05 mg/dL), and a white blood cell count of 10.7 x10^9/L. He was transferred to a tertiary center and started on empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics. Blood cultures grew a gram-positive organism, and repeat cultures remained positive after 48 hours of appropriate therapy. Transthoracic echocardiography showed new moderate mitral regurgitation with preserved ejection fraction. Subsequent transesophageal echocardiography revealed mobile echodensities on both mitral leaflets extending toward the interatrial septum, an additional left atrial wall lesion, and an annular abscess. He later developed visual hallucinations and acute encephalopathy; brain MRI showed multifocal acute infarcts in several vascular territories with a small subarachnoid hemorrhage. Dental imaging showed periodontal disease without abscess.

A 9-year-old girl with no prior medical history and up-to-date immunizations presented with several weeks of diffuse headaches and vomiting, without fever, that preceded the onset of limb weakness by about three weeks. Initial evaluation revealed severe arterial hypertension (160/110 mmHg). Brain imaging was unremarkable. A workup for secondary hypertension, including renal and adrenal imaging, renal artery assessment, and endocrine studies, did not identify a structural or endocrine cause. Urinary catecholamines were at the upper limit of normal but not considered indicative of a secreting tumor. She subsequently developed progressive limb weakness and was admitted for further evaluation. On admission she was alert (Glasgow Coma Scale 15) and afebrile; blood pressure was 130/108 mmHg on antihypertensive therapy, with a heart rate of 120 bpm. She was respiratory stable with intact swallowing, but had mild peripheral facial weakness. Neurological exam showed symmetric quadriparesis (strength 3/5 in all limbs), generalized areflexia, and preserved sensation. Ophthalmologic exam was normal. Inflammatory and infectious screens, including viral serologies and immunologic panels, were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed elevated protein (reference 15-45 mg/dL) with a normal white cell count (3 cells/mm³). Nerve conduction studies showed markedly prolonged distal motor latencies (up to 15.0 ms in the right median nerve), reduced motor amplitudes, and absent sensory responses in tested nerves.

A man in his mid-30s with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department after an episode of moderate, sudden-onset, stabbing retrosternal chest pain that began during vigorous exercise. The pain had resolved by the time he was transferred to a tertiary center, and he was hemodynamically stable on arrival with no recurrence of symptoms. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed no ST-T changes, and physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies, including white blood cell count, liver enzymes, renal function tests, and D-dimer, were all within normal limits. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated mild pericardial effusion and moderate aortic regurgitation with a central jet, with preserved left ventricular size and systolic function (end-diastolic/systolic diameters 53/33 mm; ejection fraction 68%). Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed dilatation of the aortic root (60 mm) and ascending aorta (40 mm), a small anterior pericardial effusion, and blood tracking along the aortic arch, without a clearly defined intimal flap; a subtle contour irregularity was noted along the medial aspect of the proximal ascending aorta. Because imaging findings were not definitive, the patient was admitted to intensive care for strict blood pressure control and close hemodynamic monitoring rather than immediate intervention, remaining asymptomatic throughout observation. Repeat CT imaging obtained several days later showed more clearly delineated wall changes in the proximal ascending aorta, with resolution of the periaortic blood tracking and a stable pericardial effusion.

A man in his 70s with a multi-decade history of a progressive neurologic disorder (previously treated with an interferon-based disease-modifying agent, discontinued years earlier due to intolerance, with no subsequent therapy) and chronic cholecystitis presented after a period of accelerating functional decline. Over the roughly two months before admission, his family observed progressive worsening of his gait and balance, with transition from a cane to a walker; before this he had been ambulating independently with a cane and largely independent in daily activities. He had not had neurologic follow-up in about six years. In the week before admission he developed marked bilateral leg weakness, reduced mobility, poor oral intake, and worsening swallowing difficulty, the latter a longstanding complaint. Several days before presentation he developed severe, episodic limb muscle spasms, with new confusion and slurred speech; family reported he had been taking a subtherapeutic dose of a prescribed neuropathic-pain medication. About three weeks earlier he had low-grade fever and dark urine, treated presumptively for a urinary tract infection with a completed antibiotic course ending the day before admission. He presented to the emergency department after a severe spasm episode. Sodium was high-normal, suggesting volume depletion. Laboratory testing showed markedly elevated creatinine and blood urea nitrogen with a severely reduced estimated GFR, and markedly elevated serum calcium; parathyroid hormone and vitamin D metabolite levels were not obtained. Neurologic exam showed intact mentation, dysarthria, left facial weakness sparing the forehead, decreased left facial sensation, mild left-sided and lower-extremity weakness, intact sensation/coordination, and normal reflexes without pathological signs. Noncontrast head CT showed no acute abnormality but chronic findings; brain MRI showed chronic-appearing periventricular white matter changes without contrast enhancement.

An elderly man (late 70s) with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and metastatic melanoma presented with several days of palpitations, progressive fatigue, and proximal muscle weakness, along with intermittent double vision and eyelid drooping. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, or orthopnea, and had no known history of cardiomyopathy or structural heart disease. He had begun a new systemic immunotherapy regimen for his malignancy approximately two weeks earlier. On presentation he was afebrile, with a blood pressure of 159/86 mmHg, a heart rate of 110 beats/min, and an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Cardiac and pulmonary examination were unremarkable, without peripheral edema. Laboratory testing showed elevated aspartate aminotransferase (290 U/L) and alanine aminotransferase (95 U/L), a markedly elevated troponin (11,399 ng/L), elevated C-reactive protein (28.8 mg/L), and elevated creatine kinase (6,046 U/L). Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes or conduction abnormality. Echocardiography showed preserved to hyperdynamic left ventricular systolic function without a clear regional wall motion abnormality, though the study was limited by tachycardia and technical factors; a prior echocardiogram was reportedly normal. Over the following days, despite discontinuation of the new therapy and initiation of high-dose corticosteroids, cardiac biomarkers continued to rise, and the patient developed complete heart block requiring temporary pacing, followed by severely reduced biventricular systolic function on cardiac MRI. Right heart catheterization showed elevated intracardiac filling pressures with reduced cardiac output, and coronary angiography showed no obstructive coronary disease.

train_cases.diagnosis: Benign neoplasm of unspecified adrenal gland
train_cases.note: A 12-year-old male with no significant past medical history was admitted for postoperative monitoring following an uneventful laparoscopic appendectomy. During this monitoring period, persistent elevated blood pressure was noted, prompting further evaluation. There was no family history of endocrine tumor syndromes or related hereditary conditions. On examination, the patient was well-developed and well-nourished, weighing 38 kg. Vital signs showed heart rate 120 bpm, blood pressure 162/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 35/min, and temperature 35.8°C. Cardiovascular exam revealed a regular rhythm without murmurs. The abdomen was soft and non-tender without palpable masses. No skin findings suggestive of neurocutaneous syndromes were present. The rest of the exam was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound performed as part of the hypertension workup identified an incidental mass at the upper pole of the right kidney region. Contrast-enhanced abdominal MRI subsequently showed bilateral adrenal masses measuring 5.0 cm on the right and 3.0 cm on the left, both with heterogeneous T2 hyperintensity and avid enhancement, without evidence of local invasion or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory testing showed hematocrit 27.7%, hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, WBC 14,900/µL with neutrophil predominance, elevated CRP (116 mg/L), elevated liver enzymes, and low albumin. A 24-hour urine catecholamine metabolite level was markedly elevated. Whole-body functional imaging showed no evidence of distant disease spread.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute leukemia of unspecified cell type not having achieved remission
train_cases.note: A male in his late teens presented with cervical lymphadenopathy and marked leukocytosis noted on initial evaluation. No further details regarding the duration of symptoms prior to presentation, associated systemic symptoms, past medical history, vital signs, or physical examination findings beyond the lymphadenopathy were reported. Initial laboratory assessment demonstrated a markedly elevated white blood cell count. Given the findings of lymphadenopathy and leukocytosis, further diagnostic workup including lymph node and bone marrow sampling was pursued to characterize the underlying hematologic process. Cytogenetic analysis of the marrow by conventional G-banding showed a normal karyotype without numerical or structural chromosomal abnormalities. The clinical picture prompted consideration of a hematologic malignancy, and additional histopathological and immunophenotypic studies were undertaken to establish a definitive diagnosis and guide subsequent management planning, including risk stratification for potential future therapy.

train_cases.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
train_cases.note: A man in his early 50s presented to the emergency department with new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures. He had a history of poorly controlled hyperthyroidism (previously treated with an antithyroid medication, discontinued about five years earlier with no subsequent endocrinology follow-up), type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension. Family history was notable for thyroid disease in several first-degree relatives. Per family report, symptoms began approximately eight hours before arrival, beginning with a seizure at home accompanied by loss of consciousness and urinary incontinence, followed by four additional seizures (three at home, two during transport). On arrival he was drowsy and poorly responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 11). Vital signs: heart rate 123/min, blood pressure 130/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, temperature 36.1°C, oxygen saturation 97% on room air; capillary glucose 143 mg/dL. He appeared clinically volume-depleted, with fine bilateral hand tremor and a diffusely enlarged, non-nodular thyroid gland. Cardiac auscultation revealed an irregular rhythm without murmurs; lung exam was unremarkable. Once mental status improved, neurological exam showed no focal deficits. Labs showed leukocytosis (13.18×10³/µL) with neutrophilia, mildly elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit, elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin, prolonged prothrombin time/INR and activated partial thromboplastin time, elevated fibrinogen, and normal renal function and electrolytes (potassium 3.5 mmol/L). Urinalysis showed hematuria, leukocyturia, bacteriuria, and positive nitrites, with urine culture growing two organisms. Electrocardiography showed an irregular rhythm with rapid ventricular response and absent discernible P waves. Chest radiograph showed increased pulmonary vascular markings with cephalization of flow and a small right-sided pleural effusion. Brain computed tomography showed no acute abnormality, with bilateral frontal white matter hypodensities felt to reflect chronic changes.

A man in his mid-50s presented to the emergency department with a 5-day history of progressively worsening left flank pain associated with high-grade fever, chills, nausea, and reduced oral intake. The pain was constant, severe, and radiated to the left lower abdomen, partially relieved by analgesics. He also reported dysuria and increased urinary frequency for one week, but denied hematuria, pneumaturia, vomiting, bowel disturbances, or recent trauma. He had no history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, urolithiasis, or immunosuppressive therapy, and no prior hospitalizations or urological interventions. On arrival he appeared ill and toxic, with temperature 39.2°C, heart rate 112 bpm, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. He was alert but uncomfortable, with mild pallor and dehydration. Abdominal exam showed tenderness over the left flank and costovertebral angle with guarding, no palpable mass, soft abdomen, and normal bowel sounds. Labs showed leukocytosis (18.6×10^9/L, 89% neutrophils), hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, CRP 186 mg/L, procalcitonin 12 ng/mL, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, BUN 48 mg/dL, sodium 130 mmol/L, normal glucose and HbA1c. Urinalysis showed turbid urine, positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites, numerous pus cells, and bacteriuria; urine and blood cultures grew Escherichia coli. Plain radiograph showed mottled radiolucency over the left renal region. Ultrasound showed an enlarged left kidney with echogenic foci and posterior dirty shadowing, poor corticomedullary differentiation, and mild perinephric fluid. Contrast CT showed gas within the left renal parenchyma and collecting system extending into the perinephric space, with renal parenchymal destruction and no obstructing calculi.

A previously healthy man in his late twenties presented with a four-day history of fever (39.2°C) and sore throat. One day after self-administering ibuprofen 400 mg for symptom relief, he developed a generalized rash that began at the left antecubital fossa. He was evaluated by a primary care physician and treated with intravenous paracetamol and oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for two to three days for a presumed allergic or inflammatory skin eruption, but the rash rapidly progressed despite this treatment. He subsequently developed significant mucosal involvement affecting the oral, ocular, and genital mucosae, with inability to open his eyes, dysphagia, and dysuria. He had no history of regular medications, prior drug reactions, or similar prior episodes. On presentation to the emergency department, he had diffuse dusky red macular eruptions coalescing into plaques with widespread epidermal detachment affecting approximately 90% of total body surface area, painful oral and genital mucosal ulcerations, and severe conjunctivitis with conjunctival injection and erosions. A skin punch biopsy with direct immunofluorescence was obtained for further evaluation. He was admitted for specialized multidisciplinary inpatient management including wound care and supportive therapy.

A teenage girl with a history of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder presented with five days of continuous dizziness described as a spinning sensation with a feeling that the environment was moving, preceded one day earlier by a single episode of vomiting. She also reported right upper arm soreness and transient left-sided weakness lasting about one week, intermittent involuntary twitching of the right arm occurring mainly after cold exposure, and transient numbness and tingling of the left arm. She had an unsteady gait during this period. About one year earlier she had an episode of headache, vomiting, and balance difficulty evaluated at another facility with a reportedly normal head CT and no neurology follow-up; since then she described persistent baseline gait unsteadiness that never fully resolved. She had no known prior autoimmune disease or recent infection. On arrival she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, with right upper arm tenderness and unsteady gait. During admission she developed nystagmus and intermittent blurred vision without diplopia or visual field loss. General exam was otherwise unremarkable, and she improved to a normal neurologic exam with steadier gait by discharge. Initial blood counts, metabolic panel, inflammatory markers, and glucose were normal; toxicology, B12, and viral testing were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid showed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly low glucose, mildly elevated protein, elevated IgG index and synthesis rate, and oligoclonal bands, with negative culture and negative MOG antibody. Brain, orbital, and spinal imaging showed multiple white matter lesions of varying size, some enhancing, involving periventricular, infratentorial, cervical, and thoracic cord regions, with optic nerve signal changes and no evidence of venous thrombosis or acute infarction. She was treated with high-dose intravenous steroids with marked symptomatic improvement.

train_cases.diagnosis: Acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection, unspecified
train_cases.note: A man in his late 20s presented to the emergency department with acute-onset abdominal pain and vomiting. The pain was constant, severe (9/10), located in the epigastrium with radiation to the back, non-colicky, aggravated by movement, and partially relieved by leaning forward, associated with nausea and repeated vomiting. He had no significant past medical history and took no regular medications aside from a topical cream recently started for generalized itchy skin lesions, without relief. He did not smoke or drink alcohol but reported consuming up to five energy drinks daily over the preceding year. He was married and worked in vegetable packaging. On examination he was morbidly obese (BMI 41.6 kg/m2), mildly tachycardic (pulse 101/min) and tachypneic (respiratory rate 24/min), blood pressure 143/72 mmHg, temperature 37.7°C, oxygen saturation 96% on 2 L supplemental oxygen. Cardiorespiratory exam was unremarkable. The abdomen was soft with tenderness in the epigastrium and right hypochondrium and normal bowel sounds. Initial venous blood gas showed elevated glucose with borderline ketone elevation but no significant acidosis. He was given intravenous fluids and analgesia. Cross-sectional abdominal imaging showed pancreatic enlargement with surrounding inflammatory stranding, without necrosis, gallstones, or bile duct dilation. Hours later he deteriorated with worsening tachycardia and tachypnea; repeat blood gas showed worsening acidosis with rising glucose and ketones. Subsequent blood samples were grossly lipemic, precluding measurement of several routine chemistries; the available lipid panel showed markedly elevated triglycerides and total cholesterol with very low HDL. Skin examination later revealed multiple yellowish papules over the buttocks, back, and extensor limb surfaces, without lipemia retinalis or hepatosplenomegaly. HbA1c was markedly elevated; thyroid function was normal.

A woman in her mid-50s presented to the emergency department with fever, vomiting, and a fall associated with transient loss of consciousness. Her medical history included alcohol-related chronic liver disease with portal hypertension and grade I oesophageal varices on prior endoscopy. On admission she was haemodynamically stable but febrile, with markedly elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 125 mg/L). Initial bloods showed mildly elevated ALT (63 IU/L), INR 1.3, albumin 30 g/L, ammonia 46 µmol/L, and normal bilirubin. CT head showed no acute abnormality and there were no focal neurological deficits. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, and she was started on targeted intravenous antibiotics. Common sources of bacteraemia (lines, intravenous drug use, dental work, skin/soft tissue, urinary tract) were excluded on history, examination, and imaging. There was no ascites for diagnostic paracentesis. No peripheral stigmata (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages, Roth spots, conjunctival petechiae) were found. CT abdomen/pelvis showed a cirrhotic liver, bilateral pleural effusions, and small pelvic free fluid. An initial cardiac ultrasound showed moderate aortic regurgitation without other abnormality. On day eight of antibiotics she developed hypotension, tachycardia, and persistent fever, with recurrence of the same bacteraemia on repeat cultures. Whole-body PET-CT showed no abnormal cardiac uptake. A subsequent transoesophageal cardiac ultrasound, performed ten days after the initial study, revealed severe aortic regurgitation and a small (0.5 x 0.4 cm) mobile structure on the left coronary cusp.

A woman in her mid-40s presented with a nine-month history of facial redness, abdominal bloating, and reduced cold tolerance. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, combined hyperlipidemia, and euthyroid autoimmune thyroiditis under annual surveillance. Family history was notable for early cardiac death in her father and gynecologic malignancies in maternal and paternal relatives. She had two prior cesarean deliveries and reported previously regular menstrual cycles that became irregular two months before presentation. On examination she had a rounded, plethoric face, central obesity, and possible proximal muscle wasting; the thyroid was mildly enlarged. Blood pressure was 170/100 mmHg, heart rate 80 beats/min, and body mass index 31 kg/m^2. Laboratory testing showed a fasting glucose of 8 mmol/L (144 mg/dL) and prolactin within the normal female range. Morning cortisol was markedly elevated on repeat measurement, and 24-hour urinary free cortisol was mildly above the upper reference limit. Thyroid ultrasound showed a mild multinodular goiter with more prominent nodularity on one side. Abdominal/adrenal imaging was unremarkable. Further endocrine testing showed an elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone level with a diurnal cortisol pattern that failed to suppress appropriately. Electrocardiography was within normal limits for age and sex. Pituitary MRI demonstrated a small hypoenhancing lesion with associated deviation of the pituitary stalk.

A 70-year-old woman with a history of obstructive sleep apnea, osteoporosis, obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and prediabetes presented with nausea and constipation. About three months earlier she had started a weekly injectable GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist for sleep apnea management, with the dose escalated over successive months. Lower doses caused transient first-week nausea that resolved, but after the most recent dose increase the nausea persisted and progressively worsened; she continued the medication regardless, with her last dose about 1.5 weeks before presentation. In the week prior to admission she had markedly reduced oral intake, dry heaving without vomiting, occasional hard stools without change in bowel frequency, and increased urinary frequency attributed to increased water intake. She had lost approximately 20 pounds over the preceding months and reported improved sleep continuity. Home medications included calcium and vitamin D supplements, a multivitamin containing calcium, an ACE/ARB, a statin, aspirin, and a calcium channel blocker. Outpatient labs obtained just before admission showed hypokalemia, elevated bicarbonate, mildly elevated creatinine, and hypercalcemia (baseline labs seven months earlier had been normal). On arrival, vital signs were normal (BP 131/62 mmHg, HR 72, temperature 36.2°C, RR 15, SpO2 96% on room air) with an unremarkable physical exam. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with nonspecific T-wave changes. Initial hospital labs showed severe hypokalemia, elevated bicarbonate, hypercalcemia with elevated ionized calcium, hypophosphatemia, normal magnesium, normal TSH and parathyroid hormone, normal vitamin D, and low parathyroid hormone-related protein and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.

An 84-year-old male was found to have an elevated carcinoembryonic antigen level on routine bloodwork. Chest imaging revealed a 4.8 cm mass in the left hilar region, subsequently confirmed as squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, staged as cT2bN1M0 with extensive hilar lymphadenopathy and no distant metastasis. Past medical history included hypertension and a prior transient ischemic attack on antiplatelet therapy; there was no history of interstitial lung disease or pulmonary fibrosis. He had a substantial prior smoking history but had quit decades earlier. Baseline pulmonary function testing was normal. He received three cycles of neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy, complicated by transient severe neutropenia but completed without dose reduction; the tumor decreased in size on repeat imaging. Six weeks later he underwent left upper lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection, an uncomplicated procedure with a routine intraoperative course. Recovery was initially uneventful, with early mobilization and resumption of oral intake, though chest tube drainage was required for several days for a minor air leak. On postoperative day 7 he developed leukocytosis and a marked rise in inflammatory markers, with new bilateral ground-glass opacities on CT despite the absence of respiratory symptoms; empiric antibiotics were started. Cardiac function was normal on echocardiography. Four days later he developed high-grade fever, dyspnea, and progressive hypoxemia, with worsening bilateral pulmonary infiltrates despite antibiotic escalation. Respiratory failure progressed despite corticosteroid therapy and advanced respiratory support, ultimately requiring mechanical ventilation. Microbiologic cultures remained persistently negative.

A 58-year-old woman, previously healthy and living independently, presented to the emergency department with apparent acute-onset confusion, time and place disorientation, short-term memory loss, and perseverative behavior, accompanied by marked psychomotor retardation, apathy, and transient visual hallucinations. Because she had lived alone for the prior two years, an initial history was difficult to obtain; subsequent interviews with family and coworkers revealed personality and behavioral changes evolving over the past year, worsening in recent weeks. Family history was notable for multiple maternal relatives with major neurocognitive disorders. Vital signs on admission were normal (BP 127/76 mmHg, HR 76, RR 17, temperature 36.3°C, SpO2 97%). Neurological exam showed bradykinesia, symmetric extrapyramidal rigidity, camptocormia, a positive Romberg sign, convergence insufficiency, fine spontaneous nystagmus, and left-sided Hoffman and Babinski signs with brisk reflexes; the remainder of the exam was normal. Non-contrast head CT showed symmetric ventricular enlargement with reduced gyral volume and widened frontotemporal sulci. Initial bloodwork showed elevated CRP, ESR, and fibrinogen, with normal procalcitonin, full blood count, and glucose. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed no pathological enhancement; chest/abdomen/pelvis CT was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture showed mild elevation of protein and glucose without infectious cytology; cultures were negative. Phosphorylated tau was elevated. EEG showed asymmetric sharp theta waves over the temporal region without clear epileptiform foci.

An adult patient presented with acute-onset dyspnea. Initial evaluation revealed newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Past history was notable for reduced baseline renal function (admission serum creatinine 2.0 mg/dL). The patient reported a self-limited gastrointestinal illness approximately three weeks before presentation, with no prior cardiac history. Electrocardiography at admission showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular rate, mild T-wave negativity in the anterior precordial leads, subtle non-ischemic ST-segment elevation, and a normal QT interval. Cardiac troponin was elevated. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated diffuse left ventricular hypokinesis, most pronounced in the mid-to-apical segments, with severely reduced ejection fraction (approximately 30%); right ventricular function was normal. Given acute dyspnea, troponin elevation, ECG abnormalities, and reduced ejection fraction, urgent coronary angiography performed within 24 hours showed a left-dominant coronary system without angiographically significant obstructive disease in either coronary circulation. On hospital day 1 the patient developed profound bradycardia with junctional rhythm (~30 beats/min), marked QT prolongation (620 ms), and deep precordial T-wave inversions, initially attributed to amiodarone (started for the arrhythmia, then discontinued); isoproterenol infusion was required for hemodynamic support. Spontaneous conversion to sinus rhythm occurred by day 3. Renal function worsened after contrast exposure (creatinine peaking at 4.0 mg/dL) before improving toward baseline. On day 5, despite no antiarrhythmic or bradycardic medications, junctional rhythm recurred with severe QT prolongation and diffuse T-wave inversion.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism with acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: An 80-year-old man with a history of dyslipidemia and metabolic syndrome presented to the emergency department with a two-week history of progressively worsening dyspnea. He denied chest pain, hemoptysis, or syncope. He had no prior history of thromboembolic disease, cardiac surgery, malignancy, or recent immobilization. On arrival, he was hemodynamically stable (blood pressure 124/68 mmHg, heart rate 102 bpm) with marked tachypnea (26 breaths/min) and severe hypoxemia (oxygen saturation 80% on ambient air), requiring supplemental oxygen; temperature was 37.2°C. Bilateral soft, non-pitting, painless lower limb edema was noted. Pulmonary auscultation was unremarkable. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia with right-axis deviation and complete right bundle branch block. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly, a wedge-shaped opacity in the right lower lobe, plate-like atelectasis, and suspected linear atelectasis on the left. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, white blood cells 9,800/µL, platelets 254,000/µL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate 46.46 mL/min/1.73m², D-dimer 3,120 ng/mL, C-reactive protein 205 mg/L, high-sensitivity troponin T 0.041 ng/mL, and NT-proBNP 7,500 pg/mL. Liver function tests and coagulation screening were normal.

An 11-year-old boy presented to a rural emergency department with 12 hours of worsening left groin pain. His parents had recently commented that he seemed to have only one testicle, although this had not previously been raised as a concern. There was no history of trauma, and no gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms. He was born extremely preterm at 25 weeks' gestation and had undergone bilateral inguinal hernia repairs in infancy; no prior procedure to fix the position of either testis was documented. His past history also included craniofacial abnormalities requiring surgical correction and a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. He was otherwise well and attending school. On examination, the right testis was retractile, non-tender, and easily reducible into the scrotum. The left hemiscrotum was empty. A tender, firm, immobile mass was palpable in the left inguinal region just lateral to the pubic tubercle, without overlying erythema. Attempts at manual reduction with analgesia and Valsalva manoeuvre were unsuccessful. Scrotal and inguinal ultrasound with colour Doppler was performed, demonstrating absent vascular flow and heterogeneous echotexture in the left testis, located within the inguinal canal, with normal perfusion of the right testis.

A previously healthy boy in his pre-adolescent years (10-year-old) presented to the emergency department with acute onset of high fever, painful swallowing, chest pain, and difficulty breathing. Vaccination history was complete, including four doses of a Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine, and there was no known relevant epidemiological exposure. On arrival, the patient was in respiratory distress, febrile, and appeared toxic. He avoided lying flat, kept his tongue protruded, and was drooling, though oxygen saturation remained above 96% and lung auscultation was clear bilaterally. Heart rate was 130 bpm with a capillary refill time of three seconds, prompting volume resuscitation, high-flow oxygen, nebulized adrenaline, and empiric intravenous antibiotic therapy. Physical examination showed red, enlarged tonsils. Initial laboratory testing revealed leukocytosis (21,200/μL) with neutrophilia (18,630/μL), markedly elevated C-reactive protein (32.76 mg/dL), and elevated procalcitonin (0.76 ng/mL); hemoglobin and platelet counts were normal. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. A lateral neck radiograph showed an enlarged epiglottis with a thumbprint-like appearance. After initial stabilization, indirect laryngoscopy showed inflammation and edema of the supraglottic structures without obstruction of the glottis. The patient was admitted for continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and further management.

train_cases.diagnosis: Benign neoplasm of left adrenal gland
train_cases.note: A 43-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidentally discovered left adrenal mass identified on imaging performed for unrelated reasons. She was entirely asymptomatic, denying hypertension, palpitations, or episodes of sweating. She had no significant past medical history and no relevant family history. On examination she was normotensive, and physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen showed a large, 57×53 mm cystic-solid left adrenal mass with internal septa; following contrast administration, the lesion showed slight, heterogeneous enhancement. Chest CT and physical examination did not identify any additional masses. Laboratory evaluation showed a markedly elevated plasma normetanephrine level of 1168.0 pg/ml (reference, <145 pg/ml) and a mildly elevated plasma metanephrine level of 84.6 pg/ml (reference, <62 pg/ml). Plasma catecholamine levels and 24-hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) were within normal limits. Medication history was reviewed and did not include tricyclic antidepressants, alpha-blockers, or labetalol. Plasma 3-methoxytyramine was not obtained on initial testing. Given the imaging and biochemical findings, further evaluation and surgical planning were undertaken.

train_cases.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale
train_cases.note: A woman in her 40s, recently diagnosed with hypertension and diabetes mellitus a few months prior, non-adherent to medications (previously on beta blockers), presented with a 3-day history of nausea, vomiting, and shortness of breath, without chest pain. She had used homeopathic and herbal remedies for knee pain for several years. She denied alcohol use, other substance use, prior abdominal or pelvic surgery, trauma, or immobility, and had no features suggestive of autoimmune disease. On presentation she was obese, oriented but irritable (GCS 13-14/15), tachycardic (109 bpm), hypotensive (98/57 mmHg), tachypneic (32/min), with oxygen saturation of 90% on room air and no fever. She was icteric, with decreased air entry at lung bases, a soft non-tender abdomen without organomegaly, bilateral pitting lower limb edema to mid-shin, and peripheral cyanosis of both feet. Venous blood gas showed mixed metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.27, pCO2 21, HCO3 12) and lactate of 7. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL, creatinine 2.93 mg/dL, AST 1788 IU/L, ALT 1500 IU/L, and INR 1.7. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly with fatty infiltration and patent vasculature.
