Chest X-ray showed cardiomegaly without pulmonary pathology. Viral hepatitis serologies (A/B/C/E) were negative. An intrauterine copper device was noted in situ. Over the following 48 hours she developed worsening drowsiness, tachypnea, rising oxygen requirement, and rising lactate, prompting ICU escalation and intubation.

A woman in her early 50s with end-stage kidney disease (history of biopsy-confirmed glomerular disease) on thrice-weekly hemodialysis presented to the emergency department with acute-onset right shoulder and neck pain, progressive fatigue, and abdominal pain. Her history included hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, sick sinus syndrome status post pacemaker, hypothyroidism, prior ischemic stroke, and a prior upper gastrointestinal bleed from a duodenal ulcer treated endoscopically. She also reported a prior episode of a similar rash that resolved after stopping hydralazine and recurred after re-exposure. Vital signs were stable and she was afebrile. Exam showed conjunctival pallor, abdominal distension with mild epigastric tenderness, and bilateral lower-extremity edema; no rash was noted initially. Labs showed hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL (baseline 9-10), platelets 95×10^9/L, elevated BUN, and hyperkalemia. Stool was occult-blood positive, later with melena. Upper endoscopy showed reactive gastropathy without H. pylori. She received transfusions and high-dose PPI therapy. Imaging showed gallbladder wall thickening with pericholecystic edema and mild ascites; hepatobiliary scintigraphy showed normal gallbladder function, felt due to volume overload. On hospital day three she developed painful, non-blanching violaceous purpuric macules and patches on the bilateral lower extremities extending proximally, with new arthralgias of the knees and ankles. Skin biopsy showed small-vessel inflammation with neutrophilic infiltrate, leukocytoclasia, fibrin deposition, and extravasated erythrocytes. Extensive serologic workup (ANA, ANCA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, cardiolipin, complement, ADAMTS13, DIC panel) was largely unremarkable aside from a markedly elevated homogeneous ANA titer. She improved rapidly with high-dose corticosteroids and permanent discontinuation of hydralazine.

train_cases.diagnosis: Ankylosing spondylitis of unspecified sites in spine
train_cases.note: A man in his early 50s with a history of hypertension (on perindopril, indapamide and amlodipine) presented with polyarthralgia. He reported a 10-year history of inflammatory-type low back pain with progressively limited spinal mobility, and a more recent 3-month period of asthenia, fatigue, dry cough, night sweats, fever and a 20 kg weight loss. He denied alcohol use, hepatotoxic medications, herbal supplements, and had no family history of autoimmune or liver disease. On examination he was pale, with diffuse tenderness on spinal percussion and painful limitation of lower-limb movement; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Labs showed markedly elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), severe anemia, thrombocytosis, and elevated liver enzymes with a cholestatic-predominant pattern (elevated ALP, GGT, with lesser transaminase elevation). Abdominal ultrasound excluded biliary obstruction or focal liver lesions; MRCP showed no biliary duct abnormality. Viral hepatitis serologies and metabolic/hereditary liver screens were negative. Autoimmune serologies showed positive ANA and anti-liver cytosol type 1 antibodies with mildly elevated IgG; other autoantibodies were negative. Tumor markers were normal. Fecal calprotectin was mildly elevated but endoscopy, colonoscopy and small-bowel MRI showed no bowel inflammation. Pelvic X-ray showed narrowing of the right hip joint space. CT showed syndesmophytes and sacroiliac joint changes with reactive mesenteric lymphadenopathy; pelvic MRI showed sacroiliac erosions, bone marrow edema and a subchondral cystic lesion.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A teenage female presented to the emergency department with a three-day history of polyuria and vomiting, with no prior history of diabetes. She weighed 45 kg and was 155 cm tall (BMI 18.7 kg/m^2). On examination she was alert, oriented, and cooperative, with no neurological impairment. She had marked polypnea with a respiratory rate of approximately 30/min, characterized by deep, regular, labored breathing. Blood pressure was 140/80 mmHg, heart rate 130 bpm, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Urine output was present and abundant. She reported diffuse abdominal pain, and mild abdominal tenderness was noted; abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed blood glucose 522 mg/dL, marked glycosuria (>1000 mg/dL), and ketonuria (80 mg/dL). Arterial blood gas showed pH 6.8-7.0, bicarbonate approximately 1.7 mmol/L, and pCO2 approximately 7 mmHg. Sodium was 125 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, lactate 0.9 mmol/L, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, and urea 45 mg/dL. White blood cell count was elevated at 23.1 x10^3/uL, with CRP 74.9 mg/L and procalcitonin 2.26 ng/mL; blood and urine cultures, SARS-CoV-2 testing, and a respiratory pathogen panel were all negative. Fluid resuscitation and intravenous insulin infusion were initiated, with transfer to intensive care for continuous monitoring and correction of the severe metabolic derangement, which improved progressively over approximately 24 hours.

train_cases.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
train_cases.note: A woman in her mid-40s with a four-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus complicated by retinopathy presented to the emergency department after three days of progressive decline in consciousness. Following an emotional stressor, she developed fatigue, nausea, markedly decreased oral intake, dysarthria, dizziness, and progressive shortness of breath. She had no prior episodes of similar metabolic decompensation. Her medications included an SGLT2 inhibitor, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, basal insulin, a statin, and a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor recently started by her ophthalmologist for glaucoma. On examination she appeared acutely ill and profoundly dehydrated, conscious but disoriented to time and place. Vitals showed tachycardia and marked tachypnea (respiratory rate 30-36/min). Chest was clear. Neurologic exam showed globally decreased motor power (4/5 in all limbs). Labs: random glucose 170 mg/dl; WBC 18.85x10^9/l, hemoglobin 15.53 g/dl, platelets 328.9x10^9/l; sodium 139, potassium 4.2, chloride 111 mmol/l; creatinine 0.77 mg/dl; lactate 14.6 mg/dl. Arterial blood gas showed severe acidemia: pH 6.85, bicarbonate 1.5 mmol/l, pCO2 9.4 mmHg, anion gap 27 mmol/l, base excess -31 mmol/l. Urinalysis showed glucose 3+ and ketones 3+. Brain imaging showed old ischemic changes without acute pathology; echocardiogram was normal.

A man in his 30s with a history of gastritis and crack cocaine use presented to the emergency department with gross hematuria and dizziness. He reported a three-day history of constant, sharp bilateral flank pain, right groin discomfort, and dysuria with a burning sensation at the end of urination, along with hematuria throughout the entire urinary stream without clots, a single episode of hematemesis with small blood clots, diaphoresis, and headache. He denied fever, chills, dyspnea, upper respiratory symptoms, chest or abdominal pain, extremity weakness, or fatigue. His last laboratory testing, roughly three years earlier, was reportedly normal. He denied hepatitis, HIV, autoimmune disease, intravenous drug use, or prior platelet or blood transfusions. On examination he was hemodynamically stable, with bilateral flank tenderness, scattered purpura on the chest, and mild subscapular tenderness. Initial laboratory studies showed total bilirubin 4.9 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 1,334 U/L, creatine kinase 266 U/L, hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, platelets 8,000/µL, and troponin 222 ng/L. Urinalysis revealed orange-colored urine, protein 600 mg/dL, blood 3+, RBCs greater than 200/hpf, and 10 hyaline casts. Peripheral smear showed severe thrombocytopenia without schistocytes. Hepatitis panel, HIV, and antinuclear antibody testing were negative. He was started on corticosteroids for presumed immune thrombocytopenia. Repeat evaluation 24 hours later showed worsening anemia (hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL), persistent severe thrombocytopenia (11,000/µL), rising LDH, low haptoglobin, and low vitamin B12, with a repeat peripheral smear now showing schistocytes.

A man in his late 30s with a history of Poland syndrome, a remote episode of left-sided facial palsy, a bicuspid aortic valve, a hypoplastic posterior mitral leaflet with a compensatory elongated anterior leaflet, and a known ascending aortic aneurysm presented with two days of progressively worsening weakness of the hands and feet. Symptoms began roughly one week after a self-limited flu-like illness with diarrhea. There was no sensory level, bowel or bladder incontinence, or known toxin or tick exposure. He was intubated for airway protection and transferred for further care. On arrival he was arousable to command. Examination showed complete paralysis of the hands and of ankle plantar- and dorsiflexion, minimal hip flexion/extension, preserved deltoid strength and antigravity elbow movement, globally diminished sensation, and markedly reduced deep tendon reflexes. Over the following 48 hours he progressed to flaccid quadriplegia with complete areflexia and loss of all brainstem reflexes; EEG showed preserved background activity without epileptiform discharges or cortical suppression. Initial brain imaging showed a small acute infarct in the left cerebellum and chronic left frontal encephalomalacia; cervical spine MRI was unremarkable. CT chest angiography showed a nodular right lower lung infiltrate and aortic dilation. An initial lumbar puncture was traumatic and nondiagnostic; a repeat study later showed mild pleocytosis and elevated protein. Echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 37%, a calcified unicuspid aortic valve with severe insufficiency and moderate stenosis, severe ascending aortic dilation, grade III diastolic dysfunction, and a small pericardial effusion. Blood cultures obtained on admission were later reported positive.

A woman in her seventh decade presented with a chief complaint of paroxysmal chest tightness and dyspnea for more than 10 years, with an exacerbation over the preceding 4 days. Symptoms had first begun over a decade earlier without clear triggers and had recurred intermittently; she had previously been evaluated for these episodes but received no ongoing specific therapy. Four days prior to admission, she developed recurrent chest tightness and breathlessness after cold exposure, accompanied by fever up to 40°C; after an antipyretic her temperature normalized, but chest tightness, breathlessness, abdominal distension, and generalized fatigue persisted. Past history included type 2 diabetes for over 10 years (on metformin and dapagliflozin, glucose well controlled) and hypertension for 8 years with irregular medication use and poor monitoring. No tobacco or alcohol use; no relevant family history. On admission: temperature 36.0°C, pulse 99/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 115/61 mmHg, weight 44 kg. She was alert but in poor general condition. Lungs were clear; heart rate 99/min, regular, no murmurs; abdomen soft and non-tender; neurologic exam unremarkable. ECG showed sinus tachycardia, pathological Q waves in V1–V2, ST-segment elevation in V1–V4, and T-wave inversion in V2–V6, with evolving changes on serial tracings over the following days. Initial labs showed WBC 8.47×10^9/L, elevated procalcitonin (20.0 ng/mL), markedly elevated NT-proBNP (16446 pg/mL), mildly elevated troponin and myoglobin, and mild transaminase elevation. Cardiac ultrasound showed ejection fraction 60% without significant segmental wall motion abnormality.

samples.note: A man in his late 60s with a recently diagnosed advanced-stage (locally advanced, node-positive, non-metastatic) squamous cell carcinoma of the posterior oropharyngeal wall—radiotherapy for which had been delayed pending dental clearance and due to inability to lie flat without desaturation—presented to the emergency department with throat pain and difficulty swallowing. His oncology team had raised concern for possible airway compromise. Initial physical exam revealed a visible oropharyngeal mass raising concern for airway narrowing. CT of the neck showed an increase in size of the known pharyngeal mass with moderate narrowing of the oropharyngeal airway compared with prior imaging. Shortly after admission he became increasingly somnolent and tachycardic, with oxygen saturation dropping to 86%, prompting urgent specialist evaluation. On assessment he was lethargic, with mouth open and tongue protruding, and was using abdominal, neck, and shoulder accessory muscles to breathe; lung sounds were diminished. He was on high-flow nasal cannula at 15 L/min. He aroused to verbal stimulation but was difficult to understand due to a raspy voice. Given the known airway-narrowing mass with minimal remaining airway patency, direct endoscopic airway visualization was deferred due to concern that instrumentation could precipitate complete obstruction, and the patient was taken emergently to the operating room for surgical airway management.

A man in his late 40s, employed as a painter and a chronic smoker (30 pack-years) with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, presented to the emergency department with generalised tiredness and breathlessness for 5 days. He had recovered uneventfully from a respiratory viral illness about six weeks earlier and had a prior history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis. On arrival he was drowsy, afebrile, pulse 98/min, blood pressure 150/100 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 86% on room air, and jugular venous pressure was elevated. Chest exam revealed bilateral basal rales. Arterial blood gas showed type 2 respiratory failure. He had a transient episode of supraventricular tachycardia requiring cardioversion, and later an episode of atrial fibrillation that reverted with medical therapy. Chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly with bilateral perihilar infiltrates. Labs showed neutrophilic leucocytosis (WBC 17.6x10^9/L), haemoglobin 12 g/dL, markedly elevated pro-BNP (5290 pg/mL) and elevated CRP (37.7 mg/dL). Endotracheal secretions were negative for acid-fast bacilli and other organisms; testing for atypical pneumonia and a regional tropical infection was negative. Bedside echocardiography showed an abnormal, redundant anterior mitral leaflet with moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation, dilated left atrium and ventricle, mild-to-moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary B-lines. Oral examination later revealed poor hygiene with dental plaque and caries, and a systolic murmur radiating to the axilla was noted. Blood culture drawn at admission subsequently grew a gram-positive organism.

An adult man in his late 30s presented with a three-day history of severe abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting. On examination he was hemodynamically stable but mildly tachycardic (heart rate 105 bpm). The abdomen was distended with epigastric tenderness, guarding, and absent bowel sounds. No significant past medical history was reported. Initial blood tests showed hemoglobin 132 g/L, white cell count 6.2 x10^9/L, platelets 355 x10^9/L, neutrophils 6.3 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein markedly elevated at 108 mg/L, and amylase mildly elevated at 117 U/L. Renal function was normal (urea 2.5 mmol/L, creatinine 75 umol/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L). Serum calcium was elevated at 2.94 mmol/L (adjusted), phosphate low at 0.53 mmol/L, magnesium low at 0.78 mmol/L, vitamin D low at 18 nmol/L, and parathyroid hormone markedly elevated at 18.9 pmol/L. Erect chest and abdominal radiographs demonstrated free air under the diaphragm. Subsequent CT of the abdomen showed pneumoperitoneum with localized air loculi adjacent to the pylorus and first part of the duodenum. Given hemodynamic stability, a conservative approach with nasogastric decompression, intravenous antibiotics, analgesia, and fluids was initiated with close clinical monitoring, and calcium levels were trended serially during admission with mild improvement following intravenous fluids.

A 57-year-old male, previously admitted to an inpatient pulmonology service, developed acute respiratory distress in the evening with stridorous breathing and use of accessory neck muscles, appearing agitated, with oxygen saturation of 80% on room air. He denied diplopia, nasal speech, or generalized fatigue, and no focal neurological deficits were found on exam. Blood pressure was markedly elevated at 160/120 mm Hg. Indirect laryngoscopy revealed bilateral vocal cord immobility with severe airway narrowing. His condition rapidly worsened, requiring emergency tracheostomy, ICU transfer, and mechanical ventilation for two days. History revealed that one month earlier he had sought care from his primary physician, a pulmonologist, and a cardiologist for dyspnea, chest pain, and hypertension, treated with diuretics, an ACE inhibitor, and rescue inhalers. One week before this admission he began daily systemic corticosteroids for suspected adult-onset asthma exacerbation. He had a PCR-confirmed COVID-19 infection about 10 months earlier and had not been vaccinated. During a subsequent regional rise in COVID-19 cases, he self-initiated over-the-counter magnesium supplementation for about two months without medical consultation. Surgical history was notable for thymectomy for a benign thymoma approximately six years earlier.

samples.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
samples.note: A woman in her early 40s presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of upper abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had no known history of diabetes mellitus or prior abnormal urine glucose testing. She weighed 45 kg (BMI 19 kg/m2). On arrival she was mildly disoriented with tachypnea (respiratory rate 34/min), dry oral mucosa, and mild tenderness from the epigastrium to the right hypochondrium; Murphy's sign was negative, and there were no peritoneal signs. Initial labs showed blood glucose 569 mg/dL, urine glucose 4+, urine ketones 4+, arterial pH 7.084, pCO2 9.2 mmHg, HCO3 2.7 mmol/L, base excess -24.8 mmol/L, sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 6.2 mEq/L, white blood cells 14,540/uL, glycated hemoglobin 6.9%, C-peptide <0.20 ng/mL, and negative anti-GAD and anti-IA-2 antibodies. Pancreatic amylase, lipase, and elastase were mildly elevated; C-reactive protein was normal. Plain CT of the trunk showed free gas around the porta hepatis and gastric pylorus without mediastinal gas; a contrast-enhanced CT obtained 2 hours later showed resolution of the free gas with no pancreatic inflammation, bowel necrosis, gallstones, or biliary dilation. Given the absence of peritoneal irritation, conservative management was pursued, and upper endoscopy performed once the patient improved showed no gastric or duodenal perforation or ulcer.

An approximately 8-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of periumbilical, spasmodic abdominal pain that gradually migrated to the right lower quadrant. The pain was sudden in onset, non-radiating, worsened with attempts to eat, not relieved by over-the-counter analgesics, and severe enough to cause visible distress. He also had several episodes of non-bloody, bilious vomiting containing food particles, and multiple episodes of watery, non-bloody loose stools over the same period, with no relief of pain after defecation. On examination he was alert and oriented but appeared unwell; general examination was otherwise unremarkable. Vital signs: heart rate 88/min, blood pressure 110/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, temperature 36.1°C. Abdominal examination revealed guarding, right iliac fossa tenderness, and rebound tenderness. Initial labs showed a leukocyte count of 19,200/mm3. Abdominal ultrasound showed only mild right iliac fossa probe tenderness with no other abnormality, and abdominal X-ray was unremarkable. A validated clinical scoring tool for right lower quadrant pain was calculated at 8, and the child underwent emergency open abdominal surgery. Postoperatively, rather than improving, he clinically worsened: by the second postoperative day he had passed neither stool nor flatus, heart rate rose above 110/min, respiratory rate increased to 25/min, temperature was 37.1°C, and blood pressure remained 110/80 mmHg. A repeat abdominal X-ray (supine and erect views) showed findings consistent with bowel obstruction, prompting urgent surgical re-exploration.

samples.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis, unspecified with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
samples.note: A woman in her late 60s with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and papillary thyroid carcinoma status post total thyroidectomy several years earlier (with known metastatic disease to the lung and pelvic bone, previously offered radioiodine therapy but the patient declined and elected palliative care) presented to the emergency department after being found semiconscious and febrile at home, with a home blood glucose of 45 mg/dL. She was on long-term levothyroxine replacement, with a recent outside-lab report of low TSH prompting a dose reduction, and had been seen in the emergency department days earlier for hypoglycemia-related confusion attributed to a sulfonylurea, at which time a chest infiltrate was treated with oral antibiotics. On this presentation, initial vitals showed temperature 37.4°C, heart rate 117/min, and blood pressure 174/83 mmHg. After intravenous dextrose her mental status transiently improved, then deteriorated with fever rising to 38.5°C and new supraventricular tachycardia unresponsive to adenosine and verapamil. Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis with normal C-reactive protein. Thyroid function testing revealed a markedly suppressed TSH (<0.008 µIU/mL), an elevated free T4 (>12.0 ng/dL), and elevated total T3 (5.43 ng/mL). Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed no new acute source of infection, with stable known pulmonary and pelvic lesions.

A woman in her 50s presented to the emergency department with acute onset of severe chest and upper back pain. Her medical history was notable for controlled stage II hypertension, managed with losartan; no other comorbidities were reported. On presentation, blood pressure was elevated at 170/90 mmHg. Laboratory testing showed normal kidney function. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography imaging of the chest and abdomen was obtained to evaluate the pain. Initial management included intravenous antihypertensive therapy (a beta blocker and a vasodilator) followed by oral beta blockade, which controlled blood pressure but did not relieve her symptoms. Back pain persisted for several days despite medical therapy, prompting consideration of further intervention. Imaging findings raised concern for involvement of major aortic branch vessels, including a visceral renal artery, and marked narrowing of a portion of the aortic lumen at the mid-thoracic level. Given the persistent symptoms and anatomic findings, a decision was made to pursue further treatment. The patient was hemodynamically stable at the time of intervention, without signs of end-organ hypoperfusion, stroke, or limb ischemia.

A woman in her mid-50s presented to the emergency department with dyspnea on mild exertion for one month, worsening over the preceding three days to the point that she could not complete full sentences. She also reported two months of progressive difficulty swallowing. She had been evaluated at a primary care facility for her respiratory symptoms and had been started on oral bronchodilator therapy without improvement; symptoms progressed to dyspnea at rest. On arrival, she appeared acutely unwell with a pulse of 130 beats/min, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 84% on room air. She was conscious, alert, and oriented. There was no pallor, icterus, edema, lymphadenopathy, cyanosis, or clubbing. Deep tendon reflexes were preserved bilaterally with bilateral flexor plantar responses. Bilateral drooping of the eyelids was noted, more pronounced on the left. Auscultation revealed bilateral rhonchi with coarse crepitations and wheeze over more than two-thirds of the lung fields. She was treated empirically for an obstructive airway exacerbation with bronchodilators, systemic steroids, nebulized short-acting beta-agonists, intravenous magnesium sulfate, and non-invasive ventilation, but continued to deteriorate. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.10, PaCO2 75 mmHg, PaO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 45 mEq/L, and SaO2 78%, consistent with severe hypercapnic respiratory failure, prompting elective intubation. Chest CT was subsequently reported as normal.

A woman in her mid-40s presented to the emergency department with a two-hour history of palpitations. She had a prior history of recurrent arrhythmias but no other known comorbidities and no regular medication use. On arrival she was hemodynamically stable. Initial ECG showed a narrow-complex tachycardia consistent with a supraventricular rhythm. Vagal maneuvers were attempted without success, and intravenous adenosine 6 mg was administered. Immediately afterward, the patient developed chest pain, pallor, diaphoresis, and transient hypotension. Cardiac monitoring showed a brief run of non-sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that spontaneously terminated within 30 seconds, reverting to sinus rhythm. A repeat ECG obtained after this event showed ST-segment elevation in lead aVR with ST-segment depression in the inferior and anterolateral leads. Symptoms resolved spontaneously within minutes, and a follow-up ECG several hours later showed normalization of these changes. Serial cardiac troponin measurements (both T and I) showed a rise-and-fall pattern with peak values well above the 99th-percentile reference limit. Invasive coronary angiography demonstrated no obstructive coronary lesions. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed transient hypokinesia of the basal septal segment. The patient remained clinically stable thereafter and was discharged after two days of observation.

A man in his early 50s, an African living-donor kidney transplant recipient 18 months post-transplant, presented with a one-week history of painful swelling of the right thigh, fever, and general malaise. Initial imaging of the thigh showed small fluid collections not amenable to drainage; he was treated with a course of intravenous antibiotics with improvement in swelling, pain, and fever, and was discharged. Three days later he developed left-sided weakness of the arm and leg, recurrent fever, and a single self-limited generalized tonic-clonic seizure, prompting referral to a tertiary hospital. History obtained from a family member was negative for trauma to the thigh, headache, neck stiffness, confusion, photophobia, blurred vision, or slurred speech, and there was no cough, nasal symptoms, ear pain, dysuria, or diarrhea. His only chronic condition was hypertension, which had previously caused kidney failure requiring transplantation. On examination he was febrile (37.8-39°C), pulse 84/min, blood pressure 130/82 mmHg, with a displaced apical impulse but no audible murmurs; there was no digital clubbing or splinter hemorrhages. Respiratory and abdominal exams were unremarkable. Neurologically he was obtunded (Glasgow coma scale 11/15) with left facial weakness, left-sided hemiparesis, a supple neck, negative Kernig's sign, and normal, equal pupils with intact reflexes; fundoscopy was normal. Contrast MRI of the brain demonstrated multiple bilateral, ovoid, rim-enhancing lesions of varying size across both hemispheres with surrounding edema and leftward midline shift. Further laboratory and cardiac investigations were pending.

samples.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
samples.note: A woman in her early 50s with a roughly 13-year history of diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with recurrent nausea, vomiting, and new-onset dyspnea. She had initially been managed with oral antihyperglycemic agents, but due to poor glycemic control and recurrent ketosis-prone episodes with positive pancreatic autoantibodies, she had been transitioned to insulin therapy years earlier, with persistently labile glucose control. She also had a history of dyslipidemia (elevated total cholesterol and LDL) and hyperuricemia. Six days before this presentation, she discontinued insulin and began a once-weekly injectable incretin-based antihyperglycemic agent. Shortly after the first dose she developed severe nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and poor oral intake. She was seen in the emergency department three days later with persistent vomiting; glucose was mildly elevated and venous pH was slightly low, and she was treated symptomatically and discharged. Over the following two days she developed recurrent vomiting and dyspnea, prompting return to the emergency department. On this visit she appeared ill with rapid, deep breathing. Arterial blood gas showed severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.02, low PaO2, base excess -25.5, anion gap 36 mmol/L, lactate 2.8 mmol/L), blood glucose was markedly elevated (27.85 mmol/L), HbA1c was 10.6%, and ketones were positive.

A male adolescent (early teens) presented to the emergency department with a 48-hour history of right-sided testicular pain accompanied by vague, nonspecific abdominal pain. He denied any history of trauma. He had no prior significant medical history. On examination, there was a well-defined swelling of the right hemiscrotum with marked tenderness on palpation; no local warmth or erythema was noted. Vital signs were not remarkable at presentation. Scrotal ultrasound showed the right testis enlarged, measuring approximately 1.1 x 2.2 x 2.5 cm, with heterogeneously hypoechoic echotexture; color Doppler interrogation demonstrated absence of internal vascular flow, with a small amount of surrounding fluid. The right epididymis appeared bulky, trilobed, and heterogeneous, predominantly hyperechoic, with only minimal peripheral flow on Doppler. The left testis and epididymis were sonographically normal. Incidentally, a large (approximately 1.4 cm) calculus was identified within a cystic dilation of the distal right ureter at its bladder insertion, exhibiting a twinkling artifact on color Doppler. Excretory urography demonstrated a lucent filling defect in the bladder with a classic 'cobra head' appearance of the distal ureter. Given the acute scrotal findings, urgent surgical exploration was planned.

samples.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis, unspecified with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
samples.note: A young adult male with no prior medical history, no known liver disease, and no alcohol, drug, or relevant medication use presented after being found unresponsive by family. Three days prior he developed dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and fatigue; symptoms persisted despite outpatient antiemetic and antivertigo treatment. On arrival he was stuporous (GCS 12, E4V3M5) with equal, reactive pupils (2 mm), heart rate 130 bpm, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg without vasopressor support, SpO2 96% on room air, and no fever, seizures, or meningeal signs. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.43, pCO2 34.6 mmHg, HCO3 23.1 mmol/L, base excess -1 (mild respiratory alkalosis). Glucose was 8 mmol/L; electrolytes, creatinine, eGFR, liver function tests, INR, and CRP were normal. Serum ketones were negative, urine ketones mildly positive, lactate 1.66 mmol/L. Ammonia was markedly elevated at 213 micromol/L (normal 18-72). Brain MRI showed no acute abnormality. Within three hours, level of consciousness worsened to GCS 7 (E1V1M5), with repeat ammonia rising to 284 micromol/L. CSF analysis was normal, and autoimmune encephalitis markers were negative. Thyroid studies showed elevated free T4 and free T3 with markedly suppressed TSH. Urinalysis showed cloudiness with proteinuria; urine culture was pending.

samples.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
samples.note: A woman in her 60s, with a known history of diabetes mellitus well controlled on oral metformin, presented to the emergency department with lower limb weakness for five days along with vomiting and diarrhea for three days. The diarrhea was watery, without mucus or blood, and she reported one episode of rectal bleeding. She denied fever, cough, urinary incontinence, seizures, sensory loss, falls, or headache. She had a prior hospitalization for similar complaints. On examination, Glasgow Coma Scale was 15/15, pupils were bilaterally equal and reactive, and there was no facial or tongue deviation. Tone was decreased in both lower limbs, plantar responses were down-going bilaterally, and reflexes were absent. Power was 3/5 proximally and 4/5 distally in both upper limbs, and 2/5 both proximally and distally in both lower limbs. There was no sensory deficit. The remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable. She also had sweating and tachycardia. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL (low), potassium 4.5 mEq/L, random blood sugar 208 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 12 mg/L (mildly elevated), and calcium 7.54 mg/dL (low); liver and renal function tests were normal. Nerve conduction studies performed the following day showed findings suggestive of a moderate sensory-motor axonal polyneuropathy affecting the upper limbs more than the lower limbs.

A man in his late 30s with a history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and smoking presented to the emergency department with a three-day history of sore throat, dry cough, and odynophagia, with associated myalgias. He had been seen at an urgent care clinic the day before, tested negative for COVID-19, and was prescribed an antibiotic he could not tolerate due to difficulty swallowing. He denied alcohol or illicit drug use and reported being up to date on vaccinations including influenza and COVID-19. He works in an occupation with potential inhalational exposure and had inconsistent use of protective equipment. On arrival, heart rate was 131 bpm, blood pressure 179/104 mmHg, temperature 37.1°C, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Exam showed mild respiratory distress, tachycardia, drooling, a muffled voice, and pharyngeal swelling with erythema; the rest of the exam was unremarkable. Labs showed a white blood cell count of 15,700/μL with normal differential, glucose 249 mg/dL, and hemoglobin A1c 14.3% (prior A1c 9.5% six months earlier). Electrolytes, BUN, and creatinine were normal; urine ketones and beta-hydroxybutyrate were negative. Repeat COVID-19 PCR, rapid influenza, and group A streptococcal antigen testing were negative. Blood cultures were drawn. Lateral neck imaging showed soft tissue thickening involving the upper airway structures with an appearance of preserved airway patency.

samples.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
samples.note: An older adult woman with a long-standing history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, previously managed with oral hypoglycemic agents (including metformin) and twice-daily premixed insulin, presented with decreased level of consciousness and reduced oral intake over the preceding two days. She had recently been hospitalized for a cerebrovascular event and discharged less than two weeks earlier on a new medication regimen that included an SGLT2-inhibitor class antidiabetic agent, aspirin, and a statin. She had a family history of type 2 diabetes. There were no preceding cardiovascular, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms; no fever, sore throat, cough, headache, chest pain, syncope, diarrhea, vomiting, or urinary complaints; no chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, thyroid disease, prior ischemic heart disease, or recent travel. On examination, temperature was 36.3°C, pulse 110/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and blood pressure 110/89 mmHg. She appeared moderately dehydrated with dry oral mucosa and poor skin turgor; chest and other systems were unremarkable. Non-contrast head CT showed no acute intracranial abnormality. Chest radiograph, urine culture, and septic workup were unrevealing; cardiac enzymes and ECG were negative. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.12, pCO2 38 mmHg, HCO3 12 mmol/L, sodium 149 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L, glucose 185 mg/dL, lactate 2.4 mmol/L. Serum chemistry showed sodium 139 meq/L, potassium 5 meq/L, chloride 102 meq/L, albumin 43.5 g/L, glucose 190 mg/dL, corrected sodium 140 meq/L, anion gap 25, serum osmolality 288 mOsm/kg, and urine ketones strongly positive (3+).

An adult female with a history of anxiety and depression presented to the emergency department with a two-day history of shortness of breath, nonproductive cough, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea. She had been using an albuterol inhaler throughout the day without relief and continued to feel dyspneic, prompting evaluation. She denied any prior history of asthma, childhood wheezing, or reactive airway symptoms. She reported a five-pack-year smoking history, having quit earlier in the year. On arrival, oxygen saturation was 93%, and she received two nebulized breathing treatments along with a dose of dexamethasone. Chest radiograph showed no acute abnormality. She was admitted for observation and started on a course of oral corticosteroids, scheduled inhaled ipratropium-albuterol, as-needed albuterol, and guaifenesin. The following day, vital signs showed blood pressure 152/94 mmHg, heart rate 120 bpm, and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and she became unresponsive. A venous blood gas was obtained showing pH 7.15, pCO2 82 mmHg, pO2 127 mmHg, oxygen saturation 97%, and fingerstick glucose 163 mg/dL, consistent with acute hypercarbic respiratory failure. She required transfer to the intensive care unit, escalating respiratory support, and eventually intubation for persistent severe expiratory wheezing, accessory muscle use, and markedly elevated ventilator peak pressures despite multiple sedative and paralytic trials.

A man in his 60s with diabetes mellitus (diagnosed 8 months earlier, HbA1c 12.4% at diagnosis, now on intensive insulin therapy with good glycemic control), hypertension, and benign prostatic hyperplasia (status post transurethral resection 9 years earlier) with recurrent urinary retention managed by an indwelling catheter and, more recently, intermittent self-catheterization, presented shortly after percutaneous coronary intervention with high fever and a transient episode of loss of consciousness. Vital signs on admission were relatively stable. Neurological examination showed no focal deficits. Head MRI revealed multiple acute embolic infarcts in the left parietal and posterior lobes. Blood and urine cultures grew a gram-negative organism; empiric ceftazidime was started. Fever persisted, and repeat blood cultures on day 7 grew a ceftazidime-resistant isolate, prompting a switch to levofloxacin. Transthoracic echocardiograms on days 1 and 4 were unremarkable. Symptoms resolved and the patient was discharged, but fever recurred three days later. On readmission, physical examination was unremarkable; labs showed WBC 9300/µL and total serum protein 12.5 mg/dL. Blood cultures were again positive. Repeat head MRI showed new multiple emboli with microhemorrhages in the bilateral cerebral cortex and cerebellum. Initial transthoracic echocardiogram showed no structural abnormality; transesophageal echocardiography three days later showed a mobile, hypoechoic aortic valve lesion, new severe aortic regurgitation, and a patent foramen ovale. On transfer, a pan-diastolic murmur was heard; no peripheral embolic stigmata were noted, and whole-body CT showed no other infectious focus.

A woman in her late 30s with a history of seasonal allergic rhinitis, no prior diagnosis of asthma, presented to the emergency department with a 2-month history of cough, worse at night, and recent onset of wheezing. She was a current smoker (approximately 19 pack-years) and kept hamsters at home. Several days prior, she had been evaluated by a primary care provider for cough and wheezing and started on a single extended-release dose of oral azithromycin for a presumed respiratory infection, without improvement. Two days later she developed worsening dyspnoea to the point of being unable to speak, prompting emergency evaluation. On arrival, vital signs showed a temperature of 37.1°C, oxygen saturation of 75% on room air, and a respiratory rate of 44 breaths/min. She was in marked respiratory distress. Chest radiograph showed right-sided infiltrates, and CT chest demonstrated patchy ground-glass opacity with bronchial wall thickening. Laboratory testing revealed a white blood cell count of 22,800/μL, C-reactive protein of 3.93 mg/dL, and total serum IgE of 110 IU/mL, with specific IgE positive for Japanese cedar and cypress pollen but negative for hamster epithelium. She was admitted to the intensive care unit for further management of severe respiratory compromise.

A man in his late 50s presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe, pressure-like chest pain of about 40 minutes' duration, progressively worsening and radiating to the back, accompanied by profuse sweating and blurred vision. He had a 3-year history of hypertension treated with losartan 100 mg daily, without regular blood pressure monitoring, and no other significant past medical history. He was a current smoker (20 cigarettes/day for 20 years) and reported heavy daily alcohol use (about 100 g/day for 20 years), with no relevant family history. On examination, temperature was 37.1°C, heart rate 81 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min with normal oxygen saturation, and blood pressure 92/61 mmHg. Point-of-care laboratory testing showed white blood cell count 7.1×10^9/L, lymphocytes 35.8%, platelets 106×10^9/L, potassium 3.92 mmol/L, creatinine 75 μmol/L, CK-MB 15.5 U/L, BNP 65.8 pg/mL, troponin I 0.003 μg/L, and D-dimer 4.52 mg/L (elevated). A 12-lead ECG showed ST-segment depression (>1 mm) at the J point with tall, symmetrical T waves in leads V1–V3, along with 1 mm ST-segment elevation in lead aVR.

samples.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
samples.note: A woman in her late 30s with a history of diabetes mellitus diagnosed about 1.5 years earlier, managed with metformin and an SGLT2 inhibitor, presented to the emergency department with nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath, and altered mental status. She had tested positive for a respiratory viral illness one week prior and had been quarantining at home. Since her diabetes diagnosis, her HbA1c had ranged from the mid-6% to over 9%. On presentation she was tachycardic (heart rate 115 bpm) with blood pressure 109/68 mmHg, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, and temperature 98.8°F; BMI was 32 kg/m2. Laboratory workup showed marked hyperglycemia (glucose 523 mg/dL), elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate (8.91 mmol/L), severe acidemia (pH 6.9), low bicarbonate (11 mEq/L), an elevated anion gap (25 mEq/L), hypokalemia (2.9 mEq/L), and HbA1c 10.8%. White count was mildly elevated at 13.26 K/µL; urinalysis showed marked glucosuria and ketonuria. Rapid nasopharyngeal panel was negative for influenza, parainfluenza, adenovirus, and enterovirus. Chest x-ray showed no infiltrates. She was treated with intravenous fluids, potassium repletion, an insulin drip, and intravenous bicarbonate, with resolution of hyperglycemia over two days before transition to subcutaneous insulin.

samples.diagnosis: Acute appendicitis with perforation, localized peritonitis, and gangrene, with abscess
samples.note: A woman in her late 20s presented to the emergency department with three days of worsening right lower quadrant abdominal pain, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, dysuria, and diarrhea. She had been evaluated by her primary care provider that day and was referred to the ED for further evaluation given concern for a possible acute intra-abdominal process. She described a similar, milder episode of pain about one week earlier that had resolved on its own without treatment. Past medical history was notable only for a prior cesarean section; she denied other medical problems and reported no relevant family or social risk factors. On arrival she was afebrile (36.4°C) with heart rate 85 bpm, respiratory rate 20, blood pressure 132/86 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Abdominal exam showed mild distension with marked right lower quadrant tenderness elicited even with light palpation, and voluntary guarding; there was no rigidity or rebound tenderness, and obturator and Rovsing's signs were both negative. Initial labs showed a white blood cell count of 18.9 x10^3/µL with a left shift (87% neutrophils); electrolytes and liver function tests were otherwise unremarkable. Urinalysis showed pyuria raising concern for a concurrent urinary tract infection. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained, demonstrating an enlarged, fluid-filled right lower quadrant tubular structure with wall thickening, surrounding fat stranding, and an adjacent localized fluid collection.

A man in his 30s with a history of alcohol use was found unresponsive with an unknown down time and brought to the trauma bay. Initial Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was 13, which declined rapidly after arrival; he was intubated for airway protection. Neurologic exam showed a fixed, dilated left pupil with GCS 6T after a brief sedation hold. Secondary survey revealed ecchymoses over the left chest, shoulder, and knee. CT of the head showed a left convexity acute subdural hematoma with midline shift and uncal herniation; CT chest showed a small pneumomediastinum and mild left pneumothorax. Toxicology screen was positive only for ethanol. He underwent emergent decompressive hemicraniectomy with hematoma evacuation; intraoperative bronchoscopy and endoscopy showed no additional injury. Postoperatively he improved neurologically and was extubated. On hospital day 3 he developed tachycardia and acute hypoxia with bilateral pulmonary edema on chest x-ray; ECG showed new QTc prolongation and lateral T-wave inversion, though he denied chest pain, and hypoxia improved with diuresis. On day 4, worsening T-wave inversion was noted on multiple leads with persistent QTc prolongation; troponin I was mildly elevated at 0.63 ng/mL (normal 0-0.1), then trended down. A repeat echocardiogram showed new left ventricular apical ballooning with reduced ejection fraction (about 26%) without overt heart failure symptoms; an earlier echocardiogram had been normal. Cardiac-directed medical therapy was started, with echocardiographic recovery noted on later follow-up.

A man in his mid-20s presented after sudden-onset tearing pain in the chest and back. Four days after symptom onset he became unresponsive and was found to have intracranial hemorrhage with hydrocephalus at another facility; emergency external ventricular drainage was performed and consciousness recovered afterward. Vascular imaging of the chest at that time showed an irregular, layered contour of the aortic wall extending into the abdomen, along with incidental aneurysms of the left vertebral and basilar arteries. He was transferred for further management. One week after admission, he acutely deteriorated with hypotension (blood pressure 85/58 mmHg), hypoxemia (PaO2 58 mmHg), shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal distension, without abdominal pain or peritoneal signs. Repeat CT angiography of the chest and abdomen showed persistence of the aortic wall abnormality and narrowing at the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, with a prominent vessel pattern on enhanced imaging. The small bowel was markedly dilated with imaging features of paralytic obstruction. An ileus tube was placed without significant relief of distension, and signs suggestive of peritonitis subsequently developed. No relevant chronic medical history was reported.

A middle-aged adult male with a history of hypertension and a positive COVID-19 PCR test several days prior presented to the emergency department with worsening difficulty swallowing and voice hoarseness over one day. He reported a mild sore throat that began the day before presentation, which worsened overnight and was accompanied by tongue swelling and vocal changes. He denied difficulty breathing, fever, chills, cough, chest pain, nausea, vomiting, or recent travel. He was a former smoker (quit over ten years ago) and denied excess alcohol or intravenous drug use. His hypertension had been well controlled on losartan for two years with no prior adverse reactions, and he denied any family history of angioedema. On arrival, temperature was 37.6°C, blood pressure 139/91 mmHg, heart rate 112 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. He could speak in full sentences but with noticeable voice muffling. Exam showed left neck tenderness without abdominal pain, rash, or pruritis; BMI was 24.9 kg/m2. He reported no new medications or dietary changes. Labs showed WBC 4.70 K/uL, procalcitonin 0.10 ng/mL, ferritin 152 μg/L, CRP 0.51 mg/L, and D-dimer 169 ng/mL; blood cultures and COVID-19 antibodies were negative. Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed submucosal edema and erythema of the epiglottis with surrounding secretions. Contrast CT of the neck showed thickening of the epiglottis and epiglottic folds with submucosal edema extending into the hypopharynx and mild airway narrowing.

A woman in her early 70s with no known past medical history presented to the emergency department with 4 days of atraumatic left eye pain and swelling, preceded by 2 weeks of generalized malaise. She reported thick yellow discharge and progressive swelling that prevented her from opening the eye. She denied flashes or floaters but noted she could not see out of the affected eye due to swelling. On examination, there was marked periorbital edema and erythema of the upper and lower eyelids with active mucopurulent discharge. The eye required manual assistance to open; once opened, there was proptosis and significant chemosis. Full visual acuity testing could not be tolerated due to pain and swelling, though the patient reported blurry vision in the affected eye relative to the other. Intraocular pressure was elevated in the affected eye (35 mmHg) compared to the unaffected eye (15 mmHg). Fundoscopic examination was severely limited by chemosis and swelling. Laboratory testing showed leukocytosis of 16,000/µL with 85% neutrophils. Bedside ocular ultrasound was performed given the limited direct exam and revealed extensive, well-demarcated, mobile hyperechoic debris within the posterior chamber and additional hyperechoic material within the lens. Further cross-sectional imaging of the orbit was subsequently obtained to characterize the extent of periorbital and intraorbital involvement.

A woman in her late 20s presented with a several-year history (since around 2018) of pruritic skin lesions localized mainly to the flexural/joint areas of both upper and lower limbs. She described intense itching (rated 8/10) with associated erythema, papules, edema, excoriations with occasional bleeding, oozing/exudate, dryness, scaling, and thickened (lichenified) skin over the distal joint regions, most severe on the fingers. Symptoms had progressively worsened over the past year despite topical corticosteroid and emollient therapy, and had persisted despite a recent 2-week course of oral corticosteroids, prompting the patient to discontinue treatment on her own. Symptoms fluctuated with stress and evening hours, and were aggravated by handwashing with soap, significantly impairing daily functioning and quality of life. Systemic review revealed constipation, bloating, chest tightness, and dyspepsia. Past history was notable for an appendectomy about 13 years prior; family history was unremarkable. On examination, there was erythema, papules, edema, exudation, dryness, scaling, and lichenification distributed below both limb joints, with excoriations and scratch marks on the fingers. Initial laboratory studies showed a normal total white blood cell count, mildly elevated eosinophils (17.2%, 980/μL), markedly elevated total IgE (13,419 IU/mL), and mildly elevated AST/ALT.

A woman in her 30s with a history of gastritis, depression, and obesity presented to dermatology clinic with a chief complaint of hair loss. She reported that scalp hair had been thinning progressively over about 1 year, with more rapid thinning noted over the preceding 6 months. There was minimal improvement after 3 months of daily topical minoxidil 5% foam. She had a known pituitary microadenoma present for over a decade, stable in size on recent imaging, with normal prolactin, follicle-stimulating hormone, and luteinizing hormone levels. On examination she was in no acute distress but had facial plethora and prominent truncal, facial, and nuchal adiposity. Skin examination showed diffuse nonscarring alopecia of the frontal and vertex scalp with miniaturized hairs on dermoscopy, and mildly decreased density over the temporal and occipital scalp. There were erythematous inflammatory papules and pustules on the face and mid-to-lower back, violaceous striae on the abdomen and axillae, ecchymoses on the abdomen and extremities, facial hirsutism, and patches of coarse hypertrichosis on the back. Serum ferritin, iron, thyroid-stimulating hormone, antinuclear antibody, albumin, total protein, and vitamin B12 were normal. Scalp punch biopsy showed a normal number of follicles without fibrosis, an increased ratio of catagen/telogen to anagen hairs, and a sparse peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate. Additional endocrine testing was subsequently obtained.

A middle-aged man presented with a two-week history of fever accompanied by hematuria, proteinuria, and rapidly worsening renal function despite a course of intravenous antibiotics and supportive care for the kidneys at an outside facility. He had a five-year history of untreated hypertension (peak blood pressure around 145/110 mmHg) and had recovered from an episode of pancreatitis several months earlier. He denied diabetes, alcohol use, intravenous drug use, and smoking, and had no family history of relevant disease or known environmental exposures. He worked as a farmer. On admission he was afebrile with normal mental status, pulse 92/min, respirations 18/min, and blood pressure 116/78 mmHg. Cardiac auscultation revealed a systolic murmur (3/6) at the apex and a diastolic murmur (2/6) at the aortic area; neurological exam was normal. Labs showed 1+ proteinuria (1.28 g/24h), 3+ urine occult blood with markedly elevated red cells per high-power field, white cell count 6.22×10^9/L, hemoglobin 81 g/L, albumin 32.3 g/L, globulin 48.7 g/L, creatinine 196 μmol/L, and BUN 7.7 mmol/L. Hepatitis B surface antigen, e-antigen, and core antibody were positive with detectable HBV DNA; HCV and HIV were negative, rheumatoid factor was negative. PR3-ANCA was markedly elevated (170.4 U/mL) while MPO-ANCA was normal. Blood cultures were obtained three times, with growth of an organism noted. Cardiac ultrasound showed valvular vegetations with regurgitation, and chest CT showed no obvious pulmonary infection.

samples.diagnosis: Ankylosing spondylitis of unspecified sites in spine
samples.note: A man in his early 30s presented with a 2-month history of bilateral lower extremity weakness and sensory disturbance, worsened by a recent fall. He reported progressive difficulty walking and new bowel and bladder dysfunction. He had a 10-year history of a chronic inflammatory spinal condition and had trialed rest, NSAIDs, and corticosteroids without improvement. There was no history of tuberculosis exposure, weight loss, fever, cough, or night sweats. On examination, spinal mobility was limited with tenderness over the T11-12 region. Lower extremity strength was approximately Grade II bilaterally with diminished sensation. Neurological exam showed a positive Babinski sign and ankle clonus; Lasegue sign was negative. Laboratory studies showed a positive HLA-B27, elevated ESR (56 mm/h), and elevated CRP (17.7 mg/L); complete blood count and other serum chemistries were normal. Radiographs showed syndesmophytes in the thoracic and lumbar spine with destructive changes at T11-T12. CT demonstrated increased bone density at T11-T12 with partial vertebral body resorption and intracanal osteophytes. MRI showed hyperintensity of the T11/12 disc, endplate erosion, subchondral bone marrow edema, and extradural cord compression with myelopathic signal change.

A woman in her early 70s with a history of osteoporosis presented after sustaining a low-trauma L1 vertebral fracture. She had completed a 10-year course of an oral bisphosphonate followed by a 2-year treatment break; recent bone densitometry showed a T-score of -2.5 at the spine and -1.9 at the total hip. She was started on a daily subcutaneous bone-forming injectable therapy along with calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and previously treated hepatitis C; regular medications included aspirin, a beta-blocker, a calcium channel blocker, and a statin. Baseline serum calcium was normal. After approximately 3 months of the new therapy, routine bloodwork showed markedly elevated serum calcium, confirmed on repeat testing the day after the medication was stopped. She was admitted for further evaluation and was noted to be mildly dehydrated on examination. Investigations showed normal vitamin D, suppressed parathyroid hormone, and normal parathyroid hormone-related peptide, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, serum electrophoresis, and angiotensin-converting enzyme levels. CT of the abdomen, pelvis, and thorax showed no evidence of malignancy, and an isotope bone scan excluded skeletal metastases but showed increased tracer uptake at the fracture site and in the skull. Serum calcium normalised with intravenous fluids and cessation of calcium supplementation and the injectable therapy, but recurred after the therapy was restarted, prompting a switch to an alternative osteoporosis treatment. A subsequent 24-hour urinary calcium was normal.

samples.diagnosis: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia of B-cell type not having achieved remission
samples.note: A 70-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of failed splenectomy for previously diagnosed chronic immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), following 2 years of intermittent skin ecchymoses. At initial evaluation 2 years earlier, complete blood count showed WBC 7.48×10^9/L, absolute lymphocyte count 3.58×10^9/L, and platelets 16×10^9/L; physical exam at that time showed no palpable superficial lymphadenopathy and no hepatosplenomegaly. PET-CT at that time incidentally noted multiple enlarged supraclavicular lymph nodes, which were not biopsied. Over the following two years he was treated at multiple institutions with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, recombinant human thrombopoietin, eltrombopag, and vincristine plus triptolide, with persistently poor platelet response (platelets consistently <30×10^9/L). Repeat labs approximately 6 months before admission showed WBC 11.8×10^9/L, absolute lymphocyte count 6.6×10^9/L, platelets 10×10^9/L. Splenectomy performed 1 month before admission did not improve platelet counts. On admission, exam revealed multiple enlarged, non-tender, mobile, smooth lymph nodes in the neck, supraclavicular, and axillary regions (largest approximately 2×2 cm). Labs showed peripheral lymphocyte count 8.86×10^9/L, platelets 7×10^9/L, hemoglobin 109 g/L. Ultrasound showed hypoechoic masses in the left supraclavicular and axillary regions consistent with enlarged lymph nodes. CT showed multiple small lymph nodes in the left subclavian and mediastinal regions, and enlarged prevertebral/retroperitoneal lymph nodes below the T10 vertebral level.

A man in his mid-20s presented with severe shortness of breath, with a 5-day history of fever, myalgia, arthralgia, and dry cough preceding admission. Past medical history was notable for beta thalassemia intermedia, prior splenectomy (approximately 10 years earlier), and diabetes mellitus. On examination he was tachypneic (respiratory rate 30/min) and in respiratory distress, with bibasilar crackles on lung auscultation. Body temperature was 38.3°C, and oxygen saturation on room air was 76%. Arterial blood gas showed respiratory acidosis (pH 7.31, elevated pCO2, HCO3 27.3). Initial laboratory studies revealed marked leukocytosis (WBC 41,100/µl) with 38.6% lymphocytes, hemoglobin 9.4 g/dl, RBC 3.56 x10^6/µl, and normal platelet count. Inflammatory markers were markedly elevated: ESR 97 mm/h, procalcitonin 18.3, and strongly positive CRP. Liver enzymes, BUN, creatinine, and serum electrolytes were normal. High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated multifocal, peripherally distributed ground-glass opacities involving both lungs. Given hypoxemia and respiratory distress, the patient required escalating oxygen support, including a reservoir mask and subsequent non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation, before eventual improvement and transition to nasal cannula support.

A man in his mid-40s presented to the emergency department with several days of headache, slurred speech, gait disturbance, and confusion, along with flank pain. Past medical history included HIV infection, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, recurrent kidney stones, and tobacco use disorder. He also reported a history of cosmetic silicone injections roughly two decades earlier. On arrival, blood pressure was severely elevated at 207/117 mmHg, heart rate 80 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96%. He appeared in moderate distress; abdominal exam was non-tender without peritoneal signs, though flank tenderness was present, and no neck masses were noted. Laboratory studies showed sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 2.7 mmol/L, BUN 28 mg/dL, creatinine 3.72 mg/dL, calcium 13.4 mg/dL, hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, white blood cell count 6,700/µL, and platelets 105,000/µL. Urinalysis showed pyuria and positive leukocyte esterase without significant bacteriuria. Renal ultrasound demonstrated bilateral nephrolithiasis and left-sided hydronephrosis. He was admitted for hypertensive urgency and acute kidney injury, with additional metabolic workup pursued including parathyroid hormone level and vitamin D metabolites, along with cross-sectional imaging that incidentally noted extensive soft-tissue calcific deposits in the bilateral gluteal and proximal thigh regions.

A 61-year-old male presented with insidious onset of left-sided eyelid drooping that had persisted for some time, accompanied by intermittent double vision, blurred vision, occasional difficulty swallowing, and fluctuating limb weakness that was described as milder in the morning and more pronounced by evening. He had a history of hypertension (managed with amlodipine, metoprolol, and nifedipine) and coronary artery disease (on aspirin and atorvastatin). He had end-stage renal disease diagnosed roughly a decade earlier and was on long-term maintenance hemodialysis. There was no family history of neuromuscular or autoimmune disease. On examination, there was left eyelid ptosis with reduced palpebral fissure, mild limb weakness, and difficulty swallowing solid food. Repetitive nerve stimulation showed a decremental response in the orbicularis oculi and trapezius muscles. A cholinergic challenge test produced transient improvement of the ptosis. Acetylcholine receptor antibody was positive at low titer, and anti-titin antibody was strongly positive. Chest CT showed no mediastinal mass. Antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, thyroid function, tumor markers, and infectious disease studies were negative. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia, elevated potassium (5.35 mmol/L), and markedly elevated creatinine (711 µmol/L) consistent with known renal failure; liver function was normal.

samples.diagnosis: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia of B-cell type not having achieved remission
samples.note: A man in his late 50s, employed in scientific research, presented after incidental discovery of a persistently elevated lymphocyte count identified during work-up for new-onset bilateral hip pain and arthritis; he was otherwise asymptomatic. Review of prior records showed a mildly elevated lymphocyte count roughly one year earlier, with a possible borderline elevation noted approximately three years before that, suggesting a long-standing, indolent process. Repeat testing across multiple laboratories over two months confirmed persistent mild lymphocytosis with occasional smear cells on blood film. Physical examination revealed no palpable lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly, and vital signs were unremarkable. Initial blood counts showed a white cell count of approximately 19 x10^9/L with lymphocytosis (~11 x10^9/L), normal haemoglobin (14.6 g/dL) and normal platelet count (253 x10^9/L). Immunoglobulin profile was essentially normal, CRP was low, and LDH was mildly to moderately elevated on serial testing. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood demonstrated a clonal B-lymphocyte population with light-chain restriction (lambda), variably expressing CD5, CD19, CD20, and CD23, with negative or borderline results for CD38 and a marker of proliferative activity depending on laboratory. Molecular cytogenetic studies showed no p53 deletion and hypermutated immunoglobulin genes; fluorescence in situ hybridisation showed a low-percentage 17p deletion and incomplete 13q deletion, with 11q status negative.

A middle-aged male presented with persistent, severe itching of the ear canal. He had a long-standing history of atopic dermatitis dating back to childhood, along with bronchial asthma, hypertension, cataracts, and glaucoma. He denied tobacco or alcohol use. He reported multiple drug and food allergies, including a rash from a prior xanthine bronchodilator and joint pain from a prior JAK-inhibitor trial, as well as reactions to banana, rice, wheat, and soy. Current medications included an oral antihistamine, an angiotensin receptor blocker, an oral mucolytic, and several topical corticosteroid and skin-care preparations. Over a year before the current presentation, a biologic agent targeting IL-4/IL-13 signaling had been started for his skin disease, producing marked improvement in trunk lesions with severity scores dropping substantially. Despite this, severe ear canal pruritus persisted and did not respond to topical corticosteroid ear drops or ointments, prompting specialist referral. On otoscopic examination, both external auditory canals showed erythema with abundant adherent scaling, with erythema and scaling also noted on the tympanic membranes. Laboratory testing showed a normal white blood cell count with mild eosinophilia. Serum IgE and a serum chemokine marker of allergic inflammation were markedly reduced compared to prior levels but remained above normal range. Allergen-specific IgE testing showed high sensitization to multiple environmental aeroallergens and molds. Bacterial cultures from the ear canal grew only commensal skin flora, with no pathogenic organisms identified.

A woman in her late twenties with a 3-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus (on hydroxychloroquine and corticosteroids) presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain, palpitations, and shortness of breath that began shortly after an acute emotional stressor (the death of a parent). She also reported generalized fatigue, joint pain, and anxiety. She had no prior history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or hypertension, and family history was unremarkable. On examination she was anxious and distressed; blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg, heart rate 125 bpm, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. She had recent unintentional weight loss of about 5 kg, joint pain involving the hands and knees suggestive of a flare of her underlying autoimmune disease, and occasional headaches without dizziness or syncope. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia with ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads and negative T waves. Troponin I was elevated at 1.5 ng/mL and NT-proBNP was 800 pg/mL. Coronary angiography showed normal coronary arteries. Echocardiography demonstrated a regional wall motion abnormality of the left ventricle involving the apex with reduced systolic function in that distribution. Laboratory studies showed normal renal function and electrolytes, trace proteinuria with mild hematuria, mildly decreased hemoglobin/hematocrit, and serologic markers of active autoimmune disease including positive antinuclear antibodies, elevated anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, and low complement levels.

An adult man in his 50s presented with a 1-month history of epigastric pain. He had no history of diabetes mellitus or hypertension, no history of alcohol use, but was a former smoker with a 20 pack-year history. On admission, vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed epigastric tenderness with no other abnormal findings. Laboratory studies showed normal white blood cell count, hemoglobin, platelet count, renal function, albumin, bilirubin, and transaminases, with mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase. Lactate dehydrogenase was normal. Amylase and lipase were mildly elevated. Carcinoembryonic antigen was normal, while carbohydrate antigen 19-9 was mildly elevated. Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT revealed an enhancing mass measuring 4.7 cm with anterior mesenteric soft tissue infiltration in the head of the pancreas. MRI showed a pancreatic head mass with apparent superior mesenteric vein invasion. Contrast-enhanced neck and chest CT were negative. Endoscopic ultrasound demonstrated an ill-defined hypoechoic mass in the pancreatic head. Fine-needle biopsy specimens obtained via endoscopic ultrasound showed clusters of atypical lymphoid cells with a high Ki-67 proliferation index, and a definitive diagnosis could not be established from this sample. A laparoscopic surgical biopsy was subsequently performed to obtain tissue for further histologic and immunohistochemical evaluation.

samples.diagnosis: Acute myeloblastic leukemia, not having achieved remission
samples.note: An elderly man, in his 70s, presented with progressively worsening fatigue and abdominal pain of uncertain duration, prompting hospital admission. Past medical history included a recently treated pulmonary fungal infection. On examination there was no palpable splenomegaly; other vital signs and physical findings were not detailed in the available record. Initial peripheral blood count showed marked leukocytosis (white blood cell count approximately 118 × 10^9/L), anemia (hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL), and mild thrombocytopenia (platelet count 98 × 10^9/L). Peripheral blood smear was hypercellular with approximately 90% blast forms. Bone marrow aspirate morphology showed 90% agranular blast cells of medium-to-large size. Flow cytometric immunophenotyping of the blasts demonstrated positivity for CD34, CD117, CD33, CD13, and HLA-DR, with variable expression of myeloperoxidase and CD2/CD7 markers, and no splenomegaly was noted. Cytoreductive therapy with hydroxyurea was initiated, resulting in a reduction of the white blood cell count after approximately one week of treatment.

A man in his 50s presented with a two-year history of progressive exertional dyspnea that had come to limit most physical activity, together with lower-extremity edema, orthopnea, generalized fatigue, anorexia, and abdominal distention persisting for over three years. Past medical history included chronic gout and regular alcohol use. About one year earlier he had been diagnosed with heart failure and was found to have reduced renal function (estimated glomerular filtration rate 42.4 mL/min, creatinine 160.7 μmol/L) along with an elevated parathyroid hormone level (206 pg/mL) and hypercalcemia (calcium 2.85 mmol/L). There was no history of hypertension, diabetes, or smoking. On examination, the cardiac silhouette was enlarged, heart sounds were diminished, and a grade II/VI pansystolic murmur consistent with mitral regurgitation was audible; hepatojugular reflux was positive and there was bilateral pitting lower-extremity edema. Laboratory studies showed high-sensitivity troponin I 137.7 ng/L, brain natriuretic peptide 2583.9 pg/mL, PTH 284 pg/mL, calcium 2.78 mmol/L, phosphate 0.95 mmol/L, creatinine 210.4 μmol/L, and a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 42.27 μg/mg. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia, high left ventricular voltage, and diffuse ST-T changes. Echocardiography showed severely reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (22%), dilation of all four chambers, and moderate mitral with mild tricuspid regurgitation. Cardiac MRI confirmed left ventricular dilation and myocardial thinning with a markedly reduced ejection fraction (15.2%) and linear delayed enhancement within the interventricular septum. Neck ultrasound and nuclear imaging identified a small (approximately 1 cm) hypoechoic nodule near the lower pole of the right thyroid lobe with increased vascularity on Doppler.

A woman in her early 30s was admitted for progressive numbness and weakness of the limbs over 10 days. Weakness began distally and progressed proximally, with the hands losing the ability to grasp objects and perform finger abduction/opposition. She denied fever, and had no gastrointestinal symptoms at this admission. Three months earlier she had an episode of bloody, mucopurulent diarrhea (3-5 times/day) with abdominal pain but no tenesmus or fever; colonoscopy at that time showed severe diffuse colonic inflammation, and she was treated with oral and rectal 5-aminosalicylate agents plus probiotics, with resolution of gastrointestinal symptoms before this admission. She denied hypertension, diabetes, hepatitis B, or tuberculosis. Vital signs were normal. Neurologic exam showed full alertness, normal speech, intact cranial nerves (equal reactive pupils, no nystagmus, symmetric nasolabial folds, no tongue deviation), symmetric muscle weakness (grade IV in upper limbs, IV proximally and III distally in lower limbs), normal superficial and deep sensation, and diminished deep tendon reflexes (brachioradialis, knee, ankle). She could not perform finger-to-nose or Romberg testing. No meningeal or pyramidal signs were present; abdomen was benign. Blood counts, coagulation, biochemistry, inflammatory markers, stool studies, and tumor markers were normal. Nerve conduction studies showed slowed conduction velocity, reduced amplitude, and delayed F-waves in the limbs. Brain/neck MRI showed cervical degenerative changes and a thin right vertebral artery. Chest CT was unremarkable. Abdominal imaging previously showed mild splenomegaly, bilateral renal stones, a duodenal diverticulum, and mild colorectal wall thickening. Cerebrospinal fluid showed elevated protein with a normal cell count and negative stains/cultures.

samples.diagnosis: Ankylosing spondylitis of unspecified sites in spine
samples.note: A 40-year-old man presented with a long-standing (over two decades) history of chronic inflammatory-type back pain and progressive spinal stiffness, previously managed with methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and NSAIDs, though adherence had been poor. He developed acute-onset thoracolumbar back pain after a minor fall approximately 21 months prior to presentation. At that time, examination showed point tenderness over T11-T12 with restricted spinal mobility and no neurologic deficit. Imaging showed diffuse ossification and fusion across multiple vertebral segments consistent with long-standing spinal ankylosis, plus an acute three-column fracture at T12 without significant displacement or vertebral height loss. He was managed conservatively with brace, rest, and physiotherapy but developed a progressively stooped posture and worsening pain over subsequent months. Follow-up imaging revealed pseudarthrosis with sclerosis and later an erosive lesion at the adjacent disc-vertebral junction extending to a neighboring level, with progressive kyphosis; surgery was recommended twice but declined. One year after the fall, he presented with severe back pain, perineal numbness, urinary frequency and urgency, and leg weakness. Examination showed grade IV lower-extremity strength, diminished deep tendon reflexes, negative Babinski sign, and perineal hypoesthesia. Imaging showed extension of the destructive lesion, marked kyphotic deformity, and spinal canal narrowing. Labs: ESR 24 mm/h, CRP 148.4 mg/L, HLA-B27 positive, antinuclear antibodies negative, tuberculosis screening negative, other counts and chemistries normal. No history of tumor or tuberculosis.

A man in his late 50s with a history of severe obstructive sleep apnea treated with nocturnal CPAP presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe central chest pain, described as constant and non-pleuritic, radiating to the upper abdomen, without a clear exertional trigger. Initial vital signs showed blood pressure 168/92 mmHg, heart rate 96 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and he was afebrile. Cardiovascular and respiratory examination was unremarkable, with no murmur noted. While in the department he had a transient episode of reduced responsiveness and vacant staring lasting about 20 minutes, without tonic-clonic movements, focal deficit, or post-ictal confusion, before returning to his baseline. Serial high-sensitivity troponins, electrocardiogram, and chest radiograph were unremarkable, and he was discharged with oral analgesia. Approximately ten days later he returned with acute-onset expressive language difficulty. He was hemodynamically stable but now had a new early diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge; neurological examination showed expressive aphasia without limb weakness. Brain imaging showed a subacute area of increased cortical and subcortical signal in the right posterior parietal and temporal lobes. Echocardiography demonstrated a dilated ascending aorta with a suspected intimal flap.

A woman in her 30s presented with paroxysmal cough and expectoration, followed over the subsequent weeks by progressively worsening shortness of breath and difficulty swallowing. Symptoms showed diurnal fluctuation, being milder in the morning and worsening by evening. Electrophysiological testing (repetitive nerve stimulation) showed a decremental response with low-frequency stimulation in a facial muscle. Given the severity of her condition, she received intravenous immunoglobulin pulse therapy and plasma exchange at an outside facility without significant improvement; one plasma exchange session was complicated by a transfusion-related allergic reaction, which was prevented with prophylactic medication during subsequent sessions. She was subsequently started on pyridostigmine, mycophenolate mofetil, corticosteroids, and tacrolimus. Approximately six weeks after symptom onset, due to progressive worsening, she was transferred to another facility in critical condition requiring endotracheal intubation for ventilatory support.
