Neurological examination showed bilateral incomplete eyelid closure, limited upward gaze and abduction of the eyes, grade 4 strength in all limbs, and grade 1 strength of the neck flexors. Repeat repetitive nerve stimulation again showed a low-frequency decremental response. She had weak bilateral breath sounds, elevated white blood cell count and inflammatory markers, and chest CT showing infectious lesions in both lower lobes. Sputum cultures grew multiple pathogenic bacteria consistent with pneumonia, treated with sequential antibiotics guided by culture results and inflammatory marker trends. She also developed hypoproteinemia, electrolyte disturbances, and a catheter-related thrombosis. She had no relevant past medical, surgical, or family history.

A woman in her late 50s presented with fever, vomiting, loose stools, and left-sided flank pain. She had a known history of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney dysfunction. On evaluation, she was found to have severe acute kidney injury with a serum creatinine of 8.9 mg/dL at presentation. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (total leukocyte count 16,000 cells/mm3) with neutrophilic predominance, and elevated inflammatory markers including CRP, ESR, and procalcitonin. Urinalysis demonstrated marked pyuria, strongly positive leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, significant bacteriuria, mild proteinuria, and microscopic hematuria. Given the severity of renal impairment, she was started on sustained low-efficiency daily dialysis (SLEDD). Creatinine transiently improved to 0.5 mg/dL following dialysis but rose again to 4.0 mg/dL over the subsequent five days despite treatment, indicating a fluctuating but persistent renal insult. The combination of fever, flank pain, and infected urine in the setting of poorly controlled diabetes and rapidly progressive kidney injury prompted further diagnostic workup, including cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen and kidneys, to characterize the underlying renal and urinary tract process.

A man in his 60s with a history of hypertriglyceridemia was admitted after falling from a ladder and sustaining a traumatic lumbar spine (burst) fracture, which was treated surgically with spinal fusion and laminectomy. Postoperatively he was started on subcutaneous unfractionated heparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Imaging of the spine obtained at the time of the fall showed normal-appearing bilateral adrenal glands. He was discharged to an acute rehabilitation facility. About one week later he developed fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis (white blood cell count 13.4 x10^3/uL). Lower extremity duplex ultrasound and CT angiography of the chest were negative for venous thromboembolism, though chest imaging raised concern for pneumonia, for which he received antibiotics. During this admission he also developed moderate thrombocytopenia (platelet count 57 x10^3/uL); heparin antibody testing was positive, so anticoagulation was switched to fondaparinux. A confirmatory functional platelet-activation assay returned negative several weeks later. Approximately two weeks after that, he developed unexplained tachycardia, and repeat CT chest angiography identified segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli; therapeutic anticoagulation was resumed. This same study incidentally showed bilateral adrenal gland enlargement (masses measuring about 3.9 cm on the right and 3.3 cm on the left), though dedicated adrenal imaging was not obtained at that time. He was discharged home on an oral anticoagulant. Three weeks later he was readmitted after his wife reported several weeks of poor appetite, unintentional weight loss of about 30 pounds, progressive weakness, and altered mental status, without fever, cough, congestion, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dysuria, or recent falls. On presentation he was lethargic and awake but unable to follow commands.

samples.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale
samples.note: A woman in her early 50s underwent laparoscopic myomectomy for symptomatic uterine fibroids, after presenting with episodes of abnormal uterine bleeding. The procedure lasted approximately 65 minutes, with carbon dioxide insufflation pressures of 18-20 mmHg during entry and 12 mmHg maintained intraoperatively. The surgery and anesthesia were uneventful, and she remained hemodynamically stable throughout. Approximately two hours after surgery, she acutely developed severe dyspnea with a significant drop in oxygen saturation. She reported no chest pain, fever, or other associated symptoms. She had no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, thrombophilia, or immunological disease. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen showed free air within the mediastinum and abdominal cavity, along with filling defects within the pulmonary arterial branches. No diaphragmatic defect, perforation, or other structural abnormality was identified to explain the presence of extraluminal air. Laboratory testing showed a markedly elevated D-dimer, with normal complete blood count, coagulation profile (PT, INR, APTT, fibrinogen), thyroid function, homocysteine, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-β2 glycoprotein I antibodies, protein C, protein S, and antithrombin levels. Genetic thrombophilia screening (Factor V Leiden, MTHFR variants, Factor II G20210A) was negative. Transthoracic echocardiogram and electrocardiogram were unremarkable. Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremity veins showed no evidence of deep venous thrombosis.

samples.diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
samples.note: An adolescent-to-young-adult primigravid woman presented at approximately 35 weeks and 4 days of gestation with severe hypertension and signs of pulmonary edema, prompting transfer for further evaluation and management. Her medical history was notable for type 1 diabetes mellitus managed with basal-bolus insulin therapy, with reported poor adherence to her insulin regimen for more than one week prior to presentation. She described progressive dyspnea and worsening bilateral lower-extremity swelling over the preceding days. On examination, vital signs showed elevated blood pressure and mild tachycardia; there was bilateral lower-extremity edema without focal neurologic deficits. Initial laboratory studies showed mild arterial acidemia (pH 7.32) with compensatory hypocapnia, reduced bicarbonate (17 mmol/L), mild hyponatremia, hypokalemia, trace ketonuria, and a blood glucose of 156 mg/dL, despite near-normal glucose values. Renal function, liver enzymes, and platelet count were normal; hemoglobin was mildly low. Fetal ultrasound demonstrated a cephalic singleton fetus with a reassuring heart rate and polyhydramnios. Intravenous magnesium sulfate was started for seizure prophylaxis, and subcutaneous sliding-scale insulin was initiated for glycemic control, after which glucose levels remained within the normal range. A subsequent echocardiogram, obtained due to suspected pulmonary edema, showed no evidence of structural or functional cardiac abnormality.

A female child (early school age) with a history of an unrepaired ventricular septal defect and chronic eczema presented to the emergency department with a one-week history of worsening respiratory symptoms. The illness began as mild cough and congestion and progressed over the week to include abdominal pain, poor oral intake, and fevers. Cardiology follow-up several weeks earlier had documented a small, membranous, pressure-restrictive ventricular septal defect with left-to-right shunt and trace aortic regurgitation. On arrival, temperature was 40.4°C, heart rate 178 beats per minute, respiratory rate 78 breaths per minute, and blood pressure 89/63 mmHg, with increased work of breathing and a holosystolic murmur on auscultation. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein, and elevated procalcitonin. Chest radiograph showed bilateral infiltrates. She was admitted for antibiotic and respiratory support but deteriorated over the following hours, requiring escalation of respiratory support and transfer to the intensive care unit. In the ICU, point-of-care ultrasound performed to evaluate cardiac function as a possible contributor to respiratory distress incidentally identified an echogenic, mobile structure near the tricuspid valve, prompting further evaluation. Past history was notable for the congenital heart lesion and long-standing uncontrolled eczema, with no other chronic illnesses reported.

A 73-year-old man with a history of asthma, gastroesophageal reflux disease, prior tonsillectomy, dyslipidemia, and occasional tobacco use presented to the emergency department one day after undergoing elective inguinal hernia repair under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation, reporting new difficulty and pain with swallowing. Intraoperative airway management had been uncomplicated, with routine intubation using a standard laryngoscope and cuffed endotracheal tube, followed by orogastric tube placement. On presentation he was in mild distress with a low-grade fever (38.5°C); other vital signs were unremarkable. Oral cavity and posterior pharyngeal examination were normal, though submandibular tenderness was present on palpation. Cardiopulmonary exam was normal. Labs showed neutrophilic leukocytosis (WBC 14.3x10^3/µL), elevated C-reactive protein (3.11 mg/dL), and elevated procalcitonin (2.52 ng/mL). Testing for COVID-19, influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, and blood cultures were negative. Contrast-enhanced neck CT showed mild-to-moderate soft tissue edema of the larynx extending to the epiglottis, with symmetric vocal cords and no airway narrowing. He was started on empiric antibiotics and steroids. By hospital day 3, dysphagia worsened with new hoarseness, prompting transfer to intensive care for airway monitoring; oxygenation remained normal without respiratory distress. Swallow evaluation showed pharyngeal dysphagia. Flexible laryngoscopy showed increased secretions and moderate edema of the arytenoids (right greater than left) and epiglottis, with normal vocal fold motion and no masses. Symptoms gradually improved during the ICU stay. At two-week follow-up, odynophagia and fever had resolved, with mild residual dysphagia to liquids; repeat laryngoscopy showed normal vocal cord motion, mild epiglottic erythema, and cobblestoning of the hypopharyngeal mucosa.

A woman in her late 20s, gravida 2 para 1, previously healthy, was referred with seizures, fever, and vomiting that began immediately after a spontaneous vaginal delivery complicated by intrauterine fetal death. She had received routine antenatal care with no prior comorbidities, taking only prenatal vitamins, iron-folic acid, and calcium supplements, and no other medications. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated. Symptoms developed acutely within a day of delivery. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, WBC 25,000/µL, platelets 49,000/µL, and creatinine 2.49 mg/dL. Over the following days she developed headache, decreasing urine output, and progressive visual impairment, eventually able to perceive only hand movements. On examination she had mild icterus, bilateral pitting pedal edema, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, and no focal motor, sensory, or cerebellar deficits. Repeat labs showed rising AST/ALT, elevated LDH, and worsening thrombocytopenia. Peripheral smear demonstrated schistocytes, anisocytosis, and microcytes suggestive of hemolysis; direct Coombs testing was negative. Renal function continued to worsen, requiring initiation of hemodialysis, and corticosteroids were started. Several days into admission she developed severe epigastric pain with markedly elevated serum amylase and lipase, and abdominal imaging showed a bulky pancreas with bilateral non-obstructive renal calculi. Brain imaging showed subcortical white matter edema in the parietal and occipital lobes. A renal biopsy showed near-diffuse cortical necrosis with focal microvascular changes. Complement levels (C3, C4) were normal.

A woman in her 70s with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (undetectable viral load) and metastatic, poorly differentiated vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (originally treated with radical surgery, chemotherapy, and pelvic radiation, later recurrent and treated with additional lines of chemotherapy) had started a new systemic anticancer agent 11 days prior to presentation. She presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of a painful, peeling rash, oral lesions, fevers, nausea, vomiting, cough, altered mental status, and visual hallucinations. On arrival she was febrile to 100.5°F and hypotensive (90s/50s) with a lactate of 5.4 mmol/L. Exam showed generalized abdominal tenderness, oral thrush, and areas of skin peeling in the bilateral axillae and groin; the vulva showed no discrete lesions or bleeding. Labs revealed potassium 6.5 mEq/L, WBC 0.5 cells/µL with unmeasurable absolute neutrophil count, platelets 180 cells/µL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), and BUN 34 mg/dL; respiratory viral panel was negative. CT angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed large impacted right kidney stones with hydronephrosis and findings of multifocal pneumonia. She was admitted and started on broad-spectrum antibiotics with a percutaneous nephrostomy placed. She subsequently developed progressive hypotension, tachycardia, and recurrent fever despite fluid resuscitation, with worsening skin sloughing on gentle pressure, new lesions in the mouth, underarms, and back, and lab findings including calcium 5.9 mg/dL and persistent leukopenia.

A young adult female presented with chest pain. Initial electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm at 60 bpm with low-voltage QRS complexes (≤5 mm) in the limb leads; precordial leads were normal with no ST-T changes or QT prolongation. Coronary CT angiography showed no atherosclerotic plaque in the major coronary arteries, and CT angiography of the thoracic aorta and abdomen was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed significantly elevated troponin with normal white blood cell count, neutrophil percentage, high-sensitivity CRP, procalcitonin, and interleukin-6, arguing against active infection. Cardiac MRI at that time was unremarkable. Three months later she was admitted with severe recurrent chest pain following strenuous exercise; high-sensitivity troponin rose markedly during hospitalization, peaking above 9000 ng/L, while ECG remained normal. Repeat cardiac MRI showed a region of late gadolinium enhancement involving the anterior and anterolateral left ventricular walls. Eight months after the initial presentation, she again developed persistent chest pain following an upper respiratory infection, with a further rise in troponin and similar late gadolinium enhancement on repeat imaging. There was no significant past medical history. Given the recurrent nature of these episodes, genetic testing for inherited cardiomyopathy/arrhythmia genes was performed and identified a heterozygous missense variant of uncertain significance in a desmosomal gene, also present in an asymptomatic parent but absent in other unaffected family members. She was treated supportively with metabolic adjunctive therapy, after which troponin levels normalized.

A woman in her late 30s with a history of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease), autoimmune thyroiditis, celiac disease, vitiligo, and alopecia presented to the emergency department with diaphoresis, headache, nausea, and vomiting, with inability to tolerate her usual oral medications for the preceding day. She had recent contact with a family member who had similar gastrointestinal symptoms. On arrival she appeared acutely ill and somnolent. Vital signs showed hypotension (blood pressure 75/48 mmHg), bradycardia (heart rate 46 bpm), and temperature 36.5°C. Exam revealed cool, clammy skin and diffuse skin hyperpigmentation; no focal neurologic deficits were noted, and the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Labs showed hyponatremia (sodium 125 mmol/L), normal potassium (3.9 mmol/L) and glucose (71 mg/dL), mildly elevated AST (51 U/L) and ALT (47 U/L), normal complete blood count, and normal renal function (creatinine 0.91 mg/dL, eGFR 82 mL/min). Electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia with first-degree atrioventricular block. Urinalysis and urine culture were unremarkable, blood cultures and a respiratory viral panel were negative, and abdominal ultrasound showed mild gallbladder wall thickening without cholelithiasis or cholecystitis.

A woman in her early 70s presented with a 10-day history of intermittent fatigue and profuse sweating, followed by worsening generalized myalgia. She had a 7-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with insulin and dapagliflozin, complicated by peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, and advanced diabetic kidney disease. Ten days prior, she experienced a hypoglycemic episode (fingerstick glucose 2.8 mmol/L) and self-discontinued insulin, continuing only dapagliflozin; around the same time she self-initiated bezafibrate for elevated triglycerides. Her history also included longstanding hypertension, prior ischemic stroke with residual left-sided deficits, dyslipidemia, coronary artery disease with prior myocardial infarction and percutaneous coronary intervention, pulmonary embolism with bilateral deep vein thrombosis on rivaroxaban, and recent hip fracture surgery. On examination: temperature 36.3°C, pulse 70/min, respirations 20/min, blood pressure 161/87 mmHg. She was alert and in fair general condition, with reduced pinprick, monofilament, and thermal sensation in both feet; muscle strength and tone were normal in all limbs, without edema. Labs showed random glucose 17.75 mmol/L, HbA1c 8.0%, urea 26.57 mmol/L, creatinine 329.3 μmol/L, elevated triglycerides and LDL cholesterol, and markedly elevated creatine kinase (4865 U/L, rising to 6419 U/L on repeat), CK-MB, LDH, and HBDH. Arterial blood gas showed mild acidosis with hypokalemia (potassium 3.00 mmol/L). ECG showed first-degree AV block. Vascular ultrasound demonstrated diffuse atherosclerotic plaques with arterial stenosis in the lower limb and carotid arteries.

A man in his late 60s with a history of hypertension, Crohn colitis, basal cell carcinoma, and a similar neurologic illness five years earlier (which had fully resolved over several months after inpatient treatment) presented to the emergency department with several hours of double vision, difficulty moving his eyes, voice changes, and trouble walking. Symptoms began upon waking that morning. He also reported headache and mild numbness/tingling in both lower extremities. He had noted cough and nasal congestion over the preceding several days. Vital signs on arrival were unremarkable: heart rate 86 bpm, blood pressure 155/73 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, temperature 98.9°F. He was alert and fully oriented, with normal speech articulation. Cranial nerve exam showed symmetric facial movement, intact hearing, and symmetric palate, but he had dysphonia with a hoarse, hypernasal voice. Motor strength was 5/5 throughout with normal tone, but sensation was mildly reduced at the fingertips, and he had left-sided finger-to-nose dysmetria, truncal ataxia, and could not walk without assistance. Labs showed WBC 7,000/µL, hemoglobin 13 g/dL, and glucose 135 mg/dL. Chest x-ray and inspiratory force testing were normal. Non-contrast head CT showed no acute hemorrhage but a nonacute left parietal white matter change. Lumbar puncture showed opening pressure 14 cm H2O, clear fluid, 2 WBC/µL, 0 RBC/µL, glucose 65 mg/dL, protein 56 mg/dL (elevated), and negative Gram stain.

A woman in her late 60s (height 154 cm, weight 40.4 kg, BMI 16.9 kg/m^2), previously independent in activities of daily living, presented with a several-month history of progressive neuromuscular symptoms. Approximately three months earlier she had developed a stooped, forward-flexed neck posture with impaired neck extension and difficulty swallowing. Over the following month her mobility progressively declined, and she required evaluation for gait difficulty. About one week prior to the current presentation, she developed acute worsening with difficulty moving and a decreased level of consciousness at home, and was hospitalized locally with a presumptive diagnosis of dehydration. During that admission, hypercapnia was identified on arterial blood gas analysis, and noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation was started. She was then transferred for higher level of care. On arrival, she had fatigable ptosis, symmetric proximal limb muscle weakness, and bulbar symptoms including dysarthria and dysphagia. Vital signs were notable for hypercapnic respiratory insufficiency. Chest CT revealed a nodular lesion in the anterior mediastinum. Shortly after transfer, oxygenation worsened and she underwent orotracheal intubation with initiation of mechanical ventilation, followed by ICU admission. No prior history of similar episodes was reported.

A man in his 60s with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease/emphysema, congestive heart failure, gastroesophageal reflux disease, hepatitis C virus infection, and a chronic B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder under active surveillance presented with a several-week history of painful purple skin lesions and non-healing ulcers on the lower extremities. He denied preceding trauma or new medication exposures. Vital signs were within normal limits. On examination, the bilateral lower legs showed palpable purpura and several ulcerated lesions with surrounding erythema and areas of skin breakdown; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable, without lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Complete blood count showed lymphocyte counts within the previously established range for his known lymphoproliferative disorder, without new cytopenias. Complement studies showed a normal C3 level, while C4 was reduced at less than 4 mg/dL (reference range 16-38 mg/dL), raising concern for complement consumption via the lectin or classical pathway. Renal function and urinalysis were unremarkable. A skin biopsy of one of the ulcerated lower extremity lesions was obtained for histopathology and direct immunofluorescence to further characterize the cutaneous findings.

A middle-aged man with no significant prior medical history presented with a first unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Initial neurological examination, basic metabolic panel, and non-contrast CT of the brain were normal; he was discharged after two days of observation without anti-seizure medication. He returned days later with recurrent generalised seizures; an EEG at that time was unremarkable, and he was discharged on an anti-seizure medication. About a week afterward, he presented again with further seizures, progressive anterograde memory impairment, and new difficulty performing routine occupational tasks. Repeat blood work, CT brain, and MRI brain showed no significant abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed elevated protein with a normal CSF/serum glucose ratio and normal cell count; infectious studies (bacterial culture, cryptococcal antigen, tuberculosis PCR, and viral PCR panels) were negative. During admission he developed status epilepticus requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation; repeat EEG showed generalised background slowing without epileptiform discharges. After extubation, he developed severe agitation, irritability, and disruptive behaviour that did not respond to standard antipsychotic therapy, alongside persistent though less frequent seizures despite escalating anti-seizure medications. Additional autoimmune and metabolic studies were pending at this stage.

samples.diagnosis: Other ectopic pregnancy without intrauterine pregnancy
samples.note: A 38-year-old woman, gravida 5, para 0 with 4 prior pregnancy losses, presented to the emergency department at approximately 8 weeks of gestational amenorrhea with a one-week history of mild lower abdominal pain and vaginal spotting. She appeared anxious and uncomfortable. Vital signs showed blood pressure 100/72 mmHg, pulse 110 beats/min, temperature 98.6°F, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Chest examination was unremarkable with equal bilateral air entry. The abdomen was soft and non-tender superficially, but deep palpation elicited mild rebound tenderness in the suprapubic region. Speculum examination showed a mild, thick, brown-colored discharge from the cervical os, and bimanual examination revealed mild tenderness. She had no significant medical comorbidities or known allergies. Her obstetric history included three early pregnancy losses and one mid-trimester loss at 21 weeks. Initial workup showed a serum beta-hCG level of 6,065 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrated a gestational sac measuring 3.8 x 3.6 cm with a crown-rump length of 1.1 cm, located in the right adnexal region, corresponding to approximately 8+5 weeks of gestation. Within two hours of presentation, she developed sudden, severe lower abdominal pain. Given the clinical and radiological findings, a decision was made to proceed with diagnostic laparoscopy for further evaluation and management.

A woman in her late twenties with no significant past medical history presented with sudden onset of severe pain in her left lower limb over the preceding 24 hours, associated with several days of persistent fever. On admission, she was febrile at 38.7°C, tachycardic at 120 beats/minute, with a respiratory rate of 15 breaths/minute and blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg. Examination revealed a cold, painful left lower limb with an absent ipsilateral femoral pulse but no sensorimotor deficit. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the mitral area without a gallop; there were no signs of heart failure. Neurological, pulmonary, and abdominal examinations were normal, and no cutaneous, oral, or urinary source of infection was identified. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy. Laboratory testing showed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin 8 g/dL), leukocytosis (15,000/µL), markedly elevated C-reactive protein (186 mg/dL), and a normal platelet count; renal function, electrolytes, glucose, and liver tests were normal. A single blood culture grew Staphylococcus species sensitive to vancomycin and gentamicin; urine culture and viral serologies were negative. Chest X-ray was normal. Echocardiography showed mild left heart chamber dilation, preserved biventricular systolic function, grade 3 mitral regurgitation with restricted anterior leaflet motion, and a small mobile mass attached to the atrial side of the anterior mitral leaflet. CT imaging of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and brain showed no other source of infection.

samples.diagnosis: Other specified congenital malformation syndromes, not elsewhere classified
samples.note: A 33-day-old full-term female infant, born vaginally to consanguineous parents, was referred for evaluation of failure to thrive, vomiting, and refractory hypoxemia. Birth weight, length, and head circumference were all at the third percentile. Amniotic fluid was meconium-stained and the infant had respiratory distress from birth requiring supplemental oxygen; chest imaging did not support meconium aspiration syndrome, and early workups for sepsis and respiratory viral infection were negative. By day 7 of life, respiratory status worsened, requiring high-flow nasal cannula support. On examination there was hypotonia, hypertelorism, a high-arched palate, low-set ears, a short philtrum, hypertrichosis of the elbows, and widely spaced nipples. Chest CT showed bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities with subpleural sparing and fibro-atelectatic change in the right lower lobe, without pleural or pericardial effusion; arterial blood gas showed hypoxemia without hypercapnia or acid-base disturbance. Thyroid function and alpha-1-antitrypsin levels were normal. Echocardiogram showed a small patent ductus arteriosus. Ophthalmologic exam, auditory brainstem response, and brain MRI were normal. Since birth the infant had absent sucking and gag reflexes with inability to coordinate oral feeding, requiring nasogastric feeding, with persistent poor weight gain. On day 27 of life, sudden-onset persistent regurgitation and projectile vomiting developed; abdominal ultrasound showed a thickened, elongated pylorus, and pyloromyotomy was performed with resolution of vomiting, though feeding difficulties and poor growth continued postoperatively.

A woman in her early 70s presented urgently with sudden vision loss and pain in the left eye, beginning three days after an intravitreal injection given for macular edema related to a prior branch retinal vein occlusion. She had received numerous prior intravitreal anti-VEGF injections over time for this condition. Her past medical history included prior breast cancer surgery, with ongoing surveillance follow-up; she had no hypertension or diabetes. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in the right eye and hand-motion only in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 8.6 mmHg in the right eye and 38.1 mmHg in the left eye. The right eye anterior segment was unremarkable except for cataract. The left eye showed conjunctival injection, corneal edema, a 3 mm hypopyon in the anterior chamber, and poor visibility of the ocular media due to opacity, with the posterior pole obscured. B-scan ultrasonography of the left eye demonstrated medium-reflective vitreous echoes consistent with inflammatory cellular debris, along with serous or tractional retinal detachment, retinal thickening, and increased choroidal reflectivity in the posterior pole. Given the acute, rapidly progressive nature of the presentation following the recent intraocular procedure, urgent surgical intervention was undertaken, with intraoperative collection of aqueous and vitreous samples for microbiologic culture and Gram stain, and empiric intraocular and systemic antibiotics were administered.

samples.diagnosis: Acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection, unspecified
samples.note: A woman in her late 50s with type 2 diabetes mellitus (managed with insulin glargine, semaglutide started several months prior, glimepiride, and metformin), hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented to the emergency department with one day of severe epigastric abdominal pain and repeated non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting. Symptoms began after a heavy, fatty meal the prior evening and progressively worsened overnight, prompting her family to call emergency services. She reported a hospitalization about one month earlier for abdominal pain attributed to possible gallbladder disease, though no gallstones were identified at that time. She denied alcohol use. On arrival she appeared pale and mildly dehydrated but was not in acute distress. Vital signs: blood pressure 164/66 mmHg, heart rate 93 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 37.1°C, oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Abdominal exam showed a soft, non-distended abdomen without tenderness, guarding, or rebound; cardiopulmonary exam was unremarkable, with no peripheral edema. Labs showed marked leukocytosis (WBC 25.9×10³/µL, 71.3% neutrophils), hyperglycemia (glucose 394 mg/dL), an anion gap metabolic acidosis with negative serum ketones, and a markedly elevated serum lipase (>3,000 U/L). Liver enzymes were elevated (AST 128 U/L, ALT 284 U/L, ALP 118 U/L). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed pancreatic swelling with surrounding fluid, along with mild reactive ileus, features suggestive of hepatic fibrosis, and mild retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.

An 18-year-old woman with no known chronic medical illnesses presented to the emergency department with a five-day history of fever, one day of altered consciousness, and a two-day history of right-sided weakness. According to her family, she had undergone neck manipulation (carotid massage) by a traditional healer shortly before the onset of confusion and neurological decline. On arrival she was unconscious, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7. Pupils were mid-dilated and sluggishly reactive to light. Respiratory examination showed decreased air entry over the right lung field, with oxygen saturation of 85% on room air. Vital signs: blood pressure 117/69 mmHg, pulse 81 beats per minute, random blood glucose 83 mg/dL. Neurological examination confirmed right-sided hemiplegia. Laboratory studies showed leukopenia, lymphopenia, and anemia, with elevated C-reactive protein and deranged liver and renal function. Arterial blood gas showed metabolic acidosis. Non-contrast CT of the brain showed a large area of hypoattenuation involving the left cerebral hemisphere with mass effect, mild ventricular effacement, uncal herniation, and a 3 mm midline shift. Chest CT showed extensive right-sided consolidation with air bronchograms and a small pleural effusion, with additional consolidation in the left lung. She subsequently developed hemodynamic instability with cardiac arrest requiring resuscitation, and was managed in the intensive care unit with osmotic therapy and broad-spectrum antibiotics; the family declined recommended neurosurgical intervention.

samples.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale
samples.note: A man in his late 30s was referred to hospital because of progressively worsening dyspnoea. On presentation, blood pressure was 143/108 mmHg, pulse rate 98 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on 3 L/min supplemental nasal oxygen. There was no reported history of prior venous thromboembolism, malignancy, immobilization, or recent surgery documented. Venous ultrasonography of the lower extremities identified a deep venous thrombus. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest demonstrated filling defects consistent with thrombus material within both pulmonary arteries. Transthoracic imaging additionally revealed mobile, thread-like echogenic structures approximately 4 cm in length within both atria; during diastole these structures extended across the atrioventricular valves into the ventricles. The structures appeared entrapped within an interatrial communication, positioned between the two atria. The patient was haemodynamically stable at presentation, without hypotension or signs of overt right heart failure. Given his stability, thrombolytic therapy was not pursued, and anticoagulation was initiated. Subsequent transoesophageal echocardiography performed several days later showed resolution of the intracardiac mobile structures; a bubble study demonstrated grade 2 microbubble passage into the left atrium without a Valsalva manoeuvre. Cranial MRI performed thereafter showed no evidence of cerebral infarction.

A woman in her mid-30s presented with a one-week history of fever, vomiting, and diarrhea, followed by progressively worsening confusion and two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. On arrival her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 9/15. She was febrile (temperature 38.9°C) and tachycardic (heart rate 117 bpm), with blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and respiratory rate 16/min; random blood sugar was 128 mg/dL. Abdominal examination showed a soft, non-tender abdomen without guarding or rigidity, with normal bowel sounds. Neurological examination showed reduced consciousness (GCS 9/15) without focal deficits; pupils were equal and reactive, deep tendon reflexes were preserved, and meningeal signs were absent. Initial laboratory evaluation showed anemia (hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 137,000/µL), leukocytosis, markedly elevated CRP and procalcitonin, and mild derangement of liver enzymes with elevated bilirubin; coagulation studies were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a lymphocyte-predominant pleocytosis with mildly elevated protein and normal glucose; gram stain, culture, and herpes simplex virus PCR were negative. An autoimmune antibody panel showed one weakly positive marker, with all other markers negative. Electroencephalography showed diffuse generalized slowing without epileptiform discharges. Brain MRI demonstrated diffuse cortical swelling, more pronounced posteriorly, with T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, without infarction, hemorrhage, or mass effect. She was treated empirically with broad-spectrum antimicrobials, later discontinued, followed by high-dose corticosteroids and plasma exchange, with gradual neurological improvement.

A woman in her mid-50s with a history of hypertension and long-standing (roughly 10-year) hypothyroidism on levothyroxine presented to the emergency department with nausea, vomiting, and hypoglycemia, and was transferred to the intensive care unit. Over the preceding two weeks she had experienced progressive fatigue, hypotension, and bradycardia. She had a prior transient ischemic attack about three months earlier, for which she was on antiplatelet therapy; brain imaging at that time had shown extensive small-vessel ischemic changes and an incidentally noted empty sella. She reported poor medication adherence over the preceding four months. On admission, vital signs showed marked hypotension, with blood pressure dropping as low as 70/50 mmHg, and bradycardia. During the hospital course she developed a supraventricular tachycardia at 180 bpm that did not respond to vagal maneuvers, intravenous beta-blocker, or adenosine, ultimately requiring synchronized cardioversion, after which sinus rhythm at 48 bpm was restored. Laboratory studies showed hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, hyponatremia, and a high-normal potassium level. Echocardiography demonstrated a moderately reduced ejection fraction (approximately 42%), biventricular chamber enlargement, multivalvular regurgitation, elevated estimated pulmonary artery pressure, and a mild pericardial effusion. Follow-up brain CT showed stable chronic small-vessel ischemic changes and the known empty sella, with no acute intracranial abnormality. CT pulmonary angiography excluded thromboembolism but noted pulmonary congestion and other incidental thoracic findings.

samples.diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
samples.note: An adult man in his late 30s, employed as a miner, presented to the intensive care unit with acute worsening dyspnea over the preceding 6 hours, superimposed on 3-4 days of chest tightness and shortness of breath of unclear cause, accompanied by a cough productive of small amounts of thick yellow-white sputum. He had initially been seen at a local clinic and treated symptomatically for a presumed upper respiratory infection (antipyretic and an over-the-counter herbal cold remedy, no systemic corticosteroids) without improvement. The day before transfer, evaluation revealed markedly elevated blood glucose and elevated blood ketones, and he was started on intravenous antibiotics, an insulin infusion, and fluid resuscitation. Over subsequent hours he deteriorated further, with oxygen saturation falling to 80% and altered mental status. Arterial blood gas showed severe acidemia (pH 7.27), hypoxemia (PaO2 45 mmHg), and elevated lactate (4.12 mg/dL). Additional labs showed markedly elevated D-dimer (1,844 ng/mL), mildly elevated high-sensitivity troponin T (0.024 μg/L), and markedly elevated pro-BNP (4,531 pg/mL). Due to rapid clinical deterioration he underwent emergency intubation and mechanical ventilation (FiO2 100%) and developed shock requiring high-dose vasopressor support (norepinephrine up to 1.8 mcg/kg/min, metaraminol up to 2.8 mcg/kg/min) before transfer for further critical care management. No prior medical history was documented.

A man in his 60s with a history of untreated hypertension presented with abdominal distension and decreased appetite. He reported long-standing heavy daily alcohol use, consuming roughly three liters of a spirit-based beverage per day, with estimated intake exceeding 170 g of alcohol daily. He was alert and fully oriented, with no clinical signs of encephalopathy. Physical examination revealed conjunctival icterus and bilateral lower-extremity edema, with abdominal findings consistent with ascites. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated irregularity of the liver surface, moderate ascites, and a large saccular dilation of the celiac artery measuring approximately 69 mm in diameter, arising from a calcified arterial segment. Laboratory testing showed: sodium 135 mEq/L, potassium 3.7 mEq/L, total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL, albumin 3.2 g/dL, AST 180 U/L, ALT 42 U/L, gamma-GT 939 U/L, amylase 23.4 mg/dL, BUN 8.9 mg/dL, creatinine 0.83 mg/dL, CRP 0.6 mg/dL, BNP 57.3 pg/mL, WBC 6300/µL, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, platelet count 90,000/µL, PT-INR 1.04, and D-dimer 5.9 µg/mL. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody testing were negative. Detailed vascular imaging was subsequently obtained to characterize collateral arterial circulation prior to planning definitive management.

samples.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
samples.note: A teenage girl (early-to-mid teens) was admitted with a 4-day history of sore throat and fever, and a 1-day history of yellowing of her skin and eyes. Two months earlier she had been diagnosed with a hyperthyroid disorder based on elevated thyroid hormone levels, a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone level, and a significantly elevated thyroid receptor antibody titer; she had since been taking daily methimazole for over 50 days without recent follow-up blood testing. On admission she was febrile (39.3°C), tachycardic (133 bpm), tachypneic, with borderline low blood pressure and a low body mass index. She appeared restless and diaphoretic, with mild eye bulging and an enlarged thyroid gland. Examination also showed jaundice of the skin and sclera, pharyngeal erythema, and palpable enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Blood tests showed a mildly elevated white cell count with an increased lymphocyte percentage and atypical lymphocytes on peripheral smear and bone marrow examination; a pharyngeal swab and serology indicated a recent Epstein-Barr virus infection. Liver enzymes, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin (predominantly direct) were markedly elevated, with elevated total bile acids. Coagulation studies showed mildly prolonged APTT and elevated D-dimer and fibrinogen degradation products, with normal PT/INR. Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged liver and spleen. Tests for hepatotropic viruses and autoimmune liver disease were negative. Repeat thyroid testing showed markedly suppressed TSH with very high free T3 and T4 and a markedly elevated thyroid receptor antibody level; thyroid scan showed an enlarged, hypervascular gland with increased tracer uptake. Inflammatory markers including interleukin-2 receptor, interleukin-8, interleukin-10, and TNF-alpha were elevated.

A man in his mid-30s with a history of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus skin infection, type 1 diabetes mellitus, alcohol use disorder, intravenous drug use, depression, and psychosis was found unresponsive outdoors and brought to the emergency department by emergency medical services. The duration of unresponsiveness prior to discovery was unknown, and no further history could be obtained from the patient at the time of presentation. On arrival, he was febrile to 101°F, clinically dehydrated, and hemodynamically unstable, requiring endotracheal intubation for airway protection and initiation of vasopressor support alongside intravenous fluid resuscitation. Initial laboratory evaluation revealed severe hypernatremia (sodium 154 mmol/L) with markedly elevated serum osmolality (354 mOsm/kg), hyperkalemia (potassium 5.4 mmol/L), and markedly elevated blood urea nitrogen (119 mg/dL) and creatinine (12.79 mg/dL) consistent with severe acute renal impairment. Albumin-corrected calcium was within normal limits (10.02 mg/dL), while phosphorus was markedly elevated (16.5 mg/dL). Hemoglobin was elevated at 20 g/dL. Urinalysis showed 2+ protein, 3+ blood, 21-50 red blood cells per high-power field, and trace ketones. Urine toxicology screen was positive for amphetamines. Arterial blood gas showed a severe combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis (pH 6.91, PCO2 61 mmHg, HCO3- 12.2 mmol/L) with markedly elevated lactic acid (12.1 mmol/L).

A man in his 40s was admitted to the intensive care unit with an established diagnosis of infective endocarditis, with blood cultures positive for Staphylococcus aureus and echocardiography showing a 12 mm vegetation on the mitral valve. He had no known history of intravenous drug use or prior valvular disease. Approximately five days into his hospital course, he developed an acute decline in consciousness, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9/15. Laboratory tests at that time showed elevated inflammatory markers (CRP) and leukocytosis, with a normal coagulation profile. Urgent brain MRI was obtained. Imaging showed more than twenty scattered punctate lesions distributed across both supra- and infratentorial compartments, hyperintense on T2/FLAIR sequences with diffusion restriction and hypointense signal on susceptibility-weighted imaging. A 29 × 19 mm right frontal lesion was noted with adjacent sulcal blood products and a thin (3 mm) right fronto-parietal subdural collection causing mild mass effect and roughly 4 mm leftward midline shift. A separate 19 × 15 mm left cerebellar lesion with minimal sulcal blood products was also identified. No leptomeningeal enhancement was present, the ventricular system was normal, and vascular imaging showed no aneurysm or malformation. He was treated with targeted intravenous antibiotics; anticoagulation was withheld given the intracranial blood products. Cardiac surgery was deferred because of hemorrhagic risk, and he was monitored with serial neurological assessment.

A man in his late 50s with a history of hypertension and cocaine use disorder presented to the emergency department with altered mental status and unintentional weight loss. Over the preceding two months he had gradually progressive episodes of left-sided facial grimacing with sudden flexion of the left arm, lasting several seconds and occurring multiple times daily. His wife reported progressive inattention, short-term memory loss, and behavioral changes; he had also been involved in two rear-end motor vehicle collisions with subsequent amnesia for the events. He smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily, drank two alcoholic beverages weekly, and used cocaine weekly; urine toxicology was positive for marijuana and cocaine. Vital signs on arrival were normal. He was oriented to person and place but not time, with bradyphrenia, flat affect, impaired short-term memory, and inability to perform serial sevens or spell a word backward; the remainder of the neurologic exam was nonfocal. Laboratory studies showed moderate hypotonic hyponatremia (sodium 127 mmol/L), mild microcytic anemia, elevated ESR, and normal glucose and blood gas values. Head CT was unremarkable. Brain MRI showed mild hyperintense signal changes in the bilateral temporal lobes. Video-EEG captured brief stereotyped episodes of facial and ipsilateral arm dystonic posturing without an accompanying epileptiform correlate. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed no pleocytosis and normal protein, with negative studies for infection.

samples.diagnosis: Acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection, unspecified
samples.note: A man in his early 30s was admitted to a burn unit after sustaining extensive flame burns to the head, face, neck, trunk, and extremities in an electrical panel fire approximately seven hours earlier, involving about 65% of total body surface area (15% second-degree, 50% third-degree), with suspected inhalation/airway involvement. He had no prior medical history or long-term medication use and had taken no oral intake since the injury. On arrival, heart rate was 134 bpm, blood pressure 90/55 mmHg, respiratory rate 31/min, and oxygen saturation 98%. Urine was dark brown. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 214 g/L, platelets 593×10^9/L, sodium 147.6, potassium 4.12, chloride 116.4, calcium 1.66, and magnesium 0.71 mmol/L. Urinalysis showed brown, cloudy urine with protein 2+, bilirubin 1+, specific gravity 1.020, occult blood 3+, positive ketones, and positive nitrites. He received fluid resuscitation, prophylactic antibiotics, acid suppression, and emergency burn wound debridement. On hospital day 2 he developed abdominal distension with diminished bowel sounds (1-2/min); imaging showed dilated small bowel loops with gas, managed with decompression and parenteral nutrition, with gradual improvement. On day 5 he developed new upper abdominal pain, with markedly elevated serum lipase and elevated urinary amylase. Cross-sectional imaging showed an enlarged pancreas with blurred surrounding fat planes, persistent bowel gas/fluid, dilated loops, and rectal wall thickening; further imaging showed pancreatic enlargement with surrounding signal change and diffusely restricted diffusion. He was treated with fasting, decompression, parenteral nutrition, acid suppression, and continuous somatostatin infusion, improving over two weeks, with lipase normalizing faster than amylase. Pain resolved by day 17, enteral nutrition resumed, and he was later discharged after skin grafting.

A 10-year-old girl, previously healthy, presented with fever and a widespread mucocutaneous eruption. Twenty days before admission she developed a pruritic vesicular rash over the trunk and extremities, evaluated at the time and managed with topical calamine and an oral antihistamine; a high fever partially responded to antipyretics, and the rash resolved within about two weeks without complication. Fifteen days later she developed sudden, intense nocturnal itching and a new eruption involving the mouth, elbows, knees, hands, and feet, spreading rapidly over two days into widespread confluent lesions with tense blisters surrounded by erythema, along with recurrent high fever and arthralgia limiting wrist and knee movement. Despite antipyretics at home, oral ulcers worsened with reduced oral intake and new dysphagia, prompting hospital admission. Past history included an episode of meningitis three years earlier; no chronic illness, autoimmune disease, allergies, or relevant family history. On examination she was mildly dehydrated but alert, with no meningeal signs. She had symmetric erythematous target-like lesions over the extensor forearms, hands, lower legs, feet, and ankles, with a positive Nikolsky's sign; palms showed small macules with central clearing while soles showed larger confluent target plaques. A violaceous plaque with central hyperpigmentation and scaling was noted on the forearm with satellite lesions. Oral mucosa showed diffuse erythema, erosions, and swollen, hemorrhagically crusted lips causing pain and reduced intake. Mild eye itching developed without redness or discharge. Initial labs showed low CRP, persistently elevated ESR, normal renal and hepatic function, normal coagulation, complement, immunoglobulins and autoantibodies, and negative blood cultures and viral/atypical bacterial testing.

A woman in her late 30s, multigravida (G4P3, all prior deliveries vaginal), presented at 34 weeks' gestation with a several-day history of progressive lower limb numbness and weakness, unsteady gait, urinary incontinence, sensory loss extending from the hips downward, and paraesthesia in the fingers. Symptoms began acutely and worsened over the days before admission, arising several days after a documented respiratory viral illness. There was no history of trauma or prior similar episodes. Past medical history included hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine, and previous pregnancies complicated by fetal growth restriction. She was a non-smoker with a normal booking BMI and no known drug allergies. On examination she was alert and fully oriented with stable vital signs. Motor power in the lower limbs below the knees was reduced to 2-3/5 bilaterally, with absent sensation below the knees. During admission she developed new right-sided facial weakness with features suggesting a lower motor neuron pattern, for which corticosteroids were started. MRI of the lumbar spine was unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed markedly raised protein with a normal cell count. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated axonal impairment of the facial nerve and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, without electrophysiological evidence of a demyelinating process. Liver enzymes were noted to be markedly and progressively elevated over the admission with subsequent gradual normalization, while liver ultrasound was normal. Fetal surveillance throughout remained reassuring.

An older adult male presented with a three-month history of intermittent neck pain, followed by progressive difficulty swallowing solid foods, speech that became slurred with prolonged talking, and later development of head drop. Symptoms fluctuated through the day, tending to worsen later in the day. He also reported intermittent drooping of the eyelids, at times requiring manual elevation to see, along with an unintentional weight loss of 3-4 kg. Past medical history included hypertension, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. He was on a thiazide diuretic, levothyroxine, and a statin. He was fully independent in daily activities and lived with his partner. On examination, vital signs were normal. He had bilateral facial weakness, bilateral eyelid drooping that worsened with sustained upward gaze, and speech that became more slurred with prolonged talking. Neck flexion was weak. Upper and lower limb tone, power, reflexes, coordination, and sensation were all normal. Single-breath count was 30, and there were no respiratory symptoms. Initial blood work including full blood count, C-reactive protein, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, thyroid-stimulating hormone, magnesium, calcium, phosphate, folate, and vitamin B12 were unremarkable. Electromyography of the left deltoid, trapezius, and extensor digitorum communis showed no fibrillations, with a mild excess of polyphasic motor unit potentials. Repetitive nerve stimulation showed a decremental response in the right trapezius muscle. Brain and cervical spine MRI were normal, and chest CT showed no thymic enlargement.

A 56-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department with a three-day history of abdominal pain, accompanied by cessation of bowel movements and flatus, and episodes of vomiting containing food content. On arrival he was conscious and hemodynamically stable, with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15/15. Blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg, heart rate 97 bpm, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 38.3°C. Abdominal examination showed a non-distended abdomen with generalized tenderness; digital rectal examination revealed only traces of stool. The remainder of the physical exam was unremarkable. Supine abdominal X-ray demonstrated multiple air-fluid levels predominantly in the small bowel, consistent with a mechanical small bowel obstruction, without evidence of pneumoperitoneum. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed small bowel obstruction with a clear transition point; small bowel loops proximal to the transition were dilated up to approximately 3.5 cm, with collapsed bowel distally. There were no signs of bowel ischemia (no pneumatosis or portomesenteric venous gas), no intra-abdominal collections, no significant lymphadenopathy, and no mass or hernia identified as a cause. Laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 16.5 g/dL, WBC 5,430/mm³, neutrophils 4,494/mm³, platelets 242,000/mm³, CRP 29 mg/L, lipase 11 U/L, urea 0.73 g/L, creatinine 13.9 mg/L, normal electrolytes, and normal liver enzymes and bilirubin fractions. The patient was admitted for monitoring, nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluids, analgesia, antiemetics, antispasmodics, and empiric antibiotics; surgical exploration was subsequently planned given the imaging findings of obstruction without an identifiable extrinsic cause.

A 71-year-old man presented with sudden-onset blurred vision and mild pain in the right eye. He denied any recent ocular surgery or trauma. His past medical history included oral cancer, Behçet's disease (managed with leflunomide 20 mg daily), and benign prostatic hyperplasia. On arrival to the emergency department, vital signs were stable: blood pressure 157/79 mmHg, heart rate 96 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 37.1°C, and SpO2 98%. Initial laboratory testing showed no leukocytosis and no elevation in C-reactive protein. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed best corrected visual acuity of hand motion at 1 meter, intraocular pressure of 35 mmHg, congested conjunctiva, mild corneal edema with diffuse fine keratic precipitates, anterior chamber cell grade of 3+, aqueous flare grade of 1+, a layered hypopyon, and a fundus obscured by dense vitreous opacity. Blood cultures were obtained and subsequently grew Haemophilus influenzae. Systemic workup including abdominal CT, transthoracic echocardiography, and brain CT angiography showed no abscess, valvular vegetation, or intracranial lesion. Tumor marker screening showed no evidence of malignancy progression. The patient remained afebrile throughout the evaluation.

samples.diagnosis: Acute appendicitis with perforation, localized peritonitis, and gangrene, with abscess
samples.note: A woman in her mid-20s presented with 25 days of amenorrhea, 5 days of right lower quadrant abdominal pain, and fever (peak 39.0°C). Serum β-hCG was elevated at 240 IU/L. Laboratory evaluation showed leukocytosis (WBC 13.74×10^9/L), elevated interleukin-6 (80.7 pg/mL), and mildly elevated procalcitonin (0.17 ng/mL). Transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a right lower quadrant mass measuring approximately 41×25×29 mm with internal blood flow signals on color Doppler, and an endometrial thickness of 9 mm without a definitive gestational sac visualized in the uterine cavity. Given the early stage of gestation suggested by the hCG level, absence of a visible gestational sac was considered consistent with early pregnancy dating. Intravenous antibiotic therapy was started. The following day, ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage of the right lower quadrant collection was performed, yielding 13 mL of brown, turbid fluid sent for culture. Inflammatory markers initially improved but the patient had persistent abdominal pain with only modest improvement, continued thick turbid catheter output, and by the third day recurrence of leukocytosis and rising inflammatory markers. A multidisciplinary team discussion weighed the risks of surgical intervention on the pregnancy against alternative minimally invasive endoscopic management, given ongoing suboptimal response to antibiotics and percutaneous drainage.

A woman in her late 40s was referred to an emergency care unit with a four-day history of feeling generally unwell, lethargy, bruising around the left breast and elbow, and dark urine. There was no history of trauma, fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or lower urinary tract symptoms. Past medical history included mild psoriasis, joint hypermobility, and chronic lower back pain, for which she regularly took amitriptyline. She had no known allergies, worked in an office, lived alone, was an active smoker (20 pack-years), and drank alcohol socially. Physical examination was unremarkable except for bruising over pressure areas of the joints; vital signs were not otherwise notable. Initial blood tests showed a hemoglobin of 118 g/L, white cell count 7.4x10^9/L, and a markedly low platelet count of 4x10^9/L. Urea and creatinine were elevated (20 mmol/L and 189 µmol/L respectively), with raised inflammatory markers (CRP 85 mg/L, ESR 45 mm/hr) and mildly elevated bilirubin (31 µmol/L). Reticulocyte count and coagulation profile (prothrombin time, INR, partial thromboplastin time) were within normal limits. Complement C3 was mildly elevated. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was elevated at 80 mg/mmol. Direct Coombs test was negative. Blood film showed red cell anisocytosis with tear-drop and fragmented cells, and reduced platelets without clumping.

samples.diagnosis: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
samples.note: A man in his early 30s with no known prior thyroid disease presented to the emergency department with acute-onset palpitations, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, recurrent vomiting, and agitation developing over a short period. Past history included mild intermittent bronchial asthma managed with an inhaled budesonide-formoterol combination. There was no history of chronic liver disease, acetaminophen exposure, or prior episodes of hypotension or shock. He was a non-smoker, did not drink alcohol, had no known drug allergies, and had no family history of thyroid or autoimmune disease. On examination he was febrile, markedly tachycardic, and clinically dehydrated, restless and agitated but without focal neurological deficits; there were no peripheral signs of heart failure, no palpable goiter, and no thyroid tenderness. The initial ECG showed a regular narrow-complex tachycardia consistent with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction, which progressed to an irregular narrow-complex tachyarrhythmia; synchronized cardioversion restored sinus rhythm after energy escalation. Bedside echocardiography showed a hyperdynamic circulation without wall motion abnormality or valvular disease, with findings suggesting intravascular volume depletion. Arterial blood gas showed near-normal pH with mild metabolic acidosis and normal lactate. Initial labs showed profound hypokalemia, hypernatremia, and hypercalcemia, alongside marked transaminitis, evolving coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, and elevated procalcitonin and CRP prompting empirical antibiotics. Blood and urine cultures were negative. CT head and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable.

samples.diagnosis: Other pulmonary embolism without acute cor pulmonale
samples.note: A woman in her early 50s with baseline visual impairment was brought to the emergency department by wheelchair with severe lower back pain (10/10) and mild chest discomfort that had resolved with analgesia prior to arrival. Her family reported a recent inpatient admission for a suspected demyelinating disorder, during which she underwent lumbar puncture and received high-dose corticosteroids; that admission was complicated by a drop in platelet count attributed to heparin exposure, for which heparin products were avoided. Past medical history included hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She denied limb swelling, fever, hemoptysis, or new neurological symptoms. On arrival, heart rate was 110 beats/min, blood pressure 100/75 mmHg, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, and respiratory rate was initially charted as normal but on manual recount was 31 breaths/min. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Chest auscultation revealed mild bibasal crackles. Point-of-care lung ultrasound showed a symmetric lung-sliding pattern with vertical lines in all zones bilaterally. Venous compression ultrasound of the lower limb showed a non-compressible right common femoral vein containing intraluminal echogenic material. Given the recent platelet-drop history, an oral anticoagulant was started, and CT pulmonary angiography was obtained, showing filling defects within the right main and left lower lobe pulmonary arterial branches. Initial bloodwork showed leukocytosis (16.53×10^9/L) with neutrophilia and lymphopenia, platelets 123×10^9/L, markedly elevated D-dimer (5.98 mg/L), elevated troponin T (31.18 ng/L), CRP 213.34 mg/L, glucose 9.90 mmol/L, and lactate 3.50 mmol/L.

A 46-year-old man with occupational exposure to metal dust and a prior history of cerebral infarction presented with worsening cardiac symptoms. Six months earlier he developed palpitations and chest tightness without a clear trigger; imaging at that time showed a pleural effusion, and his symptoms improved with diuretic therapy. Four days before the current admission, his symptoms acutely worsened, prompting hospital transfer. He also reported a history of recurrent oral ulcers. On examination he had intermittent fever up to 38°C, a grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the cardiac apex, and a grade 5/6 diastolic murmur over the aortic valve area. Laboratory studies showed CRP 16.3 mg/L, white blood cell count 11.4×10^9/L, absolute neutrophil count 8.13×10^9/L, BNP 458 pg/mL, high-sensitivity troponin I 127.3 pg/mL, ESR 21 mm/h, and creatinine 80 μmol/L. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an abnormal aortic valve with severe regurgitation; transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated disruption of the aortic valve annulus with prolapse of the leaflets, markedly increased vena contracta width (>0.6 cm) and effective regurgitant orifice area (>0.3 cm^2), and enlargement of the left atrium and left ventricle. Blood cultures and sputum studies were obtained. Rheumatologic and immunologic markers, including rheumatoid factor and autoantibodies, were within normal limits. Conservative medical management with inotropes, diuretics, and supportive therapy did not resolve the condition, and surgical evaluation was pursued.

samples.diagnosis: Benign neoplasm of left adrenal gland
samples.note: An adolescent boy presented with a 4-day history of abdominal pain. He denied headache, fever, nausea, vomiting, palpitations, or excessive sweating. He had no significant reported past medical history. On admission, vital signs were: heart rate 89 beats/min, blood pressure 140/73 mmHg (meeting criteria for elevated blood pressure for his age), respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and temperature 36.9°C. No orthostatic blood pressure changes were noted. Cardiorespiratory examination was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed a soft, non-tender abdomen without palpable masses, guarding, or organomegaly. Complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, chest X-ray, and electrocardiogram were all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a well-circumscribed, heterogeneously enhancing left-sided adrenal mass measuring 3.3 × 2.0 cm, without evidence of local invasion or lymphadenopathy. Plasma norepinephrine and normetanephrine levels were significantly elevated above the reference range, while plasma epinephrine and metanephrine levels were within normal limits. Additional endocrine workup was unremarkable apart from a mildly decreased morning ACTH level and an elevated neuron-specific enolase. The patient was subsequently prepared for elective surgical management of the adrenal lesion, including preoperative alpha- and beta-adrenergic blockade and fluid optimization.

A man in his early 50s presented to the eye clinic with blurred vision. Best-corrected visual acuity was reduced bilaterally, worse in the left eye, with a hyperopic correction. Slit-lamp examination revealed posterior subcapsular cataracts in both eyes, more advanced in the left. Personal and family medical history were unremarkable; he was a smoker with occasional alcohol use, took no chronic medications, and had no known allergies. He underwent uncomplicated cataract surgery with intraocular lens implantation in the left eye. On the first postoperative day, vision was good with mild discomfort and a small amount of residual material noted behind the lens. By the third day, ocular redness developed without change in visual acuity. On the fourth day, vision declined with a moderate inflammatory reaction in the anterior chamber. By the fifth day, vision had deteriorated markedly, with a pronounced anterior chamber inflammatory reaction and circular conjunctival injection, but no hypopyon, eyelid edema, purulent discharge, or severe pain. Given the rapid progressive decline in vision over several days accompanied by escalating intraocular inflammation following intraocular surgery, further diagnostic and therapeutic intervention was pursued, including surgical sampling of intraocular fluid for microbiological analysis and empiric broad-spectrum intravitreal antimicrobial therapy.

A woman in her late twenties, gravida 2 para 0, presented at 32 weeks of gestation with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that began the day before admission. She denied nausea or vomiting. There was no reported prior similar episode, and her pregnancy had otherwise been uncomplicated to this point. On examination, fetal heart rate monitoring by cardiotocography showed no evidence of fetal distress. Admission laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 11,100/µL (reference 3,300-8,600/µL) and C-reactive protein of 13.8 mg/dL (reference 0-0.14 mg/dL), with hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, hematocrit 34.7%, platelet count 218,000/µL, and normal electrolytes, renal function, and liver enzymes. Transabdominal ultrasonography was attempted but could not visualize the relevant right-sided structure clearly, leaving the source of pain undetermined. Given ongoing diagnostic uncertainty, abdominal computed tomography was performed after discussion of radiation risk with the patient. Imaging demonstrated an enlarged tubular structure in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen with surrounding inflammatory changes extending into adjacent tissue. Given these findings, surgical exploration was planned.

A young child (approximately 5 years old, male), born preterm at 36 weeks' gestation with a history of asthma, presented to an emergency department with a 3-day history of cough, rhinorrhoea, and fever. He was up to date with routine childhood immunizations per national schedule. On initial assessment he appeared well, with mild throat erythema and fever; he was discharged with a diagnosis of upper respiratory tract infection and given analgesia. Over the following 24 hours he re-presented twice with worsening malaise, reduced oral intake due to increasing throat pain, and noisy breathing noted by his mother. He did not have stridor, toxic appearance, or tripod positioning, but examination showed progressive throat inflammation, clinical signs of dehydration, and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Blood tests showed leukocytosis (16.9 x10^9/L) with neutrophilia, appearance of metamyelocytes, and markedly elevated C-reactive protein (195 mg/L). Chest radiograph was unremarkable. A lateral neck soft-tissue radiograph demonstrated thickening of the epiglottis with mild pharyngeal soft-tissue distension. He received a dose of dexamethasone, was started on intravenous antibiotics, and was admitted for further management.

A woman in her late twenties, gravida 2 para 1, at 35 weeks of gestation, was admitted with a one-week history of generalized weakness, nausea, and easy bruising. She noted bruising on her arms and legs that progressed to a petechial rash and visible purpura. She also reported mild headache and dizziness. Her obstetric history included a prior uncomplicated vaginal delivery, and she had no known medical comorbidities. There was no history of recent trauma, medication use other than routine prenatal vitamins, or infection. Prenatal screening and visits had been unremarkable to date. She denied fever, chills, or change in fetal movement. Family history was non-contributory for bleeding or thrombotic disorders. On examination she appeared acutely ill but was afebrile, with blood pressure 120/70 mmHg and heart rate 98 bpm. A palpable purpuric rash extended from the upper to lower limbs, with scattered petechiae on the chest and abdomen; there was no mucosal bleeding or active hemorrhage. Neurological exam showed mild dizziness without focal deficits. The abdomen was gravid with normal fetal heart sounds. There was no proteinuria or hyperreflexia, and cardiovascular and respiratory exams were normal. Labs showed hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, platelet count 32,000/µL, and normal white cell count. PT was 12.4 seconds and aPTT 33 seconds. Peripheral smear showed schistocytes. Reticulocyte count was elevated at 8.5%. LDH was markedly elevated at 1,250 U/L, and haptoglobin was low at 12 mg/dL. Serum creatinine was 0.8 mg/dL, and liver enzymes were normal.
